reigns.tagline: The fisherman Jesus called the rock
reigns.cameToPower: Led the apostles after the Crucifixion
reigns.previously: Jesus is crucified. A fisherman from Galilee leads his followers.
paragraphs: His name was Simon, and he fished the Sea of Galilee with his brother Andrew until a wandering preacher called Jesus told them to follow him. In Matthew's Gospel Jesus gives Simon a new name, Peter, from the word for rock, and says: on this rock I will build my church. Peter was loud, loyal and brave, right up until the night of the arrest, when he denied knowing Jesus three times before the cock crowed.

After the Crucifixion he led the little movement in Jerusalem. The Acts of the Apostles has him preaching, healing, landing in jail and arguing with Paul over whether non-Jewish converts had to keep Jewish law. Later he seems to have reached Rome. Early Christian writers agree he died there under Nero, after the great fire of 64, when the emperor blamed the Christians and had them killed in horrible ways.

Catholics count Peter as the first bishop of Rome, and every pope since as his heir. That claim to his chair is the foundation stone of the whole papacy. By tradition his followers buried him on the Vatican Hill, close to the circus where so many of them had died.

claims.text: Peter asked to be crucified upside down, feeling unworthy to die the same way as Jesus.
claims.note: The story comes from the apocryphal Acts of Peter, written in the late 2nd century, more than a hundred years after his death.

claims.text: Peter was the first bishop of Rome.
claims.note: Lists of Roman bishops starting from Peter appear in the late 2nd century, with Irenaeus. Most historians think Rome's church was led by a group of elders until well into the 2nd century.

claims.text: Peter's bones lie under the high altar of St Peter's.
claims.note: Pius XII announced in 1950 that the tomb had been found, and Paul VI said in 1968 that the bones had been identified. Archaeologists still argue over the excavations.

reigns.hook: Peter is dead, and Rome's Christians are a hunted minority. The old lists name his heir as Linus. For 250 years the bishops will live on the wrong side of the law, and most will leave little more than a name.

images.caption: Rubens painted Peter as a pope around 1610, some 1,550 years after his death; no one knows what Peter looked like.
images.alt: Painting of Saint Peter shown as a pope, wearing the pallium and holding the keys of heaven

reigns.tagline: The first name on the list after Peter
reigns.cameToPower: Named in the earliest bishop lists
reigns.previously: Peter dies a martyr in Nero's Rome.
paragraphs: Every list of popes puts the same name straight after Peter: Linus. The oldest list we have was drawn up by Irenaeus of Lyon around 180, about a century later. He says the apostles handed the care of the Roman church to Linus, and adds that this is the Linus Paul mentions in his letters to Timothy.

And that is nearly all we know. Rome's Christians at this point were a few house churches in a huge city, still reeling from Nero's purge. Later writers gave Linus a birthplace in Tuscany, a set of rules and a martyr's death, but none of it goes back anywhere near his lifetime. His name is still read out in the oldest prayer of the Roman Mass, alongside Cletus and Clement.

claims.text: Linus is the man Paul greets in 2 Timothy 4:21.
claims.note: Irenaeus says so around 180. Many scholars think 2 Timothy was written after Paul's death, and the name was not rare.

claims.text: Linus died a martyr.
claims.note: The story turns up centuries later. Irenaeus, who knew of martyrdom when it happened, names Telesphorus as the early martyr, not Linus.

claims.text: Rome had a single bishop in Linus's day.
claims.note: Most historians think a council of elders led the Roman church into the 2nd century, and the neat list was tidied up later.

reigns.hook: Linus is gone, and the list moves on to a man with two names, or possibly two men with one name. Even the early Church couldn't decide which.

reigns.tagline: One pope, two names, and centuries of confusion
reigns.cameToPower: Named in the earliest bishop lists
reigns.previously: Linus dies, a name on a list and little else.
paragraphs: Irenaeus calls him Anencletus, Greek for "blameless". Others shortened it to Cletus. That caused trouble. Some later Roman lists, including the Liber Pontificalis, treated Cletus and Anacletus as two different men and gave them separate entries, separated by Clement. It took the Church a very long time to sort the muddle out.

Tradition makes him a Roman, and later writers say he built a shrine over Peter's grave on the Vatican Hill. Nothing about his time in charge can be checked. Rome was ruled by the Flavian emperors, Vespasian, Titus and then Domitian, and the Christians kept their heads down.

claims.text: Cletus and Anacletus were two different popes.
claims.note: The split shows up in later lists such as the Liber Pontificalis. Irenaeus and Eusebius have one man, and modern scholars agree with them.

claims.text: Anacletus died a martyr.
claims.note: No early writer says so. The martyr's crown was handed to almost every early pope in the Middle Ages.

reigns.hook: Next on the list is a man whose words actually survive. A church in Greece has thrown out its elders, and Rome is about to tell it off in writing.

reigns.tagline: He wrote the letter that told Corinth to behave
reigns.cameToPower: Named in the earliest bishop lists
reigns.previously: Anacletus dies. Rome's Christians lie low under Domitian.
paragraphs: Around 96 the church of Corinth sacked its elders, and Rome wrote to tell it to take them back. That long letter, known as 1 Clement, survives complete. It is the oldest Christian writing we have outside the New Testament. It talks about order and obedience, remembers Peter and Paul as recent heroes, and never names its author: it speaks for the Roman church as a whole.

Second-century writers such as Dionysius of Corinth say Clement wrote it, and Irenaeus puts him third after Peter. Clement became famous, and stories collected around him. A later legend says Trajan exiled him to the quarries of the Crimea, where he made a spring flow for thirsty prisoners, and was then thrown into the Black Sea with an anchor round his neck.

claims.text: Clement wrote the letter to the Corinthians.
claims.note: The letter is written in the name of the church, not his. The link comes from Dionysius of Corinth and others in the 2nd century, and most scholars accept it.

claims.text: Clement was drowned in the Black Sea tied to an anchor.
claims.note: The story comes from Acts of Clement written centuries later. The anchor became his emblem in art.

claims.text: The letter shows Rome still had a council of elders, not one bishop.
claims.note: The letter speaks of bishops and elders in the plural and never names a single head of the Roman church.

reigns.hook: Clement's letter will be read aloud in Corinth for generations. His successor is a much fainter figure, a Greek with a Jewish father, if the later lists can be trusted.

reigns.tagline: A Greek bishop as the century turns
reigns.cameToPower: Named in the earliest bishop lists
reigns.previously: Clement dies, and legend sends him to the bottom of the Black Sea.
paragraphs: Irenaeus names Evaristus as the fourth bishop of Rome after Peter, and that is about all the early sources give us. The Liber Pontificalis, written hundreds of years later, fills in a biography: a Greek, son of a Jew named Judah from Bethlehem. That might preserve a real memory, or it might just be a good story.

The same book says he divided Rome's churches among the priests. That is almost certainly the later Church looking back and imagining its own parishes. He lived under Trajan, whose rule, set out a few years later in a letter to his governor Pliny, was to punish Christians if reported but not hunt them down. Evaristus was buried, says tradition, near Peter on the Vatican Hill.

claims.text: Evaristus was a Greek whose father was a Jew from Bethlehem.
claims.note: Only the Liber Pontificalis says so, and it was compiled in the 6th century from patchy older material.

claims.text: Evaristus divided Rome into parishes run by priests.
claims.note: Historians see this as later practice read back into the past. Rome's Christians still met in private houses.

reigns.hook: Evaristus dies. His successor will be remembered for things he almost certainly never did, and confused with a martyr who wasn't him.

reigns.tagline: Credited with the Mass, confused with a martyr
reigns.cameToPower: Named in the earliest bishop lists
reigns.previously: Evaristus dies, remembered only as a Greek with a Jewish father.
paragraphs: Tradition makes Alexander a Roman, and later books gave him big achievements. The Liber Pontificalis says he added the account of the Last Supper to the prayers of the Mass, and started the custom of blessing water mixed with salt to sprinkle in homes. Both are rules from a much later Church, pinned on an early pope to make them sound ancient.

His story got tangled with another man's. A martyr named Alexander was buried on the Via Nomentana north of Rome, and medieval writers decided this was the pope, giving him a dramatic death. The two are almost certainly different people. Meanwhile Trajan was conquering Dacia and pushing east, and the empire was heading for its greatest size.

claims.text: Alexander added the words of the Last Supper to the Mass.
claims.note: The claim comes from the Liber Pontificalis, centuries later. Historians see it as later liturgy credited to an early name.

claims.text: Pope Alexander I was the martyr buried on the Via Nomentana.
claims.note: Most scholars think the Via Nomentana martyr was a different Alexander, merged with the pope by later legend.

reigns.hook: Alexander is gone. The next name on the list is usually spelled Sixtus, but the oldest lists call him Xystus, and his bones would wander far from Rome.

reigns.tagline: The first Sixtus, spelled Xystus at the time
reigns.cameToPower: Named in the earliest bishop lists
reigns.previously: Alexander dies, his story tangled with another martyr's.
paragraphs: In the oldest lists his name is Xystus, a Greek word. Later Latin writers turned it into Sixtus, and it became a papal name used five times. Irenaeus calls him the sixth bishop after the apostles. Tradition says he was a Roman, son of a man named Pastor.

The Liber Pontificalis credits him with rules about the altar, such as only clergy touching the sacred vessels. Like most of the book's early rules, they belong to a later age. He served under Trajan and then Hadrian, who came to the throne in 117 and was busy building walls and touring his provinces rather than chasing Christians. A medieval story says his relics were carried to Alatri, south of Rome, in 1132.

claims.text: Sixtus ruled that only clergy may touch the sacred vessels.
claims.note: The rule comes from the Liber Pontificalis, written centuries later, and reflects the customs of its own time.

claims.text: Sixtus's relics were taken to Alatri in 1132.
claims.note: Alatri still keeps the story and the relics. It rests on a medieval account and can't be checked.

reigns.hook: Sixtus is dead. The next bishop is a Greek, and he is the first after Peter whose martyrdom has early support.

reigns.tagline: The one early pope Irenaeus calls a martyr
reigns.cameToPower: Named in the earliest bishop lists
reigns.previously: Sixtus dies. Hadrian rules, and leaves the Christians mostly alone.
paragraphs: Telesphorus was a Greek. When Irenaeus wrote his list around 180, he went through the Roman bishops with almost no comment, until he reached this one. Telesphorus, he says, died a glorious martyr's death. That makes him the first bishop of Rome after Peter whose martyrdom rests on a writer from the following generation, not on medieval legend.

Later centuries piled on extra credits. He was said to have started the midnight Mass at Christmas, the seven-week fast before Easter and the singing of the Gloria. The Carmelite friars, much later, even claimed him as one of their own, a hermit from Mount Carmel. He died in Hadrian's reign, though we don't know exactly how or why he was killed.

claims.text: Telesphorus died a martyr.
claims.note: Irenaeus says so in Against Heresies, written about 50 years later. It is the only early martyrdom on the list he states outright.

claims.text: Telesphorus started the midnight Mass at Christmas.
claims.note: The claim comes from the Liber Pontificalis. Christmas itself was not celebrated in Rome until the 4th century.

claims.text: Telesphorus was a Carmelite hermit.
claims.note: A late medieval Carmelite tradition, made to give the order an ancient pedigree.

reigns.hook: Telesphorus is dead. Under his successor, Rome attracts some brilliant and dangerous teachers, and one of them is said to have hoped to become a bishop himself.

reigns.tagline: Bishop when the clever heretics came to Rome
reigns.cameToPower: Named in the earliest bishop lists
reigns.previously: Telesphorus dies a martyr under Hadrian.
paragraphs: By now Rome was the place to be for any Christian teacher with big ideas. Irenaeus says two arrived in Hyginus's time. Valentinus, a brilliant Egyptian, taught a mystical system of secret knowledge, the kind later called gnostic. Cerdo, from Syria, said the God of the Jewish scriptures was a lesser god than the father of Jesus.

Hyginus himself is a shadow. The Liber Pontificalis says he was a Greek philosopher from Athens and that he set out the ranks of the clergy, both claims from much later. His short time in charge ended around 140, with the arguments over Valentinus and Cerdo still running. Tertullian later claimed Valentinus had hoped to be made bishop of Rome and turned rebel when passed over.

claims.text: Valentinus and Cerdo came to Rome in Hyginus's time.
claims.note: Irenaeus says so in Against Heresies, writing about 40 years later, and Eusebius repeats it.

claims.text: Hyginus was an Athenian philosopher.
claims.note: Only the Liber Pontificalis says so, compiled centuries later.

claims.text: Hyginus died a martyr.
claims.note: No early source says so. Irenaeus singles out only Telesphorus.

reigns.hook: Hyginus dies, and the next bishop has a famous brother: the author of the best-selling Christian book of the age. A rich shipowner is about to be shown the door.

reigns.tagline: His brother wrote the bestseller; he threw out Marcion
reigns.cameToPower: Named in the earliest bishop lists
reigns.previously: Hyginus dies, with Rome full of new teachers and new ideas.
paragraphs: Pius has a family. A list of approved Christian books from the late 2nd century, the Muratorian Fragment, says The Shepherd was written in Rome by Hermas while his brother Pius was bishop. The Shepherd, a book of visions about sin and second chances, was so popular that some churches read it like scripture.

Around 144 a rich shipowner from the Black Sea coast, Marcion, was expelled by the Roman church. He had tried to throw out the Jewish scriptures and kept only a trimmed gospel and Paul's letters. He set up a rival church that spread widely. Some historians think Pius may be the first true single bishop of Rome, the first to stand alone above the elders.

claims.text: Pius was the brother of Hermas, author of The Shepherd.
claims.note: The Muratorian Fragment says so. Most scholars accept it, but the fragment's own date and origin are argued over.

claims.text: Pius was the first real monarchical bishop of Rome.
claims.note: A modern theory, based on how Roman church leadership seems to change in the mid-2nd century. It can't be proved.

claims.text: Marcion was expelled from the Roman church around 144.
claims.note: The date is worked out from Tertullian's reckoning. Marcion's followers dated their church from the break.

reigns.hook: Pius dies. His successor will host a visitor who knew people who had known the apostles, and the two old men will argue about Easter.

reigns.tagline: He hosted Polycarp and agreed to disagree
reigns.cameToPower: Named in the earliest bishop lists
reigns.previously: Pius dies, and Marcion's rival church keeps growing.
paragraphs: Not long after Anicetus took over, a very old man arrived from Smyrna: Bishop Polycarp, who had known the apostle John. He and Anicetus disagreed over Easter. The churches of Asia kept it on the 14th day of the Jewish month of Nisan, whatever the weekday. Rome kept it on a Sunday. Neither man gave way, but they parted as friends, and Anicetus let Polycarp lead the Eucharist in Rome.

Rome was also a magnet for scholars. Hegesippus, a Christian from the East, came to check which teaching had been handed down, and drew up a list of Roman bishops ending with Anicetus. Justin Martyr ran a school in the city and was executed there around 165. Later tradition makes Anicetus a Syrian, from Emesa.

claims.text: Polycarp and Anicetus agreed to differ over Easter and shared the Eucharist.
claims.note: Irenaeus tells the story in a letter quoted by Eusebius. He was writing about 40 years later and knew Polycarp as a boy.

claims.text: Hegesippus drew up a succession list of Roman bishops up to Anicetus.
claims.note: Eusebius quotes Hegesippus saying so. His list is lost, but it may lie behind the later ones.

claims.text: Anicetus was a Syrian from Emesa.
claims.note: Only the Liber Pontificalis says so, compiled centuries later.

reigns.hook: Anicetus dies. His successor will send money east to churches in need, and a grateful bishop in Corinth will write back with news of an old letter from Rome.

reigns.tagline: Rome's bishop sends money, and Corinth says thanks
reigns.cameToPower: Named in the earliest bishop lists
reigns.previously: Anicetus dies, after agreeing to differ with Polycarp over Easter.
paragraphs: The Liber Pontificalis says Soter came from Fondi, in Campania. What we know for sure is that his church was generous. Rome had a habit of sending money to poorer churches and to Christians condemned to the mines, and Soter kept it up. Bishop Dionysius of Corinth wrote to thank him.

Part of that letter survives through Eusebius. Dionysius says that on the Lord's day his church read Soter's letter aloud, and that they still read Clement's old letter too. It is one of the earliest signs that Rome's letter of 96 was linked to Clement. Some scholars think Soter's Rome began keeping Easter as a yearly feast. He served under Marcus Aurelius, as plague swept the empire.

claims.text: Dionysius of Corinth thanked Soter for Rome's gifts.
claims.note: Eusebius quotes the letter in his Ecclesiastical History, Book 4.

claims.text: Soter made Easter an annual feast in Rome.
claims.note: A modern reading of Irenaeus's remarks about earlier Roman bishops. The evidence is indirect.

claims.text: Soter came from Fondi.
claims.note: Only the Liber Pontificalis says so, compiled centuries later.

reigns.hook: Soter dies. In Gaul, persecution is about to break out at Lyon, and a priest called Irenaeus will soon set off for Rome carrying letters.

reigns.tagline: The bishop on Irenaeus's list when the ink dried
reigns.previously: Soter dies under Marcus Aurelius, as trouble brews in Gaul.
paragraphs: Eleutherius was no stranger to the job. When the traveller Hegesippus came to Rome in the 150s, he found Eleutherius serving as deacon to Bishop Anicetus. Later tradition says he was a Greek from Nicopolis. When Soter died, the deacon moved up to the chair.

In 177 a mob in Lyon, in Gaul, turned on the local Christians, and dozens died in the arena. The survivors sent a priest named Irenaeus to Rome with letters for Eleutherius, partly about the Montanists, a new movement of prophets stirring up the churches of Asia Minor. Irenaeus later became bishop of Lyon and wrote a big book against heretics. In it he listed Rome's bishops from Peter down to the man in charge as he wrote: Eleutherius, the twelfth.

That list is why we know these names at all. Eleutherius died around 189. A later legend has a British king writing to ask him for missionaries, which would make him the pope who sent Christianity to Britain.

claims.text: Irenaeus's list of Roman bishops ends with Eleutherius, who held the office as he wrote.
claims.note: Against Heresies, Book 3, written around 180; Eusebius copies the list. It is the oldest surviving list of Rome's bishops.

claims.text: A British king named Lucius wrote to Eleutherius asking to be made a Christian.
claims.note: First found in the 6th-century Liber Pontificalis and spread by Bede. Many scholars think a King Lucius of Edessa got muddled with Britain.

claims.text: Eleutherius was a Greek from Nicopolis in Epirus.
claims.note: Only the Liber Pontificalis says so, writing some 350 years later.

reigns.hook: Eleutherius is dead. The next bishop comes from Africa, and he has a temper. He is about to tell half the churches of the East that they are celebrating Easter on the wrong day.

reigns.tagline: The African bishop who picked a fight over Easter
reigns.previously: Eleutherius dies around 189, the last name on Irenaeus's list.
paragraphs: Victor came from Roman Africa, by tradition, and he wanted things done one way. Most churches kept Easter on a Sunday. The churches of Asia Minor kept it on the 14th day of the Jewish month of Nisan, whatever day of the week that fell on, as they said the apostle John had taught them. Victor told them to fall into line.

Synods met across the empire, and most agreed with Rome. Bishop Polycrates of Ephesus wrote back that he would not budge. Victor tried to cut the Asian churches off from communion altogether. That was too much even for his allies. Irenaeus wrote to remind him that earlier bishops of Rome had lived happily with the difference. Victor also threw out a leather-worker named Theodotus, who taught that Jesus was just a man.
He had friends at court. Through Marcia, the mistress of Emperor Commodus, he got Christian prisoners freed from the mines of Sardinia. He died around 199.

claims.text: Victor tried to excommunicate the churches of Asia over Easter, and Irenaeus told him off.
claims.note: Eusebius quotes Polycrates's defiant letter and Irenaeus's rebuke in Book 5 of his history.

claims.text: Marcia, Commodus's mistress, asked Victor for a list of Christians in the mines and had them freed.
claims.note: Told by Hippolytus, who adds that Callixtus talked his way off the boat although his name was not on the list.

claims.text: Victor was the first bishop of Rome to write in Latin.
claims.note: Jerome says so, but none of Victor's writing survives. The Roman church mostly spoke Greek until the 3rd century.

reigns.hook: Victor is gone. His successor is a plain Roman with little learning, and the real power is about to pass to his deacon, a former slave with a very colourful past.

reigns.tagline: The plain old bishop his enemies called a puppet
reigns.previously: Victor dies around 199 after his row with Asia over Easter.
paragraphs: Zephyrinus was a Roman, and he ran the church for nearly twenty years. He had one stroke of genius. He brought back a deacon named Callixtus, a former slave freed from the mines of Sardinia, and gave him charge of the church's burial ground on the Appian Way. The catacomb Callixtus enlarged still carries his name.

The big fight of the day was about God. How could Christians worship Father, Son and Spirit and still say there was one God? Some teachers in Rome said they were three masks of the same person. Others said Jesus was a man adopted by God. Zephyrinus tried to keep the peace. A sharp-tongued priest named Hippolytus thought he was a fool for it.
Rome's church was now famous. Around 212 the young Alexandrian scholar Origen came just to see it. When Zephyrinus died around 217, his deacon stood ready.

claims.text: Zephyrinus was an ignorant, greedy man who took bribes and did whatever Callixtus told him.
claims.note: This is Hippolytus, Callixtus's bitter rival, in his Refutation of All Heresies. No friendly account survives to answer him.

claims.text: Natalius, a bishop of the adoptionist sect, was whipped all night by angels and came to Zephyrinus in sackcloth begging to be let back in.
claims.note: Eusebius quotes it from an earlier anonymous tract, the Little Labyrinth.

claims.text: Origen visited Rome in Zephyrinus's time, wanting to see its ancient church.
claims.note: Eusebius reports it in Book 6, citing Origen's own words.

reigns.hook: The old bishop is dead, and the former slave who runs the catacombs takes his chair. Hippolytus, the cleverest man in the church, refuses to accept him. Rome is about to have two bishops.

reigns.tagline: Slave, failed banker, convict, then bishop of Rome
reigns.cameToPower: Elected; Hippolytus set up a rival
reigns.reignEnded: Died in 222, maybe in a street riot
reigns.previously: Zephyrinus dies around 217. His deacon Callixtus is the obvious heir.
paragraphs: No early pope has a wilder story, though it comes from his worst enemy. Hippolytus says Callixtus was a slave who ran a bank for his Christian master, lost the depositors' money and ran for it. Caught at the port, he leapt into the sea, was fished out, and later picked a fight in a synagogue. That got him sent to the mines of Sardinia. He wangled his way out when the emperor's mistress freed the Christian prisoners there.

As deacon he ran the church's cemetery, and as bishop he ran the church his way. He let serious sinners, even adulterers, back to communion after penance. He accepted marriages between Christian noblewomen and lower-class men, which Roman law did not recognise. Hippolytus was disgusted. He gathered his own followers and set himself up as rival bishop, and is often called the first antipope.
Callixtus died around 222. He was buried on the Via Aurelia, not in the catacomb that bears his name. Archaeologists found his tomb there in the 1960s.

claims.text: Callixtus lost his master's money, jumped into the sea to escape and ended up in the Sardinian mines.
claims.note: Our only source is Hippolytus, who hated him and wrote to blacken his name.

claims.text: Callixtus was killed by a mob, thrown from a window into a well in Trastevere.
claims.note: From a late and unreliable account of his martyrdom. Nothing earlier says how he died.

claims.text: Hippolytus led a breakaway church in Rome against Callixtus and his successors.
claims.note: Hippolytus's own Refutation makes it clear. Who exactly he was, and where he was bishop, is still argued over.

reigns.hook: Callixtus is dead, but the split goes on. Hippolytus still calls himself the true bishop. The next man has to hold the church together under an emperor who leaves Christians alone.

reigns.tagline: A quiet bishop with a starring role in a fairy tale
reigns.previously: Callixtus dies around 222, and Hippolytus still claims his chair.
paragraphs: Urban had the luck to be bishop when the emperor did not care. Alexander Severus, a teenager steered by his mother Julia Mamaea, left the Christians in peace. Julia would later summon Origen for a talk about religion. For once, nobody came for Rome's bishop.

We know almost nothing about what Urban did. Eusebius gives him eight years and little else. Hippolytus's breakaway church carried on beside him. Later on, though, Urban became a star. The 5th-century story of St Cecilia, the noblewoman who sang to God at her wedding and converted her husband, has Urban baptising the couple and burying Cecilia after her martyrdom.
None of that holds up. Urban died around 230, probably in his bed. The persecution that would come for his successor was only a few years off.

claims.text: Urban baptised St Cecilia's husband and buried Cecilia after her martyrdom.
claims.note: From the Passion of St Cecilia, a romance written in the 5th century. It is the source for most of what was later said about Urban.

claims.text: When Christians and tavern keepers fought over a piece of public land, Alexander Severus gave it to the Christians.
claims.note: Told in the Historia Augusta, a famously unreliable set of imperial lives written over a century later.

claims.text: Urban was buried in the Crypt of the Popes in the Catacomb of Callixtus.
claims.note: A slab with the name Urban was found there, but the Liber Pontificalis puts his grave in another catacomb.

reigns.hook: Urban is dead and the quiet years are ending. A soldier-emperor is coming who hates the Christian leaders, and both of Rome's rival bishops are about to be shipped off to the mines.

reigns.tagline: The first pope known to have quit, in a prison mine
reigns.previously: Urban dies around 230, after years of peace under Alexander Severus.
paragraphs: With Pontian the dates suddenly get exact. A list of bishops copied into a Roman almanac of 354 gives his start, 21 July 230, and his end, to the day. Early in his time a Roman synod backed the bishop of Alexandria's condemnation of Origen, Jerome later said.

In 235 the army killed Alexander Severus and made the rough soldier Maximinus Thrax emperor. He went after the Christian leaders. Pontian was arrested along with Hippolytus, the rival bishop, and both were shipped to Sardinia to work the mines, where few lasted long.

Pontian did something no bishop of Rome had done before. On 28 September 235 he resigned, and Rome was free to choose a new bishop without waiting for him to die. He died in Sardinia soon after. Years later Fabian brought his body home to the Catacomb of Callixtus.

claims.text: Pontian resigned on 28 September 235, the first known papal resignation.
claims.note: The Liberian Catalogue in the Chronography of 354 records it with the date. It gives no reason.

claims.text: Pontian and Hippolytus made peace in the mines, ending the Roman schism.
claims.note: No one says so outright. The clue is that Rome later honoured both men on the same day, 13 August, as martyrs.

claims.text: Pontian was beaten to death with clubs in Sardinia.
claims.note: From the Liber Pontificalis, written about 300 years later. The older list says only that he was deported.

reigns.hook: Pontian has stepped down, still alive in the mines. Rome picks a Greek to replace him. Neither will see the spring.

reigns.tagline: Six weeks in the chair, then a grave you can still read
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected while Pontian was in the mines
reigns.previously: Pontian resigns in the mines of Sardinia, the first pope ever to quit.
paragraphs: Anterus was a Greek, chosen in November 235 to replace the exiled Pontian. Six weeks later, on 3 January 236, he was dead. Nobody recorded what killed him. With Maximinus Thrax on the throne, a short life was a risk that came with the job.

His real legacy is his grave. Anterus is the first bishop known to have been buried in the Crypt of the Popes in the Catacomb of Callixtus, the church's own cemetery on the Appian Way. His broken stone slab is still there, inscribed in Greek, ANTEROS EPI, short for bishop. Several of the next popes joined him in the same small room.
A later story says he had a clerk collect the official records of the martyrs' trials, and paid for it with his life.

claims.text: Anterus's Greek tomb slab survives in the Crypt of the Popes.
claims.note: Found by the archaeologist Giovanni Battista de Rossi when he uncovered the crypt in the 1850s.

claims.text: Anterus was martyred for collecting the records of martyrs' trials.
claims.note: Only the Liber Pontificalis says so, about 300 years later. The 4th-century list does not call him a martyr.

reigns.hook: Anterus is dead after six weeks. The Christians meet to elect a successor. A farmer in from the countryside is standing in the crowd, and he is not even a priest.

reigns.tagline: The layman a dove picked out of the crowd
reigns.relationToPredecessor: No relation; a layman in the crowd
reigns.cameToPower: Elected by acclaim at the vote
reigns.previously: Anterus dies after six weeks, leaving the church without a bishop.
paragraphs: Fabian came in from the country to watch the election and walked out bishop. Eusebius tells the story: a dove came down and settled on his head, and the crowd roared that he was the one. He was not even in the clergy. He turned out to be an excellent choice, and ruled for fourteen years.

He was an organiser. He split Rome into seven districts, each run by a deacon, to look after the poor and the burials. He sent for Pontian's body from Sardinia and buried it properly in the catacomb. Under easy-going emperors the church grew fast and bought property.

Then, in 249, Decius became emperor and ordered everyone in the empire to sacrifice to the gods and get a certificate to prove it. Fabian refused. He was arrested and died on 20 January 250, one of the first victims. His tomb slab is in the Crypt of the Popes.

claims.text: A dove landed on Fabian's head at the election, and the people took it as a sign.
claims.note: Eusebius tells it as something that was reported. It echoes the dove at Jesus's baptism.

claims.text: Fabian was martyred under Decius on 20 January 250.
claims.note: Cyprian of Carthage praises his death in his letters, and his tomb slab, with MARTYR added later, survives.

claims.text: Fabian divided Rome into seven church districts under deacons.
claims.note: The Liberian Catalogue of 354 says so, and Cornelius's count of seven deacons a year later fits.

reigns.hook: Fabian is dead, and Decius wants no new bishop in Rome. For fourteen months the priests run things, the cleverest of them a man named Novatian. When an election finally comes, the loser won't go quietly.

reigns.tagline: Elected in a persecution, opposed by his own priest
reigns.previously: Fabian dies under Decius. Rome goes over a year with no bishop.
paragraphs: With Decius away fighting the Goths, Rome's Christians finally elected a new bishop in March 251, a priest named Cornelius. The question that split them was what to do with the thousands who had caved in and sacrificed to the gods. Cornelius said they could come back after penance. Novatian, the brilliant priest who had run things during the vacancy, said no church could forgive them. He got three bishops to consecrate him and set up a rival church.

A synod of sixty bishops in Rome threw Novatian out, and Cyprian of Carthage backed Cornelius. A letter Cornelius wrote to the bishop of Antioch still exists. It counts the Roman clergy: 46 priests, 7 deacons, 7 subdeacons, 42 acolytes, and more than 1,500 widows and poor people fed by the church.
In 252 the new emperor Gallus started arresting Christians again. Cornelius was banished to Centumcellae, the port now called Civitavecchia, and died there in June 253.

claims.text: Decius said he would rather face a rival emperor than a new bishop of Rome.
claims.note: Cyprian says so in a letter defending Cornelius. It shows how Christians saw it, not necessarily what Decius said.

claims.text: Cornelius's letter lists 46 priests and over 1,500 widows and poor in the Roman church.
claims.note: Eusebius quotes the letter, to Fabius of Antioch, in Book 6.43. It is the earliest snapshot of the Roman church's size.

claims.text: Cornelius was beheaded for his faith.
claims.note: Cyprian calls him a martyr, but the 4th-century list says only that he died in exile. The beheading comes from later legend.

reigns.hook: Cornelius dies in exile, and Rome quickly elects his priest Lucius. Gallus sends the new bishop away too. Whether he ever comes home depends on who wins the next round of civil war.

reigns.tagline: Banished, called home, dead within months
reigns.previously: Cornelius dies in exile at Centumcellae, banished by Emperor Gallus.
paragraphs: Lucius was elected in June 253 and almost at once Gallus sent him into exile too. Then the empire changed hands. Gallus was killed by his own troops that summer, and the new emperor, Valerian, was in no rush to hunt Christians. Lucius was allowed home.

Cyprian of Carthage wrote to congratulate him on his return, saying Lucius had suffered exile for the faith like a true confessor. Lucius carried on Cornelius's line on Christians who had lapsed: they could come back after penance. Novatian's rival church kept going and would last for centuries.

Lucius died on 5 March 254, after barely eight months in office. He was buried in the Crypt of the Popes, where a fragment of his Greek epitaph survives. Cyprian later honoured him as a martyr, probably for his exile. Valerian's persecution did not begin until three years later.

claims.text: Cyprian wrote a letter congratulating Lucius on coming home from exile.
claims.note: The letter, number 61 in Cyprian's collection, survives.

claims.text: Lucius was beheaded for the faith.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis says so, writing centuries later, but there was no persecution in Rome when he died.

reigns.hook: Lucius is dead and Stephen takes his place. Stephen thinks Rome's word should settle things. In Carthage, Cyprian is about to discover that his old ally's successor is a very different man.

reigns.tagline: The pope who told Carthage to do as Rome does
reigns.cameToPower: Elected by Rome's clergy and people
reigns.previously: Lucius I dies in March 254, soon after coming home from exile.
paragraphs: Stephen picked a fight with the most respected bishop in the West. Cyprian of Carthage and his African councils said that anyone baptised by a breakaway church had to be baptised again to join the real one. Stephen said no: lay hands on them and let them in, because that was the old custom. Nothing new, he insisted, beyond what had been handed down.

Cyprian sent envoys to talk it over. Stephen wouldn't even see them, and threatened to cut off the churches of Africa and Asia Minor. What made his opponents angriest was how he argued: he sat in Peter's chair, so Rome's practice settled it. Firmilian, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, fired off a furious letter to Cyprian about Stephen's arrogance.

The quarrel was never settled in his lifetime. In 257 a new emperor, Valerian, turned on the Christians, and on 2 August Stephen died. Rome's custom won in the end: the Western Church still does not rebaptise.

claims.text: Stephen claimed authority over other churches as Peter's successor.
claims.note: Firmilian complains of exactly this in his letter to Cyprian, which survives among Cyprian's letters. It is one of the earliest known Roman appeals to Peter.

claims.text: Soldiers burst into the catacomb and beheaded Stephen as he sat on his bishop's chair.
claims.note: The story is told in later martyr legends. It looks borrowed from the very real death of his successor, Sixtus II.

reigns.hook: Stephen dies with Carthage still fuming. The next bishop, Sixtus, will make peace with Cyprian within months. He won't have long to enjoy it: Valerian's soldiers have orders to find Christian leaders.

reigns.tagline: Seized in the catacombs mid-sermon
reigns.previously: Stephen I dies in 257, still feuding with Cyprian of Carthage.
paragraphs: Sixtus mended fences fast. Without giving up Rome's position, he restored friendly relations with Carthage and the East. Cyprian's biographer Pontius remembered him as a good and peaceable bishop. Peace inside the church was just as well, because the empire had declared war on it.

Emperor Valerian first banned Christian meetings and visits to their cemeteries. In 258 he went further: bishops, priests and deacons were to be put to death at once. On 6 August soldiers found Sixtus in a cemetery on the Appian Way, teaching from his chair. He was beheaded on the spot with four of his deacons. Cyprian heard the news in Carthage and passed it on in a letter, weeks before his own execution.

Days later Rome's most famous deacon, Lawrence, was killed too. Sixtus was buried in the Crypt of the Popes in the Catacomb of Callixtus, and his name is still read out in the oldest prayer of the Roman Mass.

claims.text: Sixtus was executed in a cemetery on 6 August 258, with four deacons.
claims.note: Cyprian reports it in a letter written within weeks (Letter 80), and Pope Damasus's later verse epitaph tells the same story.

claims.text: Lawrence was roasted on a gridiron and joked: turn me over, this side is done.
claims.note: The gridiron first appears in Ambrose, a century later. Most historians think Lawrence was beheaded like Sixtus.

reigns.hook: Sixtus is dead, and Rome's church can't safely hold an election. It will go almost two years without a bishop, until news comes from the East that the emperor himself is a prisoner of the Persians.

reigns.tagline: He rebuilt the church after the storm
reigns.previously: Sixtus II is beheaded in 258. Rome goes two years without a bishop.
paragraphs: In 260 the Persian king Shapur captured Emperor Valerian in battle, and Valerian never came home. His son Gallienus called off the persecution and gave the Christians back their churches and cemeteries. Rome's Christians finally elected a bishop: Dionysius, a priest who had been prominent under Stephen, and he set about putting a wrecked church back together.

He also took on a theological row with a famous namesake. Some Christians in Libya complained that Bishop Dionysius of Alexandria talked as if the Son were a lesser being than the Father. The Roman Dionysius held a synod and wrote a careful letter warning against both mistakes, one God split into three or three names for one person. The Alexandrian wrote back to explain himself. Rome had become the place people appealed to.

He reached far beyond Italy. When Gothic raiders carried off Christians from Cappadocia, Dionysius sent letters and money to buy them back. He died at the end of 268, as a council in Antioch was deposing its own bishop.

claims.text: Dionysius sent money to ransom Christians captured by raiders in Cappadocia.
claims.note: Basil of Caesarea recalls it about a century later, in a letter to Pope Damasus.

claims.text: Dionysius rebuked Dionysius of Alexandria over the Trinity, and the Alexandrian wrote a defence.
claims.note: Athanasius quotes both in the 4th century, though he presents the exchange in the best light for his own side.

reigns.hook: Dionysius dies just as a letter from Antioch is on its way to Rome. Antioch's bishops have deposed their own leader, a showy, rich man called Paul. Paul refuses to move out, and it will take an emperor to shift him.

reigns.tagline: A pagan emperor took the bishop of Rome's word
reigns.cameToPower: Elected ten days after Dionysius died
reigns.previously: Dionysius dies in December 268 as Antioch deposes its bishop.
paragraphs: Felix inherited a scandal in the East. Paul of Samosata, bishop of Antioch, had been deposed by a council of bishops, who accused him of preaching that Jesus was an ordinary man, and of strutting about like a Roman official. Their letter went to Rome and Alexandria. But Antioch was then ruled by the breakaway Palmyrene empire of Queen Zenobia, and Paul simply stayed in the church house.

In 272 Emperor Aurelian smashed Zenobia and took Antioch back. The Christians asked him who owned the house. Aurelian, a pagan who worshipped the Unconquered Sun, gave a striking answer: it belonged to whoever the bishops of Italy and of Rome were in communion with. Paul was out, and Rome's word had decided it.
Back home, Aurelian was ringing Rome with a huge new wall against barbarian raids. Felix died at the end of 274, without having been killed for his faith.

claims.text: Aurelian ruled that the Antioch church house belonged to the bishop recognised by Rome and Italy.
claims.note: Eusebius reports the ruling in his Ecclesiastical History, Book 7, written a generation later.

claims.text: Felix died a martyr.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis says so, but it seems to have mixed him up with a martyr of the same name buried elsewhere. Early lists give him no martyrdom.

reigns.hook: Felix is gone. Within a year Aurelian is murdered by his own officers, and the emperors start changing every year or two. The next bishop will rule for nine quiet years and leave almost nothing behind.

reigns.tagline: Nine quiet years, and almost nothing to show
reigns.previously: Felix I dies in December 274, under the wall-building Aurelian.
paragraphs: Eutychian is a name, two dates and not much else. That is a sign of good times. He ruled in the long calm between Gallienus's toleration and Diocletian's persecution, when Christians built churches in the open and their numbers kept rising. Emperors rose and fell around him: Aurelian, Tacitus, Probus and Carus all died within his nine years, at least two of them killed by their own soldiers.

When he died in December 283 he was laid in the Crypt of the Popes in the Catacomb of Callixtus, beside the bishops of the persecutions. A fragment of his tombstone, carved in Greek, was dug up there in the 19th century. He was the last pope buried in that crypt.
Later writers wanted more from him. The Liber Pontificalis turned him into a martyr and gave him heroic deeds, though his own era recorded none.

claims.text: Eutychian buried 342 martyrs with his own hands.
claims.note: The figure comes from the Liber Pontificalis, written over 200 years later. There was no persecution in his time to produce martyrs.

claims.text: Eutychian's tombstone was found in the Crypt of the Popes.
claims.note: The archaeologist Giovanni Battista de Rossi recovered fragments of the popes' epitaphs there in the 1850s, Eutychian's among them.

reigns.hook: Eutychian goes into the crypt. Within a year, an army officer from Dalmatia named Diocletian takes the throne. The next bishop, said to be from Dalmatia too, will watch him rebuild the empire and then turn on the Church.

reigns.tagline: Kinsman of the emperor? Only in legend
reigns.previously: Eutychian dies after nine quiet years, in December 283.
paragraphs: Caius ruled for twelve years and history kept almost none of it. Diocletian, who took the throne in 284, spent the time fixing a broken empire. He split power between two senior emperors and two juniors, the Tetrarchy, and fought off enemies on every frontier. He left the Christians alone. Some served in his army and even worked in his palace.

The church grew in the peace. Christians put up meeting halls in the open, owned property and buried their dead in big shared cemeteries. Caius ran a church that was rich, organised and highly visible in Rome, which would make it an easy target when the mood changed.

He died in April 296 and was buried in the Catacomb of Callixtus, near his predecessors. Later legend made him a relative of Diocletian, and spun stories around a niece said to be martyred for refusing to marry into the emperor's family.

claims.text: Caius was a kinsman of Diocletian.
claims.note: It comes from the late Acts of St Susanna, a romance with little history in it. The Liber Pontificalis, which says he was from Dalmatia, does not mention it.

claims.text: Caius ruled that a man must pass through every lower order of clergy before becoming a bishop.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis credits him with this, but it likes to pin later church rules on early popes.

reigns.hook: Caius dies, and Rome's church picks a priest named Marcellinus. He will be bishop when Diocletian decides, after nineteen years of tolerance, that the Christians must be crushed.

reigns.tagline: Did the pope burn incense to the gods?
reigns.previously: Caius dies in April 296, during the long peace.
paragraphs: In February 303, at Nicomedia, Diocletian ordered churches destroyed and scriptures burned. More edicts followed: clergy were jailed, then everyone had to sacrifice to the gods or die. In Italy, his co-emperor Maximian enforced it. This was the Great Persecution, the worst the Church ever faced.

What did Marcellinus do? His enemies said he handed over the holy books and offered incense to the gods to save his skin. The Liber Pontificalis admits he sacrificed but says he repented and was beheaded. Augustine said the charge was never proved. Rome's own official list of its bishops' burial days left his name out, a silence that looks bad.
He died around 304. The persecution was so fierce, or the church so shaken, that Rome did not elect another bishop for nearly four years.

claims.text: Marcellinus gave up the scriptures and burned incense to the gods.
claims.note: The Donatists made the charge a century later; Augustine denied it was ever proved. But the Liber Pontificalis also says he sacrificed, and he is missing from the Roman list of bishops' burials of 354.

claims.text: A council of 300 bishops at Sinuessa heard him confess, and declared that no one may judge the first see.
claims.note: The acts of this council are a forgery made in Rome around 500, during a fight over whether a pope could be put on trial.

claims.text: Marcellinus repented and died a martyr.
claims.note: Only later sources say so. He is honoured as a saint, but no early evidence backs a martyrdom.

reigns.hook: Marcellinus is gone and no one dares elect a successor. When Rome finally gets a bishop, he will find a flock full of people who caved in to save their lives, and who now want back in on easy terms.

reigns.tagline: Tough on traitors, and Rome rioted
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected after a vacancy of 3+ years
reigns.previously: Marcellinus dies amid the persecution. Rome waits years for a bishop.
paragraphs: In 306 Maxentius, son of the old emperor Maximian, seized power in Rome. He had no reason to keep killing Christians and let the persecution lapse. In 308, after nearly four years without a bishop, Rome's church elected Marcellus. He set about rebuilding, but one question split his flock. What about all the Christians who had sacrificed or handed over books to save themselves?

Marcellus was strict: they could come back, but only after doing hard penance and weeping for what they had done. Many of them refused. Pope Damasus later wrote in a verse epitaph that rage, hatred and bloodshed followed, and that a man who had denied Christ even in peacetime stirred up the trouble. Maxentius wanted order, so he threw Marcellus out of Rome.
He died in exile in January 309, after less than eight months in charge.

claims.text: Marcellus's hard line on the lapsed caused riots, and Maxentius banished him.
claims.note: Damasus's epitaph for him, written about 60 years later, says so. It survives in old copies.

claims.text: Maxentius made Marcellus work as a groom in the imperial stables, and he died there.
claims.note: The story comes from a later martyr legend. The church of San Marcello al Corso is said to stand on the spot.

claims.text: Marcellus and Marcellinus were really the same man.
claims.note: Some scholars have argued this from the confusion in the early lists. Most accept two separate bishops.

reigns.hook: Marcellus dies in exile, and the brawling over the lapsed goes on. The next bishop, a Greek named Eusebius, will hold the same hard line. He will last just four months.

reigns.tagline: Four months as pope, then a boat to Sicily
reigns.previously: Maxentius banishes Marcellus I. He dies in exile in January 309.
paragraphs: Eusebius was a Greek, by tradition, and he walked straight into the fight that had sunk Marcellus. He too said the Christians who had lapsed must do penance and mourn their sins before coming back. A rival named Heraclius led the party that wanted them let in without fuss. The two sides fought in the streets.
Maxentius had had enough. He exiled both leaders to Sicily. Eusebius died there in August 310, after about four months as bishop. His body was brought home and buried in the Catacomb of Callixtus.

We know any of this only because Damasus, pope fifty years later, put up a verse inscription at his tomb. It speaks of sedition, slaughter, war and discord. Pieces of the original marble have been found in the catacomb.

claims.text: Factions led by Eusebius and Heraclius fought over the lapsed, and Maxentius exiled both to Sicily.
claims.note: Damasus's epitaph says so. The original was broken and replaced by a 6th-century copy; fragments of both survive.

claims.text: Heraclius set himself up as a rival bishop of Rome.
claims.note: The epitaph never calls him a bishop. Some historians count him as an antipope; others see a lay faction leader.

reigns.hook: Eusebius dies in exile, and Rome goes without a bishop again. Within a year Maxentius changes course. The next pope will get the church's property back, then watch a new emperor ride in under a strange new sign.

reigns.tagline: Hunted at the start, the emperor's guest by the end
reigns.previously: Eusebius dies in exile in Sicily. Rome waits a year for a bishop.
paragraphs: Miltiades, said to be an African, was elected in 311, the year the dying Emperor Galerius gave up on persecution. Maxentius sent orders to hand back everything taken from Rome's church, and Miltiades's deacons went to the prefect to collect it. Then, in October 312, Constantine marched on Rome and beat Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge. Maxentius drowned in the Tiber. Constantine said the Christian God had given him victory.

In 313 Constantine and his co-emperor Licinius agreed at Milan to let Christians worship freely. Constantine gave the bishop of Rome property at the Lateran, the start of the papal palace there. He also handed Miltiades a problem: a split in the African church, where a party later called the Donatists rejected the new bishop of Carthage.
In October 313 Miltiades held a synod in the Lateran palace and found against the Donatists. They didn't accept it and appealed to the emperor again. Miltiades died in January 314.

claims.text: The Lateran synod of 313 met in the house of Fausta, Constantine's wife.
claims.note: Optatus of Milevis gives the place and the date in his work against the Donatists, quoting the synod's records.

claims.text: Miltiades had handed over sacred books during the persecution.
claims.note: The Donatists said so, to discredit his verdict. Augustine rejected the charge and no early evidence supports it.

claims.text: Constantine saw a sign in the sky before the Milvian Bridge.
claims.note: Eusebius says Constantine told him so years later. Lactantius, writing soon after, mentions only a dream.

reigns.hook: Miltiades dies with the Donatists still protesting. His successor, Sylvester, will sit through the biggest church building boom Rome has ever seen, while the emperor quietly takes charge of the Church.

reigns.tagline: The bishop who got the emperor's gold but not his ear
reigns.previously: Miltiades dies in 314, a year after Constantine's Edict of Milan.
paragraphs: Sylvester was a Roman priest, elected three weeks after Miltiades died, and he had the luck to be bishop when the money started flowing. Constantine had already handed the bishop the Lateran palace. Now he built a huge basilica beside it, the cathedral of Rome to this day, and began the first St Peter's over the shrine on the Vatican Hill. Gold plate, silver lamps and whole estates to pay for the lighting poured in.

The emperor called the shots, though. In 314 he summoned bishops to Arles to deal with the Donatist split in Africa, and Sylvester sent two priests and two deacons. In 325 Constantine gathered hundreds of bishops at Nicaea to settle whether Christ was fully God. Sylvester stayed at home again and sent two priests, Vitus and Vincentius, to sign for Rome.

He ran Rome's church quietly for almost 22 years and died on 31 December 335. That is why New Year's Eve is still called Silvester in Germany, Austria and much of central Europe. Later Rome spun grand legends around this low-key man, turning him into the healer who baptised Constantine and the heir to half an empire.

claims.text: Constantine gave Sylvester and his heirs power over the whole western empire.
claims.note: This is the Donation of Constantine, forged in the 8th century. Lorenzo Valla proved it a fake in 1440 from its anachronistic Latin.

claims.text: Sylvester cured Constantine of leprosy and baptised him in Rome.
claims.note: A later legend. Constantine was baptised on his deathbed in 337 by Eusebius of Nicomedia, a bishop who leaned towards Arius.

claims.text: Sylvester sent two priests, Vitus and Vincentius, to the Council of Nicaea.
claims.note: Their names appear in the lists of those who signed for the council, and Eusebius notes the bishop of Rome sent deputies.

reigns.hook: Sylvester is gone, and Constantine has only 17 months left to live. The next bishop of Rome will have barely enough time to build a church.

reigns.tagline: Nine months as bishop, and two churches to show for it
reigns.previously: Sylvester dies on the last day of 335, after nearly 22 years.
paragraphs: Mark was a Roman, the son of a man called Priscus according to the Liber Pontificalis, and he was bishop for less than nine months in 336. That is about all we know of him as a person. What survives is bricks and mortar. He founded a church near the foot of the Capitol, which still stands, many times rebuilt, as San Marco beside Piazza Venezia.

He also built a cemetery church on the Via Ardeatina, on land given by Constantine, and he was buried there after he died on 7 October 336. A Roman almanac called the Chronograph of 354 records the day and the place. Dry lists like that one are what turn the bishops of this age from pious names into real men with real graves.

claims.text: Mark gave the bishop of Ostia the right to consecrate each new pope.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis credits him. The custom was certainly in place by Augustine's day, but early popes were often given credit for rules that grew up later.

claims.text: Mark's burial on 7 October is recorded in the Chronograph of 354.
claims.note: Its list of bishops' burials, compiled in Rome only 18 years later, gives the date and the cemetery of Balbina on the Via Ardeatina.

reigns.hook: Mark is dead, and next spring Constantine dies too. In the East, bishops who favour Arius are already driving the fierce Athanasius out of Alexandria, and he will come to Rome for help.

reigns.tagline: He told the East it should have asked Rome first
reigns.previously: Mark dies after nine months. Rome waits four months for a bishop.
paragraphs: Julius was a Roman, elected in February 337. Within months Constantine was dead and the fight over Arius was back on. Arius had taught that Christ was a created being, lesser than the Father. Eastern bishops friendly to his ideas drove Athanasius, the tough little bishop of Alexandria, out of his city, and around 339 Athanasius turned up in Rome.

Julius took him in, and a Roman synod cleared him. Then Julius wrote to the Easterners. Why had nobody consulted Rome, he asked, when the custom was to write to us first? It was a polite letter with an iron edge. At Serdica, modern Sofia, in 343 the Eastern bishops walked out, and the Westerners who stayed agreed that a deposed bishop could appeal to the bishop of Rome.

At home Julius built churches, among them the one across the Tiber that became Santa Maria in Trastevere. He died on 12 April 352 after 15 years and was buried on the Via Aurelia. Athanasius was back in Alexandria by then, but the emperor now in charge in the East was no friend of his.

claims.text: Julius told the Eastern bishops they should have written to Rome before judging Athanasius.
claims.note: Athanasius copied the whole letter into his Defence against the Arians.

claims.text: Julius founded the church that became Santa Maria in Trastevere.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis says he built a basilica across the Tiber. Linking it to Santa Maria in Trastevere is old tradition, and another legend credits Pope Callixtus.

claims.text: The bishops at Serdica gave Rome the right to hear appeals.
claims.note: The canons survive, though only the Western half of the council passed them. Later popes would quote them as if they came from Nicaea.

reigns.hook: Julius is dead. Constantius II is about to rule the whole empire, and he wants every bishop to condemn Athanasius. He won't take no for an answer from Rome.

reigns.tagline: Exiled by the emperor, then blamed for how he got home
reigns.previously: Julius dies in 352, after 15 years of standing by Athanasius.
paragraphs: Liberius was a Roman elected in May 352, and he soon faced the job's toughest test yet. Emperor Constantius II favoured the bishops who leaned towards Arius, and he wanted Athanasius condemned by the whole Church. Synods at Arles and Milan gave in. Liberius refused. In 355 he was hauled to Milan, argued with the emperor face to face, and was sent into exile at Beroea in Thrace.

Back in Rome the archdeacon Felix was made bishop in his place, although the clergy had sworn to accept no one else while Liberius lived. Felix is counted as an antipope. In 358 Liberius was allowed home. The price, his critics said, was signing a vague creed and dropping Athanasius. The Roman crowds drove Felix out and cheered Liberius back in.

He spent his last years quietly, building a church on the Esquiline Hill. He died on 24 September 366. Felix had died the year before, but their followers had never made peace, and the fight over who came next would be the bloodiest yet.

claims.text: Liberius bought his return by signing a compromise creed and abandoning Athanasius.
claims.note: Athanasius and Jerome both say he gave way. Letters in his name admitting it survive, but some scholars think they are forgeries.

claims.text: When Constantius proposed that Liberius and Felix share the see, the crowd chanted 'One God, one Christ, one bishop!'
claims.note: Theodoret tells the story, writing in Syria about 90 years later.

claims.text: Mary sent snow in August to show Liberius where to build her church.
claims.note: No early source tells the story; it appears centuries later. Santa Maria Maggiore still remembers it every 5 August with white petals.

reigns.hook: Liberius is dead, and two men claim his seat: the deacon Damasus and the loyalists' choice, Ursinus. Rome's Christians are about to settle it with clubs.

reigns.tagline: Elected over a pile of bodies, remembered for the Bible
reigns.previously: Liberius dies in 366. His loyalists and Felix's still hate each other.
paragraphs: When Liberius died, his loyal followers chose the deacon Ursinus. A bigger party, with money and muscle behind it, chose another deacon, Damasus. Both men were consecrated, and the fighting began. Gangs stormed the basilica where Ursinus's people were holding out, and the pagan historian Ammianus Marcellinus reports that 137 bodies were found there in a single day.

The authorities exiled Ursinus, and Damasus proved shrewd and tough. He restored the martyrs' tombs in the catacombs and wrote verse epitaphs for them, carved in elegant lettering by the calligrapher Filocalus. In 380 Emperor Theodosius ordered all his subjects to follow the faith of Damasus of Rome and Peter of Alexandria. Rome's bishop had become a yardstick of orthodoxy.

In 382 he took on a brilliant, prickly scholar named Jerome as his secretary and set him revising the Latin gospels. That work grew into the Vulgate, the Bible of the Western Church for over a thousand years. Damasus died on 11 December 384, aged about 80, and Jerome thought he knew who should be next.

claims.text: 137 bodies were found in one basilica in a single day of the election fighting.
claims.note: Ammianus Marcellinus, a pagan writing at the time, gives the number. How far Damasus himself ordered the violence is disputed; the fiercest charges come from Ursinus's backers.

claims.text: A pagan grandee joked: make me bishop of Rome and I'll become a Christian tomorrow.
claims.note: Jerome says the city prefect Praetextatus used to say it, as a dig at how rich the job had become.

claims.text: Damasus was the 'ladies' ear-tickler', a charmer of rich Roman matrons.
claims.note: The jibe comes from his opponents. He was also charged with adultery around 378 and cleared.

reigns.hook: Damasus is dead. Jerome is sure he deserves the top job, and not shy about saying so. Rome's clergy have other ideas, and Jerome is about to burn his bridges.

reigns.tagline: The first pope to lay down the law by letter

start.note: elected after the death of his predecessor

reigns.previously: Damasus dies at about 80. Jerome expects to be the next pope.
paragraphs: Siricius was a Roman deacon who had served under Liberius and Damasus, and the clergy chose him in December 384. Ursinus's old faction stirred again, but Emperor Valentinian II confirmed Siricius early in 385. Jerome took it badly. He had made enemies with his sharp tongue, and in August 385 he sailed from Rome for the Holy Land, never to return.

In February 385 Siricius answered a list of questions from Bishop Himerius of Tarragona in Spain. His reply is the oldest papal decretal that survives: a letter laying down law for another church, in the style of an imperial ruling. Priests and deacons, it said, must stop sleeping with their wives. Baptism and penance were to be handled Rome's way.

He held that line. In the early 390s he condemned the monk Jovinian, who taught that marriage was as holy as virginity. Siricius died on 26 November 399 after 15 years and was buried in the Catacomb of Priscilla.

claims.text: The letter to Himerius is the oldest surviving papal decretal.
claims.note: It is dated 10 February 385 and survives in early canon-law collections.

claims.text: Siricius was the first bishop of Rome to call himself 'pope'.
claims.note: The title 'papa' turns up for him early on, but it was used for many bishops then. Rome only claimed it for itself much later.

claims.text: Jerome left Rome because he had been passed over for bishop.
claims.note: In a letter written as he left, Jerome says almost everyone had thought him worthy of the highest priesthood. He also faced scandal over his circle of noble women.

reigns.hook: Siricius is dead. In Egypt, Bishop Theophilus is hunting the followers of the great old thinker Origen, and from Bethlehem Jerome is urging Rome to join the hunt.

reigns.tagline: Two years, one banned thinker, and Jerome's applause
reigns.cameToPower: Elected the day after Siricius died
reigns.reignEnded: Died after two years in office
reigns.previously: Siricius dies after 15 years. A row over Origen is reaching Rome.
paragraphs: Anastasius was a Roman, the son of a man named Maximus. He walked straight into a war of words over Origen, the brilliant 3rd-century Greek thinker whose ideas about souls and salvation now looked dangerous. Theophilus of Alexandria had condemned Origen's followers and wanted Rome to do the same.

Rufinus of Aquileia, who had translated Origen into Latin, sent Anastasius a statement of his own orthodoxy. Anastasius was unmoved, and around 400 he condemned Origen's writings. Jerome, Rufinus's old friend and now his bitter enemy, was delighted. He praised the pope to the skies.

Anastasius also urged the African bishops to keep up their fight against the Donatists. He died on 19 December 401. Years later, after the Goths had sacked Rome, Jerome wrote that the city had not deserved to keep such a bishop for long.

claims.text: Anastasius was the father of his successor, Innocent I.
claims.note: Jerome calls Innocent his 'son' and successor, which may mean a spiritual son. The Liber Pontificalis names Innocent's father as another Innocent, from Albano.

claims.text: Rome did not deserve him long, lest the capital of the world fall under such a bishop.
claims.note: Jerome wrote this in a letter of 414, after Alaric's sack of 410.

claims.text: Anastasius ordered priests to stand and bow while the Gospel was read.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis credits him, but it often pins later customs on early popes.

reigns.hook: Anastasius is dead, and Alaric's Goths have just crossed into Italy. His successor will be bishop when an enemy army takes Rome for the first time in 800 years.

reigns.tagline: Away at Ravenna on the day the Goths took Rome
reigns.previously: Anastasius dies after two years. Jerome mourns him from Bethlehem.
paragraphs: Innocent came from Albano, just outside Rome, and he was one of the most forceful bishops Rome had yet had. He wrote to bishops across the West as if he were their boss. Every church in Italy, Gaul, Spain and Africa, he told one of them, had been founded by Peter or his successors, so all of them should follow Rome's customs.

He backed John Chrysostom, the great preacher of Constantinople, when the eastern court threw him out in 404. Then the Goths came. Alaric besieged Rome three times. During one siege Innocent went with a Roman embassy to Emperor Honorius at Ravenna, and he was still away on 24 August 410, when the Goths broke in and sacked the city for three days.

Back in Rome he kept up the pressure on Pelagius, a British monk who taught that people could choose to be good without special help from God. In January 417 he backed the African bishops' condemnation of Pelagius. He died on 12 March 417.

claims.text: God kept Innocent away from Rome during the sack, as he saved Lot from Sodom.
claims.note: That is how Orosius, writing a few years later, explained the pope's absence.

claims.text: During Alaric's first siege in 408, Innocent let pagan priests try their old rites, as long as it was done in private.
claims.note: Only the pagan historian Zosimus says so, writing nearly a century later.

claims.text: Augustine said of Innocent's ruling: 'Rome has spoken; the case is closed.'
claims.note: A later paraphrase. In a sermon of 417 Augustine said the replies had come from the apostolic see and the case was finished.

reigns.hook: Innocent is dead and Pelagius is condemned. Or is he? The next pope is a Greek who will take a fresh look at the case, and Africa's bishops are going to be furious.

reigns.tagline: The pope who cleared Pelagius, then had to take it back
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected; a Greek priest of Rome
reigns.previously: Innocent dies in 417, weeks after condemning Pelagius.
paragraphs: Zosimus was a Greek, and his short reign was one long row. Within months Caelestius, Pelagius's right-hand man, came to Rome to plead his case. Zosimus heard him, read a statement sent by Pelagius, and declared both of them sound. He told the African bishops off for judging too hastily.

Africa hit back. Its bishops, led by Aurelius of Carthage with Augustine behind him, stood by their verdict, and in April 418 Emperor Honorius banned the Pelagians from Rome. Zosimus changed course and sent round a letter condemning them. He picked other fights too, putting Patroclus of Arles over the bishops of southern Gaul and quarrelling with Africa over a disgraced priest named Apiarius.
Even his own clergy turned against him, and some complained about him to the court at Ravenna. He fell ill and died on 26 December 418, leaving Rome's clergy split down the middle.

claims.text: Zosimus quoted canons as Nicene that really came from the Council of Serdica.
claims.note: The Africans sent to the East for copies of the Nicene canons and could not find the rules he cited.

claims.text: Zosimus reversed himself on Pelagius because the emperor forced his hand.
claims.note: He claimed he had never made a final judgement. But the emperor's ban came before the pope's letter condemning the Pelagians.

reigns.hook: Zosimus is dead, and his clergy are split. The very next day one faction seizes the Lateran and elects the archdeacon Eulalius. The other party has its own man ready.

reigns.tagline: Two popes, one Easter, and an emperor losing patience
reigns.previously: Zosimus dies, loathed by his clergy. Two factions each elect a pope.
paragraphs: The day after Zosimus died, the archdeacon Eulalius and his supporters seized the Lateran and elected him. On 28 December most of the priests met at another church and chose Boniface, an elderly Roman priest. Both men were consecrated on the same day, and Rome had two bishops.

The city prefect Symmachus backed Eulalius and told Emperor Honorius so, and at first the emperor agreed. Then he wavered and called a council, ordering both men to keep out of Rome in the meantime. Eulalius broke the order and slipped back in to hold the Easter services in 419. That finished him. Honorius threw him out and recognised Boniface in April 419.

Boniface asked the emperor to stop it happening again. Honorius ruled that if two men were ever elected, neither would get the job and the clergy must start over. Boniface spent his last years defending Rome's hold over the bishops of Illyricum against Constantinople. He died on 4 September 422.

claims.text: Honorius ruled that a disputed election should be thrown out and held again.
claims.note: The letters between the emperor, the prefect and the clergy survive in the Collectio Avellana.

claims.text: Augustine dedicated a book against the Pelagians to Boniface.
claims.note: His Against Two Letters of the Pelagians is addressed to him.

claims.text: Eulalius took his defeat well and later refused a chance to try again.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis says he turned down his supporters' call when Boniface fell ill, and ended up a bishop in the country.

reigns.hook: Boniface is dead, and this time there is no fight. Far to the east, though, a new bishop of Constantinople is about to start a quarrel about what to call Mary.

reigns.tagline: He sent a bishop to Ireland and helped topple Nestorius
reigns.previously: Boniface dies in 422, his rival Eulalius long gone.
paragraphs: Celestine was a Roman deacon, and for once the election went peacefully. He spent his first years laying down the law to bishops in Gaul and Africa. Then trouble came from Constantinople. Its new bishop, Nestorius, objected to calling Mary the Mother of God. Cyril of Alexandria, his great rival, sent Rome a dossier against him.

In August 430 a Roman synod condemned Nestorius and gave him ten days to recant. He refused. At the Council of Ephesus in 431 Cyril's party deposed him, and Celestine's legates arrived late to sign the verdict for Rome. It was a win for Rome, though Cyril had run the show.

Celestine looked north and west as well. The chronicler Prosper of Aquitaine records that in 429 he sent Bishop Germanus of Auxerre to Britain to fight Pelagian teaching, and in 431 sent Palladius as the first bishop of the Christians of Ireland. Celestine died on 27 July 432.

claims.text: Celestine sent Palladius to Ireland as its first bishop in 431.
claims.note: Prosper of Aquitaine, who later worked in Rome, records it in his chronicle.

claims.text: Celestine also sent St Patrick to Ireland.
claims.note: Patrick's own writings never mention Rome or a pope. The link appears in much later lives of the saint.

reigns.hook: Celestine is dead. His successor was once suspected of a soft spot for Pelagius, and he has a grand plan: a great church for Mary to celebrate the win at Ephesus.

reigns.tagline: The pope who built Santa Maria Maggiore
reigns.previously: Celestine dies, a year after his legates helped bring Nestorius down.
paragraphs: Sixtus was a senior priest of Rome. Years earlier he had been suspected of a soft spot for Pelagius, until he came out against him and Augustine wrote to congratulate him. As pope he played peacemaker. In 433 Cyril of Alexandria and John of Antioch, still sore from Ephesus, signed a deal ending their quarrel, and Sixtus welcomed it warmly.

His great monument still stands. He built Santa Maria Maggiore on the Esquiline, the first great church in Rome dedicated to Mary, freshly hailed at Ephesus as Mother of God. The mosaics on its arch still carry his dedication: Xystus, bishop, to the people of God. He also gave the Lateran baptistery the eight-sided shape it keeps today.

Not all was serene. The Liber Pontificalis says a nobleman named Bassus accused him of seducing a nun, and a synod cleared him. Sixtus died on 19 August 440. Rome's most able deacon, Leo, was away in Gaul patching up a quarrel between two generals, and the clergy decided to wait for him.

claims.text: Sixtus's dedication survives in the mosaics of Santa Maria Maggiore.
claims.note: The inscription XYSTUS EPISCOPUS PLEBI DEI is still on the arch above the altar.

claims.text: A nobleman named Bassus accused Sixtus of seducing a nun.
claims.note: The tale comes from a set of documents forged in Rome around 500, which the Liber Pontificalis later used.

claims.text: Sixtus had once favoured Pelagius.
claims.note: Augustine's letters to him in 418 suggest Pelagius's friends had counted on him, until he condemned them.

reigns.hook: Sixtus is dead and the clergy want Leo. He is far off in Gaul, and Rome waits weeks for him to come home and take a job he will make bigger than anyone before him.

reigns.tagline: The pope who stared down Attila
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Deacon of Rome under Sixtus III
reigns.previously: Sixtus III dies. Rome's leading deacon is away in Gaul.
paragraphs: Leo was a deacon of the Roman church, sent to Gaul to patch up a quarrel between two Roman generals, when news came that he had been elected pope. He came home and made the job bigger than anyone before him. Peter, he preached, still spoke through his heir in Rome, and bishops everywhere should listen.

The East took notice. In 449 he sent a letter on the nature of Christ, known as his Tome. At the Council of Chalcedon in 451 it helped shape the council's definition of Christ as one person with two natures, divine and human. In 452 Attila's Huns were rampaging through northern Italy. Leo rode out with two leading Romans and met him near Mantua. Attila turned back.

In 455 the Vandals under Gaiseric sailed in and took Rome. Leo met him and talked him out of burning the city and massacring its people, though the Vandals still looted it for two weeks. Leo died in November 461, the first pope buried in St Peter's. Later ages called him Leo the Great.

claims.text: Peter and Paul appeared in the sky with swords, and that is why Attila turned back.
claims.note: A later legend, painted by Raphael in the Vatican. Hunger and disease in the Hun army probably mattered more.

claims.text: At Chalcedon the bishops shouted, 'Peter has spoken through Leo!'
claims.note: The cry is recorded in the official acts of the council.

claims.text: Leo persuaded Gaiseric to spare the lives of the Romans in 455.
claims.note: Prosper of Aquitaine, who worked for Leo, records the meeting in his chronicle.

reigns.hook: Leo is dead, and the western empire has 15 years left. Rome chooses his archdeacon Hilarius, the man who once shouted 'I object!' at a rigged council and escaped from Ephesus by back roads.
