reigns.tagline: The legate who shouted no and ran for his life
reigns.cameToPower: Elected nine days after Leo died
reigns.previously: Leo the Great dies, the man who faced down Attila.
paragraphs: Hilarius was a Sardinian who had already lived through one great adventure. In 449 Leo sent him to a church council at Ephesus, which the emperor's men and a mob of monks had rigged for the bishop of Alexandria. When the council condemned the bishop of Constantinople, Hilarius stood up and shouted one Latin word, 'Contradicitur!', meaning 'I object!'. Then he slipped out of the city by back roads and made his way home to Rome.

As pope he never forgot it. He built chapels beside the Lateran baptistery, and over the door of one he thanked St John the Evangelist, Ephesus's patron saint, for setting him free. He ran the western Church with a firm hand, holding synods in Rome to sort out quarrelling bishops in Gaul and Spain. When a heretic close to the emperor Anthemius tried to set up meetings in Rome, Hilarius made the emperor promise in St Peter's to stop him.

claims.text: Hilarius escaped from the 'Robber Synod' of Ephesus by hiding and taking back roads.
claims.note: He describes it himself in a letter to the empress Pulcheria, kept among Leo's letters.

claims.text: His chapel at the Lateran baptistery carries his thanks to St John for his rescue.
claims.note: The dedication inscription over the door of the oratory still survives.

claims.text: He made Emperor Anthemius swear in St Peter's to keep heretics out of Rome.
claims.note: The story comes from a letter of Pope Gelasius I, written about 25 years later.

reigns.hook: Hilarius dies in 468. His successor will be pope when the last western emperor is pushed off his throne, and will hardly mention it.

reigns.tagline: The pope who barely noticed the fall of Rome
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Cleric from Tivoli; no known tie
reigns.previously: Hilarius dies, the pope who once fled a rigged council by back roads.
paragraphs: Simplicius came from Tivoli, in the hills east of Rome, and was pope for 15 years. In 476 a Germanic general named Odoacer deposed the teenage emperor Romulus Augustulus and sent the imperial regalia off to Constantinople. The western Roman empire was over. Simplicius's letters hardly notice. As far as the Church was concerned, there was still an emperor, and he lived in Constantinople.

That emperor was the real problem. Constantinople claimed to rank as high as Rome, and Simplicius refused to accept it. In Egypt and Syria many Christians rejected the Council of Chalcedon's teaching on Christ, and the patriarch Acacius of Constantinople seemed happy to deal with them. Simplicius protested again and again. At home he dedicated the great round church of Santo Stefano Rotondo on the Caelian Hill, which still stands.
When he died in 483, Odoacer's chief minister Basilius stepped in. He claimed that the late pope had asked for the king's man to be consulted on the next election, and laid down rules for it.

claims.text: The fall of the western empire in 476 goes almost unmentioned in Simplicius's surviving letters.
claims.note: Historians often point this out. To churchmen in Rome, the emperor in Constantinople was still the emperor.

claims.text: Simplicius dedicated Santo Stefano Rotondo on the Caelian Hill.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis credits him with it, and the building dates fit.

claims.text: Simplicius asked on his deathbed that Odoacer's minister oversee the election.
claims.note: Only Basilius said so. A Roman synod of 502 threw out his decree as a lay intrusion.

reigns.hook: Simplicius is dead, and Odoacer's court is watching the election. The man Rome picks is a nobleman who will pick a fight with Constantinople that lasts 35 years.

reigns.tagline: The nobleman who cut Rome off from the East
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Roman priest of a noble family
reigns.previously: Simplicius dies. Odoacer's minister wants a say in the next pope.
paragraphs: Felix came from an old Roman family, the son of a priest. He had been married and had children before he was ordained; his wife had died. His great-great-grandson would be Gregory the Great. Popes before the Middle Ages were often family men like this, and nobody thought it odd.

In 482 Emperor Zeno issued the Henotikon, a statement of faith meant to win back Christians who rejected the Council of Chalcedon. Rome saw it as a sell-out. Felix sent envoys to Constantinople, but they were bullied into worshipping with the patriarch Acacius. Felix sacked them, and in July 484 a Roman synod excommunicated Acacius himself. Acacius struck the pope's name from his prayers. The split between Rome and Constantinople, the Acacian schism, would last until 519.
Felix's sharpest letters were probably drafted by a clever cleric on his staff called Gelasius.

claims.text: Felix III was the great-great-grandfather of Pope Gregory the Great.
claims.note: Gregory himself calls Felix his ancestor in his writings.

claims.text: Monks smuggled the excommunication into Hagia Sophia and pinned it to Acacius's robes during a service.
claims.note: A colourful story told in later accounts; nobody at the time describes it.

claims.text: He is called Felix III, though there were only two popes Felix before him.
claims.note: The count includes Felix II, a 4th-century antipope, so some lists call him Felix II.

reigns.hook: Felix dies with East and West no longer speaking. His right-hand man takes over, and he is about to tell the emperor exactly who outranks whom.

reigns.tagline: Two powers rule the world, and the bishops' is heavier
reigns.cameToPower: Elected as soon as Felix died
reigns.previously: Felix III dies, still at war with the Church of Constantinople.
paragraphs: Gelasius was born in Rome to a family from Roman Africa, and he was the best writer the papacy had yet had. Under Felix he had drafted the letters. As pope he signed them. Italy changed hands under him: in 493 Theodoric the Ostrogoth took Ravenna and killed Odoacer with his own sword at a banquet. Gelasius got on well with the new Gothic king.

With Emperor Anastasius I he was far less polite. In 494 he wrote that the world is ruled by two powers, the sacred authority of bishops and royal power, and that the bishops' carries more weight because they answer to God even for kings. He also scolded Roman senators who still kept up the Lupercalia, an old pagan festival where young men ran through the streets in goatskins. In a time of famine he fed the poor, and they loved him for it.

claims.text: Gelasius told the emperor that priestly authority outweighs royal power.
claims.note: His letter to Anastasius I of 494, opening 'Duo sunt', survives and became a key text of medieval politics.

claims.text: He wrote against senators who wanted to keep the Lupercalia.
claims.note: His treatise against the senator Andromachus survives; the festival's end is not dated.

claims.text: He drew up the official list of books Christians should and shouldn't read.
claims.note: The 'Gelasian Decree' carries his name, but scholars think it was compiled in the 6th century, after his death.

reigns.hook: Gelasius dies after under five years. The next pope wants to make up with Constantinople, and plenty of Romans will never forgive him for trying.

reigns.tagline: The peacemaker Dante put in hell
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Roman cleric, son of a priest
reigns.cameToPower: Elected three days after Gelasius died
reigns.previously: Gelasius dies, having told the emperor that bishops outrank him.
paragraphs: Anastasius was a Roman, the son of a priest named Peter, and he wanted peace with the East. He wrote a friendly letter to the emperor, who happened to share his name, and sent envoys to talk. He even welcomed a deacon from Thessalonica who was in communion with the condemned Acacius's party. To many of the Roman clergy this was betrayal. Some of them stopped worshipping with their own pope.

He was pope for under two years and died suddenly in November 498. The Liber Pontificalis, written by his enemies' side, says he was struck down by the will of God. The smear stuck. Medieval writers muddled him up with his namesake, the emperor, and believed he had been a heretic. Dante put him in hell, in a burning tomb among the heretics, in the eleventh canto of the Inferno.

claims.text: Dante placed Pope Anastasius II among the heretics in hell.
claims.note: Inferno, canto 11. The charge rests on a medieval mix-up of the pope with Emperor Anastasius I.

claims.text: Anastasius died 'by the will of God' as punishment for his softness.
claims.note: That is the hostile verdict of the Liber Pontificalis, written by the party that opposed him.

claims.text: He wrote to congratulate Clovis, king of the Franks, on his baptism.
claims.note: The letter appeared in the 17th century, published by Jérôme Vignier, and is now regarded as one of his forgeries.

reigns.hook: Anastasius's death leaves the Roman clergy split down the middle. On the same day, two rival factions in two different churches will each crown their own pope.

reigns.tagline: Two popes, one city, and years of street fighting
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Roman deacon; no tie to Anastasius
reigns.previously: Anastasius II dies suddenly, and the Roman clergy split in two.
paragraphs: Symmachus was born a pagan in Sardinia and baptised in Rome. On 22 November 498 most of the clergy elected him pope in the Lateran, while a smaller party, backed by rich senators, elected the archpriest Laurentius at Santa Maria Maggiore. Both sides went to Theodoric, the Arian Gothic king, at Ravenna. He ruled that whoever was chosen first and by more votes should have the job: Symmachus.

That didn't settle it. In 501 his enemies accused him of celebrating Easter on the wrong date, misusing church property and keeping women. Laurentius came back, and for years the two factions fought in the streets, and priests were killed. A synod in 501 refused to put Symmachus on trial at all. His supporters backed this up with forged old documents claiming that 'the first see is judged by no one'.
Theodoric finally ordered the churches handed back to Symmachus in 506. He ruled for another eight years.

claims.text: Symmachus's supporters forged documents to prove that no one could put a pope on trial.
claims.note: The 'Symmachan forgeries' are fake records of earlier popes and councils; historians agree they were written in his circle.

claims.text: Symmachus was guilty of the charges brought against him in 501.
claims.note: Only his enemies' version, the Laurentian Fragment, says so. The synod declined to judge him.

claims.text: He was born a pagan.
claims.note: Only the Liber Pontificalis tradition, compiled decades later, says he was a Sardinian baptised in Rome; no contemporary confirms it.

reigns.hook: Symmachus dies with the East still cut off. His successor is a married deacon with a son, and the emperor in Constantinople is about to need friends badly.

reigns.tagline: The deacon who brought the East back to Rome
reigns.cameToPower: Elected the day after Symmachus died
reigns.previously: Symmachus dies after 16 years of feuding with his rival's party.
paragraphs: Hormisdas came from Frosinone, south-east of Rome. He had been married before he was ordained, and his son Silverius would one day be pope too. A loyal deacon to Symmachus, he set out to heal the split with the East on Rome's terms.

Emperor Anastasius I, facing a revolt in the Balkans, asked for talks in 515. Hormisdas sent envoys with a statement of faith for the eastern bishops to sign. The emperor tried to bribe them, then sent them home. Then Anastasius died in 518, and the new emperor Justin I wanted unity. On 28 March 519 the patriarch of Constantinople signed the Formula of Hormisdas, which said the faith had always been kept pure in the Roman see. The 35-year schism was over.

claims.text: The patriarch of Constantinople signed the Formula of Hormisdas in 519.
claims.note: The text and the reports of the papal envoys survive in a 6th-century collection of papal letters.

claims.text: Hormisdas was the father of Pope Silverius.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis says so. Hormisdas had married before he was ordained.

claims.text: Emperor Anastasius sent the papal envoys home on a leaky ship and banned them from landing.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis tells it this way; it may be dressing up a frosty send-off.

reigns.hook: Hormisdas dies with East and West at peace. But the new emperor is persecuting Arian Christians, and in Ravenna the Arian King Theodoric is beginning to suspect Rome.

reigns.tagline: The first pope in Constantinople died in a Gothic jail
reigns.previously: Hormisdas dies, having brought the eastern Church back to Rome.
paragraphs: John was old and sick when he became pope. By 525 Theodoric was in a black mood. He believed Roman senators were plotting with Constantinople, and had the great scholar Boethius executed. In the East, Emperor Justin was closing Arian churches. Theodoric, an Arian himself, sent John to Constantinople at the head of a delegation of bishops and senators to demand that the persecution stop.

No pope had ever been to Constantinople. The city gave him a hero's welcome, the emperor bowed before him, and he said Easter Mass in Hagia Sophia in Latin, in the place of honour. Justin agreed to most of Theodoric's demands but refused to let converts go back to Arianism. Theodoric decided John had failed him and threw him into prison at Ravenna. He died there in May 526, and the Romans honoured him as a martyr.

claims.text: A hermit saw the soul of Theodoric thrown into a volcano by Pope John and the senator Symmachus.
claims.note: Told by Gregory the Great in his Dialogues about 70 years later; Theodoric died in August 526, three months after John.

claims.text: Pope John I was the deacon John to whom Boethius dedicated his theological essays.
claims.note: The name and dates fit, but John was a very common name and there is no proof.

claims.text: Theodoric deliberately starved him to death.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis treats him as a martyr; how exactly he died in custody is not known.

reigns.hook: John is dead in a Gothic prison, and Theodoric doesn't trust the Roman clergy to replace him. This time the king picks the pope himself.

reigns.tagline: The Goths' pope who picked his own heir
reigns.previously: John I dies in a Gothic prison. Theodoric wants a pope he can trust.
paragraphs: Felix came from Samnium in southern Italy, and he owed his job to Theodoric, who forced him on the Romans after nearly two months of argument. Seven weeks later the old king was dead. His daughter Amalasuntha ruled for her young son Athalaric, and she treated the Church kindly. Felix stayed close to the Gothic court.

The Gothic regime gave him an old public building on the edge of the Roman Forum, and he turned it into the church of Santi Cosma e Damiano. Its apse mosaic, one of the finest in Rome, still shows him holding a model of the church, though the figure was heavily restored in the 17th century. He also sent rulings on grace and free will to Bishop Caesarius of Arles, which shaped the Council of Orange in 529.
Falling ill in 530, Felix did something new. He handed his pallium to his archdeacon Boniface and declared him his successor.

claims.text: Felix's portrait survives in the apse mosaic of Santi Cosma e Damiano.
claims.note: The figure is there, but most of it was redone in the 1600s, so the face isn't original.

claims.text: On his deathbed Felix named Boniface as his successor.
claims.note: His decree survives; the Roman senate promptly banned any discussion of a successor while a pope was alive.

reigns.hook: Felix's chosen heir is a Roman with a Gothic father. Most of the clergy refuse to accept him, and on the same day they elect a pope of their own.

reigns.tagline: The first pope with a Gothic father
reigns.cameToPower: Named heir by the dying Felix IV
reigns.previously: Felix IV dies, having named his own successor on his deathbed.
paragraphs: Boniface was born in Rome, but his father Sigibuld was a Goth, a first for a pope. Felix's choice of him was unpopular. On the day Felix died, most of the clergy elected the deacon Dioscorus, a Greek from Alexandria. Rome had two popes again, but only for three weeks: Dioscorus died in October 530. Boniface made the dead man's supporters sign a curse on his memory and filed it in the archives.

Then he tried to pull Felix's trick himself. At a synod in St Peter's he made the clergy sign a decree naming the deacon Vigilius as his heir. The outcry was huge, and at a second synod Boniface admitted it was against the rules and burned the decree in front of everyone. In 531 he approved the Council of Orange's teaching on grace. He died in October 532.

claims.text: Boniface II was the first pope of Germanic descent.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis names his father as Sigibuld, a Gothic name.

claims.text: He burned his own decree naming Vigilius as his successor.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis records both the decree and its public burning.

reigns.hook: Boniface dies, and Rome goes more than two months without a pope. Votes are being bought, and church silver is being sold to pay for them. The Gothic king has had enough.

reigns.tagline: The first pope to change his name
reigns.previously: Boniface II dies. The papacy goes on sale for over two months.
paragraphs: The vacancy after Boniface was a scandal. Candidates promised money, and some clergy pawned church treasures to pay for votes. King Athalaric issued an edict against it, capping what could be spent and ordering the rules carved in marble outside St Peter's. When the dust settled, the winner was a priest from the church of San Clemente called Mercurius.

Mercurius was the name of a pagan god, which seemed wrong for a pope, so he called himself John. Changing names only became the normal thing for popes centuries later. Far away, Justinian was now emperor, and his general Belisarius conquered Vandal Africa in 533 and 534. Justinian sent John a statement of faith and asked him to approve it. John did. Justinian's armies would soon look north, at Italy.

claims.text: John II was the first pope to take a new name, because his own was a pagan god's.
claims.note: Inscriptions at San Clemente name him as the priest Mercurius, and he signed as John.

claims.text: King Athalaric legislated against bribery in papal elections.
claims.note: His letter to the pope survives in the Variae of Cassiodorus, his minister.

reigns.hook: John dies as Justinian's armies finish off Vandal Africa. Italy is next on the list, and the Gothic king is going to send the new pope east to stop a war.

reigns.relationToPredecessor: Archdeacon; son of a slain priest
reigns.cameToPower: Elected five days after John II died
reigns.previously: John II dies, as Justinian's general conquers Vandal Africa.
paragraphs: Agapetus was a Roman archdeacon whose father, a priest named Gordianus, had been killed in the street battles under Symmachus. His first act as pope was to burn, in public, Boniface II's curse on the dead rival Dioscorus. He was a bookish man who planned a Christian school in Rome with Cassiodorus.

War came in 535. Belisarius took Sicily, and the Gothic king Theodahad sent Agapetus to Constantinople to stop the invasion. The pope had to pawn church plate to pay for the trip. Justinian wouldn't budge. But Agapetus found Anthimus, a man the Romans considered a heretic, sitting as patriarch of Constantinople with Empress Theodora's backing. Agapetus had him deposed and consecrated a new patriarch, Menas, himself. In April 536 he fell ill and died there.

claims.text: Agapetus told Justinian he had come to see a Christian emperor and found a Diocletian.
claims.note: Told by later Rome-friendly sources, comparing Justinian to the great persecutor; no neutral witness reports it.

claims.text: He pawned the church's sacred vessels to pay for his journey.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis records it, and it fits Theodahad's demand that the pope pay his own way.

claims.text: Agapetus personally consecrated Menas as patriarch of Constantinople in 536.
claims.note: The acts of the synod held in Constantinople that year record it.

reigns.hook: Agapetus dies far from home. Theodahad doesn't wait to hear what the clergy think. He has a pope in mind already: the son of a pope.

reigns.tagline: A pope's son, deposed by a general's wife
reigns.previously: Agapetus I dies in Constantinople, his mission a failure.
paragraphs: Silverius was only a subdeacon, the son of Pope Hormisdas, when Theodahad forced him on the Romans in June 536. Within months his patron was gone, killed by his own Goths. In December the pope advised the Romans to open their gates, and Belisarius marched in for Justinian. The Goths came back in force and besieged Rome in March 537.

Silverius had an enemy he never saw. Empress Theodora wanted the papacy for the deacon Vigilius, who had promised to bring back her deposed patriarch. Letters turned up saying Silverius had offered to let the Goths in by a city gate. Belisarius called him to his headquarters on the Pincian Hill, where he was stripped of his pallium, dressed as a monk and declared deposed. Vigilius was consecrated within weeks.
Silverius was shipped to Lycia, then dragged back and dumped on the island of Palmarola, where he died in December 537.

claims.text: The letters proving Silverius had plotted with the Goths were forged.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis and Liberatus of Carthage say so; the deposition clearly suited Theodora.

claims.text: Belisarius's wife Antonina arranged the deposition, and later his murder.
claims.note: Procopius says so in his Secret History, a book written to blacken Justinian's court.

claims.text: Silverius starved to death on Palmarola.
claims.note: Liberatus says he died of hunger; other accounts say he was killed, and some lists date his death to June 537.

reigns.hook: Silverius is gone, and Theodora's man is pope. Vigilius got the job by promising things. Now the empress wants paying, and Justinian wants a pope who signs what he's told.

reigns.tagline: The empress's pope, kidnapped by her husband
reigns.previously: Silverius is deposed and exiled, and dies a prisoner on Palmarola.
paragraphs: Vigilius was a Roman aristocrat and a deacon who badly wanted the top job. Pope Boniface II had once named him as heir, then backed down. Posted to Constantinople, he made a friend of Empress Theodora. In March 537 Belisarius, holding Rome for Justinian, deposed Pope Silverius as a Gothic spy, and Vigilius was consecrated in his place. Silverius died in exile on Palmarola that December.

Then Theodora's favour turned into Justinian's grip. The emperor wanted the West to condemn the Three Chapters, writings he thought would win back Christians who rejected the Council of Chalcedon. In November 545 imperial agents seized Vigilius in Rome and hauled him east. In Constantinople he agreed, retracted, hid in a church and was dragged from the altar by his legs, then fled across the water to Chalcedon.

In 553 Justinian held a council without him and struck his name from the church prayers. By the end of the year Vigilius gave in and signed. Allowed home in 555, he got as far as Syracuse and died there, ten years after leaving Rome.

claims.text: Vigilius promised Theodora he would go soft on Christians who rejected Chalcedon, in return for the papacy.
claims.note: Liberatus of Carthage and Procopius tell versions of the deal. Both were hostile, and Vigilius never actually delivered it.

claims.text: Silverius was starved to death on Palmarola by Vigilius's men.
claims.note: Liberatus says so. Procopius's Secret History blames Belisarius's wife Antonina, acting for Theodora. Nobody knows for sure.

claims.text: Imperial soldiers dragged Vigilius from the altar of a Constantinople church so hard that the altar came down.
claims.note: Described in a letter from Italian clergy who were in the city in 552, and in Vigilius's own complaint against the emperor.

reigns.hook: Vigilius dies on the way home. Justinian already has the next pope picked: Pelagius, the deacon who stood beside him in Constantinople, and whom half of Rome suspects of wanting him dead.

reigns.tagline: Justinian's man swore on the Gospels he hadn't done it
reigns.previously: Vigilius dies at Syracuse on his way home after ten years away.
paragraphs: Pelagius came from a rich Roman family and knew how to handle a crisis. When the Gothic king Totila took Rome in 546, Pelagius spent his own money feeding the starving and talked Totila out of a massacre. In Constantinople he wrote in defence of the Three Chapters and went to prison for it. Then he changed his mind. Justinian liked the new Pelagius and sent him home as pope.

Rome hated the idea. People said he had hastened Vigilius's death, and only two bishops would consecrate him, with a priest from Ostia standing in for the third. So Pelagius walked in procession to St Peter's and, holding the Gospels and the cross over his head, swore he had done Vigilius no harm.

He put the war-wrecked city back on its feet, sorting out the Church's estates and, with the general Narses, building the church of the Holy Apostles. But Milan and Aquileia refused to accept the council of 553 and broke with Rome. He died in March 561 with that split unhealed.

claims.text: Pelagius publicly swore in St Peter's that he had not harmed Vigilius.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis describes the oath, and Pelagius's own letters show how much he worried about his reputation.

claims.text: Pelagius had a hand in Vigilius's death.
claims.note: Only rumour, reported by his enemies. Vigilius died of gallstones far away in Sicily, and no source names a plot.

claims.text: Totila spared Rome's people because Pelagius begged him to.
claims.note: Procopius, who was writing in Constantinople at the time, tells of Pelagius pleading with the king after the city fell.

reigns.hook: Pelagius dies with the bishops of the north still refusing to pray for him. Rome picks a Roman nobleman's son, and within a few years a new people will pour over the Alps.

reigns.tagline: The pope who hid in a catacomb as the Lombards came
reigns.previously: Pelagius I dies, with northern Italy still refusing to pray with him.
paragraphs: John was born Catelinus, the son of a high-ranking Roman official. Very little of his paperwork survives, and the reason is plain: Italy was falling apart again. In 568 the Lombards under King Alboin crossed the Alps with their families and herds. Within a few years they held most of the north, and Constantinople, busy with Persia, sent almost nothing.

Rome's protector was the old general Narses, and the Romans couldn't stand him. They complained to the emperor that they had been better off under the Goths. John went to Naples to coax Narses back to Rome, which made the Romans furious. So the pope moved out to the catacomb of Praetextatus on the Appian Way and ran the Church from there, even consecrating bishops, until Narses died.
He still had reach. Two bishops deposed in Gaul appealed to him, and he ordered them restored. He finished Pelagius's church of the Holy Apostles. He died in July 574.

claims.text: Narses, sacked by the emperor, invited the Lombards into Italy out of spite.
claims.note: Paul the Deacon tells it two centuries later, along with a story that the empress mocked him as fit only to spin wool with the women. Most historians reject it.

claims.text: John lived in a catacomb on the Appian Way to avoid the Romans.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis, written within living memory, says so.

claims.text: John restored two Gallic bishops, Salonius and Sagittarius, after they appealed to Rome.
claims.note: Gregory of Tours, who knew the pair and thought them crooks, tells the story in his History of the Franks.

reigns.hook: John dies with Lombards loose across Italy. His successor will be elected quickly, then left waiting the best part of a year, because no messenger can get through to the emperor.

reigns.tagline: A year's wait for permission, then famine and siege
reigns.previously: John III dies. The Lombards now hold half of Italy.
paragraphs: Benedict was a Roman, the son of a man named Boniface. The Greeks called him Bonosus. Electing him was the easy part. A new pope still needed the emperor's approval before he could be consecrated, and the Lombards had cut the roads. It took almost eleven months for the go-ahead to come back from Constantinople.

Then Rome went hungry. The Lombards raided up to the walls and the fields went untilled. Emperor Justin II sent grain ships from Egypt, and they saved the city for a while. Benedict kept the Church running through it all, ordaining priests and naming bishops for towns the Lombards had wrecked.
In the summer of 579 the Lombards closed in and laid siege to Rome itself. Benedict died on 30 July with the enemy outside, and was buried in St Peter's.

claims.text: Justin II sent grain from Egypt to save Rome from famine.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis records it in Benedict's life.

claims.text: Benedict made the future Gregory the Great one of Rome's seven deacons.
claims.note: Gregory became a deacon about 578 or 579. Sources disagree whether Benedict or his successor ordained him.

claims.text: Eastern writers knew him as Bonosus.
claims.note: Greek writers of the time use the name Bonosus for him; it is close in meaning to Benedict.

reigns.hook: Benedict dies with Lombards camped outside. The clergy can't wait a year this time. They choose a Roman with a Gothic father and consecrate him at once, without asking Constantinople.

reigns.tagline: Floods, a dragon in the Tiber, and then the plague
reigns.previously: Benedict I dies with the Lombards at the gates of Rome.
paragraphs: Pelagius was Roman-born, but his father had a Gothic name, Unigild. He was consecrated in the middle of the Lombard siege, without waiting for the emperor, and then had to send an apology east. His envoy was a clever deacon named Gregory, the former city prefect, who spent years in Constantinople begging for troops. The emperor sent money and advice: bribe the Lombards, or hire the Franks.

Pelagius tried both. He wrote to the Frankish bishops for help, and around 584 the emperor put a military governor, the exarch, in Ravenna. Pelagius also picked a fight with the patriarch of Constantinople for calling himself the Ecumenical Patriarch. He rebuilt the church of San Lorenzo outside the walls, and its mosaic still shows him holding a model of it.
In late 589 the Tiber burst its banks. Plague followed. Pelagius was among the first to die, on 7 February 590.

claims.text: Pelagius was one of the first victims of the plague of 590.
claims.note: Gregory of Tours heard it from a deacon of his who was in Rome at the time.

claims.text: The 589 flood carried a great dragon and many snakes down the Tiber to the sea.
claims.note: Gregory of Tours reports it as told to him. It reads like an omen story, probably dead animals and debris.

claims.text: Pelagius refused to let the patriarch of Constantinople call himself 'ecumenical'.
claims.note: Gregory the Great's letters refer back to Pelagius's protest and continue it.

reigns.hook: Pelagius dies of the plague. Rome needs a new pope fast, and every eye turns to his deacon Gregory, the rich former prefect who only wants to be a monk.

reigns.tagline: The monk who fed Rome and sent a mission to England
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Deacon and envoy of Pelagius II
reigns.previously: Plague kills Pelagius II. The Lombards are closing in on Rome.
paragraphs: Gregory came from an old, rich Roman family and was prefect of the city, its top civil official, by his early thirties. Then he gave it all up. He turned his family's house on the Caelian Hill into a monastery and became a monk. Popes kept hauling him back out, first as a deacon, then as their envoy in Constantinople. In 590 the Romans chose him as pope. He tried to wriggle out of it, but the emperor confirmed the election.

He turned out to be brilliant at the job. With no help from Constantinople, he fed Rome from the Church's estates, paid soldiers and bargained with the Lombards himself. He wrote a handbook for bishops that was read for centuries. In 596 he sent the monk Augustine and a band of about 40 companions to convert the pagan English. Augustine baptised King Æthelberht of Kent and became the first archbishop of Canterbury.

Gregory called himself 'servant of the servants of God', a title popes still use. He was often ill with gout and stomach trouble, and he died in March 604. The Church counts him among the four great doctors of the Latin West.

claims.text: Seeing fair-haired English slave boys for sale in Rome, Gregory punned that they were angels, not Angles.
claims.note: Bede tells the story more than a century later, borrowing it from an earlier Life of Gregory written in England.

claims.text: Gregory composed or collected Gregorian chant.
claims.note: The chant took shape in the 8th and 9th centuries; the Franks credited it to Gregory to give it prestige.

claims.text: Gregory sent Augustine to England in 596.
claims.note: Gregory's own letters about the mission survive in his Register, and Bede copied several of them.

reigns.hook: Gregory leaves a city that runs on Church grain. His successor, his old envoy Sabinian, will sell that grain in a famine instead of handing it out, and the Romans will never forgive him.

reigns.tagline: He sold the grain Gregory used to give away
reigns.previously: Gregory the Great dies, having fed Rome from the Church's estates.
paragraphs: Sabinian came from Blera, near Viterbo. Gregory had trusted him enough to send him to Constantinople as his envoy. After Gregory died in March 604, Rome waited six months for Emperor Phocas to approve his election.

Then famine hit, and Sabinian made himself the most hated man in Rome. Gregory had handed out the Church's grain free. Sabinian opened the granaries and sold it. Gregory's admirers never forgave him, and the stories grew. He was also said to favour ordinary clergy over the monks Gregory had promoted.
He died in February 606, after about 17 months. The tale goes that his funeral procession had to leave the city by a side gate and loop round to St Peter's to dodge the crowds.

claims.text: Sabinian sold the Church's grain during a famine instead of giving it away.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis reports the sale. It may have been sensible rationing in a shortage, recast as greed by Gregory's fans.

claims.text: His funeral had to detour outside the walls to avoid angry Romans.
claims.note: Only in later accounts; it fits too neatly with the grain story.

claims.text: Gregory's ghost appeared to him three times to rebuke him, and finally struck him on the head, and he died.
claims.note: A much later story, told to show Gregory's goodness against Sabinian's meanness.

reigns.hook: Sabinian dies unloved. The next pope also served as envoy in Constantinople, and he is on very good terms with Phocas, the emperor who murdered his way to the throne.

reigns.tagline: Nine months, and an emperor's word that Rome came first
reigns.previously: Sabinian dies, hated by Romans who blame him for their hunger.
paragraphs: Boniface was a Roman of Greek descent. Gregory had sent him to Constantinople in 603 as his envoy, and there he made friends with Emperor Phocas, a junior officer who had seized the throne in 602 and had the old emperor Maurice and his sons killed. After Sabinian died, Rome waited almost a year before Boniface could be consecrated.

He cashed in his friendship. Phocas issued a decree that the see of St Peter in Rome was the head of all the churches. It was a slap at the patriarch of Constantinople, who had taken to calling himself 'ecumenical'. Back home, Boniface held a synod that banned anyone from discussing who the next pope should be while the current one was alive, or until three days after his burial.
Then he died, on 12 November 607, before he could make much more of it.

claims.text: Phocas declared the Roman church the head of all churches.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis records the decree. It settled nothing; Constantinople's patriarchs kept their title.

claims.text: Boniface banned election campaigns while a pope was still alive.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis reports the synod's ruling and the three-day rule.

reigns.hook: Boniface III is gone within the year. The next pope is a doctor's son from the Abruzzi hills, and Phocas has a spectacular gift lined up for him: an ancient temple.

reigns.tagline: The pope who turned the Pantheon into a church
reigns.previously: Boniface III dies after nine months, Phocas's friend in Rome.
paragraphs: Boniface came from the Marsi country in the Abruzzi, the son of a doctor named John. Under Gregory he had run the Church's finances. He wanted the monks' way of life, and as pope turned his own house into a monastery. His reign had a grim backdrop of famine, plague and floods.

His great prize was the Pantheon. Phocas gave him the old temple of all the gods, and in 609 Boniface dedicated it to the Virgin and all the martyrs, as Santa Maria ad Martyres. It was one of the first pagan temples in Rome made into a church, and that is why it survives so well. In 610 he held a synod attended by Mellitus, the first bishop of London, who took its decisions back to England.
The Irish monk Columbanus wrote him a blunt letter urging him to clear Rome of suspected heresy. Boniface died in May 615.

claims.text: Boniface IV made the Pantheon a church in 609.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis and Bede both record the emperor's gift and the dedication.

claims.text: Twenty-eight cartloads of martyrs' bones were brought from the catacombs to the Pantheon.
claims.note: The number comes from much later tradition. Relics were moved in, but the count is not in early sources.

claims.text: Columbanus wrote to Boniface telling him to prove Rome's orthodoxy over the Three Chapters.
claims.note: The letter survives among Columbanus's writings, written from northern Italy about 613.

reigns.hook: Boniface IV dies. Rome's choice falls on an old Roman priest who thinks the monks have had it too good, just as earthquake and disease are about to strike.

reigns.tagline: The clergy's pope, in a time of quake and plague
reigns.previously: Boniface IV, who made the Pantheon a church, dies.
paragraphs: He is also known as Deusdedit, 'God has given'. He was a Roman, the son of a subdeacon, and a veteran priest of the city. After Boniface IV, a monk at heart, he swung the other way, favouring the ordinary clergy and giving them back jobs Gregory had handed to monks.

Italy was in turmoil. The exarch at Ravenna was murdered, and a rebel took Naples. The new exarch, Eleutherius, crushed the trouble and stopped in Rome, where Deusdedit received him. Then, in 618, an earthquake shook the city, and a disease that covered people in sores followed. The pope is said to have visited the sick himself.
He died in November 618 and left money to every one of his clergy in his will.

claims.text: His is the oldest surviving lead seal of a pope.
claims.note: It is often cited as the earliest papal lead seal known. Earlier popes probably used seals too, but none survive to compare.

claims.text: Earthquake and an outbreak of a skin disease struck Rome in his last year.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis records both.

claims.text: Deusdedit kissed and cured lepers.
claims.note: Later saints' lives turn his care for the sick into miracle stories.

reigns.hook: Deusdedit dies. Rome waits over a year for approval of his successor, a Neapolitan, while the exarch who just restored order decides he would like to be emperor himself.

reigns.tagline: The Neapolitan who wrote to a pagan king
reigns.previously: Deusdedit dies after plague, earthquake and a rebellion.
paragraphs: Boniface came from Naples. He was not consecrated until December 619, more than a year after Deusdedit died. That year the exarch Eleutherius declared himself emperor and set out for Rome to be crowned, until his own soldiers killed him on the way.

Boniface ruled that anyone who fled into a church could not be dragged out, making churches places of refuge. He looked north to England, where Gregory's mission was still clinging on. He sent the pallium to Justus, the new archbishop of Canterbury.

He also wrote to King Edwin of Northumbria, a pagan, urging him to become a Christian, and to his queen, Æthelburh, a Christian princess of Kent, telling her to work on her husband. Boniface died in October 625, two years before Edwin was baptised.

claims.text: Boniface wrote to King Edwin and Queen Æthelburh urging Edwin's conversion.
claims.note: Bede copied both letters into his history, and scholars accept them as genuine.

claims.text: The exarch Eleutherius tried to make himself emperor in 619 and was killed by his troops.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis reports the revolt and his death on the road to Rome.

claims.text: Boniface made churches places of asylum.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis lists it among his rulings.

reigns.hook: Boniface V dies. Within two days Rome has chosen a rich nobleman who will put a bronze roof on St Peter's and a fateful phrase about Christ's will into a letter.

reigns.tagline: A brilliant pope, damned as a heretic after he died
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Chosen two days after Boniface died
reigns.previously: Boniface V dies, having written to the pagan king of Northumbria.
paragraphs: Honorius was a rich nobleman from Campania, the son of a consul, and a fan of Gregory the Great. He had money and taste. With Emperor Heraclius's permission he stripped the gilded bronze tiles off the old Temple of Venus and Rome and put them on St Peter's. He built Sant'Agnese outside the walls, where his portrait in mosaic still stands. He sent Birinus to convert Wessex.

Then came the letter. Patriarch Sergius of Constantinople wanted to end a long row over Christ's nature by saying Christ had one will. Honorius replied, around 634, agreeing to the words 'one will'. He probably meant only that Christ's human will never fought his divine one, but he had signed up to a slogan.
He died in October 638. In 681 a council in Constantinople condemned him by name as a heretic, and later popes accepted it.

claims.text: A church council condemned Honorius as a heretic in 681.
claims.note: The acts of the Third Council of Constantinople name him, and Pope Leo II confirmed the verdict.

claims.text: Honorius moved bronze roof tiles from a pagan temple to St Peter's.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis records it, with the emperor's permission.

claims.text: Honorius was never truly a heretic, only careless with words.
claims.note: His successor John IV argued so at once. In 1870 opponents of papal infallibility cited the case against it.

reigns.hook: Honorius dies just as Heraclius publishes his 'one will' decree. The next pope is elected within days, then left waiting a year and a half for approval that comes at a price.

reigns.tagline: Kept waiting 19 months, then dead in two
reigns.previously: Honorius dies, leaving a fine new roof and a dangerous letter.
paragraphs: Severinus, a Roman, was elected in October 638, a few days after Honorius died. Then nothing happened. Emperor Heraclius had just issued his decree that Christ had one will, and he wanted the new pope to sign it before he would approve him. Rome's envoys spent a year and a half in Constantinople before they got the approval, apparently by promising to show the decree to the pope.

Meanwhile Rome was robbed. An imperial official named Maurice stirred up the garrison over unpaid wages, telling them the pope was sitting on a fortune. The soldiers besieged the Lateran palace for three days. Then the exarch Isaac arrived, sealed the treasury, and stripped it, sending part of the loot to the emperor.
Severinus was finally consecrated in May 640, already an old man. He died two months later, on 2 August.

claims.text: Imperial troops looted the papal treasury at the Lateran while Severinus waited.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis describes the siege and the plunder in detail.

claims.text: Severinus condemned the 'one will' teaching.
claims.note: Some later sources say so, but he reigned only two months, and the clear condemnation came from his successor.

reigns.hook: Severinus dies. The next pope is a Dalmatian, and he has two jobs: condemn the emperor's 'one will' decree, and defend Honorius, who signed up to it.

reigns.tagline: The Dalmatian who ransomed his people and saved Honorius
reigns.previously: Severinus dies after two months, his treasury already looted.
paragraphs: John came from Dalmatia, on the Adriatic, the son of a lawyer named Venantius, and was archdeacon of Rome. Within weeks of his consecration he held a synod in Rome that condemned the emperor's 'one will' teaching. He then wrote to the new emperor defending Honorius: the old pope had only meant that Christ had no sinful human will at war with God's.

His homeland was being overrun by Slav and Avar raiders, and Christians were being carried off. John sent an abbot named Martin with plenty of money to buy back captives, and to bring home the relics of Dalmatian martyrs.
He built a chapel for those relics beside the Lateran baptistery, dedicated to St Venantius, and covered it in mosaic. He died in October 642 before it was finished.

claims.text: John IV defended Honorius in a letter to the emperor.
claims.note: His letter, known as the Apology for Pope Honorius, survives.

claims.text: Heraclius, near death, told John he had not written the 'one will' decree himself.
claims.note: John reports it, and Heraclius blamed the late patriarch Sergius. It suited both men to shift the blame.

claims.text: John paid to ransom captives from raids in Dalmatia and Istria.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis describes the mission of Abbot Martin.

reigns.hook: John dies with his chapel half done. His successor will finish it: a Greek born in Jerusalem, son of a bishop, driven west by the Arab conquest and ready to fight the 'one will' doctrine harder still.

images.caption: A painting of about 1,000 years after his death; the only likeness of him from his own time is in the San Venanzio chapel mosaic.
images.alt: Painted portrait of Pope John IV

reigns.tagline: The Jerusalem-born pope who took on two patriarchs
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected; no kin of John IV
reigns.previously: John IV dies after defending dead Pope Honorius's good name.
paragraphs: Theodore was a Greek, born in Jerusalem, the son of a bishop also called Theodore. His family was one of many that had fled to the West as the Arab armies swept through Palestine. In Rome he stepped straight into the great quarrel of the day: whether Christ had one will or two. The emperors backed 'one will' as a peace formula for the East. Rome said that was heresy.

Theodore refused to recognise the new patriarch of Constantinople, Paul II, and went after the old one, Pyrrhus. In 645 Pyrrhus lost a public debate to the monk Maximus the Confessor, came to Rome and recanted, and Theodore received him with honour. Then Pyrrhus went to Ravenna and switched back. Theodore excommunicated him in 648.

That same year Emperor Constans II issued the Typos, a decree banning all talk of wills in Christ, one or two. Theodore planned to fight it but died in May 649 before he could. The job fell to his successor.

claims.text: Theodore signed Pyrrhus's excommunication in ink mixed with consecrated wine from the chalice.
claims.note: The story is told by the Byzantine chronicler Theophanes, writing about 160 years later. No Roman source mentions it.

claims.text: Theodore's father was a bishop from Jerusalem.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis, Rome's own record of the popes, gives his birthplace and his father's office.

reigns.hook: Theodore is dead and the emperor's gag order stands. The next pope is a man from Todi who knows Constantinople well, and he is not going to wait for anyone's permission.

reigns.tagline: The pope the emperor dragged away in chains
reigns.cameToPower: Elected; didn't wait for the emperor
reigns.previously: Theodore I dies before he can answer the emperor's gag order.
paragraphs: Martin came from Todi in Umbria and had served as the pope's envoy in Constantinople, so he knew exactly whom he was defying. He had himself consecrated without asking the emperor. Within months he called a council at the Lateran, helped by Greek monks who had fled the East. In October 649 it condemned the 'one will' teaching and the emperor's decree, the Typos.

Constans II took that as treason. He sent his exarch Olympius to arrest Martin, but Olympius rebelled instead and soon died in Sicily. The next exarch did the job. On 17 June 653 his soldiers seized Martin, sick in bed in the Lateran, and smuggled him out of Rome by night.

After a slow, miserable voyage he was put on trial in Constantinople, stripped of his robes in public and condemned to death. The sentence was cut to exile in Cherson, in the Crimea. His last letters complain of hunger and that Rome had forgotten him. He died there in September 655.

claims.text: Martin's Lateran Council of 649 condemned the emperor's Typos.
claims.note: The council's acts survive in Greek and Latin and were later read out at the Third Council of Constantinople.

claims.text: The exarch's swordbearer, sent to stab Martin at Mass, was struck blind at the altar.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis tells this to explain why Olympius changed sides. It reads as pious storytelling.

claims.text: Martin is the last pope the Church honours as a martyr.
claims.note: He died as a prisoner of the emperor, and the Roman and Orthodox churches both keep his feast. His letters and an account of his trial survive.

reigns.hook: Martin is in a cell in Constantinople, and Rome can't sit without a bishop forever. With the emperor leaning hard, the clergy elect a replacement while the real pope is still alive.

reigns.tagline: The stand-in pope whose own congregation said no
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected while Martin I still lived
reigns.reignEnded: Died; the emperor was busy elsewhere
reigns.previously: Martin I is seized in the Lateran and shipped off to Constantinople.
paragraphs: Eugene was a Roman, a long-serving priest from the city's own clergy. He was chosen in August 654 while Martin was still alive in exile, because Constantinople wanted a more pliable pope. Eugene tried to be one. He sent envoys east, and they came back having signed up to a fudge that spoke of one will and two wills at once.

In 656 the new patriarch's letter, setting out that compromise, was read in the church of Santa Maria Maggiore. The Romans in the pews were having none of it. Clergy and people blocked Eugene from finishing Mass until he promised to reject it. He did. The emperor was furious, but the Arabs were hammering his fleets and provinces, and Eugene died in June 657 before Constans could reach him.

claims.text: The Roman crowd would not let Eugene finish Mass until he rejected the patriarch's letter.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis records the scene, written in Rome within living memory.

claims.text: Constantinople threatened to treat Eugene the way it had treated Martin.
claims.note: The threat is reported in the record of Maximus the Confessor's interrogations, written by his supporters, who had every reason to stress imperial menace.

claims.text: Martin accepted Eugene as his successor.
claims.note: One of Martin's letters from exile prays for the shepherd now over Rome. Whether he meant Eugene, and approved, is read both ways.

reigns.hook: Eugene's flock has shown it will stop a Mass over theology. The next pope, a man from Segni, decides the smart move is to stop arguing with Constantinople altogether.

reigns.tagline: He welcomed the emperor, who then stole the roof
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected; no kin of Eugene I
reigns.previously: Eugene I dies before Constans can punish him.
paragraphs: Vitalian came from Segni, south-east of Rome, and played it cool. He sent friendly letters to Constantinople that steered round the 'one will' question, and his name went back into the prayers of the Byzantine church. In 663 he got his reward, of a sort. Constans II came to Rome, the first emperor to set foot there in about two centuries, and Vitalian met him outside the city with all his clergy.

Constans stayed twelve days, prayed at St Peter's and left gifts. Then his men stripped the city of bronze, including the gilded tiles from the roof of the Pantheon, and shipped it off. In 666 he made the church of Ravenna independent of Rome, a deliberate slap. Two years later Constans was murdered in his bath in Sicily.

Vitalian's longest legacy was in England. After the Synod of Whitby in 664, the English needed an archbishop. In 668 Vitalian consecrated Theodore of Tarsus, a learned Greek monk in his sixties, who went on to organise the English church for over twenty years.

claims.text: Constans II stripped the bronze tiles from the Pantheon's roof.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis describes the looting, and it was written in Rome close to the event.

claims.text: Vitalian sent Theodore of Tarsus to be archbishop of Canterbury.
claims.note: Bede tells the story in detail, including how Abbot Hadrian was sent along to keep an eye on him.

claims.text: Vitalian brought the organ into church music.
claims.note: The claim appears in much later writers and has no support in early sources.

reigns.hook: Vitalian dies after fourteen years of careful peace. His successor is a gentle monk from the Caelian Hill, and in Constantinople the emperor is about to face an Arab siege.

reigns.tagline: A kindly monk-pope in a quiet, cold war
reigns.previously: Vitalian dies after fourteen years of keeping the peace.
paragraphs: Adeodatus was a Roman, son of a man named Jovinian, and a monk at the monastery of St Erasmus on the Caelian Hill. As pope he went on spending on it and enlarging it. The Liber Pontificalis remembers him for one thing above all: he was kind to everyone, and especially to pilgrims and strangers.

Relations with the East were frozen. The patriarchs of Constantinople still held to the 'one will' teaching, and Rome would not accept their letters. But the emperor, Constantine IV, had bigger problems. From 674 Arab fleets besieged Constantinople year after year. Adeodatus died in June 676 with nothing settled.

claims.text: Adeodatus was famous for his kindness to pilgrims.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis praises his generosity; it is nearly all it says about him.

claims.text: Adeodatus freed the abbey of St Martin at Tours from its bishop's control.
claims.note: A privilege in his name survives, but historians question whether it is genuine.

reigns.hook: Adeodatus is gone. The Roman clergy choose an old man who will spend his short reign paving, repairing and clearing out a nest of foreign heretics.

reigns.tagline: The old builder who got Ravenna back in line
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected; no kin of Adeodatus II
reigns.previously: Adeodatus II, the kindly monk-pope, dies in June 676.
paragraphs: Donus was a Roman, son of Maurice, and already old when he was elected. He spent his short reign on the fabric of the city. He paved the great open forecourt in front of St Peter's with marble and restored other churches. He also found a group of Syrian monks in a Roman monastery who held the Nestorian view of Christ. He split them up among other houses and gave their monastery to Roman monks.

In his time the archbishop of Ravenna, independent since Constans II's decree, came back under Rome. And Constantine IV, battered by the Arab siege, wanted peace in the Church. He wrote to Donus proposing talks to end the 'one will' quarrel for good. The letter arrived after Donus had died in April 678.

claims.text: Donus paved the forecourt of St Peter's with marble.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis records the work.

claims.text: Ravenna's archbishop submitted to Rome again under Donus.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis puts it in his reign, but the formal end of Ravenna's independence is usually dated a few years later.

reigns.hook: The emperor's peace letter is sitting in Rome with no pope to read it. It will land on the desk of a Sicilian monk who, the stories say, is already over a hundred.

reigns.tagline: The aged monk whose letter settled a 50-year fight
reigns.previously: Donus dies just as the emperor offers peace talks.
paragraphs: Agatho was a Sicilian Greek and a monk. He seized the emperor's offer. At Easter 680 he gathered 125 bishops in Rome and sent legates east with a long letter setting out the Roman faith: Christ had two wills, a human one and a divine one. That November the Third Council of Constantinople opened in the palace, with Constantine IV in the chair.

The council took Agatho's letter as its guide, and the bishops cried out that Peter had spoken through Agatho. It condemned the 'one will' teaching and everyone who had backed it, including a dead pope, Honorius I. Agatho also heard the appeal of Bishop Wilfrid of York, thrown out of his see, and found in his favour. He died in January 681, months before the council ended.

claims.text: The council acclaimed: 'Peter has spoken through Agatho.'
claims.note: The phrase is in the council's own acts, and later popes quoted it often.

claims.text: Agatho was more than a hundred years old when elected.
claims.note: The figure comes from much later tradition. No early source gives his age.

claims.text: Agatho ruled in favour of Wilfrid of York.
claims.note: Wilfrid's biographer Stephen of Ripon and Bede both describe the hearing in Rome in 679.

reigns.hook: Agatho is dead and the council's verdict must be signed in Rome. His successor will have to put his name to a sentence condemning one of his own predecessors as a heretic.

reigns.tagline: He signed off on calling a pope a heretic
reigns.cameToPower: Elected; waited 18 months to take office
reigns.previously: Agatho dies before the council condemns the 'one will' creed.
paragraphs: Leo was a Sicilian, a fine singer and at home in both Greek and Latin. He was elected soon after Agatho died but had to wait about a year and a half for the emperor's approval. Only in August 682 was he consecrated. His big task was to accept the decrees of the Third Council of Constantinople.

He did, in full, including the condemnation of Pope Honorius. In letters to the emperor and to the bishops of Spain he said Honorius had let the pure faith be stained instead of defending it. The emperor, pleased, ended Ravenna's independence: its archbishops would be consecrated in Rome again. Leo died in July 683, after less than eleven months.

claims.text: Leo II accepted the council's verdict that Pope Honorius I was a heretic.
claims.note: Leo's letters confirming the council survive. Defenders of papal infallibility in 1870 argued he blamed Honorius for negligence, not false teaching.

claims.text: Leo II ended the independence of the church of Ravenna.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis records the emperor's decree restoring Rome's authority over Ravenna's archbishops.

reigns.hook: Leo is dead after barely ten months, and once again Rome must wait for the emperor's nod. The next pope will wait almost a year, and decide this has to change.

reigns.tagline: The pope sent locks of the emperor's sons' hair
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected; no kin of Leo II
reigns.cameToPower: Elected; waited a year for approval
reigns.previously: Leo II dies after confirming that Honorius was a heretic.
paragraphs: Benedict was a Roman, son of a man named John, who had served in the Church since boyhood and was trained in scripture and chant. He was elected soon after Leo II died in 683, but the emperor's approval took almost a year to come. He was finally consecrated in June 684.

Constantine IV now got on well with Rome. He sent Benedict locks of hair from his two sons, Justinian and Heraclius, a gesture that made the pope a kind of spiritual father to them. According to the Liber Pontificalis he also let future popes be consecrated once the exarch in Ravenna approved, with no wait for Constantinople. Benedict died in May 685.

claims.text: Constantine IV sent Benedict locks of his sons' hair.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis records the gift. Sending hair was a Byzantine gesture of adoption or spiritual sonship.

claims.text: The emperor let popes be consecrated on the exarch's approval alone.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis says so, but historians argue over what exactly was granted and whether it lasted.

reigns.hook: Benedict is gone. The next pope is a Syrian from Antioch, the first of a long line of popes from the East, and he was there in Constantinople when Honorius was condemned.

reigns.tagline: The Syrian who carried the council home
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected; no kin of Benedict II
reigns.reignEnded: Died after a year of illness
reigns.previously: Benedict II dies, and the emperor's sons are now the pope's 'sons'.
paragraphs: John came from Syria, from the region of Antioch, and his election began a long run of eastern popes. As a deacon he had been one of Rome's legates at the Third Council of Constantinople, and he had carried its decrees back to Rome himself. In July 685 the clergy, army and people of Rome chose him together, and thanks to the new rule he was consecrated within weeks.

The emperor kept up his good will and lifted heavy taxes on the papal estates in Sicily and Calabria. But John was sick for almost his whole reign and could hardly carry out his duties. He was generous all the same, handing out large gifts to the clergy and the poor. He died in August 686, a year after his election.

claims.text: John V had been a papal legate at the Third Council of Constantinople.
claims.note: His name appears among the Roman delegates in the council's acts.

claims.text: Constantine IV cut the taxes on papal estates in Sicily and Calabria.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis records the tax relief granted in John's time.

reigns.hook: John V is dead, and Rome is split: the clergy want one man, the army another. Locked in a standoff, they settle on an old, kindly priest whom nobody is afraid of.

reigns.tagline: The harmless old compromise who nobody feared
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected; no kin of John V
reigns.previously: John V dies after a year spent mostly in his sickbed.
paragraphs: When John V died, the clergy backed the archpriest Peter and the army backed a priest named Theodore. Neither side would give way, and the standoff dragged on for weeks. In the end they settled on Conon, the son of an officer from the Thracesian army in Asia Minor, schooled in Sicily. He was old, dignified and simple.

He was also sick for most of his eleven months. He annoyed the Roman clergy by giving the rich Sicilian estates of the Church to a deacon from Syracuse. As Conon lay dying, his archdeacon Paschal bribed the exarch to make him the next pope.

claims.text: Archdeacon Paschal promised the exarch 100 pounds of gold to become pope.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis tells the story and names the sum. It comes from the next pope's biography, so it was written by the winning side.

claims.text: Conon sent the Irish missionary Kilian to convert Franconia.
claims.note: It comes from a Life of Kilian written well over a century later.

reigns.hook: Conon is dead and Rome has two rival popes camped in different halves of the Lateran Palace, one of them with the exarch's gold on his side. The city needs a third way.

reigns.tagline: He said no to the emperor, and the army had his back
reigns.cameToPower: Picked to end a double election
reigns.previously: Conon dies; his archdeacon has already bribed the exarch.
paragraphs: Sergius was born in Sicily to a Syrian family from Antioch. When Conon died, the archpriest Theodore and the archdeacon Paschal each grabbed part of the Lateran Palace and claimed the throne. Rome's leading men chose Sergius instead and broke into the Lateran to install him. Theodore gave in. Paschal secretly sent for the exarch, who came and demanded the gold he'd been promised. Sergius had to pay it.

In 692 Justinian II held a council in his palace that condemned Roman customs, such as celibate priests. Sergius refused to sign. Justinian sent an officer to arrest him, as Constans had arrested Martin. This time the soldiers of Ravenna marched on Rome to defend the pope, and the terrified officer hid under Sergius's bed.
Sergius baptised King Cædwalla of Wessex in 689, and consecrated Willibrord as archbishop for the Frisians in 695. He died in September 701.

claims.text: The emperor's officer hid under the pope's bed to escape the troops.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis tells the scene in vivid detail, written in Rome soon after.

claims.text: Sergius added the Agnus Dei, 'Lamb of God', to the Mass.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis says so. Some historians link it to the 692 council's ban on showing Christ as a lamb, but that is a guess.

claims.text: Cædwalla died in Rome days after his baptism, still in his white robes.
claims.note: Bede tells the story and gives his epitaph in St Peter's.

reigns.hook: Sergius has shown that Italian troops will fight for a pope. His successor, a Greek, will need them to fight for the emperor's man instead.

reigns.tagline: A Greek pope who bought peace with silver
reigns.previously: Sergius I dies, having faced down Justinian II's soldiers.
paragraphs: John was a Greek, one of a long run of popes from the eastern Mediterranean. Soon after he took over, the emperor's governor in Italy, the exarch Theophylact, arrived in Rome. The local Italian troops hated him and marched on the city to get at him. John sent priests out to calm the soldiers and kept the exarch safe.

Then Gisulf, the Lombard duke of Benevento, swept through Campania burning and taking prisoners. Constantinople sent no help, so John sent priests with church money to buy the captives back and pay Gisulf to go home. In 704 the stormy English bishop Wilfrid turned up in Rome to appeal against his enemies, and John's synod backed him. John died in January 705 after just over three years.

claims.text: John protected the exarch from his own mutinous troops.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis tells the story; it is one sign that by now the pope, more than the emperor's man, held Rome together.

claims.text: Wilfrid of York won his appeal before John's synod.
claims.note: Told by Wilfrid's biographer Stephen of Ripon, who wrote within a few years of his death and was firmly on his side.

reigns.hook: John is gone. His successor is the son of the man who looked after the emperor's palace in Rome, and he loves fine mosaics more than he loves a fight.

reigns.tagline: The pope who left his own face in mosaic
reigns.previously: John VI dies, having bought off a Lombard duke with church silver.
paragraphs: John VII was the first pope whose father was a Byzantine official: Plato had looked after the old imperial palace on the Palatine. John moved the papal residence up there, beside the church of Santa Maria Antiqua in the Forum, and filled the church with paintings. In St Peter's he built a chapel to the Virgin and put himself in its mosaics, holding a model of the building. A fragment of that portrait survives.

His trouble came from Justinian II, back on the throne in 705 with a slit nose and a grudge. Justinian sent Rome the canons of his council of 692, which Sergius I had refused, and asked the pope to say which he accepted. John simply sent them back untouched. The Lombard king Aripert II returned church estates in the Cottian Alps. John died in October 707.

claims.text: John returned the council canons unsigned because he was afraid.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis says he did it out of "human weakness". Some historians read it as a cautious refusal to commit, not plain fear.

claims.text: The mosaic fragment in the Vatican shows John himself, made in his lifetime.
claims.note: It comes from his chapel in Old St Peter's, demolished in the early 1600s; an inscription there named him as builder.

reigns.hook: John is dead. The next pope is a Syrian so crippled by gout he cannot lift food to his mouth. He will not last the winter.

reigns.tagline: Twenty days on the throne, too sick to feed himself
reigns.previously: John VII dies, having sent Justinian II's canons back unsigned.
paragraphs: Sisinnius was a Syrian, the son of a man named John, and by the time he was chosen he was very ill. The papal biographer says his gout was so bad he could not even feed himself. The Romans had waited three months for a pope and got one who could barely move.

He still tried. He ordered lime to be burned so the crumbling walls of Rome could be repaired, and he consecrated a bishop for Corsica. Then, twenty days after his consecration, he died. The repairs he started would be finished by the popes who came after him. His successor was another Syrian, and was in place within two months.

claims.text: Sisinnius's gout was so bad he could not feed himself.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis, written in Rome at the time, says so plainly.

claims.text: He ordered lime burned to rebuild the walls of Rome.
claims.note: The same papal biography records the order; Gregory II later carried the work on.

reigns.hook: Sisinnius is dead in under three weeks. The next Syrian pope will be called east by the most dangerous man in the empire, and will go.

reigns.tagline: The last pope to sail to Constantinople for 1,250 years
reigns.previously: Sisinnius dies after 20 days, too crippled by gout to feed himself.
paragraphs: Constantine was a Syrian. In 710 Justinian II summoned him to Constantinople, and everyone remembered what had happened to Martin I. He went anyway, taking a young deacon called Gregory. In 711 the emperor met him at Nicomedia, wearing his crown, threw himself down and kissed the pope's feet. He took communion from him and confirmed the Roman church's privileges. They seem to have settled the old quarrel over the canons of 692.

Constantine got home in October 711. Within weeks Justinian was overthrown and killed. The new emperor, Philippicus, revived the old heresy that Christ had only one will. Rome refused to put his image in churches or his name in the Mass, and there was fighting in the streets. He fell in 713 and his successor was orthodox. Two English kings, Cenred of Mercia and Offa of Essex, came to Rome as pilgrims and became monks. Constantine died in 715.

claims.text: Justinian II kissed the pope's feet at Nicomedia.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis describes it; the author probably got it from people on the trip.

claims.text: No pope set foot in Constantinople again until Paul VI in 1967.
claims.note: Paul VI's visit to Istanbul in July 1967 was the first since Constantine's.

claims.text: Two Anglo-Saxon kings became monks in Rome in his time.
claims.note: Bede reports Cenred and Offa going to Rome and taking vows.

reigns.hook: Constantine dies. The young deacon who argued theology in front of Justinian II is now the obvious choice. He will need every bit of that nerve.

reigns.tagline: He sent Boniface to the Germans and told an emperor no
reigns.relationToPredecessor: His deacon, who went east with him
reigns.previously: Constantine dies, home from Constantinople, the emperor's friend.
paragraphs: Gregory was a Roman, raised in the papal household, who had impressed Justinian II on Constantine's trip east. As pope he sent the Englishman Wynfrith to preach to the Germans in 719, renamed him Boniface, and later made him a bishop. Boniface went on to organise the Church across Germany. Gregory also restored the ruined abbey of Monte Cassino.

Emperor Leo III wanted more tax from Italy, and Gregory refused. Leo's men in Italy plotted to kill the pope, and the Romans, and even some Lombards, rallied to protect him. When Leo turned against religious images, Gregory would not go along. Meanwhile the Lombard king Liutprand took the town of Sutri and in 728 handed it to the pope, not the emperor. It was the papacy's first piece of land held as a ruler. Gregory died in 731.

claims.text: Liutprand gave Sutri to the pope in 728.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis says he handed it to the apostles Peter and Paul; historians call it the Donation of Sutri, the first seed of the Papal States.

claims.text: Imperial officials plotted to assassinate Gregory.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis names the plotters, including the exarch Paul; the Romans and Lombards protected him.

reigns.hook: Gregory is dead. At his funeral the crowd seizes a Syrian priest and makes him pope on the spot. He will be the last to ask the emperor's leave.

reigns.tagline: The last pope who asked the emperor's permission
reigns.cameToPower: Acclaimed by the crowd; exarch approved
reigns.previously: Gregory II dies, having defied the emperor and gained Sutri.
paragraphs: Gregory III was a Syrian priest, picked out by the crowd at his predecessor's funeral. He waited over a month for the exarch at Ravenna to approve him, the last pope ever to do so. Then he went straight at the emperor. His synod of November 731 cut off anyone who destroyed holy images. Leo III struck back by seizing the papacy's rich estates in Sicily and southern Italy.

Meanwhile the Lombard king Liutprand was eating up towns around Rome. Gregory backed the dukes of Spoleto and Benevento against him, and in 739 Liutprand struck back, seizing four towns close to Rome. Gregory sent the keys of St Peter's tomb to Charles Martel, ruler of the Franks, and begged for help. Charles was Liutprand's ally and did nothing. Both men died in late 741, Charles in October and Gregory in November.

claims.text: Gregory III was the last pope to seek the emperor's approval.
claims.note: After him popes simply told Constantinople they had been elected.

claims.text: He was the last pope born outside Europe until Francis in 2013.
claims.note: He was a Syrian; Francis was born in Buenos Aires.

claims.text: Leo III took the papal estates in Sicily and Calabria to punish him.
claims.note: The seizure is certain, but historians argue over its date, anywhere from the 730s to the 750s.

reigns.hook: Gregory is dead, and so is Charles Martel. Liutprand is still at the gates. The next pope won't write letters; he will go to meet the Lombard king in person.

reigns.tagline: The last Greek pope talked kings into anything
reigns.cameToPower: Elected within days of Gregory III
reigns.previously: Gregory III dies, his appeal to Charles Martel unanswered.
paragraphs: Zachary was a Greek from Calabria and a born negotiator. In 742 he went to meet Liutprand at Terni and talked him into giving back four captured towns and a 20-year peace. In 749 the next Lombard king, Ratchis, besieged Perugia. Zachary went to his camp and persuaded him to leave. Soon after, Ratchis gave up his crown and became a monk.

Zachary's biggest move came in 751. Pepin the Short, the real power among the Franks, asked whether a puppet king should keep his title. Zachary backed Pepin, who deposed the last Merovingian and took the crown. Back home, Zachary bought a cargo of slaves from Venetian traders in Rome to stop them being sold to Muslim Africa, and set them free. He died in March 752, the last of the Greek popes.

claims.text: Zachary said the man with real power should be king.
claims.note: The Royal Frankish Annals say so, but they were written decades later at the court of Pepin's family, which wanted papal approval on record.

claims.text: Zachary bought slaves from Venetian merchants and freed them.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis tells the story; it is one of the earliest mentions of Venetian traders in Rome.

reigns.hook: Zachary dies. The Lombard king is at Rome's door, and the emperor won't help. The next pope is about to do something no pope has ever done: cross the Alps.

reigns.tagline: The pope who crossed the Alps and came back with a state
reigns.previously: Zachary dies, having blessed Pepin's grab for the Frankish crown.
paragraphs: First, the numbering. After Zachary died, a priest named Stephen was elected but died of a stroke a few days later, before he could be consecrated. Some lists count him and some don't, so this pope turns up as Stephen II or Stephen III depending on the book. Within days the Romans picked a deacon, also called Stephen.

The Lombard king Aistulf had taken Ravenna and wanted Rome, and Constantinople sent nothing. So late in 753 Stephen did what no pope had done before: he crossed the Alps to the Frankish court. He met Pepin the Short in January 754. That summer at Saint-Denis he anointed Pepin king, along with his two young sons. One of them was the future Charlemagne.

Pepin paid him back. He marched into Italy and beat Aistulf twice, and in 756 handed the conquered lands, Ravenna and a band of territory across central Italy, to the pope instead of the emperor. This was the Donation of Pepin, the birth of the Papal States. The pope was now a ruler of land and people, and would stay one for 1,100 years. Stephen died in April 757.

claims.text: At their first meeting Pepin walked beside the pope's horse like a groom.
claims.note: The papal biography says so. Frankish sources instead have Stephen kneeling in sackcloth before Pepin. Each side told it its own way.

claims.text: Stephen was the first pope to cross the Alps.
claims.note: His journey is described in his life in the Liber Pontificalis and in Frankish annals.

claims.text: The forged Donation of Constantine was made in Rome around this time to back papal claims.
claims.note: Many historians date it to the mid or late 8th century, but exactly when, where and why it was forged is still argued.

reigns.hook: Stephen has a state. His younger brother Paul means to keep it in the family, but part of the clergy wants the archdeacon instead, and the new Lombard king has no plan to hand over a single town.
