reigns.tagline: His brother built a state; Paul had to keep it
reigns.reignEnded: Died at St Paul's in the heat
reigns.previously: Stephen II dies, the first ruler of the new Papal States.
paragraphs: Paul was Stephen II's younger brother and had been his right hand. Not everyone wanted the job to stay in the family: a rival group backed the archdeacon Theophylact. Paul's party won, and he wrote to Pepin to announce his election, much as popes had once written to the emperor.

The new Lombard king, Desiderius, had promised to hand over towns and then kept finding reasons not to. Paul's letters to Pepin begging for help survive in a collection Charlemagne later had copied. He became a spiritual co-parent of Pepin's baby daughter Gisela. The Lombard raids had wrecked the catacombs outside Rome, so Paul moved martyrs' bones into city churches, including his own family home, now San Silvestro in Capite. He died in June 767.

claims.text: Paul moved martyrs' relics from the catacombs into Rome.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis and the foundation of San Silvestro in Capite both record it; later popes did the same on a bigger scale.

claims.text: Paul fell ill and died at St Paul's, where he had gone to escape the summer heat.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis says so.

reigns.hook: Paul is dead. Before the clergy can meet, a duke from Nepi marches armed men into Rome and makes his brother pope, though the brother isn't even a priest.

reigns.tagline: Elected after a coup, a blinding and a one-day pope
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected after the layman usurper fell
reigns.cameToPower: Elected after the coup was crushed
reigns.previously: Paul I dies, and a duke's armed men put a layman on the throne.
paragraphs: When Paul died, Duke Toto of Nepi forced his brother Constantine, a layman, onto the papal throne. A year later the papal official Christophorus and his son Sergius came back with Lombard help and threw him out. A Lombard priest then made a monk called Philip pope, and he lasted a day. Finally Stephen, a Sicilian monk, was elected. Constantine was blinded and his backers mutilated.

Stephen's synod of 769 ruled that only a cardinal priest or deacon could be elected pope, never a layman, and backed holy images. Stephen was no strongman. In 771 the chamberlain Paul Afiarta, working with the Lombard king Desiderius, turned on Christophorus and Sergius, who were blinded; Christophorus died soon after. Stephen also wrote to warn Charlemagne off marrying Desiderius's daughter. Charlemagne married her anyway. Stephen died in January 772.

claims.text: Constantine II, the layman pope, was deposed and blinded.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis, written by the winning side, describes his downfall in grim detail, and the acts of the 769 synod survive.

claims.text: Stephen let his own protectors be blinded to please Desiderius.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis blames Paul Afiarta; Stephen's own letter to the Franks suggests he went along with it. How far he was complicit is argued.

claims.text: In a letter to Charlemagne he called the Lombards a foul and faithless race.
claims.note: The letter survives in the Codex Carolinus.

reigns.hook: Stephen is dead, and Desiderius's man still runs the papal court. The cardinals choose a Roman noble who will see him off and call in Charlemagne.

reigns.tagline: Charlemagne's friend, and the longest reign for 1,000 years
reigns.cameToPower: Elected a week after Stephen died
reigns.previously: Stephen III dies, with a Lombard puppet running the papal court.
paragraphs: Hadrian came from a noble Roman family and was raised by his uncle Theodotus, a top papal official. He started by exiling Paul Afiarta. Desiderius answered by grabbing papal towns and threatening Rome. So Hadrian called in Charlemagne, who crossed the Alps in 773 and besieged the Lombard capital, Pavia. At Easter 774 Charlemagne came to Rome and swore to honour his father Pepin's grant of land to the pope. Pavia fell that June.

With the Lombard kingdom gone, Hadrian rebuilt. He repaired Rome's walls and aqueducts and set up big church-run farms to feed the city. His legates attended the Second Council of Nicaea in 787, which restored holy images in the East. He reigned nearly 24 years, a record no later pope beat until Pius VI. He died on Christmas Day 795, and Charlemagne wept at the news.

claims.text: Charlemagne wept at Hadrian's death and sent an epitaph to Rome.
claims.note: Einhard, who knew Charlemagne, mentions the tears. The marble epitaph, with verses usually credited to Alcuin, survives at St Peter's.

claims.text: At Easter 774 Charlemagne promised the pope most of Italy.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis says he did, listing huge territories. The Franks never handed most of them over, and some historians doubt the list.

reigns.hook: Hadrian's death leaves his powerful nephews out in the cold. The new pope comes from a humbler family, and they don't intend to put up with him for long.

reigns.tagline: The pope who made an emperor on Christmas Day
reigns.cameToPower: Elected the day after Hadrian died
reigns.previously: Hadrian I dies on Christmas Day. Charlemagne weeps for him.
paragraphs: Leo was a career churchman from an ordinary family, elected the day after Hadrian died. Hadrian's relatives held top jobs at the papal court and loathed him. On 25 April 799, as Leo rode in a procession through Rome, a gang led by Hadrian's nephew Paschal dragged him from his horse and tried to cut out his eyes and tongue. They locked him in a monastery, but he got away by night.

He fled north to Charlemagne at Paderborn. His enemies sent charges after him, including adultery and perjury. Charlemagne sent him home under escort and came to Rome himself late in 800. On 23 December, before an assembly in St Peter's, Leo swore on the Gospels that he was innocent. It was agreed that no one could sit in judgement on the pope.

Two days later, at Christmas Mass in St Peter's, Leo put a crown on Charlemagne's head and the crowd hailed him emperor of the Romans. The West had an emperor again for the first time in over 300 years, and a pope had crowned him. Leo outlived Charlemagne and died in June 816. He left a precedent popes would lean on for centuries: emperors got their crowns from Rome.

claims.text: His attackers did cut out his eyes and tongue, and God healed him by a miracle.
claims.note: Leo's supporters said so. Frankish sources say he was attacked; most historians think the mutilation simply failed.

claims.text: Charlemagne would never have entered the church that day had he known what the pope planned.
claims.note: Einhard says so. Historians argue whether Charlemagne was truly surprised or just disliked the pope taking the credit.

claims.text: Leo swore an oath of innocence two days before the coronation.
claims.note: Recorded in the Liber Pontificalis and the Frankish annals for 23 December 800.

reigns.hook: Leo and Charlemagne are both gone. Rome's new pope, Stephen IV, sets out over the Alps to anoint Charlemagne's son. Out at sea, Arab raiders know exactly where Rome's richest church stands.

reigns.tagline: Seven months, one trip north, one emperor anointed
reigns.cameToPower: Elected days after Leo III died
reigns.reignEnded: Died in Rome after seven months
reigns.previously: Leo III dies in 816, sixteen years after crowning Charlemagne.
paragraphs: Stephen came from a noble Roman family and had served in the Lateran since boyhood. He was consecrated ten days after Leo III died, without waiting for word from the emperor. To smooth that over he made the Romans swear loyalty to Louis the Pious, Charlemagne's son and heir, and then set off over the Alps to meet him in person.

In October 816, in the cathedral at Reims, Stephen anointed Louis and crowned him emperor, and crowned his wife Ermengard too. Louis had already been crowned at Aachen in 813 on his father's orders. Now the pope had added Rome's blessing, and the idea that a real emperor needed one took another step. Stephen came home loaded with gifts and with the Roman exiles of Leo's reign pardoned. He died in January 817.

claims.text: The crown Stephen placed on Louis's head had belonged to Constantine the Great.
claims.note: Said in Frankish accounts of the ceremony. There is no way to trace a 4th-century crown to Reims, and it was surely meant as a statement, not a provenance.

claims.text: Stephen crowned Louis the Pious emperor at Reims in October 816.
claims.note: Recorded in the Royal Frankish Annals, Thegan's life of Louis, and the court poet Ermold the Black.

reigns.hook: Stephen is dead after seven months. The very next day the Romans pick Paschal, an abbot from beside St Peter's, and once again nobody waits for the emperor's permission.

reigns.tagline: Square halo, bloody hands, no tomb in St Peter's
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected the day after Stephen IV died
reigns.previously: Stephen IV dies after crowning Louis the Pious at Reims.
paragraphs: Paschal was a Roman priest who ran the monastery of St Stephen beside St Peter's. Elected in a hurry, he wrote to Louis the Pious to explain, and got a handsome reward: the Pactum Ludovicianum of 817, a charter confirming the pope's lands and promising free papal elections. He spent lavishly, rebuilding Santa Prassede, Santa Cecilia and Santa Maria in Domnica. In their mosaics he still stands among the saints, wearing the square halo of the living.

His rule turned dark. In 823, months after he crowned Louis's son Lothair co-emperor at Easter, two senior papal officials who leaned to the Franks were blinded and beheaded inside the Lateran. Paschal swore an oath before imperial envoys that he had no part in it, but he shielded the killers, saying the dead men were traitors. When he died in February 824 the Romans would not let him be buried in St Peter's.

claims.text: Paschal ordered the murder of the two officials in the Lateran.
claims.note: Frankish annals report the killing and Paschal's oath of innocence. He refused to hand over the killers, which kept suspicion alive.

claims.text: St Cecilia appeared to Paschal in a dream and showed him where her body lay.
claims.note: Paschal's own account, recorded in the Liber Pontificalis. He moved remains from a catacomb to her church in Trastevere.

claims.text: His mosaics show him with a square halo.
claims.note: Visible today in Santa Prassede and Santa Cecilia. The square halo marked someone still alive when the image was made.

reigns.hook: Paschal dies hated, and the Romans want a change. The nobles push their man Eugene, Lothair hurries to Rome, and the emperor is about to rewrite the rules for every future election.

reigns.tagline: The pope who had to swear loyalty first
reigns.previously: Paschal I dies, and the Romans refuse him a tomb in St Peter's.
paragraphs: Eugene was archpriest of Santa Sabina on the Aventine. When Paschal died, the clergy had their own candidate, but the Roman nobles wanted Eugene and got him. The Franks were ready to step in. Lothair, the young co-emperor, came to Rome in late 824 and laid down a Roman Constitution: imperial envoys would oversee justice in the city, and every new pope had to swear loyalty to the emperor before he could be consecrated.

Eugene accepted it. The papacy had gained a protector and lost a slice of its freedom. In 826 he held a synod at St Peter's that passed rules for the clergy, including schools at bishops' churches to teach letters and doctrine. He died in August 827, after three quiet years under the emperor's eye.

claims.text: Lothair's Roman Constitution of 824 made a new pope swear loyalty to the emperor before consecration.
claims.note: The text survives in the Frankish capitularies and is reported in the Royal Frankish Annals.

claims.text: Eugene's synod of 826 ordered schools to be set up for the clergy.
claims.note: The synod's canons survive, including one requiring teachers at bishops' churches and other places where needed.

reigns.hook: Eugene dies in August 827. The Romans choose a young deacon who has been the darling of two popes. His name is Valentine, and he will not see out the autumn.

reigns.tagline: The only Pope Valentine lasted barely a month

start.note: elected after the death of his predecessor

reigns.cameToPower: Chosen by clergy, nobles and people
reigns.previously: Eugene II dies after three quiet years under Lothair's eye.
paragraphs: Valentine was a Roman from the Via Lata district. As a young cleric he caught the eye of Paschal I, who made him archdeacon, and Eugene II kept him close too. When Eugene died, clergy, nobles and people agreed on him at once, a rare thing in a city that liked a fight. They took him to the Lateran and enthroned him before he had even been consecrated.

Then he died. His papacy lasted roughly a month, perhaps a little more. Nothing he did as pope is recorded, because there was no time to do anything. He is still the only pope ever to take the name Valentine.

claims.text: Valentine reigned for exactly forty days.
claims.note: That is the Liber Pontificalis figure. Modern lists, working from other dates, put it at about five weeks.

claims.text: Pope Valentine is the Valentine of St Valentine's Day.
claims.note: A modern mix-up. The saint of 14 February was a 3rd-century Roman martyr, more than 500 years earlier.

reigns.hook: Valentine is buried almost before he is known. Next comes Gregory, a priest of noble blood, and this time the rules are followed: no consecration until the emperor's man says yes.

reigns.tagline: He went to make peace and watched an emperor fall
reigns.previously: Valentine dies after barely a month as pope.
paragraphs: Gregory was a Roman noble and priest of San Marco, where his apse mosaic still shows him with a square halo. Under the new rules he had to wait months for the emperor's envoy before he could be consecrated. Then the Frankish empire started to tear itself apart. Louis the Pious's grown sons rebelled against their father, and in 833 Gregory crossed the Alps with Lothair, saying he came to make peace.

Near Colmar, in June 833, the two armies faced each other. Gregory went over to talk to Louis. While the talks went on, Louis's men drifted across to his sons until he had almost no one left. Louis surrendered and was deposed. The spot was later called the Field of Lies, and Gregory went home with his name tarnished. Louis was back on his throne within a year.

In Italy the danger was at sea. Arab forces were taking Sicily, and Gregory built a fortified town at Ostia, Gregoriopolis, to guard the mouth of the Tiber. He died in January 844, after sixteen years.

claims.text: Gregory was tricked into helping Louis's sons depose their father.
claims.note: Louis's loyal biographers blamed the pope's presence for the betrayal. Others think he knew exactly whose side he was on.

claims.text: Gregory spread the feast of All Saints on 1 November across the Frankish lands.
claims.note: Frankish sources say Louis made it a feast at Gregory's urging around 835. The date was already kept in Rome and parts of England.

claims.text: The Field of Lies took place in June 833.
claims.note: Described by Nithard, Thegan, the Astronomer and the Annals of St-Bertin.

reigns.hook: Gregory is dead. A deacon's mob seizes the Lateran; the nobles crush it and crown their own man, the elderly Sergius. Nobody asks the emperor first, and the emperor is about to send an army.

reigns.tagline: Gout, a greedy brother, and pirates at St Peter's

start.note: elected after the death of his predecessor

reigns.cameToPower: Nobles beat a deacon's rival bid
reigns.previously: Gregory IV dies in January 844 after sixteen years.
paragraphs: Sergius was an elderly Roman noble. When Gregory died, a crowd tried to make a deacon named John pope and stormed the Lateran. The nobles broke it up, put Sergius in, and had him consecrated at once without the emperor's say. Lothair was furious. He sent his son Louis with an army and the bishop of Metz to sort it out. Sergius met them at St Peter's, crowned Louis king of the Lombards, and kept his job.

Sergius suffered badly from gout, and his brother Benedict, bishop of Albano, ran affairs and sold church posts. Then came disaster. In August 846 an Arab fleet came up the Tiber. St Peter's and St Paul's lay outside the walls, and the raiders stripped both of their treasures. Rome was shaken to the core. Sergius died five months later.

claims.text: Sergius's brother Benedict openly sold bishoprics and church offices.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis, written soon after, is scathing about both brothers. It is the main source.

claims.text: Arab raiders plundered St Peter's and St Paul's in August 846.
claims.note: Reported by the Liber Pontificalis, the Annals of St-Bertin and other Frankish annals.

reigns.hook: Sergius dies with St Peter's stripped bare. The Romans want a fighter, fast, and they don't wait for the emperor. Their choice is Leo, a priest with walls on his mind.

reigns.tagline: He walled in the Vatican and beat the raiders
reigns.previously: Sergius II dies, months after Arab raiders loot St Peter's.
paragraphs: Leo was a Roman who had trained as a monk and served at the Lateran. With the raiders likely to return, the Romans consecrated him without waiting for the emperor. He started on a wall right round the Vatican hill, paid for with help from the emperor and labour from across the papal lands. It was finished in 852. The district inside it is still called the Leonine City.

In 849 a raiding fleet threatened Ostia. Ships from Naples, Amalfi and Gaeta joined the papal forces, Leo blessed them, and a storm finished off the enemy. Prisoners were set to work on the new wall. In 853 Wessex sent a four-year-old prince named Alfred to Rome, and Leo honoured the boy with the insignia of a Roman consul. Leo died in July 855, a hero to his city.

claims.text: In the 850s a woman disguised as a man reigned as Pope Joan until she gave birth during a procession.
claims.note: First told in the 13th century, about 400 years later. Coins, letters and the papal lives run straight from Leo IV to Benedict III with no gap for her.

claims.text: Leo invested the young Alfred with a consul's sash and sword.
claims.note: A fragment of Leo's own letter to Alfred's father survives. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle later said he anointed Alfred king.

claims.text: Raphael's fresco of the Battle of Ostia shows this victory.
claims.note: Painted for Leo X in the Vatican in 1514 to 1515, with the Renaissance pope's face on Leo IV.

reigns.hook: Leo dies a hero. The Romans pick a quiet priest called Benedict, but the emperor's envoys have another man in mind, a brilliant scholar Leo had excommunicated, and they mean to seat him by force.

reigns.tagline: Stripped of his robes, he still won the throne
reigns.cameToPower: Beat a rival backed by imperial envoys
reigns.previously: Leo IV dies in 855, the Vatican safe behind his new wall.
paragraphs: Benedict was a Roman priest with a name for learning and piety, and the clergy and people chose him. The emperor Louis II's envoys had other ideas. They backed Anastasius, a gifted scholar whom Leo IV had excommunicated. Anastasius marched into the Lateran with the envoys, pulled Benedict off the throne, stripped him of his robes and locked him up.

It backfired. The clergy and people of Rome would not budge, and after a few days of standoff the envoys gave up. Benedict was consecrated on 29 September 855. He let Anastasius off lightly, and the scholar would come back as a key adviser to later popes. That same year King Æthelwulf of Wessex came to Rome with young Alfred and lavish gifts. Benedict died in April 858.

claims.text: Anastasius seized the Lateran and had Benedict stripped of his vestments.
claims.note: Told in detail by the Liber Pontificalis, written by Benedict's supporters soon after.

claims.text: Anastasius, the failed rival, is the same man as Anastasius the Librarian, later the papacy's chief scholar.
claims.note: Most historians identify the two. A few have doubted it, as the Liber Pontificalis is silent on his later career.

reigns.hook: Benedict dies in April 858. Emperor Louis II is close to Rome when the Romans choose, and the man they pick is a deacon of iron will. Nicholas will tell kings and patriarchs what to do.

reigns.tagline: He made a king take his wife back
reigns.reignEnded: Died in Rome after long illness
reigns.previously: Benedict III dies after facing down the emperor's envoys.
paragraphs: Nicholas was the son of a Roman official, trained at the Lateran, and he believed the pope answered to no one on earth. In Constantinople the patriarch Ignatius had been forced out and a learned layman, Photius, rushed into his place. Nicholas refused to accept it, and in 863 a Roman synod deposed Photius. Photius hit back in 867 by having a council depose Nicholas. The split between Rome and the Greek church grew deeper.

In the West he went toe to toe with kings. Lothair II wanted to dump his wife Teutberga and marry his mistress Waldrada, and his bishops agreed. Nicholas deposed the two archbishops who arranged it, faced down Emperor Louis II when he marched on Rome, and forced Lothair to take Teutberga back. He also humbled the mighty Hincmar of Reims and the archbishop of Ravenna.

In 866 the newly Christian Bulgarians sent him a long list of questions. His patient answers covered everything from fasting to whether women could wear trousers. He died in November 867, and was soon called the Great.

claims.text: Nicholas told the Bulgarians it did not matter whether their women wore trousers.
claims.note: In his Responses to the Questions of the Bulgarians, 866. The letter survives.

claims.text: Nicholas built his claims on the forged Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals.
claims.note: The forgeries were circulating in Francia by his time and he may have known them. Historians argue over how far he used them.

claims.text: The quarrel with Photius started the Great Schism of 1054.
claims.note: It poisoned relations and set precedents, but the two churches were reconciled for long stretches afterwards.

reigns.hook: Nicholas dies in November 867. The cardinals turn to a kindly old priest who has said no to the job twice before. He is a married man, and his family is about to pay a terrible price.

reigns.tagline: A married pope whose family was murdered
reigns.previously: Nicholas I, the pope who bossed kings, dies in November 867.
paragraphs: Hadrian came from a noble Roman family that had already given two popes. He had married before he became a priest, as was allowed, and had a daughter. He had turned down the papacy twice, in 855 and 858. This time, aged about 75, he said yes. He was gentler than Nicholas and tried to calm the quarrels Nicholas had left behind.

In 868 tragedy hit. Eleutherius, a brother of Anastasius the Librarian, abducted Hadrian's wife Stephania and their daughter, then killed them both when the emperor's men caught up with him. Anastasius was briefly disgraced. That winter Hadrian also welcomed the missionaries Cyril and Methodius, who brought him the bones of Pope Clement, and he backed their work among the Slavs. He died in December 872.

claims.text: Eleutherius abducted and murdered Hadrian's wife and daughter in 868.
claims.note: Reported by the Annals of St-Bertin, a well-informed Frankish source of the time.

claims.text: Hadrian laid the Slavonic service books on the altar of Santa Maria Maggiore to bless them.
claims.note: Told in the Life of Methodius, written by his followers. No Roman source mentions it.

claims.text: King Lothair II died soon after Hadrian gave him communion, as a judgement for lying about his marriage.
claims.note: Lothair did die of fever on the way home in 869. Chroniclers drew the moral.

reigns.hook: Hadrian dies at about 80. The new pope is his archdeacon John, a street-fighting politician who will crown two emperors, pay off pirates and die at the hands of his own people.

reigns.tagline: The first pope said to be murdered by his own
reigns.previously: Hadrian II dies, his wife and daughter murdered four years before.
paragraphs: John had been archdeacon of Rome for years and knew every faction in the city. He spent his reign hunting for a protector. On Christmas Day 875 he crowned Charles the Bald emperor, and in 881 Charles the Fat. Meanwhile Arab raiders roamed southern Italy. John built a wall round St Paul's, took to sea against them, and in the end paid them protection money.

In Rome he crushed his enemies, Formosus among them, excommunicating them in 876. When the duke of Spoleto seized Rome in 878, John fled to France. He backed Methodius and the Slavonic liturgy, and made peace with Photius. In December 882, the Annals of Fulda say, a relative poisoned him, and when it worked too slowly he and others beat him to death with a hammer.

claims.text: John VIII was poisoned by a relative, then finished off with a hammer.
claims.note: Only the Annals of Fulda, written far away in Germany, tell the story. Nothing in Rome confirms or denies it.

claims.text: John paid Arab raiders tribute to keep them off Rome.
claims.note: His own letters, many of which survive in a register, complain of the payments he had to make.

claims.text: John crowned Charles the Bald emperor on Christmas Day 875.
claims.note: Recorded in the Annals of St-Bertin and other Frankish annals.

reigns.hook: John VIII lies murdered. His successor is already a bishop, a veteran envoy called Marinus, and one of his first acts is to bring home the man John had cast out: Formosus.

reigns.tagline: The bishop who broke the rules to become pope
reigns.cameToPower: Elected the day John VIII died
reigns.previously: John VIII is murdered by his own household in December 882.
paragraphs: Marinus was a priest's son from Gallese, north of Rome, and a seasoned diplomat. He had gone to Constantinople on papal missions in the long fight with the patriarch Photius. When John VIII was murdered he was already bishop of Caere, and old church law said a bishop could not swap his see for another. Rome ignored the rule and chose him anyway.

He undid the old feuds. Formosus, whom John VIII had thrown out, was forgiven and sent back to his see at Porto. Marinus met the emperor Charles the Fat at Nonantola in 883. He was also a friend to England: he let off the English quarter in Rome from its taxes and sent King Alfred a gift, a piece of the True Cross. He died in May 884, after just seventeen months.

claims.text: Marinus was the first man already bishop of another see to become pope.
claims.note: Often said, but some count earlier cases. What is clear is that it broke the old canons, and Formosus's enemies later made it a weapon.

claims.text: Marinus sent Alfred a piece of the True Cross.
claims.note: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records the gift and the freeing of the English quarter from tax.

claims.text: Later popes called Martin IV and V are misnumbered because of him.
claims.note: Medieval lists misread Marinus I and II as Martin II and III, so no popes ever took those numbers.

reigns.hook: Marinus is dead after barely a year and a half. The Romans pick one of their own, a hard man who settles scores with a blinding and a public whipping.

reigns.tagline: Sixteen months, a blinding and an unfinished journey
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected; a Roman of the city
reigns.cameToPower: Elected by Roman clergy and people
reigns.reignEnded: Died on the road to Germany
reigns.previously: Marinus I dies in May 884 after seventeen months.
paragraphs: Hadrian III was a Roman, son of a man named Benedict, and Rome in 884 was a city of feuding families. He struck hard. A powerful official, George of the Aventine, was blinded on his orders, and the widow of a murdered courtier was whipped naked through the streets. Under all that lay a fight between John VIII's friends and his enemies.

In 885 the emperor Charles the Fat called him north to a great meeting at Worms. Charles had no legitimate son and wanted the pope's help to settle his throne. Hadrian set out up the Po valley and never got there. He died near Modena in September 885 and was buried at the abbey of Nonantola, where people soon prayed to him as a saint.

claims.text: Hadrian had a noblewoman whipped naked through Rome.
claims.note: It comes from a short surviving fragment of the Liber Pontificalis, with little context. Nothing else confirms the details.

claims.text: Hadrian is a saint.
claims.note: Nonantola honoured him for centuries, and Rome formally confirmed the cult in 1891.

claims.text: Hadrian was going north to help Charles the Fat make his illegitimate son Bernard his heir.
claims.note: The Annals of Fulda give the purpose of the meeting; whether Hadrian had promised to help is guesswork.

reigns.hook: Hadrian dies on the road and is buried far from Rome. The Romans don't wait to ask the emperor. They choose a rich nobleman and consecrate him at once.

reigns.tagline: The rich pope who fed Rome and lost the Slavs
reigns.previously: Hadrian III dies near Modena on his way to the emperor.
paragraphs: Stephen came from a noble Roman family and was elected and consecrated in a rush, without waiting for Charles the Fat to approve. The emperor was furious and sent men to remove him, then backed down when told the vote had been unanimous. Stephen found the papal palace looted, so he paid for Rome's poor through a famine out of his own fortune. Older books call him Stephen VI: a pope-elect of 752 counts or not, depending on the list.

His big mistake came in the east. After the missionary Methodius died in 885, Stephen banned the Slavonic-language Mass he had won from earlier popes. Methodius's followers were driven out of Moravia and fled to Bulgaria, where their alphabet took root instead. At home the dukes of Spoleto were rising. Stephen adopted Duke Guy as his son and crowned him emperor in February 891, then died that September.

claims.text: Stephen fed starving Romans from his family's own wealth.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis says so; it was written by his own people and is warm towards him.

claims.text: Stephen's ban helped send the Slavonic liturgy to Bulgaria.
claims.note: His letter against it survives, and the Lives of Clement of Ohrid tell how Methodius's disciples were expelled and welcomed in Bulgaria.

claims.text: Charles the Fat sent envoys to depose Stephen.
claims.note: Only the papal biography tells it, and it is keen to show the emperor backing down.

reigns.hook: Stephen V is dead, and the Spoleto clan holds the imperial crown. The man the Romans pick next is an old bishop John VIII once threw out. His name is Formosus.

reigns.tagline: The pope whose troubles began after his funeral
reigns.previously: Stephen V dies. The dukes of Spoleto hold the imperial crown.
paragraphs: Formosus had a career before he had a throne. As bishop of Porto he was sent to Bulgaria in 866, and the Bulgarian ruler liked him so much he asked for him as archbishop. Rome said no. Then he made enemies. In 876 John VIII accused him of plotting and excommunicated him, and Formosus fled. A later pope lifted the ban, and in 891, already old, Formosus was elected pope himself.

Italy was a mess. The imperial title had fallen to Guy, duke of Spoleto, and Formosus crowned Guy's son Lambert as co-emperor in 892. But the Spoleto family leaned hard on Rome, so the pope wrote north to Arnulf, king of the East Franks. Arnulf marched into Italy, took Rome, and was crowned emperor by Formosus in February 896.

It went wrong at once. Arnulf fell ill and went home, and the Spoleto party was still there. Weeks later, on 4 April 896, Formosus died. He was buried in St Peter's. The Spoleto faction, and Lambert's fierce mother Ageltrude, had a long memory.

claims.text: The Bulgarian ruler Boris asked for Formosus as his archbishop.
claims.note: Papal letters and the Liber Pontificalis record the request and Rome's refusal.

claims.text: Formosus plotted against John VIII.
claims.note: The charges came from John VIII's camp in a time of bitter factions. Many historians think they were political.

claims.text: Arnulf was poisoned on Ageltrude's orders.
claims.note: Liutprand of Cremona tells it decades later. Arnulf probably had a stroke or similar illness.

reigns.hook: Formosus lies in his tomb in St Peter's. A riotous crowd picks Boniface VI, a priest twice thrown out of the clergy. And Formosus's enemies have not finished with him.

reigns.tagline: Twice defrocked, then pope for fifteen days

start.note: elected after the death of his predecessor

reigns.previously: Formosus dies weeks after crowning Arnulf emperor.
paragraphs: Formosus was barely in his tomb when a mob filled the streets of Rome and shouted for Boniface. He was a Roman, the son of a bishop named Hadrian, and a strange choice. He had been thrown out of the clergy twice for immorality, once as a subdeacon and once as a priest, and John VIII had never let him back. The crowd did not care.

He lasted about fifteen days. Then he was dead, and most sources say it was gout. Two years later a synod under John IX went back over his election, and ruled that it had been void from the start. The faction that backed him had a far bigger plan for the late Formosus.

claims.text: Boniface had twice been degraded from holy orders.
claims.note: The Roman synod of 898 says so when it cancelled his election, and John VIII's acts back it up.

claims.text: He died of gout.
claims.note: This is the usual report. Some historians suspect he was pushed aside or killed to make way for Stephen VI, but no source says so.

reigns.hook: Boniface is gone in a fortnight. His successor owes his bishopric to Formosus, and he hates him for it. Within a year he will drag his old patron out of the grave.

reigns.tagline: The pope who put a corpse on trial
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected; backed by the Spoleto clan
reigns.previously: Boniface VI dies after barely two weeks.
paragraphs: Stephen was a Roman and bishop of Anagni, and Formosus himself had consecrated him. That did not save Formosus. In January 897, with the Spoleto family back in charge of Rome, Stephen had his body dug up after nine months in the grave. It was dressed in full vestments and propped on a throne in the Lateran. A terrified deacon stood beside it to answer the charges.

Stephen raged at the corpse himself. The court found Formosus guilty of moving between sees and grabbing the papacy. They cut off the fingers he blessed with and threw the body in the Tiber. All his ordinations were cancelled, which suited Stephen, who could then count as a proper pope. Soon after, the Lateran basilica fell down. A Roman uprising threw Stephen in jail, and that summer he was strangled there.

claims.text: Formosus's corpse was tried, condemned and thrown in the Tiber.
claims.note: Writers of the next generation, Auxilius and Liutprand among them, describe it, and synods of 897 and 898 condemned the trial.

claims.text: The young emperor Lambert and his mother Ageltrude came to Rome to push for the trial.
claims.note: Their party clearly backed it, and some historians place them in Rome that winter; no source of the time puts them in the hall.

claims.text: The Lateran's collapse was God's verdict on the trial.
claims.note: The basilica really did fall about then, likely in an earthquake. The link was made by writers keen to see a sign.

reigns.hook: Stephen VI is strangled in his cell. The next pope probably sides with Formosus, but he won't last long enough to prove it.

reigns.tagline: Four months, then he simply vanishes
reigns.previously: A Roman rising throws Stephen VI in jail, where he is strangled.
paragraphs: Romanus came from Gallese, the same small town north of Rome as Marinus I, and was a cardinal priest when Stephen VI fell. He was probably on Formosus's side, and the Romans chose him in the late summer of 897 as the city cooled off after the trial of the corpse.

That is almost all we know. He reigned for about four months. Then, around November, he was removed, and the record goes quiet. The old lists say only that he was made a monk. We do not know who pushed him out, why, or when he died. A few small silver coins struck in his name are almost all that is left of him.

claims.text: Romanus was deposed and forced to become a monk.
claims.note: The early lists say he was later a monk, which may mean he was pushed out. They give no reason and no date.

claims.text: Romanus was a Formosan.
claims.note: Usually assumed, because his successor, who clearly was, followed so quickly. No act of his own survives to prove it.

reigns.hook: Romanus is gone, no one quite knows how. The next pope will last only about twenty days, but in that time he'll give Formosus his funeral back.

reigns.tagline: Twenty days to give a dead pope his tomb back
reigns.previously: Romanus is quietly removed after four months.
paragraphs: Theodore was a Roman, the son of a man named Photius, and his reign lasted about twenty days. He used them well. He called a synod that tore up the verdict of the Cadaver Synod. The priests and bishops Formosus had ordained, who had been stripped of their rank, got it back.

Then he dealt with the body. Formosus had been fished out of the Tiber after the trial, and Theodore had him carried back to St Peter's and buried again with full honours, in his vestments. Within weeks Theodore himself was dead, of what no one says. The fight over Formosus was far from over.

claims.text: Theodore reburied Formosus in St Peter's with full honours.
claims.note: Auxilius and Flodoard, writing within a generation, both say so.

claims.text: As the corpse was carried into St Peter's, the saints' images bowed to greet it.
claims.note: Liutprand of Cremona tells it decades later, as he heard it from pious old Romans.

reigns.hook: Theodore dies within weeks. The anti-Formosus party has its candidate ready, a deacon called Sergius. But a monk from Tivoli gets the throne instead.

reigns.tagline: The monk who banned putting the dead on trial
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected; rival of the future Sergius III
reigns.previously: Theodore II reburies Formosus, then dies within weeks.
paragraphs: John was a Benedictine monk from Tivoli, ordained a priest by Formosus himself. In early 898 two parties each chose a pope. One picked Sergius, a bishop who had sat at the Cadaver Synod. The other picked John, and John won, with the emperor Lambert of Spoleto behind him. Sergius was driven out and excommunicated. He would be back.

John made peace with real rules. Synods at Rome and Ravenna confirmed Formosus as a true pope, ordered the records of the Cadaver Synod burned, and banned trials of the dead. To stop riots, new popes were to be consecrated only with imperial envoys present. Then Lambert died in a hunting accident in October 898. John lost his protector, and Magyar raiders were already in northern Italy when he died in early 900.

claims.text: John's synods banned any future trial of a corpse.
claims.note: The decrees of the Rome and Ravenna synods of 898 survive.

claims.text: Sergius was elected pope in 898 and driven out by John's side.
claims.note: Sergius's own later epitaph says he was elected then; the Formosan writers call him an intruder.

reigns.hook: John IX is dead and his protector Lambert is gone too. The Romans choose a nobleman who will put a new emperor on the throne.

reigns.tagline: Kindly pope, blind emperor
reigns.previously: John IX dies, and his ally Lambert of Spoleto is already dead.
paragraphs: Benedict was a Roman nobleman, the son of a man named Mammalus, and another priest ordained by Formosus. In a grim age he had a good name. Flodoard of Reims praised his kindness to the poor. He backed his friends: in 900 he excommunicated the men who had murdered Archbishop Fulk of Reims.

Italy still needed an emperor, and Benedict picked young Louis of Provence, who had come over the Alps. He crowned him in Rome in February 901. It went badly. Berengar of Friuli fought back, and four years later caught Louis and blinded him. Benedict did not see that. Magyar horsemen were raiding northern Italy, and he died in the summer of 903. Rome's next election would not go quietly.

claims.text: Benedict crowned Louis of Provence emperor in 901.
claims.note: Louis's own charters and coins show the title, and coins naming Benedict and Louis survive.

claims.text: Benedict was unusually good and generous for his time.
claims.note: Flodoard says so in his verses on the popes. He wrote kindly of most Formosan popes.

reigns.hook: Benedict IV is dead. The clergy pass over the cardinals and choose a parish priest from the countryside. His own chaplain is already plotting against him.

reigns.tagline: A country priest betrayed by his own chaplain
reigns.previously: Benedict IV dies in the summer of 903.
paragraphs: Leo came from Ardea, south of Rome, and he was a plain parish priest. That was unusual. Popes were normally chosen from the cardinals of the city, and Leo was an outsider with no faction of his own. It did him no good at all.

Within about a month his own chaplain, a priest named Christopher, threw him off the throne and into prison, then took the papacy himself. The Church today counts Christopher as an antipope. He did not last either. In January 904 Sergius, the rival of 898, came back with soldiers, threw Christopher in the same prison, and became pope. Before long both prisoners were dead.

claims.text: Leo V and Christopher were both murdered in prison on Sergius III's orders.
claims.note: Auxilius and Eugenius Vulgarius say so, but they were pro-Formosan writers who hated Sergius. Other sources simply have the two men die.

claims.text: Leo was not a cardinal when elected.
claims.note: The papal lists call him a priest from outside Rome's cardinal clergy, which was rare.

reigns.hook: Leo rots in a cell, and Christopher soon joins him. The man who walks into Rome with soldiers is Sergius, who sat at the Cadaver Synod and never forgave Formosus.

reigns.tagline: He judged a corpse, then came back to rule with an army
reigns.previously: Leo V lasts weeks before his own chaplain throws him in jail.
paragraphs: Sergius was a Roman noble whom Formosus had made a bishop, and he still sat in judgement at the Cadaver Synod in 897. The next year Formosus's enemies chose him as pope, but the other side won, and he spent about six years in exile in Tuscany. Early in 904 he came back with soldiers lent by Alberic, Marquis of Spoleto. He threw out Christopher and took the throne.

Leo V and Christopher both died in prison soon after. Sergius then declared Formosus's ordinations void all over again, so priests and bishops had to be ordained a second time. He rebuilt the Lateran basilica, which had fallen down in the 890s. His muscle came from Theophylact, a noble who ran Rome's treasury and militia, and from Theophylact's wife Theodora and their daughter Marozia.
He died in April 911, still the Theophylact family's man. Their grip on Rome would last another forty years.

claims.text: Sergius had Leo V and Christopher strangled in prison.
claims.note: Auxilius and Eugenius Vulgarius, who wrote for Formosus's party, say so. They were his enemies, and no neutral source confirms it.

claims.text: Marozia, still a teenager, was Sergius's mistress and bore him the future John XI.
claims.note: Liutprand of Cremona, who loathed the Romans, says so. A brief papal list also calls John XI Sergius's son, so many historians accept it.

claims.text: Sergius rebuilt the Lateran basilica after its collapse.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis notice of his reign records the rebuilding.

reigns.hook: Sergius is dead, but Theophylact's family still holds the keys of Rome. Their next pope is a quiet Roman named Anastasius, and almost nothing he does will make it into the record.

reigns.tagline: Two quiet years under the eye of Rome's first family

start.note: elected after the death of his predecessor

reigns.previously: Sergius III dies in 911, leaving Theophylact's family in charge.
paragraphs: Anastasius was a Roman, son of a man named Lucian. He came to the throne in 911 with Theophylact and Theodora firmly in control of the city, and nothing suggests he ever tried to shake them off. A few of his grants survive, and a silver penny carries his name. That is close to all we have.

Trouble came in a letter from Constantinople. Sergius's envoys had approved the fourth marriage of the Byzantine emperor Leo VI, which Eastern church law banned. The patriarch Nicholas Mystikos, deposed for opposing it and now back in office, wrote to Anastasius in fury. Anastasius died in 913 and was buried in St Peter's.

claims.text: Nicholas Mystikos wrote to Anastasius protesting at Rome's approval of Leo VI's fourth marriage.
claims.note: The letter survives among Nicholas's collected letters.

claims.text: Anastasius was Sergius III's illegitimate son.
claims.note: A late and unsupported story. No source from the time says so.

reigns.hook: Anastasius is gone after two years. Theophylact's circle picks a Sabine noble named Lando. His reign will be short, but his name will stand alone for over a thousand years.

reigns.tagline: Six months, and a name no pope has used since
reigns.previously: Anastasius III dies around 913 after two quiet years.
paragraphs: Lando came from a noble family in the Sabine hills north-east of Rome; his father was called Taino. He was elected in 913, again with Theophylact's family running the city, and reigned about six months. Almost nothing he did is recorded.

His real claim to fame is his name. No later pope has ever chosen it, so he was the last pope with a name of his own until John Paul I in 1978. He died early in 914, and Theodora's party had a stronger man ready.

claims.text: Lando was the last pope with an unused name until John Paul I in 1978.
claims.note: It depends how you count. John Paul I combined two old names, and Francis in 2013 was the first truly new one since Lando.

claims.text: Lando was Theodora's puppet.
claims.note: Likely, given who ran Rome, but nothing he did or said is recorded either way.

reigns.hook: Lando dies within months. The new pope is the Archbishop of Ravenna, and Liutprand will claim he got the job because Theodora was in love with him.

reigns.tagline: The warrior pope who fought the Saracens and lost to Marozia
reigns.previously: Lando dies early in 914 after about six months.
paragraphs: John was born at Tossignano near Imola, served as a deacon in Bologna and became Archbishop of Ravenna. In 914 Theophylact's party brought him to Rome as pope. He was a doer. In December 915 he crowned Berengar I emperor. That year he stitched together Italian princes and a Byzantine fleet against the Saracen base on the Garigliano, and rode with the army that wiped it out.

Theophylact and Theodora died, and their daughter Marozia took over. John tried to build his own power, using his brother Peter and courting Hugh of Arles, the future king of Italy. Marozia married Guy of Tuscany and struck first. In 928 her men killed Peter in the Lateran in front of the pope.
John was deposed and locked up, probably in Castel Sant'Angelo. He died in prison, probably in 929.

claims.text: Theodora got John his archbishopric and then the papacy because she was his lover.
claims.note: Only Liutprand of Cremona says so, writing decades later and keen to smear Rome. The dates of his career fit badly.

claims.text: John X was smothered with a pillow in prison on Marozia's orders.
claims.note: Liutprand again. Flodoard of Reims, writing at the time, just says he died in custody.

claims.text: The pope rode with the army that destroyed the Saracen base on the Garigliano in 915.
claims.note: Liutprand and other Italian and Byzantine sources agree.

reigns.hook: John X sits in a cell, still alive. Marozia doesn't wait for him to die. She names a new pope, a Roman priest called Leo, while his predecessor is locked up across the city.

reigns.tagline: Elected while the last pope was still alive in a cell
reigns.previously: Marozia throws John X into prison and has his brother killed.
paragraphs: Leo was a Roman, son of an official named Christopher, and a cardinal priest of Santa Susanna. Marozia put him on the throne in 928 while John X was still alive in prison. He lasted about seven months.

Almost nothing he did is known. One letter survives, telling the bishops of Dalmatia to obey their archbishop at Split and to keep within their own dioceses. He died in December 928, and Marozia was still choosing popes.

claims.text: Leo VI was elected while John X was still alive in prison.
claims.note: John was deposed in 928 and Flodoard puts his death in custody later. Only the exact months are uncertain.

claims.text: Leo VI's letter to the Dalmatian bishops survives.
claims.note: It survives only in later copies, kept with the records of the Church of Split.

reigns.hook: Leo VI is dead, and Marozia's son is still too young to be pope. She needs someone harmless to keep the seat warm for a couple of years.

reigns.tagline: Keeping the throne warm for Marozia's son
reigns.previously: Leo VI dies after seven months. Marozia picks again.
paragraphs: Stephen was a Roman, son of a man named Theodemund, and cardinal priest of Sant'Anastasia. He took the throne at the end of 928, the second pope in a row chosen by Marozia while John X lay in prison.

He reigned a little over two years. A few charters survive, granting rights to monasteries in Italy and France. Beyond that the record is blank. He died early in 931, and Marozia's son was now old enough.

claims.text: Stephen was only keeping the seat warm until Marozia's son came of age.
claims.note: It fits the timing, and John XI followed him at once. No writer of the time says it outright.

claims.text: Charters of Stephen VII for monasteries survive.
claims.note: A handful of his grants are known from copies kept by the houses that received them.

reigns.hook: Stephen VII is dead. Marozia finally has the pope she has been waiting for: her own son, barely in his twenties.

reigns.tagline: Marozia's son, made pope by her and caged by his brother
reigns.reignEnded: Died a puppet of Alberic II
reigns.previously: Stephen VII dies early in 931. Marozia's son is now old enough.
paragraphs: John was Marozia's son, in his early twenties, and his mother made him pope in 931. In 932 she married her third husband, Hugh of Arles, King of Italy, in Castel Sant'Angelo, aiming to rule Rome as queen. Her other son, Alberic, had other plans. He raised the Romans against them. Hugh fled over the walls and Marozia was locked up. As far as anyone knows, she never came out.

Alberic now ruled Rome as prince. He kept his brother on the throne but confined him to church business, much like a prisoner in the Lateran. John could still sign papers, and in 931 he had granted Cluny Abbey the right to reform other monasteries. He died at the end of 935.

claims.text: John XI was the son of Sergius III.
claims.note: Liutprand of Cremona says so, and a brief papal list agrees. Some historians think his father was Marozia's first husband, Alberic I.

claims.text: Alberic turned on Hugh after the king slapped him for spilling water as he washed his hands.
claims.note: Liutprand tells the story. It may be a tidy explanation for a power grab that was coming anyway.

claims.text: Alberic left John only his spiritual duties.
claims.note: Flodoard of Reims, writing at the time, has John held under his brother's control; modern histories agree Alberic left him only church business.

reigns.hook: John XI is dead and Alberic chooses the next pope himself. His pick is a monk, and together they will invite the most famous abbot in Europe to clean up Rome.

reigns.tagline: The prince's pope who invited Cluny to Rome
reigns.previously: John XI dies, a prisoner in all but name of his brother Alberic.
paragraphs: Leo was a Roman, probably a monk, picked by Alberic II, who now ran Rome as its prince. Alberic wanted a pope who would pray, not plot. Leo fitted the bill.

His big move was to bring Odo, Abbot of Cluny, to Rome to reform its run-down monasteries. Alberic gave his own family house on the Aventine to become a monastery. Odo also tried to make peace between Alberic and his stepfather Hugh, King of Italy. Leo made Archbishop Frederick of Mainz his vicar in Germany. He died in July 939.

claims.text: Alberic gave his own house on the Aventine for a monastery reformed by Odo of Cluny.
claims.note: John of Salerno, Odo's disciple and biographer, records Odo's work in Rome; the site became Santa Maria on the Aventine.

claims.text: Leo told Frederick of Mainz not to force Jews to be baptised, but let him expel those who refused.
claims.note: Leo's letter to Frederick survives. Historians read it as a grim mix of restraint and pressure.

reigns.hook: Leo VII is dead. Alberic picks another pope he can trust, and this one will try to settle quarrels in faraway France.

reigns.tagline: Alberic's pope who took sides in France
reigns.previously: Leo VII dies in July 939, Alberic's quiet pope to the end.
paragraphs: Stephen was a Roman, and like Leo before him he owed his throne to Alberic. Inside Rome he had little room to act.

Abroad he could make a noise. In France the young king Louis IV, back from exile in England, was fighting his own great lords. In 942 Stephen sent a legate who told the Frankish nobles to accept Louis as king or be excommunicated. Some of them gave in. Stephen died in the autumn of 942.

claims.text: Stephen threatened the Frankish nobles with excommunication unless they submitted to Louis IV.
claims.note: Flodoard of Reims, who was close to events, records the legate's message.

claims.text: Alberic's men mutilated Stephen for plotting against him.
claims.note: The story appears in a chronicle written centuries later and is not found in any source from the time.

reigns.hook: Stephen VIII is dead. Alberic's next pope will be so obedient that a chronicler says he would not lift a finger without the prince's say.

reigns.tagline: The pope who did nothing without the prince's nod
reigns.previously: Stephen VIII dies in 942, after backing Louis IV of France.
paragraphs: Marinus was a Roman and Alberic's man from start to finish. He kept to church business, backing the reform of monasteries and guarding church property.

His name caused a muddle later. Medieval copyists confused Marinus with Martin, so the two popes Marinus were counted as Martin II and Martin III. That is why the next Pope Martin, in 1281, called himself Martin IV. Marinus died in the spring of 946.

claims.text: Marinus did nothing without Alberic's say-so.
claims.note: A 10th-century source says so. It fits everything else known of Alberic's grip on Rome.

claims.text: Because of a copying mistake, there were never popes called Martin II and Martin III.
claims.note: The Marinus-Martin confusion is well documented; Martin IV took his number from it in 1281.

reigns.hook: Marinus is dead. The next pope will win respect across Europe, but at home Alberic still holds the keys, and a German king is about to knock at the door.

reigns.tagline: He kept a German king out of Rome, for a while
reigns.previously: Marinus II dies in 946, Alberic's obedient pope to the end.
paragraphs: Agapetus was a Roman, and unlike the popes before him he made a mark abroad. In 948 his legate chaired a council at Ingelheim, in Germany, with King Otto I and Louis IV of France. It settled who was the rightful Archbishop of Reims and backed Louis against his rebels.

In 951 Otto took the Italian crown and asked to come to Rome to be crowned emperor. Agapetus said no, almost certainly because Alberic told him to. In 954 Alberic fell ill. Before he died he gathered the Roman nobles in St Peter's and made them swear to elect his son Octavian at the next vacancy. Agapetus died late in 955.

claims.text: Agapetus turned Otto I away in 952 on Alberic's orders.
claims.note: Flodoard reports the refusal. That Alberic was behind it is a near-certain guess, not a recorded fact.

claims.text: Alberic made the Romans swear to elect his son as the next pope.
claims.note: Benedict of Soracte and other sources record the oath, and the Romans kept it.

claims.text: The Ingelheim council of 948 met under a papal legate.
claims.note: Flodoard describes it in detail, and its acts survive.

reigns.hook: Agapetus II is dead, and the Romans keep their oath to Alberic. The new pope is his son Octavian, about 18, who would rather hunt and party than pray.

reigns.tagline: The teenage pope who crowned an emperor, then crossed him
reigns.reignEnded: Died, said to be in a lover's bed
reigns.previously: Alberic dies. The Romans have sworn to make his son pope.
paragraphs: Octavian, son of Alberic II, was prince of Rome and then pope, taking the name John XII. He was about 18. His enemies said he gambled, hunted and kept a harem in the Lateran. When Berengar, king of Italy, threatened the papal lands, John called in Otto I of Germany. On 2 February 962 he crowned Otto emperor in St Peter's, and Otto promised to protect the pope's territory.

Almost at once John started plotting with Otto's enemies. Otto came back in late 963, and John fled with the papal treasure. Otto's synod in St Peter's put him on trial in his absence, and the charges were spectacular: perjury, murder, incest and toasting the devil. In December he was deposed and a layman, Leo VIII, was made pope in his place.

As soon as Otto's back was turned, John returned and took his revenge on the men who had judged him. One had his hand cut off, others were whipped or mutilated. Then, in May 964, John suddenly collapsed and died. He was about 27.

claims.text: John XII died after being struck down in bed with a married woman, by the devil or by her husband.
claims.note: Liutprand of Cremona, Otto's spokesman and John's enemy, says the devil struck him. The jealous husband appears in later retellings.

claims.text: The synod's charges, such as toasting the devil, were true.
claims.note: Our account comes from Liutprand, who wrote for Otto. Even so, few historians doubt John lived wildly.

claims.text: Otto I promised in writing to protect the pope's lands in 962.
claims.note: The Diploma Ottonianum survives in a fine copy in the Vatican archives.

reigns.hook: The Romans elect Benedict V; Otto carts him off to Germany. For the next eighty years emperors and Roman clans will make and break popes, and one young pope will try to sell the job.

reigns.tagline: The scholar pope Otto dragged off to Hamburg
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Rival of Otto's pope, Leo VIII
reigns.reignEnded: Deposed by Otto, exiled to Germany
reigns.previously: John XII collapses and dies in May 964, aged about 27.
paragraphs: When John XII died, Rome already had another pope. Otto I had installed Leo VIII months earlier, but the Romans had never accepted him. They elected a cardinal deacon of their own, a learned man nicknamed the Grammarian, and he became Benedict V. The Romans swore to stand by him. To Otto, camped in Italy, it was plain rebellion.

The emperor marched on Rome and sealed it off. As food ran short, the city's nerve broke. In late June 964 the Romans opened the gates and handed Benedict over. At a synod in the Lateran, Leo VIII stripped him of his papal robes and broke his pastoral staff over his head. Benedict was allowed to stay a deacon, then sent north as a prisoner.

Otto put him in the care of Archbishop Adaldag of Hamburg, who treated him kindly. Benedict lived out his days there, teaching and praying on the northern edge of Christendom. He died in Hamburg, probably in July 965, and was buried there.

claims.text: Leo VIII broke Benedict's pastoral staff over his head at the synod.
claims.note: Told by the continuator of Regino's chronicle, who wrote for Otto's side. The scene may be dressed up, but the deposition itself is certain.

claims.text: Benedict V was the rightful pope and Leo VIII the usurper.
claims.note: Still argued. Leo was made pope while John XII was alive, Benedict was elected against the emperor's will, and the Vatican list counts both men.

claims.text: Otto III later had Benedict's bones brought back to Rome.
claims.note: Reported in medieval accounts, but the date and details of the move are unclear.

reigns.hook: Leo VIII is back on the papal throne, with an army to guard him. The Romans haven't forgotten their grammarian, and Leo has less than a year to live.

reigns.tagline: The layman made pope in a day, kept there by an army
reigns.previously: Otto starves Rome until it hands over Benedict V.
paragraphs: Leo was a Roman official, the city's chief notary, and not a priest at all. In December 963 Otto I needed a pope to replace John XII, whom his synod had just deposed. Leo was rushed through every grade of holy orders, from doorkeeper to priest, in a single day and consecrated bishop of Rome on 6 December. Church law banned that kind of shortcut, and his enemies never let anyone forget it.

The Romans hated him. They rose against Otto in January 964 and were cut down in the streets. As soon as the emperor left, John XII came back, and Leo fled to Otto's camp. A council under John declared him deposed. Then John died, the Romans chose Benedict V, and in June 964 Otto brought Leo back at the head of an army.

His second spell was short and quiet. He held the synod that broke Benedict's staff and relied on Otto for everything. He died early in 965. A century later, forgers put his name on documents that handed the emperor the right to choose popes.

claims.text: Leo was a layman rushed through all the holy orders at once.
claims.note: Reported by Liutprand of Cremona and the continuator of Regino, both on Otto's side, so this is not slander from his enemies.

claims.text: Leo VIII granted the emperor the right to choose all future popes.
claims.note: The so-called privileges of Leo VIII are forgeries, made in the fight between Henry IV and the reforming popes around the 1080s.

claims.text: Leo VIII, not Benedict V, was the lawful pope in 964.
claims.note: The Vatican list counts both men, and canon lawyers have argued over it ever since.

reigns.hook: Leo is dead, and the Romans ask for their grammarian back. Otto has other plans. His envoys are coming to watch the next election, and the city's barons are already plotting.

reigns.tagline: Otto's pope, jailed by the Romans and avenged
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Otto I's choice after Leo VIII
reigns.cameToPower: Elected with Otto I's envoys present
reigns.previously: Leo VIII dies in 965, with Benedict V still exiled in Hamburg.
paragraphs: After Leo VIII died, the Romans asked Otto to give them back Benedict V, but Benedict died in exile first. Otto sent envoys to oversee the next election. Their man was John, bishop of Narni, a Roman with a long career in the papal offices. He was elected on 1 October 965. He came from Rome's nobility, yet the city's barons saw him as the emperor's puppet.

Within three months they struck. In December 965 the city prefect Peter and his allies seized John, held him in Castel Sant'Angelo and then sent him off to a prison in Campania. He escaped, found protection with Pandulf Ironhead, prince of Capua, and in November 966 was back in Rome. Otto arrived soon after, in a fury.

The emperor hanged twelve leaders of the revolt. Prefect Peter was hung by his hair from the bronze horseman by the Lateran, the statue of Marcus Aurelius, then paraded on a donkey. With order restored, John crowned Otto's son Otto II co-emperor at Christmas 967. In April 972 he married Otto II to the Byzantine princess Theophanu and crowned her empress. He died that September.

claims.text: Prefect Peter was hung by his hair from the statue of Marcus Aurelius.
claims.note: Told in the short Roman life of John XIII. The statue stood by the Lateran and was then believed to show Constantine.

claims.text: John XIII belonged to the Crescentii clan.
claims.note: Some later sources link him to the family of John Crescentius and Theodora; others call him simply a Roman. The evidence is thin.

claims.text: John XIII crowned Theophanu empress in St Peter's on 14 April 972.
claims.note: Her marriage charter, written in gold on purple parchment, survives in the state archive at Wolfenbüttel.

reigns.hook: John is dead, and Otto I is getting old. When the emperor goes, the Roman clans will strike, and the next pope will learn how cold the cells of Castel Sant'Angelo can be.

reigns.tagline: Strangled in a castle cell once his emperor died
reigns.previously: John XIII dies in 972, after crowning a Byzantine bride empress.
paragraphs: Benedict was a Roman, the son of a man named Hildebrand, and a cardinal deacon. Elected in the autumn of 972, he had to wait months for the emperor's approval and was only consecrated on 19 January 973. He owed everything to Otto I, and the Roman clans knew it.

On 7 May 973 Otto died in Germany. His son Otto II was young and had his hands full north of the Alps. In June 974 Crescentius, head of Rome's strongest clan, rose with a deacon named Franco. They seized Benedict and locked him in Castel Sant'Angelo. Franco had himself made pope as Boniface VII.

An imperial envoy, Count Sicco, was on his way to demand Benedict's release. Before he got there, a priest called Stephen strangled the prisoner on Boniface's orders. Benedict had been pope for about eighteen months.

claims.text: Benedict VI was strangled in prison on the orders of Boniface VII.
claims.note: The outline is reported in the brief Roman lives of the popes and by later chroniclers. Boniface is now counted as an antipope.

claims.text: Crescentius directed the murder.
claims.note: Crescentius is named as leader of the revolt, but how far he was behind the killing itself is unclear.

reigns.hook: Boniface VII has the throne, but the Romans are turning on him and the emperor's men are coming. He grabs what he can from the papal treasury and runs for Constantinople. He'll be back.

reigns.tagline: The calm pope who outlasted a murderer
reigns.previously: Benedict VI is strangled in prison, and Boniface VII grabs the throne.
paragraphs: Boniface VII didn't last. The Romans turned on him, imperial troops closed in, and after about six weeks he fled to Constantinople with much of the papal treasure. The emperor's envoy, Count Sicco, then oversaw a fresh election in October 974. The choice fell on the bishop of Sutri, a nobleman from the family later known as the Counts of Tusculum.

Benedict VII brought something Rome had not had for years: calm. He ruled for almost nine years, backed monastic reformers and granted privileges to churches across Europe. When Boniface tried to come back in 980, Benedict had to leave Rome for a while, but Otto II brought him back the next year.

Otto spent Easter 981 in Rome with him, and that year a synod in St Peter's banned simony, the buying and selling of church posts. Benedict died in July 983 and was buried in Santa Croce in Gerusalemme. Rome's calm did not outlive him.

claims.text: Boniface VII fled to Constantinople with the papal treasure.
claims.note: Reported in the brief Roman lives and by later writers. How much he really took is unknown.

claims.text: Benedict VII belonged to the family later called the Counts of Tusculum.
claims.note: Later sources tie him to the kin of Alberic II, but the exact relationship is uncertain.

claims.text: A synod under Benedict VII condemned simony in 981.
claims.note: Its decree survives. Simony became the great target of church reformers in the century that followed.

reigns.hook: Benedict is dead. Otto II is in Rome and wants a pope he can trust, so he picks his own chancellor. But the emperor himself has only months to live.

reigns.tagline: The emperor's chancellor who died in a papal prison
reigns.previously: Benedict VII dies in July 983, after nine calm years.
paragraphs: Otto II did not trust the Romans to choose. In late 983 he named his own man: Peter Canepanova, bishop of Pavia and his chancellor for Italy. Peter took the name John XIV. No pope has ever called himself Peter II.

Within weeks his protector was gone. Otto II, only 28, fell ill with fever in Rome and died on 7 December 983. He was buried in the forecourt of St Peter's, the only Holy Roman emperor laid to rest there. His heir, Otto III, was three years old and far away in Germany.

That left John alone. In April 984 Boniface VII came back from Constantinople, with Byzantine money behind him. John was seized, beaten, deposed and thrown into Castel Sant'Angelo. He died there four months later, on 20 August 984, starved or poisoned.

claims.text: Boniface VII had John XIV starved or poisoned in his cell.
claims.note: The Roman sources agree he died in Boniface's prison. How he died is told in different ways, and the accounts are hostile to Boniface.

claims.text: Peter Canepanova changed his name so as not to be Peter II.
claims.note: Often said, and no pope has used the name since, but no writer of his own time gives his reason.

claims.text: Otto II is the only Holy Roman emperor buried in St Peter's.
claims.note: His sarcophagus now stands in the Vatican Grottoes beneath the basilica.

reigns.hook: Boniface VII is pope again, but not for long. Within a year he'll be dead, his body dragged through the streets, and the next pope will have to live with the Crescentii.

reigns.tagline: The pope who made the first official saint
reigns.previously: Boniface VII dies in 985, and the Romans drag his body through Rome.
paragraphs: Boniface VII died suddenly in July 985, perhaps murdered, and the Romans dragged his body through the city. Weeks later they elected John, a Roman cardinal priest and the son of a priest named Leo. Real power lay with Crescentius II, head of the Crescentii, who called himself patrician of the Romans. John lasted over ten years by keeping on the right side of him.

He mattered more abroad than at home. In 991 his envoy made peace between King Æthelred of England and Duke Richard of Normandy. Around the same time Mieszko I of Poland placed his lands under St Peter's protection. In 993 John declared Bishop Ulrich of Augsburg a saint, the first canonisation by a pope that we know of.

At home his name was poor. Critics said he loved money and gave posts to his relatives. In 995 he fell out with Crescentius and the clergy, fled to Tuscany and called on young Otto III for help. The Romans made peace and took him back, but he died of fever in March 996, before Otto arrived.

claims.text: John XV's canonisation of Ulrich in 993 was the first by a pope.
claims.note: His bull survives. Before this, saints were made by local acclaim or by bishops.

claims.text: John XV was greedy and gave church posts to his family.
claims.note: The charge comes partly from French bishops he crossed over the see of Reims, who painted Rome as corrupt.

claims.text: Mieszko I of Poland gave his lands to St Peter.
claims.note: Known from the Dagome iudex, a short summary copied a century later into Cardinal Deusdedit's collection of church law.

reigns.hook: Otto III is 15 and on his way to Rome to be crowned. With the papal throne empty, he won't wait for the Romans to choose. He has a cousin in mind.

reigns.tagline: The first German pope, and a terrible revenge
reigns.previously: John XV dies of fever, waiting for Otto III to rescue him.
paragraphs: Otto III, aged 15, was on his way to Rome when John XV died. He simply chose the next pope: his chaplain and cousin Bruno, son of the Duke of Carinthia and a great-grandson of Otto I. Bruno, about 24, became Gregory V, the first German pope. On 21 May 996 he crowned Otto emperor in St Peter's.

Rome had no love for a foreign pope. Months after Otto left, Crescentius II drove Gregory out. In 997 Crescentius set up a rival: John Philagathos, a Greek from Calabria who was Otto's own godfather. He called himself John XVI. Gregory, stuck in northern Italy, excommunicated Crescentius and waited.

In early 998 Otto came back. Philagathos fled but was caught. His eyes were put out, his nose, ears and tongue cut off, and he was paraded through Rome backwards on a donkey. Crescentius held out in Castel Sant'Angelo until April, then was beheaded and his body hung up for all to see. Gregory died in February 999, aged about 27.

claims.text: Gregory V was poisoned.
claims.note: Rumoured at the time. Nothing proves it, and fevers killed many northern visitors to Rome.

claims.text: Pope as well as emperor was to blame for Philagathos's treatment.
claims.note: The life of St Nilus of Rossano, who begged for mercy for Philagathos, blames them both. Other accounts put it on Otto's men.

claims.text: Gregory V was the first German pope.
claims.note: Earlier popes were Romans, Italians, Greeks or Syrians. Bruno came from the Salian family of Worms.

reigns.hook: Otto III needs a new pope. He turns to the cleverest man he knows, his old teacher, a scholar so brilliant that people will say he got his learning from the devil.

reigns.tagline: The genius pope of the year 1000, called a wizard
reigns.previously: Gregory V dies at about 27, a year after Otto's bloody return.
paragraphs: Gerbert of Aurillac was a poor boy from the Auvergne who became the most learned man in Europe. Trained as a monk, he studied in Catalonia, on the border of Muslim Spain, then made the cathedral school at Reims famous. He taught arithmetic on an abacus, showed the stars with spheres and wrote on geometry. Kings and emperors wanted him.

Politics was harder. His election as archbishop of Reims in 991 was challenged, and Pope John XV refused to accept it. Otto III took him in, made him his tutor and then archbishop of Ravenna. When Gregory V died, Otto made Gerbert pope, the first from France. He chose the name Sylvester, after the pope of Constantine's day. The hint was plain: Otto would be the new Constantine.

Together they dreamed of ruling a revived Roman Empire from Rome. Sylvester set up an archbishopric for Poland at Gniezno. In 1001 the Romans rose and drove both men out. Otto died in January 1002, aged 21. Sylvester went back to a Rome run by the Crescentii and died there in May 1003.

claims.text: Gerbert sold his soul to the devil and owned a brass head that answered questions.
claims.note: Told by William of Malmesbury about 1125. A scholar who had studied near Muslim Spain looked like a wizard to later monks.

claims.text: Gerbert helped bring Arabic numerals to Christian Europe.
claims.note: His abacus used counters marked with symbols close to Hindu-Arabic numerals, but how much he spread them is argued.

claims.text: Sylvester sent King Stephen of Hungary his crown.
claims.note: Hungarian tradition says so, and Thietmar says Stephen got a crown with the pope's blessing. The Holy Crown kept today is later work.

reigns.hook: Otto and Gerbert are both dead. Rome belongs to John Crescentius, son of the man Otto beheaded, and he wants popes who know their place.

reigns.tagline: The family man who was pope for five months
reigns.previously: Sylvester II dies in May 1003, a year after his emperor.
paragraphs: With Otto III dead and the new German king, Henry II, busy at home, Rome belonged to John Crescentius, son of the man Otto had beheaded. He called himself patrician and ran the city. When Sylvester II died, he made sure the next pope was his man: a Roman named Giovanni Sicco, who became John XVII.

Very little is known about him. Before he took holy orders he seems to have been married and had sons, which was not rare among Roman clergy then. He ruled for about five months and died on 6 November 1003, leaving Crescentius free to choose again.

claims.text: John XVII had been married and had sons.
claims.note: Recorded in later papal catalogues. Nothing more is known about his family.

claims.text: John Crescentius chose the popes from 1003 to 1012.
claims.note: Roman and German sources agree the Crescentii controlled papal elections until the clan's fall in 1012.

reigns.hook: Crescentius needs another pope. This time he picks a cardinal of St Peter's who will last longer, and who will win the favour of the new German king.

reigns.tagline: The pope who blessed Bamberg and ended as a monk
reigns.reignEnded: Said to have retired to a monastery
reigns.previously: John XVII dies in November 1003, after barely five months.
paragraphs: John Fasanus was a Roman, the son of a priest, and a cardinal priest of St Peter's when John Crescentius chose him around the turn of 1004. He lasted much longer than his predecessor, over five years, and kept on good terms with both the Crescentii and the German king, Henry II.

His best-known act came in 1007. Henry wanted a new bishopric at Bamberg, a favourite town of his, partly to spread the faith among the Slavs to the east. John gave it his blessing and placed it under papal protection. Bamberg Cathedral, where Henry and his wife Cunigunde lie buried, grew from that decision. In 1009, by most accounts, John gave up the papacy and died as a monk at St Paul Outside the Walls.

claims.text: John XVIII abdicated and died a monk at St Paul's.
claims.note: Reported in later papal catalogues. No writer of his time says why he went, or exactly when.

claims.text: John XVIII approved the new bishopric of Bamberg in 1007.
claims.note: Thietmar of Merseburg describes its founding, and the papal privilege for Bamberg survives.

reigns.hook: John XVIII is gone. Crescentius picks a shoemaker's son next, and his short reign will bring news from Jerusalem that shocks Christendom.

reigns.tagline: Pig's Snout, the shoemaker's son on Peter's throne
reigns.previously: John XVIII steps down and ends his days as a monk.
paragraphs: Pietro was a shoemaker's son from Rome who rose to be bishop of Albano. His nickname was Bucca Porci, Pig's Snout. Elected on 31 July 1009, he took the name Sergius instead of keeping his own name, Peter. As usual in those years, John Crescentius had approved the choice.

Within months came shocking news from the East. The Fatimid caliph al-Hakim ordered the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem torn down. A letter in Sergius's name calls on Christians to sail east and avenge it, which would make it the first call to crusade. Most historians think the letter was forged around the time of the First Crusade, nearly 90 years later.

Sergius was remembered for feeding the poor in a famine. He died on 12 May 1012. His patron John Crescentius died within days of him, and Romans whispered that both had been murdered. Either way, the Crescentii had lost their grip, and a rival clan was ready.

claims.text: Sergius IV called for a holy war after the Holy Sepulchre was destroyed.
claims.note: Aleksander Gieysztor argued that the letter is a forgery from about 1096, and most scholars agree. A few still defend it.

claims.text: He was nicknamed Pig's Snout.
claims.note: The name Bucca Porci is recorded in the papal catalogues. It may describe his face or be a family name.

claims.text: Sergius and John Crescentius were murdered.
claims.note: Their deaths so close together started the rumour. No source names a killer.

reigns.hook: Pope and patron are both dead. The Crescentii and the Counts of Tusculum each rush to name a pope, and the winner will decide who rules Rome for a generation.
