reigns.tagline: The count's son who crowned Henry II and fought pirates
reigns.previously: Sergius IV and his patron Crescentius die within days of each other.
paragraphs: The Counts of Tusculum, from the hills south-east of Rome, saw their chance. They put up Theophylact, son of Count Gregory, and he became Benedict VIII in May 1012. The Crescentii elected a rival, Gregory, who hurried north to King Henry II for support. Henry backed Benedict instead, and the rival faded from history.

On 14 February 1014 Benedict crowned Henry and his wife Cunigunde emperor and empress in St Peter's. Henry was surprised that Rome did not sing the Creed at Mass, as the Germans did, and Benedict agreed to add it, including the words saying the Holy Spirit comes from the Father and the Son. That line would sharpen the quarrel with the Greek Church.

Benedict was more warlord than scholar. In 1016 a fleet he raised with Pisa and Genoa beat Saracen raiders at Luni. He backed rebels against Byzantine rule in the south, and in 1020 went to Bamberg to rally Henry. In 1022, at Pavia, he attacked married priests. He died in April 1024, and his family kept the job.

claims.text: Benedict VIII had the Creed sung at Mass in Rome at Henry II's request.
claims.note: Berno of Reichenau, who came to Rome with Henry in 1014, reports the conversation.

claims.text: Benedict encouraged the first Norman adventurers to fight in southern Italy.
claims.note: Some chroniclers credit him with backing Melus of Bari and his Norman hirelings in 1017. The evidence is indirect.

reigns.hook: Benedict's brother Romanus has been running Rome as a layman. Now he'll go from layman to pope almost overnight. The Tusculans own the papacy outright.

reigns.tagline: A layman in the morning, pope by nightfall

start.note: elected after the death of his predecessor

reigns.previously: Benedict VIII dies in April 1024, and his family isn't letting go.
paragraphs: Romanus of Tusculum was the dead pope's brother and the real boss of Rome, a layman with the titles of consul and senator. The family wasn't about to let the throne slip. So he was rushed through every grade of holy orders in a single day and came out the other end as Pope John XIX.

Envoys from Constantinople soon arrived with gifts, asking him to let their patriarch call himself 'ecumenical', the universal bishop of the East. Reformers in the West howled, and the deal died. At Easter 1027 John crowned the German king Conrad II emperor in St Peter's, with Cnut, king of England and Denmark, in the crowd. Cnut came away with cheaper tolls for English pilgrims. John died in October 1032.

claims.text: John XIX nearly sold the Byzantines the title of 'ecumenical patriarch' for cash.
claims.note: Only Rodulfus Glaber tells it, and he says the outcry stopped it. No Greek or papal record mentions the deal.

claims.text: Cnut stood by at Conrad II's imperial coronation in Rome in 1027.
claims.note: Cnut's own open letter to the English, written on the journey home, describes the coronation and the concessions he won.

claims.text: The musician Guido of Arezzo showed John his new way of writing music, and the pope learned to sing a line at sight.
claims.note: Guido tells the story himself in a letter to a fellow monk, so it is his own word on it.

reigns.hook: The Tusculans have now held the papacy for 20 years. When John dies they go one better and put his nephew on the throne, a young man who will become the most notorious pope of the century.

reigns.tagline: The young count's son handed the keys of Rome

start.note: elected after the death of his predecessor

reigns.relationToPredecessor: Nephew of John XIX and Benedict VIII
reigns.reignEnded: Driven out by a Roman revolt
reigns.previously: John XIX dies in October 1032. His family already has a candidate.
paragraphs: Theophylact was the son of Count Alberic III of Tusculum and the nephew of the last two popes. His father paid for the votes, and the young man became Benedict IX. He was probably about 20, though one chronicler made him a mere boy.

He wasn't idle. He met Emperor Conrad II and did his bidding, excommunicating the rebel archbishop of Milan in 1038. But his enemies remembered him for his private life. Decades later Victor III wrote of rapes, murders and worse. In September 1044 the Romans had had enough. A revolt drove him out of the city, and the Tusculans' old rivals, the Crescentii, prepared a pope of their own.

claims.text: Benedict IX was only about ten or twelve when he became pope.
claims.note: Rodulfus Glaber says so, but he wrote from far away in Burgundy. Most historians think he was nearer 20.

claims.text: Benedict committed rapes and murders as pope.
claims.note: Victor III wrote this decades later as a committed reformer, and Peter Damian was just as fierce. Both were hostile witnesses.

claims.text: In 1038 he excommunicated Archbishop Aribert of Milan at Conrad II's request.
claims.note: Recorded in German and Italian sources on Conrad's campaign in Italy.

reigns.hook: Benedict has fled to the family castles in the hills. In January 1045 the rebels elect a bishop from the Sabine country. He has bought his way in too, they say, and he won't last long.

reigns.tagline: Seven weeks on the throne, then back to the hills
reigns.previously: A revolt drives Benedict IX out of Rome in September 1044.
paragraphs: John, bishop of Sabina, was the man the rebels picked. He was enthroned as Sylvester III on 20 January 1045, and the story went round that he had paid for the honour. He was very likely the Crescentii's man, the clan that had fought the Tusculans for Rome for half a century.

His reign was short. By 10 March Benedict IX's family had fought their way back into the city and Sylvester was out. He went home to his see in the Sabine hills and kept on being its bishop. At Sutri in December 1046 a synod deposed him anyway. It seems nobody bothered to enforce that, because he was still signing as bishop of Sabina years later.

claims.text: Sylvester III paid bribes to get elected.
claims.note: Later reform writers say so. They had every reason to paint all three of the 1046 claimants as simoniacs.

claims.text: He was a true pope, not an antipope.
claims.note: The Vatican's official list still counts him, but many historians call him an antipope because Benedict IX had not resigned.

claims.text: He was still bishop of Sabina into the 1060s.
claims.note: His name turns up on church documents as bishop there long after Sutri.

reigns.hook: Benedict IX is back on the throne. Then he does something no pope has ever done. He sells the job to his own godfather.

reigns.tagline: Back by force, then the papacy goes on sale
reigns.reignEnded: Sold the papacy to his godfather
reigns.previously: Sylvester III is thrown out of Rome after seven weeks.
paragraphs: Benedict IX had his throne back, and seven weeks later he seemed to want rid of it. His godfather, John Gratian, was a respected priest. He was worried about the state of the Church and had money to hand.

So they made a deal. On 1 May 1045 Benedict stepped down in Gratian's favour, and a large sum changed hands. Gratian saw it as buying the Church out of a bad man's grip. Many reformers agreed and cheered him on. Benedict retreated to the family lands, money in pocket, but he never quite accepted that he was finished.

claims.text: Benedict IX sold the papacy to John Gratian in 1045.
claims.note: The sources differ on the details and the price, but agree that money was paid and Benedict stood down.

claims.text: He gave up the papacy because he wanted to marry.
claims.note: The story of a bride, sometimes a cousin, only shows up in later writers. No source from 1045 says it.

claims.text: The sum was a thousand or two thousand pounds of silver.
claims.note: Different chroniclers give different figures, and none was there.

reigns.hook: John Gratian takes the name Gregory VI. He is honest and well meaning, but he bought the job. Soon three men will claim to be pope, and the German king is coming to Italy.

reigns.tagline: The honest man who bought the papacy
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Benedict IX's godfather; paid him off
reigns.previously: Benedict IX sells the papacy to his godfather for a fat sum.
paragraphs: John Gratian, archpriest of St John at the Latin Gate, became Gregory VI. Reformers like Peter Damian wrote to him full of hope. His chaplain was a young Roman cleric named Hildebrand, who would be heard from again. But Rome was broke and lawless, and Benedict IX and Sylvester III were still out there, each saying he was the true pope.

In 1046 the German king Henry III came south to be crowned emperor, and he needed a pope beyond reproach to do it. At Sutri, north of Rome, on 20 December he held a synod. Gregory admitted the money and was deposed, or resigned under pressure. Days later Benedict was deposed in Rome. Gregory was taken to Germany, Hildebrand going with him, and died there about a year later.

claims.text: Gregory VI resigned of his own free will at Sutri.
claims.note: Some accounts say he stepped down, others that the synod deposed him. Henry's men preferred the version that made the king look gentle.

claims.text: Hildebrand chose the name Gregory VII in his honour.
claims.note: A natural guess given their bond, but Hildebrand never said so.

claims.text: Henry III removed three claimants in December 1046.
claims.note: Sylvester and Gregory were dealt with at Sutri and Benedict at a synod in Rome a few days later.

reigns.hook: Henry III wants a clean sweep. His candidate, a German bishop, is elected on Christmas Eve and crowns him emperor the next day. The reformers have arrived.

reigns.tagline: The emperor's bishop who kept his old job
reigns.previously: At Sutri, Henry III clears out three rival popes at once.
paragraphs: Suidger, a Saxon noble and bishop of Bamberg, didn't want the job, but Henry III did not take no for an answer. He was elected on Christmas Eve 1046 as Clement II. The next day, Christmas Day, he crowned Henry and his wife Agnes emperor and empress in St Peter's. The Romans also gave Henry the title of patrician, which meant a say in every papal election from now on.

Clement got straight to work. A synod in January 1047 came down hard on simony, the buying and selling of church posts. He kept his Bamberg diocese too, a sign of where his heart lay. That autumn he fell ill on a journey and died at a monastery near Pesaro on 9 October. His body was carried back over the Alps to Bamberg, where it still lies, the only pope buried in Germany.

claims.text: Clement II was poisoned with lead.
claims.note: A study of his bones in the 1950s found high levels of lead. Rumour blamed Benedict IX's friends; lead was also used in medicine, so nobody can be sure.

claims.text: He is the only pope buried in Germany.
claims.note: His tomb is in Bamberg Cathedral, where his remains were examined in the 20th century.

claims.text: He crowned Henry III emperor on the day after his own election.
claims.note: Contemporary German annals give 25 December 1046 for both his consecration and the coronation.

reigns.hook: Clement is dead, Henry is back in Germany, and Rome has no pope. A familiar face slips back into the Lateran, for the third time.

reigns.tagline: Pope for the third time, and the last
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Seized the vacancy after Clement II
reigns.cameToPower: Took the Lateran with Tuscan help
reigns.previously: Clement II dies suddenly in October 1047, far from Rome.
paragraphs: Benedict IX had been deposed in Rome in December 1046, but he hadn't gone away. When Clement II died, Benedict marched back into the city on 8 November 1047. This time he had a powerful friend: Margrave Boniface of Tuscany, the strongest prince in northern Italy.

Henry III was having none of it. He named a new German pope and told Boniface to take him to Rome. Boniface stalled, until a furious letter from the emperor changed his mind. On 16 July 1048 Benedict was forced out for good. Summoned later to answer for his crimes, he never came, and he was excommunicated. He slipped back into the Tusculan hills and out of history, dying around 1056.

claims.text: Benedict IX died a penitent monk at Grottaferrata.
claims.note: The abbey near his family's lands claimed him and keeps a gravestone, but the story comes from much later monastic tradition.

claims.text: Boniface of Tuscany backed Benedict's return until the emperor threatened him.
claims.note: Told by Bonizo of Sutri and accepted by modern histories of the papacy. The emperor's letter itself does not survive.

claims.text: Benedict IX is the only man to have been pope three separate times.
claims.note: No other pope held the office in three separate spells.

reigns.hook: Benedict is gone, and Henry's next German bishop rides into Rome under Tuscan guard. It's the middle of summer, the season when Rome kills strangers.

reigns.tagline: Twenty-three days, then the summer fever
reigns.previously: Benedict IX is driven out of Rome for good in July 1048.
paragraphs: Poppo was a Bavarian and bishop of Brixen in the Alps. Henry III picked him at Christmas 1047, but it took more than six months, and an imperial threat to Boniface of Tuscany, to get him into Rome. He was enthroned as Damasus II on 17 July 1048.

Rome in July was a dangerous place for a man from the mountains. Within weeks Damasus had left for the hill town of Palestrina to escape the heat. It didn't help. He died there on 9 August, just 23 days after his enthronement, and was buried in San Lorenzo outside the walls. Two German popes in a row had died within a year of arriving.

claims.text: Damasus II died of malaria.
claims.note: The most likely explanation for a sudden death in the Roman summer, but no source names the illness.

claims.text: Benedict IX's followers poisoned him.
claims.note: The rumour went round at the time, as it had for Clement II. There is no evidence for it.

claims.text: He was buried in San Lorenzo fuori le Mura.
claims.note: His tomb is still in the basilica.

reigns.hook: The Romans are muttering that the papacy kills Germans. Henry needs a man who isn't afraid, and he turns to his own cousin, a tough Alsatian bishop who has a condition of his own.

images.caption: His tomb in the basilica of San Lorenzo outside the walls, Rome. No portrait of him survives.

reigns.tagline: The travelling pope who rode out to war
reigns.cameToPower: Named by Henry, acclaimed by Rome
reigns.reignEnded: Died in Rome after Norman captivity
reigns.previously: Damasus II dies of fever at Palestrina after just 23 days.
paragraphs: Bruno of Egisheim-Dagsburg, Alsatian count's son and bishop of Toul, was the emperor's kinsman. He said yes on one condition: Rome itself must elect him. He walked in dressed as a pilgrim and was enthroned as Leo IX in February 1049. He brought in sharp reformers: Humbert, Frederick of Lorraine, and the young Hildebrand back from exile.

Then he hit the road. At Reims in 1049 he made every bishop swear whether he had paid for his office, and sacked the ones who couldn't. Few popes had ever been seen north of the Alps, and Leo crossed them again and again. In 1053 he led an army against the Normans in the south, and they crushed it at Civitate on 18 June. He spent nine months as their honoured prisoner and died in Rome soon after his release.

Three months after his death his legate Humbert walked into Hagia Sophia and slammed a bull of excommunication on the altar against Patriarch Michael Cerularius. The patriarch excommunicated him back. It became the symbol of the split between East and West.

claims.text: Leo came to Rome barefoot as a pilgrim and refused to be pope unless the Romans chose him.
claims.note: Told in his Life, written by an admirer soon after his death, which makes the scene suspiciously perfect.

claims.text: Humbert's bull of 1054 was legally void, since the pope who sent him was already dead.
claims.note: Canon lawyers have long argued it, though Humbert acted as Leo's legate in good faith.

claims.text: Miracles were reported at his tomb, and he was soon venerated as a saint.
claims.note: His followers recorded the miracles; he has been honoured as St Leo IX ever since.

reigns.hook: Leo is dead and the Normans are stronger than ever. Henry III takes his time choosing again. In the end he gives up his most trusted adviser, and he doesn't do it happily.

reigns.tagline: The emperor's right-hand man, at his deathbed
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Henry III's adviser, chosen after Leo
reigns.previously: Leo IX dies in Rome, and the see stays empty for almost a year.
paragraphs: Gebhard, bishop of Eichstätt, was Henry III's closest adviser, and the emperor hated to lose him. It took a year of talks with a Roman delegation led by Hildebrand before Gebhard agreed, on terms of his own. He was enthroned as Victor II in April 1055, and he kept his German diocese, just in case.

He held a big reform synod at Florence with Henry in 1055. In 1056 he went north and was at Henry's bedside when the emperor died that October. The heir, Henry IV, was five. Victor got the princes to accept the boy, with his mother Agnes as regent, and made peace between the crown and its enemies. Back in Italy, he died of fever at Arezzo in July 1057.

claims.text: The people of Ravenna seized Victor's body on its way home to Eichstätt and buried it in their own city.
claims.note: An Eichstätt writer tells it. It explains why he lies in Ravenna, but the story may have grown in the telling.

claims.text: Victor was with Henry III when he died and took charge of the succession.
claims.note: German annals record him at Bodfeld in October 1056 and at the settlement that followed.

claims.text: He drove a hard bargain before agreeing to be pope.
claims.note: Contemporary sources say he demanded that Henry return lands taken from the Roman church.

reigns.hook: Victor II was the last of Henry's German popes, and now Henry is gone too. With a child on the German throne, the reformers in Rome decide not to wait for anyone's permission.

reigns.tagline: The abbot elected without asking the Germans
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Leo IX's chancellor, elected in Rome
reigns.cameToPower: Elected in Rome without German say
reigns.reignEnded: Died at Florence after eight months
reigns.previously: Victor II dies at Arezzo. With Henry III gone, Rome acts alone.
paragraphs: Frederick of Lorraine had been Leo IX's chancellor, and he stood beside Humbert in Hagia Sophia in 1054. His brother, Duke Godfrey the Bearded, had married the widow of Boniface of Tuscany and now ruled half of northern Italy. That made Frederick suspect to Henry III, and he took refuge as a monk at Monte Cassino and became its abbot in 1057.

When Victor died, the Romans elected Frederick within days. Nobody waited to hear from the German court; Hildebrand was sent north afterwards to get the regent's blessing. As Stephen IX he made the fiery hermit Peter Damian a cardinal and pushed reform hard. But he was already ill. He died at Florence on 29 March 1058, after ordering that no pope be chosen until Hildebrand returned.

claims.text: Stephen IX planned to make his brother Godfrey emperor.
claims.note: Leo of Ostia, the Monte Cassino chronicler, hints at it. There is no proof of a real plan.

claims.text: He was elected without waiting for the German court's approval.
claims.note: Contemporary sources agree, and Hildebrand's mission to Empress Agnes came afterwards.

claims.text: He ordered that no election be held until Hildebrand came back from Germany.
claims.note: Reported by Peter Damian and others close to the reformers.

reigns.hook: The dying pope's orders are ignored. Within a week the Roman nobles have crowned their own pope, Benedict X. Hildebrand races home with a candidate of his own.

reigns.tagline: The pope who gave the vote to the cardinals
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected by reformers against Benedict X
reigns.cameToPower: Chosen at Siena, enthroned by force
reigns.previously: Stephen IX dies at Florence, and the Roman nobles grab the papacy.
paragraphs: The Tusculans and their allies made John, bishop of Velletri, pope as Benedict X. The reform cardinals fled and met at Siena in December 1058. There they elected Gerard, bishop of Florence, a Burgundian. Duke Godfrey's soldiers took him to Rome, Benedict ran, and Gerard was enthroned in January 1059 as Nicholas II.

At a Lateran synod that April he issued a decree that changed everything: from now on the cardinal bishops would pick the pope, the other cardinals would agree, and the clergy and people would just cheer. In August he went to Melfi and made peace with the Normans, Leo IX's old enemies. Robert Guiscard knelt as the pope's vassal and became duke of Apulia, Calabria and, once he conquered it, Sicily.

claims.text: The 1059 election decree put the choice of pope in the hands of the cardinals.
claims.note: The decree survives, though in two versions; one of them gives the German king a bigger role and is probably a later forgery.

claims.text: The Normans helped hunt down Benedict X.
claims.note: Norman troops besieged him at Galeria in 1059, and he gave himself up.

claims.text: German bishops declared Nicholas's decrees void in 1061.
claims.note: Reported by Peter Damian, an angry witness. The details of the German synod are unclear.

reigns.hook: Nicholas is dead, and the cardinals get to try out his new rules. The German court is furious at being left out and picks a pope of its own. Rome is heading for a schism.

reigns.tagline: Elected by cardinals, opposed by the court
reigns.relationToPredecessor: First pope elected under the 1059 rules
reigns.previously: Nicholas II dies at Florence. The cardinals will choose alone.
paragraphs: Anselm of Baggio was a Milanese noble, bishop of Lucca and a friend of the street reformers of Milan, the Patarenes. On 30 September 1061 the cardinals elected him under the new rules, and the Normans got him into Rome. The German court and the Lombard bishops answered by naming Cadalus, bishop of Parma, as Honorius II. For two years the rivals fought in and around the city.

A palace coup in Germany in 1062 swung the court behind Alexander, and a council at Mantua in 1064 settled it. Through it all Hildebrand, now archdeacon, was his right hand. Alexander pushed reform from Milan to Spain and backed the Normans in Sicily. In 1066 he gave his blessing to Duke William of Normandy's invasion of England. He died in Rome in April 1073.

claims.text: Alexander II sent William of Normandy a papal banner for the invasion of 1066.
claims.note: William of Poitiers, the duke's own chaplain, says so. No papal record survives.

claims.text: Cadalus held out in Castel Sant'Angelo for a long time, helped by the Roman Cencius family.
claims.note: Reform writers and his own supporter Benzo of Alba both mention it; how long he held out is unclear.

claims.text: Hildebrand ran the papacy behind Alexander.
claims.note: Enemies said so. Alexander was a reformer in his own right, but Hildebrand's hand is plain in many of his acts.

reigns.hook: April 1073. At Alexander II's funeral the crowd starts shouting a name. It belongs to the little archdeacon who has been running things for years.

reigns.tagline: The monk who made an emperor stand in the snow
reigns.previously: Alexander II dies. His archdeacon has run things for years.
paragraphs: Hildebrand was small, plain and fearless. The crowd at Alexander II's funeral demanded him, and the cardinals agreed. As Gregory VII he set out to free the Church from lay control. In his register sits a list of claims called the Dictatus Papae. Among them: the pope can be judged by no one, and the pope alone may depose emperors.

The clash came over who appointed bishops, the Investiture Controversy. The young German king Henry IV had his bishops declare Gregory deposed. Gregory excommunicated Henry, and the German princes began to desert their king. In January 1077 Henry crossed the Alps in winter and stood outside the castle of Canossa as a penitent until Gregory lifted the ban.

The peace didn't last. Gregory excommunicated Henry again in 1080, and Henry set up his own pope, Clement III. In 1084 Henry took Rome. Gregory's Norman allies under Robert Guiscard drove him out, then sacked the city. The Romans blamed the pope. Gregory left with the Normans and died at Salerno the next year.

claims.text: Henry IV stood barefoot in the snow at Canossa for three days.
claims.note: Gregory's own letter says Henry stood three days at the gate, barefoot and in wool. The snow and cold come from the chronicler Lampert. Both were hostile to Henry.

claims.text: His dying words were: 'I have loved justice and hated iniquity, therefore I die in exile.'
claims.note: Reported by his admirers. It echoes Psalm 45, which makes it sound like a line polished afterwards.

claims.text: The Dictatus Papae was written in Gregory's papal register in 1075.
claims.note: The original register survives in the Vatican. Whether the list was ever published at the time is unclear.

reigns.hook: Gregory dies in exile, with Henry's pope sitting in Rome. His cardinals want Desiderius, the rich abbot of Monte Cassino, who wants nothing to do with it. Victor III will not last long.

reigns.tagline: The abbot who ran away from the papacy
reigns.previously: Gregory VII dies in exile at Salerno, with Henry's antipope in Rome.
paragraphs: Desiderius came from the ruling family of Benevento and ran away from home to become a monk. As abbot of Monte Cassino from 1058 he made Saint Benedict's old house the grandest abbey in Italy. He rebuilt its church, brought in mosaic artists from Constantinople, filled its library and stayed friends with the Normans of the south, whose swords kept the reform popes alive.

Gregory VII died in May 1085, and for a year nobody wanted the job. On 24 May 1086 the cardinals dragged Desiderius into it as Victor III. Four days later riots drove him out of Rome. He went home to his abbey, took off the papal robes and refused to come back. Only in March 1087, at a synod in Capua, did he give in.

Norman troops took him to St Peter's, and he was consecrated there on 9 May 1087, while the antipope Clement III's men still held other parts of the city. That summer he held a council at Benevento that renewed the ban on lay investiture. Then he fell ill. He went back to Monte Cassino, urged the cardinals to choose Odo of Ostia, and died there on 16 September 1087.

claims.text: Desiderius appears in a fresco at Sant'Angelo in Formis with a square halo, the sign of a living donor.
claims.note: The fresco in the church he paid for near Capua survives, painted while he was abbot. It is a donor portrait in a set style, so how far it shows his real face is unknown.

claims.text: Victor blessed an Italian fleet that sacked the Muslim port of Mahdia in North Africa in 1087.
claims.note: Said by the Monte Cassino chronicle. Pisan and Genoese sources describe the raid but say little about the pope's part.

claims.text: Victor was poisoned.
claims.note: A rumour picked up by some chroniclers in the north. The Monte Cassino writers, who were there, describe a long illness.

reigns.hook: Victor is dead, and Rome is still split between two popes. His cardinals take his advice and turn to Odo of Ostia, a French noble who trained at Cluny.

reigns.tagline: The pope who launched the First Crusade
reigns.previously: Victor III dies at Monte Cassino, months after his consecration.
paragraphs: After Gregory VII came Victor III, the abbot of Monte Cassino, who was ill and lasted only a year. Then the cardinals met at Terracina, south of Rome, because the antipope Clement III held the city. They chose Odo, a French nobleman, a former monk of Cluny and bishop of Ostia. He took the name Urban II. For years he could barely set foot in his own capital.

Urban was smoother than Gregory. He won friends, built alliances and slowly took back Rome. In March 1095 envoys from the Byzantine emperor came to his council at Piacenza asking for soldiers against the Turks. Urban had a bigger idea. On 27 November 1095, in a field outside Clermont in France, he called on the knights of the West to march east and free Jerusalem.

The response stunned everyone. Tens of thousands took the cross. After three brutal years the crusaders took Jerusalem on 15 July 1099 and slaughtered many of its people. Urban died in Rome two weeks later, on 29 July, before the news could reach him.

claims.text: The crowd at Clermont roared 'Deus vult!', 'God wills it!'
claims.note: Our versions of the speech were written years later by men such as Robert the Monk and Fulcher of Chartres, and they differ a lot.

claims.text: Urban died without learning that Jerusalem had fallen.
claims.note: He died on 29 July 1099, two weeks after the city fell. News took weeks to travel from Palestine to Rome.

claims.text: Urban promised crusaders full remission of the penance for their sins.
claims.note: A canon of the Council of Clermont says so, though exactly what was promised was soon inflated.

reigns.hook: The crusaders hold Jerusalem, but the man who sent them never knew. The new pope, Paschal II, will soon learn what Henry IV's son thinks of popes.

reigns.tagline: The pope who was arrested in St Peter's
reigns.cameToPower: Elected two weeks after Urban died
reigns.previously: Urban II dies in Rome two weeks after his crusaders take Jerusalem.
paragraphs: Raniero was a monk from near Viterbo whom Gregory VII had made a cardinal. Elected in August 1099, he quickly saw off the antipope Clement III, who died in 1100, and then three more short-lived rivals. In England he settled the fight over bishops with Henry I in 1107: the king gave up investing them with ring and staff, and they still paid him homage for their lands.

The new German king, Henry V, wanted his imperial crown. In February 1111 Paschal offered a startling bargain: the bishops would hand back every land and right they held from the crown, and Henry would stop investing them. When the deal was read out in St Peter's on 12 February, the bishops exploded. Henry seized the pope and his cardinals on the spot.

After two months as a prisoner Paschal gave Henry the right of investiture and crowned him emperor on 13 April 1111. Reformers howled, and in 1112 a Lateran synod tore up the grant. Paschal never quite recovered his standing. When Henry returned to Rome in 1117 the pope fled south, and he died in January 1118, soon after coming back to the city.

claims.text: Henry V arrested Paschal and his cardinals in St Peter's in February 1111.
claims.note: Described in several accounts, including the papal biography in the Liber Pontificalis and the German chronicler Ekkehard of Aura, from opposite sides.

claims.text: Paschal was a monk of Cluny before Gregory VII made him a cardinal.
claims.note: Later writers say so, but no record from Cluny itself confirms it, and some historians doubt it.

reigns.hook: Paschal dies with Henry V's army never far away. The cardinals rush to elect his old chancellor, John of Gaeta, and forget to ask the Frangipani.

reigns.tagline: Beaten, chained and chased out of Mass
reigns.previously: Paschal II dies in Rome, never free of his surrender to Henry V.
paragraphs: John of Gaeta had run the papal chancery for almost thirty years and given its letters a polished new Latin style. On 24 January 1118 the cardinals met quietly in a monastery on the Palatine and elected him. Within minutes Cencio Frangipane, head of a powerful Roman clan, broke in with armed men, grabbed the new pope by the throat, kicked him and dragged him off in chains.

The Romans rescued him, but then Henry V marched into Rome. Gelasius fled by boat to his home town of Gaeta and was consecrated there. Henry answered by making the archbishop of Braga pope as Gregory VIII. When Gelasius slipped back to Rome that summer, the Frangipani attacked him again while he said Mass at Santa Prassede, and he escaped on horseback, still half in his vestments.

He gave up on Rome and sailed for France. He reached Cluny, the great Burgundian abbey, already sick, and died there on 29 January 1119, a year and five days after his election. The few cardinals with him chose his successor on the spot.

claims.text: Cencio Frangipane seized Gelasius by the throat, beat him and carried him off in chains.
claims.note: Told by Pandulf, a papal clerk who was there, in his life of Gelasius in the Liber Pontificalis. He is on the pope's side, but the attack is not in doubt.

claims.text: Gelasius fled Santa Prassede on horseback, still dressed for Mass.
claims.note: Pandulf again; the details of his escape may have grown in the telling.

reigns.hook: Gelasius is dead in a monastery far from Rome. The cardinals at his bedside need someone the emperor can't bully. They turn to a man with kings in his family.

reigns.tagline: The count's son who ended the investiture war
reigns.previously: Gelasius II dies at Cluny, a year after being dragged off in chains.
paragraphs: Guy of Burgundy was a count's son with royal connections everywhere: his niece was queen of France, and his brother had married the heiress of Castile. As archbishop of Vienne he had already excommunicated Henry V in 1112. The handful of cardinals at Cluny elected him in February 1119, and he took the name Callixtus II. Rome accepted him, and he entered the city in triumph in 1120.

The emperor's pope, Gregory VIII, had fled to Sutri. In April 1121 Callixtus's troops took the town and dragged the antipope back to Rome on a camel, facing its tail, while the crowds jeered. He spent the rest of his life locked in monasteries.

Then Callixtus made peace. The Concordat of Worms, sealed on 23 September 1122, ended half a century of fighting: churches would elect their bishops freely, and the emperor could watch and grant them their lands. The First Lateran Council confirmed it in 1123, the first general council held in the West. Callixtus died in Rome on 13 December 1124.

claims.text: The antipope Gregory VIII was paraded into Rome on a camel, facing backwards.
claims.note: Reported by several chroniclers. A camel was a deliberate insult: it marked him as a mock pope.

claims.text: Under the Concordat of Worms the emperor gave up investing bishops with ring and staff.
claims.note: Both halves of the agreement survive. In Germany the emperor could still be present at elections and hand over the lands with a sceptre.

reigns.hook: Callixtus dies in Rome. As the cardinals install their choice, the Frangipani burst in with swords and shout for a different man, the bishop who wrote the Worms treaty.

reigns.tagline: Made pope at sword-point, then elected properly
reigns.previously: Callixtus II dies in Rome, two years after the Concordat of Worms.
paragraphs: Lamberto Scannabecchi came from a modest family near Imola and rose to be cardinal-bishop of Ostia. He had negotiated the Concordat of Worms for Callixtus. In December 1124 the cardinals chose another man, who took the name Celestine. In the middle of the ceremony the Frangipani clan burst in with armed men and acclaimed Lamberto instead. Celestine stepped aside. Lamberto resigned a few days later and was elected again, properly this time.

As Honorius II he backed Lothair of Supplinburg as German king in 1125 and approved new orders, the Premonstratensian canons in 1126 and the Knights Templar at the Council of Troyes in 1129. He tried to stop Roger II of Sicily taking over the Norman south, failed, and in 1128 had to make him duke of Apulia.

When he fell gravely ill in February 1130, his chancellor Haimeric and the Frangipani had him carried to the monastery of San Gregorio on the Celian Hill, their stronghold. He died there on the night of 13 February, and his allies made sure they controlled what happened next.

claims.text: Honorius took office only after the Frangipani forced out the cardinals' first choice, Celestine.
claims.note: Told in the papal biography and by other contemporaries. Lamberto's resignation and re-election were meant to clean it up.

claims.text: Honorius approved the Rule of the Knights Templar.
claims.note: The rule was drawn up at the Council of Troyes in 1129 under his legate, Matthew of Albano. No papal approval from Honorius himself survives.

reigns.hook: Honorius is barely cold. That same night a few cardinals elect one man in secret and bury the old pope in a hurry. By morning the rest have chosen someone else.

reigns.tagline: Elected at night, exiled by day, saved by a saint
reigns.previously: Honorius II dies in a monastery held by the Frangipani clan.
paragraphs: Gregorio Papareschi was a Roman from Trastevere. On the night of 13 February 1130, with Honorius dying, a minority of cardinals led by the chancellor Haimeric elected him in secret. Hours later most of the other cardinals chose Pietro Pierleoni, from a rich Roman family of Jewish descent, as Anacletus II. Anacletus had the money and the city. Innocent fled to France.

Then Bernard of Clairvaux took up his cause. The great Cistercian abbot travelled Europe and won over the kings of France and England and the German king Lothair. Only Roger II of Sicily backed Anacletus, who made him a king. Lothair escorted Innocent to Rome and was crowned emperor in 1133. The schism ended when Anacletus died in 1138 and his successor gave in.

In 1139 Innocent held the Second Lateran Council and marched against Roger, who ambushed and captured him. To get free he had to confirm Roger as king of Sicily. Innocent rebuilt Santa Maria in Trastevere, where his mosaic portrait still survives. In 1143 the Romans, furious at his deal with their rival Tivoli, rose, set up a senate and defied him. He died that September.

claims.text: Anacletus II was mocked by Innocent's side as the 'Jewish pope'.
claims.note: His great-grandfather was a Jewish convert. Bernard of Clairvaux and other Innocent supporters used this against him.

claims.text: Innocent was captured by Roger II's army at Galluccio in July 1139.
claims.note: Recorded by Falco of Benevento and other southern chroniclers. The Treaty of Mignano followed days later.

reigns.hook: Innocent dies with the Romans in open revolt. The cardinals pick an elderly scholar who studied under Abelard, the man Innocent condemned.

reigns.tagline: Abelard's old pupil, first in a famous fake prophecy
reigns.cameToPower: Elected two days after Innocent died
reigns.previously: Innocent II dies with the Romans in revolt and a senate defying him.
paragraphs: Guido came from Città di Castello in Umbria and had studied under Peter Abelard, the brilliant and much-condemned teacher. He kept Abelard's books and stayed loyal to his old master even after Innocent II condemned him. The cardinals elected Guido unanimously within two days of Innocent's death. He took the name Celestine II.

He was old and he had only five months. His best-known act was making peace with Louis VII of France, lifting the interdict Innocent had laid on the king's lands after a fight over who would be archbishop of Bourges. Meanwhile the Roman commune and its new senate kept their grip on the city. Celestine died in Rome on 8 March 1144.

claims.text: Celestine is the first pope named in the 'Prophecy of St Malachy', which gives a motto for every pope to the end of the world.
claims.note: The list was first printed in 1595 and is almost certainly a forgery of about 1590. Its mottoes are uncannily apt up to then and vague after.

claims.text: Celestine had been a pupil of Peter Abelard.
claims.note: Generally accepted. Letters show Abelard's opponents worried about Guido's loyalty to him, but where and when he studied is unclear.

reigns.hook: Celestine dies after five months. His successor, a Bolognese chancellor, will try to take back the Capitol from the Romans by force.

reigns.tagline: The pope who stormed the Capitol
reigns.previously: Celestine II dies after five months, with the commune ruling Rome.
paragraphs: Gherardo Caccianemici came from Bologna, had been a canon and a papal legate in Germany, and served as chancellor under Innocent II. As Lucius II he inherited a city in revolt. The Roman commune had made Giordano Pierleoni, brother of the dead antipope Anacletus, its patrician and demanded that the pope give up all his worldly power and live on tithes and offerings.

Lucius asked the German king Conrad III for help, and none came. In February 1145 he led an armed force of his own against the senators on the Capitol. The attack failed. Within days, on 15 February, he was dead.

claims.text: Lucius was hit by a stone during the attack on the Capitol and died of his injuries.
claims.note: Godfrey of Viterbo tells it decades later. Writers closer to the time say only that he died soon after the failed assault.

claims.text: The commune made Giordano Pierleoni its patrician in 1144.
claims.note: Recorded by Otto of Freising and other chroniclers.

reigns.hook: Lucius is dead after storming the Capitol. On the same day the cardinals pick a Cistercian abbot who isn't even a cardinal, and Bernard of Clairvaux can hardly believe it.

reigns.tagline: The monk who launched the Second Crusade
reigns.previously: Lucius II dies after leading a failed assault on the Capitol.
paragraphs: Bernardo of Pisa was abbot of a small Cistercian house outside Rome and had once been a monk at Clairvaux under Bernard himself. The cardinals elected him the day Lucius died. The Romans would not let him be consecrated, so he slipped away to the abbey of Farfa. He spent most of his reign outside Rome, which the commune and the radical preacher Arnold of Brescia held.

When news came that the crusader county of Edessa had fallen to Zengi, Eugene issued a bull in December 1145 calling a new crusade. Bernard preached it, and the kings of France and Germany took the cross. The Second Crusade ended in humiliation outside Damascus in 1148. Bernard wrote him a long book of advice, On Consideration, warning him about the pomp of the papal court.

In 1153 Eugene made a treaty at Constance with the new German king, Frederick Barbarossa: Frederick would restore papal rule in Rome, and the pope would crown him emperor. Eugene had come to terms with the Romans by then, but he died at Tivoli on 8 July 1153 before Frederick came.

claims.text: Bernard of Clairvaux wrote to the cardinals asking what they were thinking, electing a simple monk.
claims.note: His letter survives, mixing surprise with blessing.

claims.text: Eugene read the visions of Hildegard of Bingen at a synod at Trier in 1147–48 and approved them.
claims.note: Told in Hildegard's own Life, written by admirers. No papal letter from the synod confirms it.

reigns.hook: Eugene is dead before Barbarossa reaches Rome. The cardinals choose an old Roman who once held the city for Innocent II, and the Romans actually let him live there.

reigns.tagline: An old Roman, at peace with Rome at last
reigns.reignEnded: Died in Rome of old age
reigns.previously: Eugene III dies at Tivoli before Barbarossa can come to Rome.
paragraphs: Corrado was a Roman from the Suburra district, a cardinal-bishop who had held Rome for Innocent II when that pope fled to France in the 1130s. Elected as Anastasius IV in July 1153, he was about 80, and he was gentle and conciliatory. He made peace with the commune and lived in the Lateran, something few popes of the century managed.

He settled a long English quarrel by restoring William FitzHerbert, whom Eugene III had deposed, as archbishop of York and sending him the pallium. He built a palace by the Pantheon and set aside a grand tomb for himself. He died on 3 December 1154, after seventeen months.

claims.text: Anastasius took over the porphyry sarcophagus of Empress Helena, Constantine's mother, for his own burial.
claims.note: The great carved coffin was moved to the Lateran for him. It is now in the Vatican Museums.

claims.text: He was about 80 when he was elected.
claims.note: No birth record survives. The age is an estimate from his long career.

reigns.hook: Anastasius dies in peace. The next day the cardinals elect a foreigner: the son of a poor English clerk, fresh from bringing order to the churches of Norway.

reigns.tagline: The only English pope, and he made an emperor kneel
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected the day after Anastasius died
reigns.previously: Anastasius IV dies in Rome after seventeen quiet months.
paragraphs: Nicholas Breakspear grew up near St Albans, the son of a poor clerk who became a monk. He went to France, joined the canons of St Ruf near Avignon and rose to be their abbot. His canons complained he was too strict. Eugene III made him a cardinal instead and sent him to Scandinavia, where he set up an archbishopric for Norway. In December 1154 he became Adrian IV.

Rome was in Arnold of Brescia's hands. When a cardinal was attacked in the street, Adrian put the whole city under interdict in Holy Week 1155: no Masses, no Easter. The Romans gave in and expelled Arnold, who was caught, hanged and burned. That June Frederick Barbarossa refused to hold Adrian's stirrup at their first meeting near Sutri. He did it the next day, and Adrian crowned him emperor.

The friendship soured. In 1156 Adrian made peace with the Normans of Sicily, the emperor's enemies. At Besançon in 1157 a papal letter seemed to call the empire a fief of the pope, and Frederick's men nearly lynched the legate. Adrian died at Anagni on 1 September 1159, at odds with the emperor and with the cardinals split over him.

claims.text: Adrian's bull Laudabiliter granted Ireland to Henry II of England.
claims.note: The text survives only through Gerald of Wales. John of Salisbury says Adrian did grant Ireland and sent a ring, but historians still argue over the bull.

claims.text: Adrian choked to death on a fly in his wine.
claims.note: A tale from hostile and later writers. His friend John of Salisbury and other contemporaries point to a throat illness.

claims.text: As a young man he was turned away by the monks of St Albans.
claims.note: Matthew Paris tells it about a century later. It may be a local story that grew with his fame.

reigns.hook: Adrian is dead, and the cardinals are hopelessly split. When they meet to replace him, the election turns into a brawl over a scarlet cloak.

reigns.tagline: The pope who humbled Barbarossa and outlasted four antipopes
reigns.previously: Adrian IV, the English pope, dies at Anagni, at odds with Barbarossa.
paragraphs: Rolando of Siena was a lawyer and the papal chancellor, and Frederick Barbarossa already hated him. At a meeting at Besançon in 1157 he had brought a letter from Adrian suggesting the empire was a papal gift, and a German noble nearly cut him down. When most cardinals chose Rolando in 1159, a minority chose Cardinal Octavian as Victor IV. The emperor backed Victor, and the Church had two popes again.

The schism lasted 18 years and Alexander spent much of it far from Rome, three years of it in France. Barbarossa kept naming new antipopes. But the cities of northern Italy formed the Lombard League against the emperor, and even named a new town Alessandria after the pope. In 1176 the League's foot soldiers beat Barbarossa at Legnano. In Venice in July 1177 the emperor knelt and kissed the pope's feet.

England gave him a crisis too. In 1170 Henry II's knights murdered Archbishop Thomas Becket in Canterbury Cathedral. Alexander made Becket a saint in 1173, and Henry did public penance. In 1179 the Third Lateran Council ruled that a pope needs a two-thirds majority of the cardinals, which is still the rule. Alexander died in 1181, still unable to live safely in Rome.

claims.text: Octavian tore the scarlet papal mantle off Rolando and put it on himself, back to front in his haste.
claims.note: The vivid version comes from Alexander's own side, notably his biographer Cardinal Boso. Victor's supporters told a different story.

claims.text: Barbarossa prostrated himself and kissed the pope's feet at Venice in 1177.
claims.note: Described by eyewitnesses including Romuald of Salerno. The story that Alexander put his foot on the emperor's neck is a later legend.

claims.text: The two-thirds rule for electing a pope dates from Alexander's council of 1179.
claims.note: The decree Licet de vitanda of the Third Lateran Council. Popes have tinkered with it since, but it stands.

reigns.hook: Alexander is gone after 22 years. His successor is an old man the Romans won't have in their city, and far away Saladin is gathering his armies.

reigns.tagline: An old man the Romans wouldn't let stay in Rome
reigns.previously: Alexander III dies in 1181, still unable to live safely in Rome.
paragraphs: Ubaldo Allucingoli came from Lucca and had served the popes for decades. As cardinal-bishop of Ostia he was Alexander III's closest adviser. In 1181, already about 80, he became the first pope chosen under Alexander's new two-thirds rule. He tried living in Rome, but the city's commune wanted the popes' rights for itself, and within months he was gone again.

He spent the rest of his reign on the road. In 1184 he met Frederick Barbarossa at Verona, and together they issued Ad abolendam, which condemned the Cathars, the Waldensians and other heretics. Bishops were to hunt them out in their own dioceses and hand them over to the secular power to be punished. It was a big step towards the Inquisition.

The meeting went sour on everything else. Lucius would not crown Barbarossa's son Henry as co-emperor, and the two argued over the lands of Countess Matilda of Tuscany, which both claimed. Lucius died at Verona in November 1185 with nothing settled, and was buried in the cathedral there.

claims.text: The Romans blinded a group of clergy loyal to Lucius, all but one, and sent them back to him riding on donkeys.
claims.note: Reported by chroniclers of the time. The details vary, and they come from writers on the pope's side, but some atrocity of this kind seems to have happened during the fighting around Tusculum.

claims.text: Ad abolendam (1184) told bishops to seek out heretics in their dioceses and hand the guilty to the secular power.
claims.note: The decree survives and was later included in Church law. Historians see it as a forerunner of the inquisitions set up in the 1230s.

reigns.hook: Lucius dies at Verona. The cardinals there pick an archbishop of Milan, a city Barbarossa once razed to the ground. He hasn't forgotten, and neither has the emperor.

reigns.tagline: A Milanese pope with a grudge against Barbarossa
reigns.cameToPower: Elected at Verona the same day
reigns.previously: Lucius III dies at Verona, still at odds with Barbarossa.
paragraphs: Uberto Crivelli was archbishop of Milan, and his family had suffered when Barbarossa sacked the city in 1162. The cardinals at Verona chose him on the day Lucius died. He kept Milan for himself as well, so its rich income stayed out of the emperor's hands. The emperor took that as a declaration of war.

Barbarossa struck first. In January 1186 his son Henry married Constance, heiress of Sicily, in Milan itself, the pope's own city. A Sicilian kingdom joined to the empire would squeeze the Papal States from north and south. Urban hit back by consecrating an archbishop of Trier the emperor had rejected. Henry's troops then overran papal lands, and Urban found himself shut up in Verona.

By 1187 he was ready to excommunicate Barbarossa. The people of Verona begged him not to do it in their city, so he set off for Ferrara, where he fell ill and died in October. That summer Saladin had crushed the crusader army at Hattin, and on 2 October Jerusalem surrendered.

claims.text: Urban died of grief at the news that Jerusalem had fallen.
claims.note: Told by later chroniclers. Jerusalem surrendered on 2 October, and the news could hardly have reached Ferrara by the 20th. Grief at the defeat at Hattin, in July, is more plausible.

claims.text: Henry VI married Constance of Sicily in Milan on 27 January 1186.
claims.note: Recorded by many chroniclers. The marriage later gave the Staufer Sicily, which caused the popes trouble for 80 years.

reigns.hook: Urban is dead and Jerusalem has fallen. At Ferrara the cardinals choose the papal chancellor, an old man in a terrible hurry to raise a crusade.

reigns.tagline: Fifty-seven days, and the call for the Third Crusade
reigns.previously: Urban III dies at Ferrara just as Jerusalem falls to Saladin.
paragraphs: Alberto di Morra came from Benevento and had been chancellor of the Roman church for nine years. Years before, he was one of the legates who made peace with Henry II of England after the murder of Thomas Becket. The cardinals at Ferrara chose him the day after Urban died. He was over 80, devout and known as a peacemaker.

He moved fast. Within days he issued Audita tremendi, a letter to all Christians mourning the loss of Jerusalem and calling them to a new crusade. He promised the usual remission of sins and ordered fasting. He also made peace with the emperor, dropping Urban's quarrel at once. Then he travelled to Pisa to end its feud with Genoa, because the crusade would need both cities' fleets.

He never got further. Gregory caught a fever at Pisa and died there on 17 December 1187, after 57 days as pope. But his call worked. Within two years the emperor, the king of France and the king of England had all taken the cross.

claims.text: Gregory issued Audita tremendi, the bull calling the Third Crusade, about a week after his election.
claims.note: The text survives, dated 29 October 1187. Chroniclers including Roger of Howden copied it.

claims.text: Gregory was one of the legates who absolved Henry II at Avranches in 1172 for Becket's murder.
claims.note: English chroniclers name Cardinal Albert and Cardinal Theodwin as the two legates.

reigns.hook: Gregory is dead at Pisa. The cardinals there pick a Roman, and that matters: the popes have been shut out of their own city for years.

reigns.tagline: The Roman who got the popes back into Rome
reigns.previously: Gregory VIII dies at Pisa after just 57 days.
paragraphs: Paolo Scolari was born in Rome and was cardinal-bishop of Palestrina. Being a Roman was his great asset. In 1188 he struck a deal with the city's commune: the Senate kept its powers, but its senators swore loyalty to the pope and he got back his rights and his revenues. For the first time in years a pope could live in the Lateran.

His other job was the crusade. Philip II of France and Henry II of England took the cross in January 1188, and Barbarossa at Mainz that spring. Clement raised money and kept the kings talking. Barbarossa marched east in 1189 and drowned crossing a river in Anatolia in June 1190. Henry II was dead by then, and his son Richard sailed with Philip.

Sicily was trouble. When William II of Sicily died in 1189, Barbarossa's son Henry claimed the kingdom through his wife Constance. Clement backed a rival, Tancred of Lecce, rather than see the empire wrap around the Papal States. He died in March 1191, with Henry already on his way to Rome for his crown.

claims.text: The pact of 1188 with the Roman Senate let the pope return to Rome after years in exile.
claims.note: The treaty survives. It left the commune in place, which kept Rome a difficult city for popes for generations.

claims.text: Clement agreed to let the Romans destroy their old enemy Tusculum.
claims.note: Part of his deal with the city. The Romans finally razed the town in 1191, just after he died.

reigns.hook: Clement is dead, and Henry is outside Rome demanding an imperial crown. The cardinals turn to the oldest man in the room, a deacon of 85 who has been a cardinal for almost 50 years.

reigns.tagline: Elected at 85, and outlived everyone's expectations
reigns.previously: Clement III dies, with Henry VI on his way to Rome for a crown.
paragraphs: Giacinto Bobone, of the Roman family later called the Orsini, had been a cardinal since 1144. As a young man he stood up for Peter Abelard at the council of Sens. When he was elected in 1191 he was only a deacon, so he was made priest, then bishop, and on Easter Monday he crowned Henry VI and Constance in St Peter's. Part of the price was Tusculum, which the Romans then razed.

Henry was the most dangerous emperor yet. In 1192 Duke Leopold of Austria captured Richard the Lionheart on his way home from crusade and handed him to Henry, who held him for a huge ransom. Celestine excommunicated Leopold for laying hands on a crusader. In 1194 Henry took Sicily too. The Papal States were caught in a vice, and the old pope could only bend.

Then Henry died suddenly in 1197, aged 32. Celestine, over 90, wanted to resign and name his successor himself, but the cardinals refused. He died on 8 January 1198. That same day they chose the youngest of them all.

claims.text: At Henry VI's coronation Celestine kicked the imperial crown off his head, to show that popes make and unmake emperors.
claims.note: Told only by the English chronicler Roger of Howden, who wasn't there. No Roman or German account mentions it.

claims.text: Celestine excommunicated Leopold of Austria for imprisoning Richard I, a crusader under the Church's protection.
claims.note: Recorded by English and German chroniclers. Leopold died in 1194, still excommunicate, after a fall from his horse.

claims.text: Celestine offered to resign at Christmas 1197 if the cardinals would elect his chosen man.
claims.note: Reported by the chronicles of the time. The cardinals would not accept a pope naming his heir.

reigns.hook: The old man is gone at last. The cardinals pick a nobleman of 37, trained in Paris and Bologna, who thinks the pope stands above every king on earth.

reigns.tagline: The most powerful pope of the Middle Ages
reigns.cameToPower: Elected the day Celestine III died
reigns.previously: Celestine III dies in his nineties. The cardinals turn to a man of 37.
paragraphs: Lotario dei Conti was a young noble trained in theology at Paris and law at Bologna. Elected at just 37, he believed the pope was Christ's vicar, set over kings as the sun is over the moon. He meant it. He took back control of the Papal States, ruled on disputed German elections, and turned kings into vassals.

His crusades went wild. The Fourth Crusade was meant for Egypt, but the crusaders sacked the Christian city of Zara and then, in April 1204, Constantinople itself, against his orders. In 1209 he launched a crusade against the Cathar heretics in southern France, which became a bloodbath. He put England under interdict in a fight with King John, who caved in 1213 and made England a papal fief. Two years later Innocent annulled Magna Carta.

He also saw what was new. In 1209 or 1210 he gave his blessing to a scruffy band from Assisi led by Francis. In 1215 he gathered more than 400 bishops at the Fourth Lateran Council, which ordered every Catholic to confess yearly and made Jews wear distinctive dress. He died suddenly at Perugia in July 1216, planning yet another crusade.

claims.text: Innocent dreamed that the Lateran basilica was falling and a small poor man held it up, and recognised Francis as that man.
claims.note: Told in the lives of Francis written decades later, notably by Bonaventure. It is a pious story, not a record.

claims.text: On the night he died, thieves stripped his body almost naked as it lay in the church at Perugia.
claims.note: Jacques de Vitry, who arrived in Perugia that week, says he saw it himself. It is a single witness, but a credible one.

reigns.hook: Innocent is dead, and his former ward Frederick II rules Sicily and Germany. The cardinals at Perugia pick the gentle Honorius III, who thinks he can talk Frederick into a crusade.

reigns.tagline: The gentle pope who couldn't get an emperor on crusade
reigns.previously: Innocent III dies at Perugia, his body stripped by thieves.
paragraphs: Cencio Savelli was a Roman who had run the papal treasury and in 1192 compiled the Liber Censuum, the great list of everything owed to the pope. Two days after Innocent III died, two cardinals chosen to settle the matter picked him at Perugia. He was old, kindly and patient, everything Innocent was not.

He blessed the new friars. He approved Dominic's Order of Preachers in December 1216, and in 1223 he confirmed the rule of Francis of Assisi, which is still the Franciscan rule today. In England he backed the boy-king Henry III against the French invasion. In 1220 he crowned Frederick II emperor in St Peter's, after Frederick swore yet again to go on crusade.

That oath was the problem. The Fifth Crusade took Damietta in Egypt in 1219, waited for Frederick, and lost everything in 1221. Honorius kept nagging. In 1225 Frederick promised to sail by August 1227 or be excommunicated. Honorius died in March 1227, before the deadline came.

claims.text: Honorius had been Frederick II's tutor when the emperor was a boy in Sicily.
claims.note: Often said since the Middle Ages, but there is little firm evidence that he actually taught the boy.

claims.text: Honorius approved the final Franciscan rule in 1223 with the bull Solet annuere.
claims.note: The bull survives, dated 29 November 1223.

claims.text: Honorius wrote a book of black magic, the Grimoire of Pope Honorius.
claims.note: The grimoire appeared centuries later, in the 17th century or after, and borrowed his name to sell it.

reigns.hook: Honorius dies with Frederick still in Italy. The next pope is old, fierce, a friend of Francis and Innocent III's kinsman, and he will not wait.

reigns.tagline: He called the emperor the beast from the sea
reigns.reignEnded: Died as Frederick's army closed in
reigns.previously: Honorius III dies, Frederick II's crusade still not sailed.
paragraphs: Ugolino of Segni was related to Innocent III and had been cardinal-bishop of Ostia for 20 years. He was a friend of Francis of Assisi and protector of his friars. Some say he was about 80 when elected; others think 60. Either way he had a temper. Within six months, when Frederick II's crusade fleet turned back with sickness on board, Gregory excommunicated him.

Frederick went anyway, still excommunicate, and in 1229 talked the Sultan of Egypt into handing over Jerusalem without a fight. Gregory sent an army into Frederick's kingdom of Sicily while he was gone. Peace came in 1230, but it didn't last. Meanwhile Gregory made Francis a saint in 1228, sent papal inquisitors after heretics from 1231, and in 1234 published the Decretals, the backbone of Church law for 700 years.

In 1239 he excommunicated Frederick again. He called a council to depose him, but in 1241 Frederick's fleet captured a whole convoy of bishops sailing to Rome. Frederick's army was in sight of the city when Gregory died in the August heat.

claims.text: Gregory's 1239 manifesto called Frederick the beast rising from the sea, from the Book of Revelation.
claims.note: The letter, opening Ascendit de mari, survives. Frederick's chancery answered in kind, calling the pope the great dragon.

claims.text: Gregory's bull Vox in Rama started a mass killing of cats across Europe, which later let rats spread the Black Death.
claims.note: The bull (1233) describes a black cat in a heretics' ritual, but says nothing about killing cats. The plague link is a modern invention.

claims.text: Gregory was nearly 100 when he died.
claims.note: Some chroniclers say so. Many historians put his birth around 1170, which would make him about 70.

reigns.hook: Gregory is dead, Frederick's men hold two cardinals, and the rest are in Rome. The city's boss decides they will not leave until they pick a pope, however long it takes.

reigns.tagline: Chosen in a locked, stinking ruin; dead in 17 days
reigns.previously: Gregory IX dies with Frederick II's army outside Rome.
paragraphs: Rome's senator Matteo Rosso Orsini wanted a pope who would stand up to Frederick, and fast. So he rounded up the ten cardinals in Rome and locked them in the Septizodium, a crumbling ancient building on the Palatine, with armed guards outside. It was the first real conclave, a word that means locked with a key. One of the cardinals, the Englishman Robert of Somercotes, fell ill and died there.

After weeks of misery they settled on Goffredo da Castiglione, an elderly Milanese cardinal-bishop of Sabina, as a stopgap. He was already sick. He died on 10 November 1241, seventeen days later, before anyone could crown him. The cardinals did not wait to be locked up again. Most fled the city at once.
They then refused to meet for a year and a half. Frederick held two of them prisoner and was busy wasting the land around Rome. The Church had no pope until June 1243.

claims.text: The guards relieved themselves on the roof of the Septizodium so that it leaked onto the cardinals below.
claims.note: The grim conditions are described in a letter from the cardinals and in Matthew Paris. This detail is told by later writers and may be embroidered.

claims.text: Cardinal Robert of Somercotes died during the 1241 conclave.
claims.note: Matthew Paris reports it, and English sources mourned him. Some at the time suspected poison, without proof.

reigns.hook: Celestine is dead and the cardinals have scattered. When they finally meet again they choose a Genoese lawyer, once Frederick's friend, who will chase the emperor off his throne.

reigns.tagline: The lawyer pope who deposed an emperor
reigns.reignEnded: Died at Naples after a defeat
reigns.previously: Celestine IV dies within weeks, and the papacy sits empty.
paragraphs: Sinibaldo Fieschi came from a family of Genoese counts and was one of the best canon lawyers alive. Frederick II thought him friendly and welcomed the election. He was wrong. Talks went nowhere, and in June 1244 Innocent slipped out of Italy in disguise, reaching Genoa by ship and then Lyon, safely outside the emperor's reach.

In 1245 he held a council at Lyon. It declared Frederick deposed for perjury, sacrilege and suspected heresy, and freed his subjects from their oaths. Innocent preached a crusade against him and backed rival kings in Germany. That same year he sent the friar John of Plano Carpini all the way to the Mongol khan, with a letter asking him to stop attacking Christians.

Frederick died in 1250 and Innocent came back to Italy, determined to finish the Staufer. In 1252 his bull Ad extirpanda let inquisitors use torture. He offered Sicily to Edmund, son of Henry III of England. But Frederick's son Manfred beat a papal army at Foggia, and Innocent died at Naples days later.

claims.text: When Innocent was elected, Frederick said he had lost a friend among the cardinals, because no pope can be a Ghibelline.
claims.note: A famous line found in later chronicles. It sums up the story so neatly that it may have been invented after the fact.

claims.text: Innocent gave cardinals the red hat at the Council of Lyon in 1245.
claims.note: Reported by later chroniclers. The early evidence is thin.

claims.text: Ad extirpanda (1252) allowed inquisitors to use torture to make suspects confess.
claims.note: The bull survives, dated 15 May 1252. It set limits: no loss of limb or life.

reigns.hook: Innocent dies at Naples, and the cardinals there quickly pick Gregory IX's nephew. Frederick's son Manfred is winning the south, and the new pope is no fighter.

reigns.tagline: A kind man in a cruel war he couldn't win
reigns.previously: Innocent IV dies at Naples, days after Manfred routs his army.
paragraphs: Rinaldo of Segni was Gregory IX's nephew and cardinal-bishop of Ostia, a pious, easygoing man who looked after the Franciscans. He was elected at Naples five days after Innocent IV died. He inherited a war with Manfred, Frederick II's son, and lost it. In 1258 Manfred had himself crowned king of Sicily at Palermo, and the pope's armies could do nothing.

His own city wasn't safe. Rome's tough senator Brancaleone ran it and the pope mostly lived at Viterbo and Anagni. In 1256 he united several small groups of hermits into the Augustinian friars. At Paris, where the professors were trying to throw the friars out of the university, he backed the friars and condemned their chief critic's book.
In 1260 Manfred's allies from Siena smashed the Guelphs of Florence at Montaperti. Alexander died at Viterbo in May 1261, having made few cardinals, so only eight were left to choose the next pope.

claims.text: Alexander created the Order of Augustinian Friars in 1256 by joining several hermit groups.
claims.note: The bull Licet ecclesiae catholicae, 9 April 1256, known as the Great Union.

claims.text: Alexander was too gentle to rule, easily led by those around him.
claims.note: The view of some chroniclers of the time. Historians note he still pressed the war against Manfred and the tyrant Ezzelino da Romano.

reigns.hook: Alexander dies with Manfred unbeaten. The eight cardinals at Viterbo argue for three months, then pick a cobbler's son from Troyes who isn't even a cardinal.

reigns.tagline: The cobbler's son who never set foot in Rome
reigns.previously: Alexander IV dies at Viterbo; only eight cardinals are left.
paragraphs: Jacques Pantaléon was the son of a cobbler in Troyes. He studied at Paris and rose to be patriarch of Jerusalem. He was at Viterbo on business when the deadlocked cardinals chose him in August 1261. That July the Greeks had retaken Constantinople, ending the Latin empire the Fourth Crusade had set up.

Urban never entered Rome. He lived at Viterbo and Orvieto and filled the college with French cardinals, which changed the papacy for a century. His big plan was to get rid of Manfred. He offered the crown of Sicily to Charles of Anjou, brother of Louis IX of France, an ambitious man who wanted a kingdom of his own.

As archdeacon at Liège years before, Urban had known the local push for a feast in honour of the Eucharist. In 1264 he made Corpus Christi a feast for the whole Church. That autumn Manfred's allies threatened Orvieto, and Urban fled to Perugia, where he died in October, with Charles still not in Italy.

claims.text: Thomas Aquinas wrote the prayers and hymns for Urban's new feast of Corpus Christi, including Pange lingua.
claims.note: The traditional attribution, accepted by most scholars; a few have argued the office was by others.

claims.text: Urban's feast was inspired by the Miracle of Bolsena of 1263, when a consecrated host bled onto the altar cloth.
claims.note: The miracle story is told from later medieval sources. Urban's bull Transiturus (1264) does not mention it.

claims.text: Urban IV was the son of a cobbler.
claims.note: Contemporary sources say so, and a church he founded in Troyes, Saint-Urbain, stands on the site of his father's shop.

reigns.hook: Urban dies before Charles of Anjou arrives. The cardinals choose a Frenchman who used to be a married lawyer, a friend of Louis IX, and he will finish the deal.

reigns.tagline: The widower pope who handed Sicily to the French
reigns.previously: Urban IV dies at Perugia; Charles of Anjou has yet to come.
paragraphs: Guy Foulques was a lawyer from the south of France with a wife and daughters, and a trusted counsellor of Louis IX. When his wife died he became a priest, then bishop of Le Puy, archbishop of Narbonne and a cardinal. He was away on a mission to England when the cardinals at Perugia elected him, and he had to travel to Italy in disguise.

He finished Urban's plan. Charles of Anjou was crowned king of Sicily in Rome in January 1266, and the next month he killed Manfred in battle at Benevento. In 1268 Frederick II's grandson Conradin, aged 16, came south to win his inheritance back. Charles beat him at Tagliacozzo and had him beheaded in the market square at Naples in October.

Clement kept his own family at arm's length. He told his relatives not to expect any favours and married his daughters to modest husbands. He also asked the English friar Roger Bacon to send him his writings, which led to the Opus Maius. He died at Viterbo in November 1268, a month after Conradin's death.

claims.text: Clement said: 'The life of Conradin is the death of Charles; the death of Conradin is the life of Charles.'
claims.note: The line is quoted by later chroniclers to blame Clement for the beheading. There is no reliable record that he said it.

claims.text: Clement wrote to Roger Bacon in 1266 asking for his work, and Bacon sent him the Opus Maius.
claims.note: Clement's letter survives, and Bacon addresses the work to him.

claims.text: Clement travelled from France to Perugia disguised as a monk to avoid capture by Manfred's men.
claims.note: A common account. That he travelled secretly is likely; the exact disguise varies in the telling.

reigns.hook: Clement is dead at Viterbo. The French and Italian cardinals there can't agree on anything. Months pass, then years, and the people of Viterbo start to lose patience.

reigns.title: The Longest Conclave
reigns.tagline: Nearly three years without a pope
reigns.previously: Clement IV dies at Viterbo, a month after Conradin's beheading.
paragraphs: When Clement died, about 18 cardinals met at Viterbo. They split down the middle: the French wanted a pope friendly to Charles of Anjou, now master of southern Italy and senator of Rome, and the Italians wanted anyone but. Neither side could reach two-thirds. Weeks became months, then years.

The people of Viterbo ran out of patience. Their officials locked the cardinals in the bishop's palace and cut their food to bread and water. In March 1271 the vacancy turned bloody. Guy de Montfort, whose father Simon had been killed and mutilated at Evesham, found his cousin Henry of Almain at Mass in a Viterbo church and murdered him in revenge.

Three cardinals died during the wait. At last, on 1 September 1271, the survivors gave the choice to a committee of six. They picked Teobaldo Visconti, archdeacon of Liège, who wasn't a cardinal or even a priest. He was in Acre, on crusade.

claims.text: The people of Viterbo tore the roof off the palace to force a decision.
claims.note: The lock-in and rationing are well recorded. The roof story is widely told and partly documented, though it may have been smaller than the legend says.

claims.text: An English cardinal joked that they should take off the roof, because the Holy Spirit couldn't get through so many layers.
claims.note: The quip is attributed to Cardinal John of Toledo. It turns up in later accounts and is surely too good to check.

claims.text: Henry of Almain was murdered in a church at Viterbo by Guy de Montfort in March 1271.
claims.note: Reported across Europe at the time. Dante puts Guy in the river of boiling blood in Inferno 12.

reigns.hook: A messenger rides for the coast with the news. Teobaldo Visconti is in the Holy Land with Edward of England, and he will take months getting home. The Church now has a pope who isn't yet a priest.

reigns.tagline: Elected in Italy while he was praying in Acre
reigns.cameToPower: Picked by a committee of six
reigns.previously: Three years locked in at Viterbo; the cardinals pick a man at Acre.
paragraphs: Teobaldo Visconti was a churchman from Piacenza, archdeacon of Liège, who had never been ordained a priest. In 1271 he was in the Holy Land with Prince Edward of England when word came that he was pope. He sailed home, reached Viterbo in early 1272, and was ordained and crowned in Rome that March. His heart stayed in the East. Everything he did was meant to raise one more crusade.

In 1274 he gathered a great council at Lyon. Envoys of the Byzantine emperor Michael VIII accepted union with Rome, on paper at least, Bonaventure died while it sat, and Thomas Aquinas died on his way there. The council also passed his decree Ubi periculum: cardinals locked in, food cut after three days and again after eight. He backed Rudolf of Habsburg as German king, then died at Arezzo on his way back to Rome.

claims.text: Gregory's decree Ubi periculum is the root of the modern conclave.
claims.note: Its lock-in and rationing rules were suspended soon after, restored by Celestine V and Boniface VIII, and still shape papal elections.

claims.text: Gregory sent letters and two Dominican friars to Kublai Khan with Niccolò, Maffeo and Marco Polo.
claims.note: The story is in Marco Polo's book. It fits the dates, but no papal record of the mission survives, and the friars turned back early.

reigns.hook: Gregory is buried at Arezzo, and his tough new rules get their first test there. The cardinals pick a famous Dominican teacher in a single day.

reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected; a cardinal under Gregory X

reigns.reignEnded: Died in Rome after five months
reigns.previously: Gregory X dies at Arezzo, his crusade still a plan on paper.
paragraphs: Pierre de Tarentaise came from the Alps of Savoy and joined the Dominicans young. He taught theology at Paris alongside Thomas Aquinas and wrote a long commentary on Peter Lombard's Sentences, the textbook every student had to master. Gregory X made him archbishop of Lyon and then a cardinal, and at the council of 1274 he preached the funeral sermon for Bonaventure.

Locked in at Arezzo under Gregory's new decree, the cardinals chose him in January 1276 on the first day. He was the first Dominican pope. He went to Rome, was crowned, and set to making peace: between Genoa and Charles of Anjou, and between Pisa and Lucca. He wanted Gregory's crusade too. He had five months. He died in Rome in June, and Leo XIII beatified him in 1898.

claims.text: Innocent V was the first Dominican to become pope.
claims.note: Recorded in all the standard lists; the order of preachers was only about 60 years old.

claims.text: He was elected on the first day of the first conclave held under Ubi periculum.
claims.note: The cardinals met at Arezzo in January 1276 and finished quickly.

reigns.hook: Innocent is dead, and Charles of Anjou wants a friendly pope. The Rome conclave is hot, cramped and miserable. The man it chooses will scrap the rules that made it so, then die before he can even be ordained.

reigns.cameToPower: Elected in a sweltering Rome conclave
reigns.previously: Innocent V dies in Rome after five months as pope.
paragraphs: Ottobuono Fieschi was a Genoese noble and a nephew of Innocent IV, who made him a cardinal. He knew England well. As papal legate from 1265 to 1268 he helped make peace after the barons' war against Henry III, and his church laws, issued in London in 1268, stayed part of English church law until the Reformation. Prince Edward, the future Edward I, took the cross from him.

He was elected in Rome in July 1276, in a conclave run with Charles of Anjou breathing down the cardinals' necks. His first act was to suspend Gregory X's harsh conclave rules. Then he left the summer heat for Viterbo, fell ill and died on 18 August. He was still only a deacon: never ordained priest, consecrated or crowned. Arnolfo di Cambio's workshop is credited with his tomb in Viterbo.

claims.text: Adrian V died without ever being ordained a priest, consecrated a bishop or crowned.
claims.note: He was a cardinal deacon when elected and died 38 days later. Popes were not yet expected to be ordained before taking office.

claims.text: Dante places Adrian in Purgatory among the greedy, confessing that only becoming pope cured him of loving money.
claims.note: Purgatorio 19. Dante's charge of avarice has no clear support in the record; some think he confused him with another pope.

reigns.hook: Adrian is buried at Viterbo, and the cardinals meet there again. They choose a Portuguese doctor who knows more about medicine and logic than politics. He will be killed by his own building.
