reigns.tagline: The doctor pope killed by his own ceiling
reigns.previously: Adrian V dies at Viterbo after 38 days, never ordained.
paragraphs: Peter of Spain, from Lisbon, is still the only Portuguese pope. He was a physician, credited with a popular handbook of cheap cures, and had been Gregory X's personal doctor. He chose the name John XXI, but there was never a John XX: clerks had miscounted the earlier Johns, and the mistake stuck. In January 1277 he asked the bishop of Paris to look into errors at the university, which led to a sweeping list of condemned ideas.

He left much of the daily business to Cardinal Giovanni Gaetano Orsini and stayed with his books. At Viterbo he had a new study built onto the papal palace. In May 1277 its ceiling collapsed on him. He was pulled from the rubble and died a few days later. Dante, who rarely had a kind word for a pope of his age, put him in Paradise as a scholar.

claims.text: There is no Pope John XX.
claims.note: Medieval lists counted an antipope and a phantom pope among the Johns, so the numbering jumped from XIX to XXI.

claims.text: John XXI was the logician Peter of Spain, author of the Summulae logicales, the most used logic textbook of the Middle Ages.
claims.note: Long accepted and still the usual view, but some scholars argue the logician was a different Peter of Spain, a Dominican.

claims.text: Chroniclers said the collapse was God's punishment for a pope who dabbled in magic.
claims.note: Hostile writers, mostly friars he had snubbed, turned a scholar's accident into a judgement. There is no evidence of magic.

reigns.hook: The pope is dead under his own ceiling. Cardinal Orsini, who has run things for him, wants the job himself. The deadlock lasts six months, and then the Roman nobleman gets it.

reigns.tagline: An Orsini pope who filled the Church with Orsini
reigns.previously: John XXI dies at Viterbo, crushed by his new study's ceiling.
paragraphs: Giovanni Gaetano Orsini came from one of Rome's great baronial families and had been a cardinal for 33 years. After half a year of deadlock at Viterbo he got the votes. He was able, proud and very much a Roman. He talked Rudolf of Habsburg into handing over the Romagna in 1278, a big gain for the Papal States, and he pushed Charles of Anjou out of the post of senator of Rome by banning foreign rulers from holding it.

He looked after his family too. Three relatives became cardinals, and Orsini kinsmen got castles and posts across the Papal States. He rebuilt the papal palace by St Peter's and laid out gardens there. In August 1280, at his castle at Soriano near Viterbo, he died suddenly of a stroke. Twenty years later Dante put him in hell for it.

claims.text: Dante shows Nicholas upside down in a hole in hell, his feet on fire, among the popes who sold Church offices.
claims.note: Inferno 19. Dante's Nicholas mistakes the poet for Boniface VIII, who is due to replace him in the hole.

claims.text: Nicholas III was the first pope to live at the Vatican rather than the Lateran.
claims.note: He built heavily at the Vatican and stayed there often, but popes kept using the Lateran, and earlier popes had lived at St Peter's for spells.

reigns.hook: Nicholas is dead, and Charles of Anjou wants his Rome back. When the Italian cardinals stall the vote, two Orsini cardinals are hauled out and locked up. The way is clear for a Frenchman.

reigns.tagline: Charles of Anjou's pope, and a weakness for eels
reigns.previously: Nicholas III dies suddenly of a stroke at Soriano.
paragraphs: Simon de Brion had been Louis IX's chancellor and a cardinal for 20 years. He was elected at Viterbo after a six-month fight and took the name Martin IV, though there had only been one Martin before. He never went to Rome. The Romans made him their senator, and he handed the post to Charles of Anjou, living at Orvieto and Perugia instead. He was France's man, and he let Charles run Italy.

He excommunicated the Byzantine emperor, wrecking the union made at Lyon, so Charles could attack Constantinople. Then on Easter Monday 1282 Sicily rose against the French at the Vespers in Palermo. Peter III of Aragon took the island. Martin excommunicated him, declared him deposed and offered Aragon to a French prince, which meant a crusade against Christians. Charles died in January 1285 and Martin followed in March.

claims.text: Two Orsini cardinals were locked up at Viterbo to break the deadlock and let Martin win.
claims.note: Contemporary chroniclers say the Viterbese, with Charles's backing, seized them. How far Charles ordered it is unclear.

claims.text: He is numbered Martin IV although only one Pope Martin came before him.
claims.note: Medieval clerks read the two popes named Marinus as Martin II and III, and the error stuck.

claims.text: Dante puts him on the terrace of the gluttons, fasting off the eels of Lake Bolsena that he cooked in sweet wine.
claims.note: Purgatorio 24 says exactly that. Early commentators add that he loved the dish, which may have come from the poem.

reigns.hook: Martin and Charles are both gone, and the French grip slips. At Perugia the cardinals pick a Roman nobleman so crippled by gout he cannot stand.

images.caption: A manuscript miniature made some decades after his death.

reigns.tagline: A pope too lame to stand, and a quiet two years
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected; a Roman, not a Frenchman
reigns.previously: Martin IV dies at Perugia, two months after Charles of Anjou.
paragraphs: Giacomo Savelli was a Roman noble, a great-nephew of Honorius III, and he took the same name. He had studied at Paris and been a cardinal since 1261. The cardinals chose him at Perugia within days of Martin's death. He was old and so crippled by gout that he could hardly stand or use his hands. He went straight to Rome, where the people welcomed a Roman again, and lived in his family's palace on the Aventine.

His brother Pandolfo became senator, and the city was calm. Outside, the war over Sicily ground on. Charles of Anjou's son, Charles II, was a prisoner of the Aragonese, and Honorius kept backing the French side while trying to make peace. He favoured the friars. He died in Rome in April 1287. His tomb effigy lies in Santa Maria in Aracoeli.

claims.text: Honorius was so crippled that he said Mass sitting down and needed a device to raise the host.
claims.note: Told by chroniclers and repeated in later histories. His gout is well attested; the details of the device are less certain.

reigns.hook: Honorius dies in April, and the cardinals meet in Rome in the summer fever season. Six of them will die. One man stays put at Santa Sabina, and in the end he is the only choice left.

reigns.tagline: The first Franciscan pope, and the fall of Acre
reigns.previously: Honorius IV dies in Rome, two years in.
paragraphs: Girolamo Masci, from the hills near Ascoli, had followed Bonaventure as head of the Franciscans and gone to Constantinople as a papal envoy. He was the first Franciscan pope. He got the job the hard way: fever killed six cardinals in the Roman summer of 1287 and the rest fled. He refused at first and took the tiara only when they voted again. He leaned on the Colonna family, so heavily that Romans joked about it.

He looked east. In 1288 he received Rabban Sauma, a Christian monk sent from Mongol Persia, and in 1289 he sent the friar John of Montecorvino on the long road to China. But in May 1291 Acre fell to the Mamluks, ending the crusader states in the Holy Land. His crusade never sailed. He died in Rome in April 1292, and the mosaics he paid for still glow in Santa Maria Maggiore.

claims.text: Nicholas IV was the first Franciscan pope.
claims.note: Elected in February 1288, sixty years after Francis was made a saint.

claims.text: Rabban Sauma took communion from Nicholas's own hand on Palm Sunday 1288.
claims.note: Sauma's own account, kept in a Syriac history of the Nestorian church, describes it in detail.

claims.text: While the other cardinals fled the fever, Masci stayed alone at the palace and kept the vacancy alive.
claims.note: Repeated by later historians; the contemporary record says only that he stayed and others left.

reigns.hook: Nicholas is dead, and the cardinals split between the Orsini and the Colonna. The Church will be without a pope for 27 months, until a hermit sends them a warning from his mountain.

reigns.tagline: The hermit who was pope, then wasn't
reigns.previously: Nicholas IV dies, and the cardinals deadlock for over two years.
paragraphs: Pietro da Morrone was a hermit from the hills of Molise, about 80, famous for fasting and for founding a strict order of monks. In 1294 he sent the cardinals, stuck at Perugia for 27 months, a warning that God would punish them if they did not choose. The dean read it out and named him. Messengers climbed to his cell to tell him. He rode into L'Aquila on a donkey, led by King Charles II of Naples, and was crowned there.

He moved to Naples and lived in Charles's castle. He named twelve cardinals, mostly the king's men, and handed out favours to whoever asked. He had a cell built so he could pray in peace. By December he wanted out. He issued a decree that a pope could resign, then did so on 13 December 1294. He hoped to go home. Instead his successor caught him and locked him in Fumone castle, where he died in 1296.

claims.text: Cardinal Caetani spoke through a tube into his cell, pretending to be the voice of God telling him to resign.
claims.note: A tale spread by Boniface VIII's enemies after the fact. Caetani did advise him that resigning was lawful.

claims.text: The soul who made 'the great refusal' out of cowardice in Dante's hell is Celestine V.
claims.note: Dante never names him in Inferno 3. Early commentators mostly said Celestine; others suggest Pontius Pilate or Esau.

claims.text: Celestine's pardon for pilgrims to Santa Maria di Collemaggio is still celebrated in L'Aquila every August.
claims.note: The Perdonanza, from his bull of 1294, is held each year at the basilica where he was crowned and is buried.

reigns.hook: The hermit is free to go home to his mountain. Or so he thinks. The cardinal who advised him on resigning is about to become pope, and wants no rival on the loose.

reigns.tagline: The proudest pope, and the slap that broke him
reigns.previously: The hermit pope Celestine V resigns after five months.
paragraphs: Benedetto Caetani was a brilliant canon lawyer from Anagni, and he had helped Celestine find the legal way out. Elected eleven days later, he wasn't taking chances. Celestine was caught trying to flee and locked up in the castle of Fumone, where he died in 1296. Boniface moved the court back to Rome, made war on the Colonna clan, who said his election was invalid, and razed their town of Palestrina.

In 1300 he declared the first Jubilee, and pilgrims poured into Rome for the pardon he offered. But he picked a fight he couldn't win. Philip IV of France wanted to tax his clergy. Boniface forbade it, and in 1302 issued Unam Sanctam: every human being must be subject to the pope to be saved.

Philip's answer was force. On 7 September 1303 his minister Guillaume de Nogaret and Sciarra Colonna burst into the papal palace at Anagni and seized the old man. The townspeople freed him after a few days, but he was broken. He went back to Rome and died a month later. Dante had already saved him a place in hell.

claims.text: Sciarra Colonna slapped the pope in the face with an iron gauntlet at Anagni.
claims.note: The famous 'slap of Anagni' isn't in the earliest reports, which describe threats and insults. It grew in the telling.

claims.text: Dante put Boniface in hell while he was still alive.
claims.note: Inferno is set in 1300, so Dante has Pope Nicholas III, in the pit of the simoniacs (canto 19), expecting Boniface to arrive.

claims.text: Boniface was a heretic and a blasphemer who didn't believe in the afterlife.
claims.note: Charges made by Philip IV's lawyers in a posthumous trial they pushed for years. Political smears, never proved.

reigns.hook: Boniface is dead, and the French king has won. One of the two cardinals who stood by him at Anagni now takes his place, and Philip is watching.

reigns.tagline: The friar who stood by Boniface, then died fast
reigns.previously: Boniface VIII dies, broken by the attack at Anagni.
paragraphs: Niccolò Boccasini, from Treviso, was a Dominican who had risen to head his order. Boniface made him a cardinal, and at Anagni in 1303 he was one of only two cardinals who stayed beside the old pope when the French broke in. The conclave in Rome chose him in a day. He was gentle and careful, and his job was to calm the fight with France without betraying the man he had stood beside.

He lifted most of Boniface's penalties on Philip IV and his kingdom, and eased those on the Colonna. But in June 1304 he excommunicated Nogaret, Sciarra Colonna and the others who had seized the pope at Anagni. Rome was too wild for him and he moved to Perugia. There, on 7 July 1304, after eight months as pope, he died suddenly. He was beatified in 1736.

claims.text: Benedict was one of the two cardinals who stood by Boniface VIII during the attack at Anagni.
claims.note: The other was the Spaniard Pedro Rodríguez. The rest of the curia fled or kept away.

claims.text: He was poisoned with figs, perhaps on Nogaret's orders.
claims.note: The rumour went round at once and suited Philip's enemies. Nothing was ever proved, and a sudden illness is just as likely.

reigns.hook: Benedict is dead, and Perugia's conclave splits for eleven months between Boniface's friends and France's. They settle on a Gascon archbishop who will never set foot in Rome.

reigns.tagline: The Gascon pope who never saw Rome
reigns.previously: Benedict XI dies suddenly at Perugia after just eight months.
paragraphs: The cardinals at Perugia were split down the middle, pro-French against anti-French, and it took them eleven months to agree. They picked someone from outside the room: Bertrand de Got, archbishop of Bordeaux, a Gascon whose duke was the king of England. He asked to be crowned at Lyon. As the procession passed, a wall packed with spectators collapsed. Duke John II of Brittany was among the dead.

He meant to go to Italy, but he never did. In 1309 he settled at Avignon, on the Rhône, and Philip IV of France pushed him hard. When Philip had every Templar in France arrested in 1307 and tortured into confessions, Clement protested, then gave way. At the Council of Vienne in 1312 he dissolved the order without condemning it.

He filled the college with Frenchmen, several of them his own relatives, and he was ill for much of his reign. In March 1314 the last Templar grand master, Jacques de Molay, was burned in Paris. A month later Clement was dead at Roquemaure, and before the year was out Philip followed him.

claims.text: Burning on his pyre, Jacques de Molay summoned pope and king to God's judgement within the year.
claims.note: Both men did die in 1314, but the curse turns up only in later chroniclers. It reads like a story written after the fact.

claims.text: A wall collapsed during his coronation procession at Lyon, killing the duke of Brittany.
claims.note: Reported by chroniclers at the time; the pope himself was thrown from his horse.

claims.text: The Templars were guilty of the heresy and idolatry they confessed to.
claims.note: The confessions were extracted by torture and many were retracted. Clement's bull suppressed the order without a verdict of guilt.

reigns.hook: Clement is dead, and his cardinals fight on for over two years. In the end a French prince locks them in at Lyon, and they choose a tiny old man everyone expects to die soon.

reigns.tagline: The stopgap pope who ruled for 18 years
reigns.previously: Clement V dies at Roquemaure, weeks after the Templar master's pyre.
paragraphs: Jacques Duèze was the son of a Cahors burgher, small and frail-looking, and already about 72. After a vacancy of more than two years, Philip of Poitiers shut the cardinals in at Lyon until they chose. They took Duèze, bishop of Avignon, as a safe stopgap. He lived to about 90, ran the Church from his old palace at Avignon, and built a ruthless tax system that filled the treasury.

He picked fights on every side. In 1323 he declared it heresy to say that Christ and the apostles owned nothing, which split the Franciscans. Their leaders, with William of Ockham, fled to Louis of Bavaria, whom John refused to accept as king. Louis replied by having himself crowned in Rome in 1328 and setting up a friar as an antipope.

Then the old man preached that the souls of the blessed do not see God until the Last Judgement. Theologians in Paris were horrified. On his deathbed, on 3 December 1334, he took it back, and died the next day.

claims.text: He left a treasury of 18 million gold florins, plus jewels worth 7 million more.
claims.note: The figure comes from the Florentine chronicler Giovanni Villani. Modern studies of the papal accounts put it far lower.

claims.text: He withdrew his teaching on the beatific vision on his deathbed.
claims.note: The retraction was read out before the cardinals on 3 December 1334, the day before he died.

claims.text: Four Spiritual Franciscans who refused to obey were burned at Marseille in 1318.
claims.note: Recorded by the inquisition that tried them; the Spirituals remembered them as martyrs.

reigns.hook: John dies with his chests full of gold. The cardinals sit down expecting a long fight, and by surprise they elect a stout Cistercian who once hunted heretics in the Pyrenees.

reigns.tagline: The heretic-hunter who built a fortress for popes
reigns.previously: John XXII dies at about 90, having recanted his strange sermon.
paragraphs: Jacques Fournier came from a modest family in the County of Foix and became a Cistercian monk and an abbot. As bishop of Pamiers he ran his own inquisition against the Cathars in the mountain villages, questioning peasants for hours and having every word written down. That register still survives in the Vatican Library.

As pope he cleared up John XXII's mess. In 1336 he ruled that the souls of the saved see God at once. He set out to reform the monks and friars, cut back the scramble for jobs at court, and refused to make his own family rich. He also started building the great fortress-palace at Avignon, which says a lot about where he expected the popes to stay.

He tried to make peace with Louis of Bavaria, but the French king blocked it. When England and France went to war in 1337, he tried to stop that too, and failed. He died in April 1342, leaving the palace half built.

claims.text: He told the cardinals who elected him: "You have chosen an ass."
claims.note: A story told by later chroniclers. It fits his reputation for bluntness but has no early source.

claims.text: His Pamiers inquisition register is the source for Montaillou, the famous portrait of a medieval village.
claims.note: Emmanuel Le Roy Ladurie built his 1975 book from the depositions Fournier had recorded.

claims.text: "To drink like a pope" was coined for Benedict XII.
claims.note: Later writers pinned the Latin phrase on him; there is no evidence he drank more than anyone else.

reigns.hook: Benedict dies with the palace half built. His successor is his opposite: a nobleman and a dazzling preacher who thinks a pope should live like a prince.

reigns.tagline: The prince-pope who stayed put through the Black Death
reigns.previously: Benedict XII dies, leaving his fortress-palace half built.
paragraphs: Pierre Roger was a Benedictine from a noble Limousin family, a star preacher and a friend of the French king. As pope he spent like a prince. He added a grand new wing to the palace, with painted walls, threw feasts, and handed out jobs and favours. Several relatives got red hats, among them a nephew of 18. In 1348 he bought Avignon itself from Queen Joanna I of Naples for 80,000 florins.

That same year the Black Death reached the city. Clement stayed. He paid doctors, had the dead buried, and granted a full pardon to all who died of it. Mobs across Europe were murdering Jews, blaming them for the plague. Clement issued two bulls in 1348 forbidding it, pointing out that Jews were dying of it too.

He fixed the next Jubilee for 1350, and a million pilgrims are said to have gone to Rome. He himself never went. He died at Avignon in December 1352 and was buried at La Chaise-Dieu, the abbey where he had become a monk.

claims.text: He said his predecessors "did not know how to be pope".
claims.note: The remark is quoted in later accounts of his reign. It fits his free-spending style, but it is hard to trace to a source at the time.

claims.text: He issued bulls defending the Jews, who were being blamed for the plague.
claims.note: Two bulls of July and September 1348 told Christians the Jews were not responsible and banned attacks on them.

claims.text: Huguenot soldiers burned his remains at La Chaise-Dieu in 1562.
claims.note: The Wars of Religion left his tomb damaged; the marble effigy survives.

reigns.hook: Clement leaves a dazzling palace and an empty treasury. The cardinals sign a pact to tie the next pope's hands, then elect an old lawyer who tears it up within months.

reigns.tagline: The thrifty lawyer who sent a soldier to win Italy
reigns.previously: Clement VI dies, and his spending has emptied the treasury.
paragraphs: Étienne Aubert was a Limousin who had taught law at Toulouse and worked his way up to cardinal. Before the election the cardinals had all sworn to a pact limiting the new pope's powers. Aubert signed it, and once elected he declared it void. Then he cut back the lavish court and sent many hangers-on home.

His big move was Italy. In 1353 he sent the Spanish cardinal Gil Albornoz, who had fought the Moors in his youth, to win back the Papal States, which local lords had carved up. Albornoz did it, town by town, with armies and a new law code. In 1355 a papal legate crowned Charles IV emperor in Rome.

At home, war bands left over from the fighting between England and France roamed the Rhône valley. In 1360 one of them seized Pont-Saint-Esprit, upriver from Avignon, and the pope paid them to go away. Plague returned in 1361. He died the next September, and was buried in the charterhouse he had founded across the river.

claims.text: He tore up the pact the cardinals had sworn before his election.
claims.note: His bull of July 1353 declared the agreement invalid, saying it limited powers that came from God.

claims.text: Cardinal Albornoz reconquered the Papal States for him.
claims.note: His campaigns from 1353 and the Egidian Constitutions of 1357 are well documented.

claims.text: Cola di Rienzo, the self-styled tribune of Rome, was sent back with Albornoz and killed by a Roman mob in 1354.
claims.note: Told by the anonymous Roman chronicler of the period.

reigns.hook: Innocent dies, and the cardinals cannot agree on any of their own. They reach outside the college for a Benedictine abbot who is away in Italy on the pope's business.

reigns.tagline: The monk who took the papacy home, then lost his nerve
reigns.reignEnded: Died soon after returning to Avignon
reigns.previously: Innocent VI dies, and the cardinals cannot agree on one of their own.
paragraphs: Guillaume de Grimoard was abbot of St Victor at Marseille, and when the news came he was in Italy as a papal envoy. As pope he kept wearing his black Benedictine habit and kept a monk's routine. He spent on students, not feasts, and paid for many hundreds to study.

He also took the plunge his predecessors had avoided. In 1367 he sailed for Italy and entered Rome in October, the first pope there in over 60 years. He found the Lateran burned and the city shabby. In 1368 Emperor Charles IV came to him, and in 1369 the Byzantine emperor John V, desperate for help against the Turks, made a personal submission to the Roman Church.
But Rome was hard work and the French cardinals wanted to go home. In September 1370 Urban sailed back to Avignon. By December he was dead. He was beatified in 1870.

claims.text: Bridget of Sweden warned him he would die soon if he left Rome.
claims.note: Her revelations, recorded by her followers, say so. His death three months later made it look like prophecy.

claims.text: He returned to Rome in 1367, the first pope there since 1305.
claims.note: He entered the city on 16 October 1367.

claims.text: He paid for the studies of over 1,000 students.
claims.note: Figures of about 1,400 come from his early biographers; the exact number is hard to check.

reigns.hook: Urban is barely buried when the cardinals choose again, in a day or so. Their man is the nephew of Clement VI, a cardinal since he was a teenager.

reigns.tagline: The last French pope, coaxed home by a saint
reigns.previously: Urban V gives up on Rome and dies back in Avignon.
paragraphs: Pierre Roger de Beaufort was made a cardinal by his uncle Clement VI at 18, then went off to study law properly at Perugia. Elected at about 41, he was ordained priest only after he became pope. He was gentle, pious and often ill, and he meant to finish the move back to Rome.

Italy got in the way. Florence, fearing papal power, went to war with him in 1375, the War of the Eight Saints, and stirred up revolts across the Papal States. Gregory hired mercenaries. In February 1377 his legate Robert of Geneva let Breton troops loose on the town of Cesena, and thousands were killed.

Catherine of Siena, a young Dominican laywoman, came to Avignon in 1376 and urged him to go. He sailed that autumn and entered Rome on 17 January 1377. In 1377 he also condemned propositions of the English theologian John Wyclif. He died in Rome on 27 March 1378.

claims.text: Catherine of Siena talked him into returning to Rome.
claims.note: Her letters and visit are real, but he had planned the move before she came; she gave him courage, not the idea.

claims.text: Breton mercenaries massacred the people of Cesena in 1377 under his legate's command.
claims.note: Reported by many chroniclers; estimates of the dead run from about 2,500 to 5,000.

claims.text: He was the last French pope.
claims.note: No Frenchman has been elected since.

reigns.hook: For the first time in decades, the cardinals must hold a conclave in Rome. Outside, a mob is shouting for a Roman pope, or at least an Italian one.

reigns.tagline: The pope so savage his cardinals elected another
reigns.cameToPower: Elected with a mob at the door
reigns.previously: Gregory XI brings the papacy back to Rome, then dies there.
paragraphs: Bartolomeo Prignano, archbishop of Bari, was a Neapolitan who had run the papal chancery for years. He was not a cardinal. As a crowd outside roared for a Roman, the cardinals settled on him. When the mob broke in, they propped up an old Roman cardinal in the robes to buy time, and ran.

Elected, Prignano turned savage. He insulted the cardinals to their faces and called them liars. By the summer the French ones had fled to Anagni, and they declared the election void because it had been forced. In September they chose a rival, and now there were two popes. Urban made 29 new cardinals and fought on.
He grew wilder. In 1385, besieged at Nocera, he had six cardinals arrested for plotting against him and tortured. Five of them were never seen again. He died in Rome in October 1389.

claims.text: The cardinals dressed the elderly Cardinal Tebaldeschi in papal robes to fool the mob.
claims.note: Described by several witnesses in the inquiries both sides held afterwards.

claims.text: Five of the arrested cardinals were murdered on Urban's orders.
claims.note: Dietrich of Nieheim, who was with the curia, describes the torture. Nobody knows exactly how the five died.

claims.text: He was poisoned.
claims.note: Rumour at the time, never proved. He had been badly hurt in a fall from his mule the year before.

reigns.hook: The cardinals Urban has insulted slip away and tell Europe his election was forced. Their choice for a new pope is the man whose troops butchered Cesena.

reigns.tagline: The butcher of Cesena, crowned as a rival pope
reigns.cameToPower: Elected by rebel cardinals at Fondi
reigns.reignEnded: Died of a stroke at Avignon
reigns.previously: Urban VI's rages drive his cardinals out of Rome.
paragraphs: Robert of Geneva was the son of the count of Geneva and a cousin of the French king. A cardinal at 29, he had led the papal army in 1377, and Cesena would stick to his name. At Fondi, under the protection of Queen Joanna of Naples, the rebel cardinals elected him on 20 September 1378. He took the name Clement VII.

He tried to take Rome first, but his mercenaries were beaten near Marino in 1379, and he sailed back to Avignon. Europe split along its usual lines. France, Scotland and Naples backed him, then Castile and Aragon. England, most of the Empire and northern Italy stuck with Urban.

He lived well, fed a big court, and squeezed the French clergy to pay for it. Urged to resign for the sake of unity, he never did. He died of a stroke at Avignon in September 1394. The Church today counts him as an antipope.

claims.text: At Cesena he ordered "blood and more blood".
claims.note: Hostile Italian chroniclers put the words in his mouth. That the massacre happened under his command is not in doubt.

claims.text: France, Scotland, Castile and Aragon recognised him as pope.
claims.note: The allegiances of the schism are well documented in the records of each kingdom.

claims.text: His election was planned before the cardinals ever declared Urban's invalid.
claims.note: Urban's supporters said so. The cardinals insisted they had acted only once they were free of Rome.

reigns.hook: Back in Rome, Urban VI has died in 1389. If his few cardinals elect nobody, the schism could end now. They elect a young Neapolitan instead.

reigns.tagline: Young, smooth and selling everything
reigns.previously: Urban VI is dead, but Clement VII still reigns at Avignon.
paragraphs: Pietro Tomacelli came from a poor branch of an old Neapolitan family. He was about 39, handsome and tactful, a cardinal created by Urban VI. Where Urban had raged, he charmed, and he made peace with Naples by recognising the young King Ladislaus.

He badly needed money. He held a Jubilee in 1390 and another in 1400, sold church posts, charged fees for every favour, and handed out indulgences. His brothers and nephews did very well. In 1398 he finally took full control of the city of Rome, ending its independent commune, and fortified Castel Sant'Angelo.
He would not meet the other side halfway. In 1404 envoys from Avignon came to Rome to talk. He refused their terms, the talks turned bitter, and days later he was dead.

claims.text: He sold church offices and indulgences on a huge scale.
claims.note: Dietrich of Nieheim, who worked in his curia, says so bluntly. Historians agree he raised money hard, but the worst stories come from critics.

claims.text: He held two Jubilees, in 1390 and 1400.
claims.note: The 1390 Jubilee had been proclaimed by Urban VI; Boniface held both.

claims.text: The Avignon envoys were jailed after he died.
claims.note: Reports say the Romans briefly held them responsible; they were released for a ransom.

reigns.hook: Boniface dies still refusing to talk. His rival in Avignon has been sitting there for ten years: a hard Aragonese who has sworn to resign for unity and never will.

reigns.tagline: The stubborn Aragonese who would not quit
reigns.previously: Boniface IX dies in Rome, refusing to the end to compromise.
paragraphs: Pedro de Luna was an Aragonese noble and canon lawyer, made a cardinal by Gregory XI. He voted for Urban VI in 1378, then went over to Clement and won Spain for him. When Clement died in 1394, the Avignon cardinals all swore that whoever won would resign if that would end the schism. They elected de Luna, who had sworn too. He never resigned.

France lost patience and withdrew its obedience in 1398. Troops besieged him in the Avignon palace for years until he escaped in 1403. The Council of Pisa deposed him in 1409. In 1416 even Aragon gave up on him. The Council of Constance deposed him on 26 July 1417.

He retreated to the seaside castle of Peñíscola, on a rocky headland on the coast of Valencia, with a handful of loyal cardinals. He went on calling himself pope until he died there in 1423, in his nineties.

claims.text: The Spanish phrase "seguir en sus trece", to stick to your thirteen, comes from him.
claims.note: Popular etymology ties it to Benedict XIII's refusal to give up. Linguists are not sure.

claims.text: He escaped the siege of Avignon in disguise in 1403.
claims.note: He did slip out in March 1403; the details of the disguise vary between chroniclers.

claims.text: Someone tried to poison him at Peñíscola in 1418.
claims.note: The attempt was investigated at the time and a friar was punished; he survived it.

reigns.hook: In Rome, Boniface's cardinals elect a successor while Benedict's envoys are still in the city. Their choice is a mild old lawyer. His nephew is not mild at all.

reigns.tagline: A gentle pope undone by a murderous nephew
reigns.previously: Boniface IX is dead, and Benedict XIII's envoys are in Rome.
paragraphs: Cosimo de' Migliorati was a lawyer from Sulmona, in the Abruzzi, who had taught law and spent years collecting papal revenues in England. Urban VI made him a cardinal. The eight Roman cardinals had sworn to work for unity, and he promised to resign if it would help. He did little to make it happen.

His real trouble was Rome. The city was in uproar, and King Ladislaus of Naples was pulling strings. In August 1405 the pope's nephew Ludovico seized eleven Roman leaders who had come to negotiate and had them murdered, and their bodies thrown into the street. The city rose, and Innocent fled to Viterbo.
The Romans asked him back in 1406. He returned, excommunicated Ladislaus, and revived the university of Rome. He died suddenly that November, after barely two years.

claims.text: His nephew Ludovico murdered eleven Roman citizens in 1405.
claims.note: Reported by contemporaries in Rome; the killings forced the pope out of the city.

claims.text: Innocent knew of his nephew's plan.
claims.note: Nothing shows he did, but he protected Ludovico afterwards, which did him no good with the Romans.

claims.text: He died of a stroke.
claims.note: Contemporary sources say he died suddenly; the cause is not reliably recorded.

reigns.hook: Innocent is gone. This time the Roman cardinals make every candidate swear to resign the moment Benedict does. The winner is a frail old Venetian.

reigns.tagline: The pope who resigned to end the schism
reigns.cameToPower: Elected on a promise to resign
reigns.previously: Innocent VII dies after barely two years.
paragraphs: Angelo Correr was a Venetian noble and Latin patriarch of Constantinople, made a cardinal by Innocent VII. He was elected on a promise: if Benedict XIII resigned, he would too. He agreed to meet Benedict at Savona in 1407. Both men edged closer along the coast, but neither would take the last step, and they never met.

In 1408 he broke another promise and made new cardinals, two of them his nephews. Most of his cardinals walked out. With Benedict's, they called a council at Pisa, which deposed both popes in 1409 and elected a third. Gregory clung on, with only a few allies in Italy and Germany behind him.

At Constance he played his last card well. On 4 July 1415 his envoy formally summoned the council in his name, so that it existed by his authority, and then announced his resignation. He died at Recanati in 1417, weeks before a new pope was elected.

claims.text: He and Benedict XIII never met, though at one point they were a day's journey apart.
claims.note: Gregory at Lucca and Benedict at Portovenere kept finding reasons not to move. Contemporaries saw it as a farce.

claims.text: He was the last pope to resign until Benedict XVI in 2013.
claims.note: No pope resigned between 1415 and 2013.

claims.text: He fled the council he held at Cividale in 1409 disguised as a merchant.
claims.note: Reported by chroniclers; details vary.

reigns.hook: Gregory's own cardinals have walked out on him. At Pisa they join Benedict's, put both popes on trial, and pick a third: a Franciscan born on Crete.

reigns.tagline: The council's answer to two popes was a third
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Rival of Gregory XII and Benedict
reigns.cameToPower: Elected by the Council of Pisa
reigns.reignEnded: Died at Bologna after ten months
reigns.previously: Gregory XII clings on. In 1409 the cardinals try a council at Pisa.
paragraphs: By 1409 cardinals from both camps had had enough of their own popes. Neither Gregory XII in Rome nor Benedict XIII in Avignon would step down, so the rebels called a general council at Pisa. On 5 June it declared both men schismatics and heretics and deposed them. Then the cardinals went into conclave and chose a new pope for everyone.

Their man was Pietro Philarghi, a Greek born on Venetian Crete. He had grown up poor, joined the Franciscans, studied at Oxford and Paris and risen to archbishop of Milan. He took the name Alexander V. Most of Europe accepted him, but Gregory and Benedict simply refused to go. So the Church now had three popes instead of two.

Alexander never even reached Rome. He settled at Bologna, where the powerful legate Baldassare Cossa ran things, and died there on 3 May 1410, less than a year after his election. Cossa was elected in his place within a fortnight.

claims.text: Baldassare Cossa poisoned Alexander V to clear his own way to the papacy.
claims.note: The rumour went round at once and was repeated by Cossa's enemies, such as Dietrich of Nieheim. There is no evidence, and Alexander was about 70.

claims.text: Philarghi was a homeless orphan who begged in the streets of Crete before the Franciscans took him in.
claims.note: Told by later writers and by Philarghi's own circle as a rags-to-riches story. His early life is poorly documented.

claims.text: Rodrigo Borgia's choice of the name Alexander VI in 1492 counted Philarghi as Alexander V.
claims.note: The Pisan popes were widely held legitimate at the time. Alexander V is listed as an antipope today, but the numbering was never changed.

reigns.hook: Alexander is dead after ten months. The cardinals at Bologna turn to the man who was really running things: Baldassare Cossa, a hard Neapolitan noble with a soldier's reputation.

reigns.tagline: He called the council that sacked him
reigns.reignEnded: Deposed by the Council of Constance
reigns.previously: Alexander V dies at Bologna in May 1410, ten months into his reign.
paragraphs: Baldassare Cossa came from a noble Neapolitan family, studied law at Bologna and became a cardinal under Boniface IX. As legate of Bologna he ruled the city like a war lord. Elected by Alexander's cardinals in May 1410, he took the name John XXIII. He fought his way into Rome with the help of Louis of Anjou, then lost it in 1413 when King Ladislaus of Naples sacked the city.

Desperate for an ally, he turned to Sigismund, King of the Romans. Sigismund's price was a general council in his own territory, at Constance, and it opened in November 1414. John hoped it would confirm him. Instead it voted by nations, not by bishops, so his packed Italian vote was useless, and talk turned to all three popes going.

In March 1415 John slipped out of Constance and fled to Schaffhausen. It was a disaster. He was caught, brought back and deposed on 29 May. After years as a prisoner in Germany he submitted to Martin V, who made him a cardinal. He died in Florence in 1419, and Donatello and Michelozzo made his tomb.

claims.text: Cossa had been a pirate in his youth.
claims.note: His enemies said so, and piracy was among the charges against him at Constance. There is no firm evidence; the charges were drawn up to justify deposing him.

claims.text: John fled Constance disguised as a groom or a servant.
claims.note: He did escape in March 1415 with help from Duke Frederick of Austria. The chroniclers disagree on the disguise.

claims.text: When Angelo Roncalli chose the name John XXIII in 1958, he settled that Cossa had been an antipope.
claims.note: Roncalli said publicly that the number was free. The Church had long counted the Roman line as the true one.

reigns.hook: Cossa is deposed and locked up. Gregory XII sends word that he will resign, on his own terms. Benedict XIII won't. For two years, the council itself will run the Church.

reigns.title: The Council Rules
reigns.tagline: No pope for two years, and a council in charge
reigns.previously: John XXIII is deposed. Gregory XII has agreed to resign.
paragraphs: On 4 July 1415 Gregory XII's envoy formally convoked the council in his name and then read his resignation. Rome's line had bowed out with dignity. Now there was no pope, and the council ran the Church itself. In April it had already declared, in the decree Haec sancta, that its power came straight from Christ and that even a pope had to obey it.

It used that power hard. Two days after Gregory quit, on 6 July, it had the Czech reformer Jan Hus burned as a heretic, though Sigismund had promised him safe conduct. His friend Jerome of Prague followed in 1416. Meanwhile Sigismund went to Perpignan and Narbonne to talk Spain out of backing Benedict XIII, who still would not resign. On 26 July 1417 the council deposed him.

In October it passed Frequens, ordering councils to meet regularly from then on. Then 23 cardinals and 30 delegates, six from each of the five nations, went into conclave in the town's merchants' hall. On 11 November 1417, St Martin's Day, they chose a Roman cardinal, Oddone Colonna.

claims.text: Haec sancta made a general council superior to the pope.
claims.note: That is what it says. Later popes held that a council without an undisputed pope could not bind the papacy, and the decree's force is still argued over.

claims.text: Hus was burned despite a safe conduct from Sigismund.
claims.note: The text of Sigismund's safe conduct survives. The council later decreed that a safe conduct could not shield a heretic from judgement.

claims.text: Benedict XIII, deposed, called his castle at Peñíscola the true ark of Noah, holding the whole Church.
claims.note: A colourful saying attached to him by later tradition. He did hold out there with a tiny court until 1423.

reigns.hook: Oddone Colonna takes the name Martin, after the day's saint. He is a Roman, and the one pope everyone can accept. But his city is half in ruins, and he has never ruled anything.

reigns.tagline: One pope again, and a Roman to put the city back together
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected by the council; no rival
reigns.reignEnded: Stroke, as Basel was about to meet
reigns.previously: The council has deposed the last rival pope. Christendom needs one.
paragraphs: Oddone Colonna came from one of Rome's great baronial families. He had backed the Council of Pisa and been made a cardinal by Innocent VII. Elected at Constance on St Martin's Day 1417, he took the saint's name. He was the first pope in nearly 40 years whom all of Western Europe accepted, apart from a few die-hards still loyal to Benedict XIII in Spain.

He took his time going home. He reached Rome only in September 1420, after a long stay in Florence, and found it shabby, half empty and crumbling. He set about mending churches and walls, bringing back order and getting the Papal States to pay taxes again. He also gave towns and castles to his Colonna relatives, who did very well out of him.

Constance had told him to hold councils regularly. He called one to Pavia in 1423, moved it to Siena when plague struck, and shut it down as soon as he could. He named Basel for the next. On 20 February 1431, just as it was due to open, he died of a stroke.

claims.text: He took the name Martin because he was elected on the feast of St Martin of Tours.
claims.note: The election fell on 11 November, St Martin's Day, and the chroniclers of the council make the link.

claims.text: Martin V cared more about his family's estates than about church reform.
claims.note: Critics at the time and since say so. Historians such as Peter Partner credit him with rebuilding papal government almost from nothing.

reigns.hook: Martin dies just as the Council of Basel gathers. The cardinals pick a stern Venetian, Gregory XII's nephew, who has no love for the Colonna or for councils that want to give popes orders.

reigns.tagline: Stoned out of Rome, he still beat the council
reigns.previously: Martin V dies of a stroke as the Council of Basel opens.
paragraphs: Gabriele Condulmer was a Venetian, an Augustinian canon and a nephew of Gregory XII, who made him a cardinal. As pope he went after the Colonna at once to get back what Martin had given them. He also tried to shut down the Council of Basel, which refused and began acting as if it ruled the Church. Under pressure, he backed down in 1433.

In 1434 Rome rose against him and set up a republic. Eugene escaped down the Tiber in a small boat while people on the banks pelted him with stones, and he spent most of the next nine years in Florence. There, in 1436, he consecrated the cathedral under Brunelleschi's new dome.

He beat Basel by stealing its best card. The Byzantine emperor John VIII, desperate for help against the Turks, came to his rival council at Ferrara and then Florence, and in July 1439 the Greek and Latin churches signed a union. Basel deposed Eugene and elected Duke Amadeus VIII of Savoy as Felix V, but few followed. Eugene returned to Rome in 1443 and died there in 1447.

claims.text: Eugene fled Rome in 1434 dressed as a monk, under a shower of stones from the riverbanks.
claims.note: Contemporaries agree on the boat and the stones. The details of the disguise vary from account to account.

claims.text: The union with the Greek Church signed at Florence in 1439 soon fell apart.
claims.note: The decree Laetentur caeli was signed on 6 July 1439. Back home most Greek clergy and people rejected it.

claims.text: Felix V, chosen by Basel in 1439, was the last antipope.
claims.note: He was a widowed duke of Savoy. He gave up in 1449 under Nicholas V, and no later claimant won real support.

reigns.hook: Eugene dies back in Rome. The cardinals choose a doctor's son from Liguria, a cardinal for barely three months, who loves books more than anything and spends like it.

reigns.tagline: The book-mad pope who planned a new Rome
reigns.previously: Eugene IV dies in Rome, the Council of Basel all but beaten.
paragraphs: Tommaso Parentucelli was a doctor's son from Sarzana who had worked as a tutor in Florence and drew up a model library list for Cosimo de' Medici. He was a cardinal for only three months before his election. He was a peacemaker. In 1449 the antipope Felix V gave up, Basel broke up, and the last schism of the Middle Ages was over.

He loved books and scholars. He collected Greek and Latin manuscripts by the hundred, paid humanists to translate Greek classics into Latin, and took on Lorenzo Valla, the man who had exposed the Donation of Constantine. He had Fra Angelico paint his private chapel and drew up plans to rebuild St Peter's. The 1450 Jubilee brought huge crowds and money, and a deadly crush on the Ponte Sant'Angelo.

In 1452 he crowned Frederick III in St Peter's, the last emperor crowned in Rome. Then things went wrong. In January 1453 the Roman Stefano Porcari plotted to overthrow papal rule and was hanged. In May Constantinople fell to the Turks. Nicholas called a crusade that never sailed, and died in March 1455.

claims.text: Nicholas V founded the Vatican Library.
claims.note: He built up a collection of over a thousand manuscripts and meant it for public use. Sixtus IV formally set up the library in 1475, so both get the credit.

claims.text: About 200 pilgrims died in a crush on the Ponte Sant'Angelo during the 1450 Jubilee.
claims.note: The disaster is well recorded. The death toll varies between chroniclers.

claims.text: His bull Dum diversas of 1452 let the king of Portugal enslave Muslims and pagans he conquered.
claims.note: Issued to Afonso V in June 1452 and widened by Romanus pontifex in 1455. It is cited as a charter for the Atlantic slave trade.

reigns.hook: Nicholas is dead and the crusade has gone nowhere. The cardinals deadlock and settle on the oldest man in the room: a Spanish lawyer of 76, who has one burning ambition and a lot of nephews.

reigns.tagline: The first Borgia pope, and he only wanted a crusade
reigns.previously: Nicholas V dies, two years after Constantinople fell to the Turks.
paragraphs: Alfons de Borja was a lawyer from near Valencia who served King Alfonso V of Aragon. He had helped end the last flicker of the Avignon line in 1429, talking Benedict XIII's successor into giving up. The cardinals chose him because he was 76 and expected to die soon. He took the name Callixtus and in Rome became Borgia.

He had one goal: drive the Turks back. He sold church treasures, taxed the clergy and built a fleet. In 1456 he ordered church bells rung every day at noon to call Christians to pray for victory. That July, John Hunyadi broke the Turkish siege of Belgrade. The same year his commission overturned the condemnation of Joan of Arc.

He also brought in the family. His nephew Rodrigo became a cardinal in his mid-twenties and then vice-chancellor of the Church, another nephew captain-general and prefect of Rome. The Romans loathed the Spaniards around him. When he died in August 1458 they hunted the Catalans through the streets.

claims.text: Callixtus excommunicated Halley's comet in 1456.
claims.note: The story grows out of Platina's account of prayers ordered against the comet and the Turks. No bull against a comet exists.

claims.text: The noon bell rung in Catholic churches dates from his order of 1456.
claims.note: His bull of June 1456 ordered the bells and prayers. After Belgrade held, the custom became a thanksgiving.

claims.text: His commission cleared Joan of Arc's name in 1456.
claims.note: He authorised the retrial at her family's request. The court quashed her 1431 sentence on 7 July 1456.

reigns.hook: The old Borgia is dead and his nephews run for cover. The cardinals pick a famous writer instead: a man who once wrote a racy love story, and who now dreams of leading a crusade himself.

reigns.tagline: The poet who became pope and wrote his own memoirs
reigns.reignEnded: Died at Ancona awaiting his fleet
reigns.previously: Callixtus III dies, and Rome turns on the Borgias' Spanish friends.
paragraphs: Aeneas Silvius Piccolomini had lived a lot before he was pope. He was a secretary at the Council of Basel, served the antipope Felix V and then Emperor Frederick III, who crowned him poet laureate. He walked barefoot to a shrine in Scotland, fathered at least two children, and wrote The Tale of Two Lovers, a racy best-seller. He was ordained only in his forties.

As Pius II he wanted one thing: a crusade. He called the princes to Mantua in 1459, and few came. He banned appeals from a pope to a council, and told those who quoted his old pro-council writings to "reject Aeneas, accept Pius". He rebuilt his home village as Pienza, a model Renaissance town, and wrote his Commentaries, frank memoirs of his reign.
In 1464 he took the cross himself and travelled, ill, to Ancona to sail against the Turks. Hardly anyone turned up. He died there on 14 August, days after the Venetian galleys finally arrived.

claims.text: Pius II is the only pope to have written a full autobiography.
claims.note: His Commentaries, written in the third person, cover his life and reign. No other pope left anything like them.

claims.text: He wrote a long letter to Sultan Mehmed II inviting him to become a Christian, and offering to recognise him as emperor.
claims.note: The letter of 1461 survives and was widely copied, but it may never have been sent. Some read it as a rhetorical piece for a Western audience.

claims.text: After a rough crossing to Scotland in 1435 he walked barefoot to a shrine of Our Lady and was crippled by gout ever after.
claims.note: He tells the story himself in the Commentaries. The link to his gout is his own belief.

reigns.hook: Pius dies at Ancona and the crusade melts away. The cardinals write rules to keep the next pope in check. Their pick, a rich Venetian who loves jewels, will tear them up.

reigns.tagline: Jewels, carnival races and humanists on the rack
reigns.previously: Pius II dies at Ancona, and his crusade dies with him.
paragraphs: Pietro Barbo was a rich Venetian and a nephew of Eugene IV, who made him a cardinal in his early twenties. Before electing him the cardinals all swore to a set of rules limiting the next pope's power. Once elected, Paul set them aside. He loved splendour: jewels, cameos, fine fabrics, and the huge palace he built beside San Marco, now the Palazzo Venezia.

He was popular with ordinary Romans. He held carnival horse races down the old Via Lata, which is why it became the Corso. The humanists hated him. When he scrapped the jobs of a group of papal writers in 1464, the scholar Platina protested and was jailed. In 1468 Paul arrested members of the Roman Academy on charges of plotting and paganism and had some tortured, Platina among them.
Abroad, he excommunicated King George of Poděbrady of Bohemia in 1466 and backed a war against him. On 26 July 1471 he died suddenly of a stroke, aged 54.

claims.text: Paul wanted to call himself Formosus, "handsome", until the cardinals talked him out of it.
claims.note: Told by Platina, who had been jailed and tortured by Paul and hated him.

claims.text: Paul II died of a stroke after eating two large melons.
claims.note: A story passed on by Platina and later writers. The stroke is well attested; the melons are gossip.

claims.text: The Via del Corso in Rome is named after Paul's carnival races.
claims.note: He moved the carnival races to the Via Lata in the 1460s, and the street took its name from the corsa, the race.

reigns.hook: Paul is dead, his jewels still in their boxes. In the summer heat the cardinals turn to a Franciscan friar from Liguria, who arrives with a crowd of ambitious nephews.

reigns.tagline: The Franciscan who built a chapel and a family empire
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected; a cardinal Paul II made
reigns.previously: Paul II dies suddenly. The cardinals meet in the summer heat.
paragraphs: Francesco della Rovere came from a modest family on the Ligurian coast and became a star Franciscan preacher and head of his order. As pope he took the name Sixtus, and he turned out to be a builder. He threw the Ponte Sisto across the Tiber for the Jubilee of 1475, reopened the Vatican Library to scholars and put up a big new chapel in the Vatican. It still carries his name: the Sistine.

He also looked after his family like no pope before him. Nephews became cardinals, lords and generals. That's where the word nepotism comes from: nipote, nephew. One nephew, Girolamo Riario, wanted Florence, and on 26 April 1478 his allies the Pazzi struck at Mass in Florence cathedral. Giuliano de' Medici was stabbed to death. His brother Lorenzo got away bleeding, and Florence hanged the plotters, an archbishop among them.

Sixtus answered by excommunicating Lorenzo and going to war with Florence. The same year he let Ferdinand and Isabella set up their own Inquisition in Spain. He died in August 1484, leaving the Sistine walls freshly painted by Botticelli, Perugino and Ghirlandaio, and a College of Cardinals stuffed with his relatives.

claims.text: Sixtus knew about the plot to kill the Medici brothers in the cathedral.
claims.note: The hired soldier Montesecco confessed that Sixtus wanted the Medici gone but said no one should die. Historians still argue over how much he knew.

claims.text: The Sistine Chapel is named after Sixtus IV.
claims.note: He built it in the 1470s and early 1480s; the name comes from Sisto, Italian for Sixtus.

claims.text: The word nepotism comes from popes promoting their nephews.
claims.note: It comes from the Italian nipote, nephew. Sixtus is the classic example, though plenty of popes before and after did the same.

reigns.hook: Sixtus is dead and his nephews are rich. The cardinals pick a genial Genoese who won't hide his children, while a Spanish vice-chancellor waits his turn.

reigns.tagline: The pope who owned his children and kept a sultan's brother
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected; a cardinal Sixtus IV made
reigns.cameToPower: Election run by Giuliano della Rovere
reigns.previously: Sixtus IV dies, and Rome riots against his nephew Girolamo Riario.
paragraphs: Giovanni Battista Cibo was a Genoese nobleman who had a son and a daughter before he was ordained. As pope he made no secret of them, the first pope to do so openly. His election was managed by Cardinal Giuliano della Rovere, Sixtus IV's nephew, who went on to steer much of his policy. He married his son Franceschetto to Maddalena de' Medici, Lorenzo the Magnificent's daughter, and made Lorenzo's 13-year-old son Giovanni a cardinal.

In December 1484 his bull Summis desiderantes backed the German inquisitor Heinrich Kramer in his hunt for witches. Kramer printed it at the front of his witch-hunters' manual, the Malleus Maleficarum. From 1489 Innocent held Cem, the rebel brother of Sultan Bayezid II, in the Vatican, and Bayezid paid him a yearly fee to keep him there.
Money was always short, and he sold offices to raise it. Rome cheered when Granada fell to Ferdinand and Isabella in January 1492. That July Innocent died, and Cem passed to the next pope.

claims.text: Bayezid II paid Innocent 40,000 ducats a year to keep his brother Cem a prisoner.
claims.note: The deal is in the diplomatic record. The sultan also sent the relic of the Holy Lance to Rome in 1492.

claims.text: On his deathbed Innocent was given the blood of three boys, who died, in the first blood transfusion.
claims.note: Nothing in the earliest accounts describes a transfusion. Infessura mentions boys paid to give blood, possibly to drink, but he was hostile and the tale grew later.

claims.text: Innocent's bull of 1484 gave the Malleus Maleficarum papal approval.
claims.note: The bull backed Kramer's inquisition in Germany, and he printed it with his book. But it does not mention or approve the book, which appeared about two years later.

reigns.hook: Innocent is dead. The vice-chancellor Rodrigo Borgia, Callixtus III's nephew, has been waiting 35 years, and he knows every cardinal's price.

reigns.tagline: The Borgia pope and the family that shocked Rome
reigns.cameToPower: Won a conclave said to be bought
reigns.previously: Innocent VIII dies. Columbus is about to sail west.
paragraphs: Rodrigo Borgia was a Spaniard from Valencia and the nephew of Pope Calixtus III, who made him a cardinal young. He ran the papal chancery for decades and grew very rich. In August 1492 he was elected pope. Rome buzzed with talk that he had bought the votes with mule-loads of silver. He was clever, charming and tireless, and he made no secret of his children.

His mistress Vannozza dei Cattanei had given him Cesare, Juan, Lucrezia and Jofré. In 1493 his bull Inter caetera split the newly found lands across the Atlantic between Spain and Portugal. In 1494 Charles VIII of France marched through Italy and into Rome. In 1497 Juan was murdered and his body fished out of the Tiber. A year later the preacher Savonarola, who had denounced Alexander, was hanged and burned in Florence.

Cesare left the Church and carved out a state for the family in the Romagna, with his father's money and troops. Then in August 1503 father and son both fell ill after a dinner. Cesare survived. Alexander died, and his body swelled so badly it had to be forced into its coffin. Rome said poison. With the pope gone, Cesare's power crumbled.

claims.text: Rodrigo Borgia bought the papacy with bribes to the cardinals.
claims.note: Diplomats and chroniclers said so at the time, and gifts to cardinals did follow his election. Simony was common, so how decisive it was is argued.

claims.text: The Banquet of Chestnuts: an orgy in the Vatican in October 1501, watched by the pope and his children.
claims.note: It comes from the diary of Johann Burchard, the papal master of ceremonies, but may be gossip he wrote down. Many historians doubt it.

claims.text: Alexander was poisoned, perhaps by a cup meant for someone else.
claims.note: The rumour was everywhere. But it was a deadly malaria season in Rome, and fever is the likelier cause.

reigns.hook: The Borgia is dead and his son Cesare is sick. The cardinals pick an old, gouty compromise, and everyone knows he is only keeping the seat warm.

reigns.tagline: The stopgap pope who lasted twenty-six days
reigns.previously: The Borgia pope dies in August 1503, and Rome says poison.
paragraphs: Francesco Todeschini was the son of Pius II's sister. His uncle gave him the Piccolomini name, the archbishopric of Siena and, in 1460, a cardinal's hat, when he was only 20. He spent over forty years as a quiet, decent cardinal in a greedy age, and he paid for the library in Siena cathedral where Pinturicchio painted his uncle's life.

When Alexander VI died, French and Spanish armies were near Rome and Cesare Borgia still commanded the Spanish cardinals. Giuliano della Rovere wanted the throne, and so did the French cardinal Georges d'Amboise. Neither could win. On 22 September 1503 they settled on Piccolomini, 64 and crippled by gout. He took his uncle's name. He was only a deacon, so he was made priest, then bishop, and crowned on 8 October.

He talked of reform and a council, but he never had the time. Cesare, sick and losing his grip, came back into Rome under his protection, until the Orsini rose against him and he ran for Castel Sant'Angelo. On 18 October Pius died, 26 days after his election. Della Rovere, who had helped put him there, was ready.

claims.text: Pius III was poisoned.
claims.note: Rumours said so, as they did for most popes who died quickly. He was old, gouty and suffering from an ulcerated leg, which is the likelier cause.

claims.text: He was ordained priest and consecrated bishop only after his election.
claims.note: The papal master of ceremonies, Johann Burchard, records the ceremonies: priest on 30 September, bishop on 1 October, crowned on 8 October.

reigns.hook: Pius is dead within a month. This time the cardinals barely need to meet: Giuliano della Rovere, the Borgia's old enemy, has promised everyone what they want, and he is in a hurry.

reigns.tagline: He wore armour, and he hired Michelangelo
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Nephew of Sixtus IV; Borgia's foe
reigns.cameToPower: Elected in a conclave of a day
reigns.previously: Pius III, old and ill, dies 26 days after his election.
paragraphs: Giuliano della Rovere owed his red hat to his uncle Sixtus IV. He spent the Borgia years in exile in France, plotting. Elected pope in a single day in 1503, he took a name many heard as a nod to Julius Caesar, and he lived up to it. He wanted the Papal States back under Rome's control, and in 1506 he rode out at the head of his army and took Perugia and Bologna.

That same year 150 Swiss soldiers marched into Rome as his guard; their successors are still there. On 18 April 1506 he laid the first stone of a new St Peter's, to Bramante's design. He put Raphael to work on his rooms and talked Michelangelo into painting the Sistine ceiling, which took four years and a lot of shouting on both sides. It was unveiled in 1512.

His wars were a tangle of shifting alliances, first against Venice, then against France. During the fight over Bologna, which he lost again in 1511, he grew a beard and swore not to shave until the French were out of Italy. Raphael painted him like that, old and brooding. The French were pushed out in 1512, and Julius died in February 1513.

claims.text: Julius beat Michelangelo with a stick during one of their rows.
claims.note: The story comes from Ascanio Condivi's life of Michelangelo, written with the artist's help decades later.

claims.text: Erasmus wrote 'Julius Excluded from Heaven', a satire in which St Peter turns the pope away.
claims.note: It circulated anonymously from 1514. Erasmus always dodged the question; most scholars think it was his.

claims.text: The Swiss Guard first arrived in Rome on 22 January 1506.
claims.note: A company of about 150 Swiss reached Rome that day; the date is kept as the guard's founding day.

reigns.hook: The warrior is dead. The cardinals pick a 37-year-old Medici who isn't even a priest yet, and he has very different ideas about how to enjoy the job.

reigns.tagline: The Medici pope who spent lavishly and met Luther
reigns.previously: Julius II, the warrior pope, has died with the French driven out.
paragraphs: Giovanni de' Medici was the son of Lorenzo the Magnificent, and his father got him made a cardinal at 13. When he was elected pope in March 1513 he was only a deacon, so he was ordained priest and bishop in the days that followed. He loved music, hunting, theatre and jokes, and he spent money as fast as the Church could raise it.

Portugal sent him a white elephant called Hanno, who paraded through Rome and became a pet. To pay for the new St Peter's, Leo backed a sale of indulgences. In Germany it was preached hard, and on 31 October 1517 a friar called Martin Luther sent off 95 theses against it. Leo was slow to take him seriously. He finally excommunicated Luther in January 1521.

That October he named Henry VIII 'Defender of the Faith' for a book attacking Luther. Then in December 1521 he fell ill with a fever and died within days, aged 45. He left huge debts and a Church starting to crack in two.

claims.text: Leo said: 'God has given us the papacy, let us enjoy it.'
claims.note: It comes second-hand, in a Venetian ambassador's report of what Leo supposedly told his brother Giuliano.

claims.text: Leo was not yet a priest when he was elected pope.
claims.note: He was ordained priest on 15 March 1513, after the election.

claims.text: Leo was poisoned.
claims.note: Rumours flew, as they did for many Renaissance popes. There was no proof, and a malarial fever is more likely.

reigns.hook: Leo is dead and Luther is winning. The cardinals pick Adrian of Utrecht, a strict Dutch scholar who knows Rome is rotten. The Romans can't stand him.

reigns.tagline: The Dutch carpenter's son the Romans couldn't stand
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected in absence; Charles V's tutor
reigns.previously: Leo X dies suddenly, leaving huge debts and Luther unbeaten.
paragraphs: Adriaan Florensz was born in Utrecht in 1459, the son of a ship's carpenter. Brains got him out. He became a theology professor at Leuven and then tutor to the boy who grew up to be Charles V. Charles sent him to Spain, where he became a bishop, a cardinal, Grand Inquisitor and, while Charles was away, regent through a great revolt.

In January 1522 a deadlocked conclave elected him though he wasn't there, and some cardinals hardly knew who he was. He kept his own name and took eight months to reach Rome. Once there he cut the court to the bone, refused to hand out favours and lived like a monk. The Romans, who lived off papal spending, loathed him. So did the artists: he had no time for pagan statues.

He was frank about the rot. In early 1523 his envoy told the German Diet at Nuremberg that the Church's sickness had started at the top, in the Curia. It won him nothing from Luther's side. Rhodes fell to Suleiman the Magnificent at the end of 1522 while Christian kings squabbled. Adrian died on 14 September 1523. No non-Italian would be pope again until 1978.

claims.text: His envoy Francesco Chieregati admitted at Nuremberg that the Church's troubles began in the Roman Curia.
claims.note: The instruction Adrian sent was read to the Diet in January 1523 and survives; it shocked Rome and delighted the Lutherans.

claims.text: When he died, Romans hung a garland on his doctor's door hailing him as the saviour of the fatherland.
claims.note: A famous anecdote that shows how unpopular he was, but it is told by later writers and hard to pin down.

claims.text: Adrian wanted to throw the statue of Pasquino, where Romans pinned up insults, into the Tiber.
claims.note: Told by later writers; he was supposedly warned that Pasquino, like a frog, would only croak louder under water.

reigns.hook: Adrian is dead, and Rome celebrates. Cardinal Giulio de' Medici, Leo X's cousin, wants the job back for his family. He will get it, after a conclave lasting 50 days.

reigns.tagline: The pope who watched Rome burn from a castle
reigns.previously: Adrian VI, the stern Dutch reformer, dies after 20 months.
paragraphs: Adrian VI, Charles V's old tutor, tried to clean up Rome and was mocked for it. He was the last non-Italian pope for 455 years. Next came Giulio de' Medici, born a month after his father Giuliano was killed in the Pazzi plot. Cousin Leo had made him a cardinal. He was a good administrator but, as pope, couldn't pick a side between France and the Emperor, so he picked both, one after the other.

It went horribly wrong. On 6 May 1527 an unpaid imperial army stormed Rome. The Swiss Guard died fighting on the steps of St Peter's while Clement ran along the raised passage to Castel Sant'Angelo. Rome was looted for months, and the pope was a prisoner until December. He grew a beard in mourning. In 1530 he made peace and crowned Charles V emperor at Bologna.

Meanwhile Henry VIII wanted his marriage to Catherine of Aragon, Charles V's aunt, annulled. Clement stalled for years and would not give it. England began breaking from Rome. Near the end he asked Michelangelo to paint the Last Judgement in the Sistine Chapel. He died in September 1534.

claims.text: 147 of the Swiss Guard were killed defending the pope on 6 May 1527.
claims.note: The figure is the guard's own tradition and is widely accepted; about 40 survived and escorted Clement to safety.

claims.text: Clement slipped out of Castel Sant'Angelo disguised as a servant.
claims.note: Several accounts say he escaped in disguise in December 1527, but his release had been negotiated, and the details vary.

claims.text: Clement was poisoned by eating death cap mushrooms.
claims.note: A rumour at the time. He had been ill for months, and nothing supports it.

reigns.hook: Clement is dead and England is lost. The cardinals turn to a 66-year-old who got his first red hat from the Borgia pope, some say thanks to his sister.

reigns.tagline: A Borgia-era playboy who launched the fight back
reigns.previously: Clement VII is dead. Rome was sacked and England is lost.
paragraphs: Alessandro Farnese was the ultimate Renaissance insider. Alexander VI made him a cardinal in 1493, and gossips said that was thanks to his beautiful sister Giulia, the Borgia pope's mistress. He had children before he became a priest. Within weeks of becoming pope he made two teenage grandsons cardinals, and he later carved the duchy of Parma out of the Papal States for his son Pier Luigi.

Yet this old-style pope started the fight back against Protestantism. He named serious reformers as cardinals. In 1540 he approved a new order, Ignatius of Loyola's Society of Jesus. In 1542 he set up the Roman Inquisition. And in December 1545 the long-awaited council finally opened at Trent.

Rome looked up too. Michelangelo's Last Judgement was unveiled in 1541, and in 1547 the old artist took charge of St Peter's. Titian painted Paul as a sharp, hunched old man. He died in November 1549, worn out and furious with his grandson Ottavio, who had defied him over Parma.

claims.text: Romans called him 'the petticoat cardinal' because his sister Giulia won him his red hat.
claims.note: It was a nickname of the time. Giulia was close to Alexander VI, but Alessandro was able and well connected on his own.

claims.text: Paul III approved the Jesuits in 1540.
claims.note: The bull Regimini militantis ecclesiae of 27 September 1540 founded the Society of Jesus.

claims.text: His final illness was brought on by rage at his grandson's betrayal.
claims.note: Contemporaries told it that way; he was 81 and fever was enough.

reigns.hook: The council at Trent is stuck, and Protestant Europe is growing. The cardinals deadlock for ten weeks, then choose Giovanni del Monte, Trent's old president, who would rather be at his villa.

reigns.tagline: A council, a party villa and a boy made cardinal
reigns.previously: Paul III dies, furious with his grandson. Trent is stuck.
paragraphs: Giovanni Maria Ciocchi del Monte was a Roman lawyer-bishop who had served as one of the presidents at the opening of the Council of Trent. When Paul III died, the conclave dragged on for ten weeks, split between French, imperial and Farnese cardinals. In February 1550 they settled on del Monte. He had promised to back the council, and in 1551 he sent it back to work at Trent.

It did not last. In 1552 German Protestant princes rose against Charles V, and the bishops fled. Julius did not try again. He preferred his new Villa Giulia outside the walls, with its gardens and fountains, and the pleasures of the papal court. He made Palestrina choirmaster at St Peter's. In 1553 the Inquisition burned copies of the Talmud in the Campo de' Fiori, with his approval.

The scandal was Innocenzo. Julius's brother had adopted a teenage boy, said to have been picked up on the streets of Parma, and months after his election Julius made the youth, about 17, a cardinal. Tongues wagged across Europe. There was better news from England, where Mary I brought the country back to Rome in 1554. Julius died in March 1555, crippled by gout.

claims.text: He made a teenager his brother had adopted a cardinal.
claims.note: Innocenzo Ciocchi del Monte was made a cardinal in May 1550, aged about 17, and became the cardinal-nephew. His later crimes embarrassed the next popes.

claims.text: Julius and Innocenzo were lovers.
claims.note: Ambassadors' reports and Protestant writers said so. No firm evidence survives, and the gossip was useful to his enemies.

reigns.hook: Julius is dead. The cardinals elect a scholar so keen to clean house that he bans his own relatives from Rome. He has three weeks to live.

reigns.tagline: The real reformer, pope for just three weeks
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected; a Trent legate like Julius
reigns.previously: Julius III dies in March 1555, gout-ridden and gossiped about.
paragraphs: Marcello Cervini came from the Marche and made his name as a scholar. He was secretary to Paul III's grandson, became a cardinal in 1539, and sat as one of the presidents at Trent. He ran the Vatican Library and was known for living plainly. When Julius died the reformers finally got their man, elected on 9 April 1555.

He kept his own name, Marcellus, and no pope has done that since. He cut the coronation celebrations right back. He told his nephews and other relatives to stay away from Rome, which in that age was almost unheard of. Everyone expected an honest, hard-working papacy. On 1 May, after just 22 days, a stroke killed him.

claims.text: Palestrina's Mass for Pope Marcellus convinced the Council of Trent not to ban polyphonic church music.
claims.note: The story grew up decades later. Trent did discuss music, but there is no evidence this Mass changed anyone's mind.

claims.text: He told the papal choir to sing so that the words could be heard.
claims.note: His secretary Angelo Massarelli's diary records him calling the singers together on Good Friday 1555 to say so.

claims.text: Marcellus II was the last pope to keep his own name.
claims.note: Adrian VI had done it in 1522; every pope since 1555 has taken a new one.

reigns.hook: Marcellus is dead after three weeks. The cardinals now pick the most frightening man in the college: Gian Pietro Carafa, 78, head of the Inquisition, who hates Spain and heresy in equal measure.

reigns.tagline: The inquisitor pope who built the Roman ghetto
reigns.previously: Marcellus II, the reformers' hope, dies after 22 days.
paragraphs: Gian Pietro Carafa was a Neapolitan noble who had served as a papal envoy in England and Spain. In 1524 he helped found the Theatines, a strict order of priests. He talked Paul III into setting up the Roman Inquisition in 1542 and ran it with zeal. Elected in May 1555, he was 78 and as fierce as ever.

Within two months his bull Cum nimis absurdum shut Rome's Jews into a walled ghetto by the Tiber, with one synagogue, and made them wear yellow hats. He hated Spain, which ruled his native Naples, and let his nephew Cardinal Carlo Carafa drag him into war. The Duke of Alba's Spanish army came close to Rome, and in 1557 the pope had to make peace.

He jailed Cardinal Giovanni Morone, a respected reformer, on suspicion of heresy, and in 1559 issued the first papal Index of Forbidden Books, so sweeping that booksellers despaired. That January he finally learned what his nephews had been up to and threw them out of Rome. When he died in August, crowds burned the Inquisition's offices, freed its prisoners and smashed his statue.

claims.text: Paul IV said that if his own father were a heretic, he would gather the wood to burn him.
claims.note: Attributed to him by contemporaries and repeated ever since; the exact words vary and may be polished.

claims.text: The bull Cum nimis absurdum created the Roman ghetto.
claims.note: Issued 14 July 1555; the Roman ghetto lasted until the papal government fell in 1870.

claims.text: Romans knocked the head off his statue on the Capitol when he died.
claims.note: Many reports describe the riot; the rioters also attacked the Inquisition's palace and freed its prisoners.

reigns.hook: Paul IV is dead and the Romans are celebrating. The conclave will drag on for almost four months before it settles on a genial Milanese lawyer, who has plans for the Carafa nephews.
