reigns.tagline: The easy-going Milanese who finished the Council of Trent
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected; out of favour under Paul IV
reigns.previously: Paul IV dies in August 1559, and Rome riots against him.
paragraphs: Giovanni Angelo Medici was a Milanese, no relation of the Florentine Medici. His brother had been a famous mercenary general, and he himself was a smooth lawyer who had worked his way up the papal service. Paul IV disliked him. On Christmas Day 1559, after a conclave of almost four months, the cardinals chose him, and the mood in Rome changed at once.

He went straight after his predecessor's family. Cardinal Carlo Carafa and his brother the Duke of Paliano were tried for crimes including murder, and in March 1561 the cardinal was strangled in Castel Sant'Angelo. Meanwhile Pius reopened the Council of Trent in 1562. Against the odds he steered it to a finish in December 1563 and confirmed its decrees.

His nephew Charles Borromeo, a cardinal at 21, did much of the work and later became a saint. Pius gave Rome Michelangelo's Porta Pia and the church of Santa Maria degli Angeli, built inside the ruined Baths of Diocletian. One band of fanatics even plotted to kill him, and were executed. He died in December 1565, with Borromeo at his bedside.

claims.text: Pius IV had Cardinal Carlo Carafa put to death.
claims.note: Carafa was strangled in Castel Sant'Angelo in March 1561. Pius V later reopened the case and cleared the family's name.

claims.text: Pius IV confirmed the decrees of Trent in January 1564.
claims.note: The bull Benedictus Deus is dated 26 January 1564, and the decrees were printed in Rome that year.

reigns.hook: Pius IV is dead. Borromeo swings the conclave behind a stern Dominican friar and inquisitor, a shepherd boy from Piedmont, who will keep wearing his white habit as pope.

reigns.tagline: The friar pope who excommunicated a queen
reigns.previously: Pius IV dies, with Trent finished and its decrees confirmed.
paragraphs: Antonio Ghislieri looked after sheep as a boy in Piedmont, joined the Dominicans at 14 and took the name Michele. He rose as an inquisitor, so hard-line that Paul IV made him chief of the Roman Inquisition. Elected in January 1566, he kept wearing his white friar's habit, fasted, prayed for hours and wanted Rome to live like a monastery.

He drove prostitutes out of central Rome, came down hard on blasphemy and adultery, and in 1569 expelled the Jews from the Papal States except Rome and Ancona. He turned Trent's decrees into books: a Catechism in 1566, a Breviary in 1568 and the Missal of 1570, the standard Catholic Mass for 400 years. In 1570 his bull Regnans in Excelsis declared Elizabeth I a heretic and freed her subjects from obeying her.

His great project was a crusade. He pushed Spain and Venice into a Holy League with the papacy, and on 7 October 1571 its fleet destroyed the Ottoman navy at Lepanto, off Greece. Pius set up a yearly feast to give thanks. He died on 1 May 1572 and was made a saint in 1712.

claims.text: Pius V saw the victory at Lepanto in a vision, the moment it happened.
claims.note: Told in his early biographies; the official news reached Rome by courier more than a week later.

claims.text: Popes wear white because Pius V kept his white Dominican habit.
claims.note: A popular explanation, but popes wore white long before him. He may have fixed the custom.

claims.text: Regnans in Excelsis freed Elizabeth I's subjects from obeying her.
claims.note: Issued 25 February 1570. It made English Catholics look like traitors and helped harden Elizabeth's laws against them.

reigns.hook: Pius V is dead and Lepanto is won. The cardinals elect a Bologna law professor in a day. He has a son from before his ordination, and he is about to change the calendar.

reigns.tagline: The pope who deleted ten days
reigns.previously: Pius V, the saintly inquisitor of Lepanto, has died.
paragraphs: Ugo Boncompagni was a law professor from Bologna who had worked at Trent. Before he was ordained he had a son, Giacomo, whom he later made governor of Castel Sant'Angelo. In August 1572, three months into his reign, news came of the St Bartholomew's Day massacre of Protestants in Paris. Gregory had a Te Deum sung and a medal struck to celebrate it.

His big legacy was time itself. The old Julian calendar had drifted ten days out against the sun, which threw off Easter. Astronomers worked out a fix, and Gregory's bull of February 1582 ordered it. In Catholic lands Thursday 4 October 1582 was followed by Friday 15 October. Protestants dragged their feet: Britain waited until 1752, and Russia until 1918.

He poured money into colleges for training priests, including the Jesuits' Roman College, now the Gregorian University. To pay for it he seized land from nobles, and bandits overran the Papal States. In March 1585 he welcomed four young Japanese envoys to Rome, and he died weeks later.

claims.text: Gregory celebrated the St Bartholomew's Day massacre with a Te Deum and a medal.
claims.note: The medal survives, showing an angel striking down the Huguenots, and Vasari painted the massacre in the Vatican's Sala Regia.

claims.text: Ten days simply vanished from the calendar in October 1582.
claims.note: Spain, Portugal, Poland and the Papal States switched at once; France followed in December.

claims.text: Rioters demanded 'Give us our eleven days!' when Britain switched in 1752.
claims.note: Based on a Hogarth print. Historians have found no real evidence of calendar riots.

reigns.hook: Gregory is dead and bandits rule the roads. The cardinals elect a farmer's son who is said to have herded pigs as a boy. He'll have heads on the bridges within months.

reigns.tagline: The swineherd pope who rebuilt Rome in five years
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected; out of favour under Gregory
reigns.previously: Gregory XIII is dead. Bandits rule the roads of the Papal States.
paragraphs: Felice Peretti came from a poor family in the Marche and joined the Franciscans as a boy. As Cardinal Montalto he kept his head down under Gregory XIII. As pope he was a whirlwind. He went after the bandits without mercy, and the heads of the executed were stuck up on the Ponte Sant'Angelo. Within two years the roads were safe and the treasury full.

Then he rebuilt Rome. He drove long straight streets between the great churches, and he brought water back to the hills with a new aqueduct, the Acqua Felice. In 1586 his engineer Domenico Fontana moved the huge Egyptian obelisk to the front of St Peter's, using hundreds of men and horses. In 1590 the dome of St Peter's was finally closed.

He also fixed the number of cardinals at 70 and reorganised the Curia into departments. But he rushed out his own edition of the Latin Bible, and it was full of mistakes. He died in August 1590, and the Romans, who had hated his taxes, tried to pull down his statue.

claims.text: He hobbled into the conclave on a crutch, pretending to be feeble, and threw it away once elected.
claims.note: The tale comes from Gregorio Leti's lively 17th-century biography, which is full of inventions.

claims.text: 'Water on the ropes!': a sailor broke the order of silence to save the obelisk when its ropes began to burn.
claims.note: A much-loved Roman tale, written down long after the event.

claims.text: Sixtus's Vulgate Bible was so full of errors that it was recalled after his death.
claims.note: Copies were called in and a corrected edition, the Clementine Vulgate, came out in 1592.

reigns.hook: Sixtus is dead. The next pope, Urban VII, is said to ban smoking in church, and he dies of malaria before he's even crowned. Rome is in for a run of very short reigns.

reigns.tagline: Thirteen days: the shortest papacy on record
reigns.previously: Sixtus V, the builder, dies hated by the Romans.
paragraphs: Giovanni Battista Castagna was a Roman of Genoese family and a career papal diplomat. He had been archbishop of Rossano, sat at Trent, spent years as nuncio in Spain and governed towns in the Papal States. Sixtus V made him Inquisitor General. When Sixtus died in August 1590, Spain pushed hard for Castagna, and on 15 September he was elected.

He took the name Urban and had a name for kindness and for frowning on nepotism. But it was the fever season in Rome. Within days he caught malaria, and on 27 September 1590 he died, 13 days after his election and before he could even be crowned. No pope has had a shorter reign. He left his fortune to pay dowries for poor girls.

claims.text: Urban VII issued the world's first known ban on smoking, threatening excommunication for using tobacco in or near churches.
claims.note: Often repeated in histories of smoking. The better-documented papal tobacco bans came later, under Urban VIII (1624) and Innocent X.

claims.text: He left his estate to fund dowries for poor girls.
claims.note: His will left it to the Archconfraternity of the Annunciation in Rome, which used it for that purpose.

reigns.hook: Urban VII is dead before his coronation. The cardinals fight for two months, then choose Spain's man: a pious, sickly Milanese bishop who will send papal troops into France's religious war.

reigns.tagline: Spain's pope, and a ban on betting on popes
reigns.cameToPower: Picked from Spain's list of names
reigns.previously: Urban VII dies of malaria after 13 days, never crowned.
paragraphs: Niccolò Sfondrati came from a family of Milanese senators; his father became a cardinal after being widowed. Niccolò was bishop of Cremona for 30 years, attended Trent, and was a friend of Charles Borromeo and Philip Neri. He was devout, gentle and often ill. After a two-month conclave in which Spain named the men it would accept, he was elected on 5 December 1590.

France was in the middle of a religious civil war, and the Protestant Henry of Navarre claimed the throne. Gregory sided with Spain and the Catholic League. He renewed Henry's excommunication, sent money and an army under his nephew Ercole Sfondrati, and called on the French clergy to abandon Henry. Another nephew, Cardinal Paolo Emilio Sfondrati, ran much of the business.

Rome itself was suffering famine and plague. Gregory did stamp out one popular vice: in March 1591 he banned betting on papal elections, on how long a pope would last and on new cardinals, on pain of excommunication. He died on 16 October 1591, after ten months.

claims.text: Gregory XIV banned betting on papal elections.
claims.note: His bull Cogit nos of March 1591 targeted the wagers Roman bankers and merchants took on conclaves and cardinals.

claims.text: He died of a huge gallstone.
claims.note: Contemporary reports speak of a large stone found after his death; his health had always been poor, and details vary.

reigns.hook: Gregory XIV is dead within the year. Spain's men in the conclave try again, and they choose an old Bolognese cardinal who helped build the Holy League of Lepanto. He is sick too.

reigns.tagline: Two months in the chair, and one walk too many
reigns.previously: Gregory XIV dies after ten months, in a hungry, plague-hit Rome.
paragraphs: Giovanni Antonio Facchinetti was born in Bologna in 1519 and trained as a lawyer. He worked for Cardinal Alessandro Farnese, became bishop of Nicastro in Calabria, and went to the Council of Trent. As nuncio in Venice he helped put together the Holy League that fought at Lepanto. Gregory XIII made him a cardinal in 1583.

In October 1591 Spain's cardinals got their way again and elected him, aged 72. He kept to Gregory XIV's line, backing the Catholic League in France against Henry of Navarre. But he was already worn out. He fell ill after a pilgrimage round the churches of Rome, and died on 30 December 1591, two months after his election.

claims.text: He caught his fatal chill on a pilgrimage to Rome's great churches.
claims.note: Reported at the time; at 72 and in poor health, any winter illness could have killed him.

claims.text: Four popes died between August 1590 and December 1591.
claims.note: Sixtus V, Urban VII, Gregory XIV and Innocent IX; Rome held four conclaves in under eighteen months.

reigns.hook: Four popes are dead in sixteen months. This time the cardinals pick a younger, tougher man, Ippolito Aldobrandini, who will last thirteen years and make peace with the King of France.

reigns.tagline: The pope who forgave a French king and burned a philosopher
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected; made cardinal by Sixtus V
reigns.cameToPower: Elected once Spain's man fell short
reigns.previously: Innocent IX dies after two months, the third pope lost since 1590.
paragraphs: Ippolito Aldobrandini came from a Florentine family of lawyers driven out by the Medici. He was a careful, hard-working canon lawyer who wept easily at Mass and went to confession almost every day. After four conclaves in a year and a half, Rome finally had a pope who would last. He brought out a corrected Latin Bible in 1592 to replace the error-ridden one Sixtus V had rushed into print.

His big gamble was France. Henry IV, a Protestant, had turned Catholic to win Paris, and Spain wanted the pope to refuse him. Clement absolved him in 1595 anyway, and France came back into the fold. When the last Este duke of Ferrara died in 1597 without a legitimate son, Clement took the city into the Papal States.

His Rome was harsh. In 1599 young Beatrice Cenci was beheaded for her part in her father's murder, and on 17 February 1600, in the middle of the Holy Year, the philosopher Giordano Bruno was burned alive in the Campo de' Fiori. Clement died in March 1605, after 13 years.

claims.text: Clement tasted coffee, liked it, and 'baptised' it so Christians could drink the Muslims' drink.
claims.note: A popular story with no source from his time; it appears in print only centuries later.

claims.text: Giordano Bruno was burned in the Campo de' Fiori on 17 February 1600.
claims.note: Records of his trial and execution survive; a statue put up in 1889 marks the spot.

claims.text: Beatrice Cenci was a victim, driven to kill a brutal father, and Clement wanted her family's fortune.
claims.note: Romans pitied her and the legend grew in novels and plays. Historians agree the father was violent; the greed charge is unproven.

reigns.hook: Clement is dead. France's friends are backing a Medici cardinal of almost seventy, and Spain can't stop him. He will barely have time to unpack.

reigns.tagline: The Medici pope who lasted less than a month
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected; Clement VIII's legate to France
reigns.previously: Clement VIII dies in March 1605, after 13 years and a Holy Year.
paragraphs: Alessandro de' Medici was a Florentine from a junior branch of the great family, and his mother was a niece of Pope Leo X, so he took the name Leo. He had been archbishop of Florence and Clement VIII's legate in France, where he helped bring Henry IV's kingdom back to Rome. Henry repaid him: French money and French cardinals got him elected on 1 April 1605, to Spain's fury.

Paris celebrated. Rome barely had time to notice. On 17 April Leo rode in procession to take possession of the Lateran, his cathedral, on a cold spring day. He fell ill soon afterwards and died on 27 April, aged 69. His reign lasted 27 days, one of the shortest in papal history.

claims.text: Leo caught the chill that killed him at his Lateran procession.
claims.note: Contemporaries blamed the long ride in the cold. He was nearly seventy, and the exact illness is not known.

claims.text: On his deathbed Leo refused to make his great-nephew a cardinal, though he was urged to.
claims.note: Told in older Catholic histories as proof of his integrity; the source is pious tradition and hard to check.

claims.text: Henry IV spent a fortune to get Leo elected.
claims.note: Envoys reported large French sums going to cardinals. How much changed hands, and to whom, is unclear.

reigns.hook: Leo is dead after 27 days. The great historian Cardinal Baronius is the favourite, but Spain says no. The conclave settles on a stern canon lawyer named Borghese.

reigns.tagline: The pope who put his name across St Peter's
reigns.previously: Leo XI, the Medici pope, is dead 27 days after his election.
paragraphs: Camillo Borghese was a Roman canon lawyer from a Sienese family, a dry man who believed Church law should be enforced to the letter. He tested that on Venice in 1606, when the republic jailed two priests and limited new church building. Paul put the whole city under interdict. Venice ordered its priests to ignore him, threw out the Jesuits, and let the friar Paolo Sarpi argue its case. After a year France brokered a deal and the pope backed down.

At home he built. Carlo Maderno finished the nave and façade of St Peter's, with PAULUS V BORGHESIUS across the front in giant letters. His nephew, Cardinal Scipione Borghese, grew enormously rich, built the Villa Borghese and gave the young Bernini his first big commissions. In 1615 Japanese envoys from the lord Date Masamune reached Rome.

In 1616 the Holy Office ruled that the Earth moving round the sun was against Scripture, and Galileo was warned not to hold or defend it. Paul died in January 1621, as the Thirty Years War was beginning.

claims.text: Paul V put Venice under interdict in 1606 and the city defied him.
claims.note: The bulls, Sarpi's pamphlets and the 1607 settlement brokered by France all survive. Venice never formally backed down.

claims.text: Galileo was formally ordered never to teach Copernicanism 'in any way whatever' in 1616.
claims.note: An unsigned note in the file says so, but Cardinal Bellarmine's certificate for Galileo records only a warning. It mattered at his trial in 1633.

claims.text: Paul's stroke came during a procession giving thanks for the Catholic win at White Mountain.
claims.note: Repeated in papal histories from accounts of the time; the timing fits, but details vary.

reigns.hook: Paul is dead and Catholic armies are winning in Bohemia. The cardinals choose a frail archbishop of Bologna, and his 25-year-old nephew is ready to run the show.

reigns.tagline: Two short years that changed how popes are chosen
reigns.previously: Paul V dies in January 1621, his name blazing across St Peter's.
paragraphs: Alessandro Ludovisi was a Bolognese lawyer and archbishop, schooled by the Jesuits, frail and often ill. Everyone expected a short reign. His nephew Ludovico, just 25, was made a cardinal within days and ran the government. The Ludovisi grew rich fast, and Gregory brought his fellow Bolognese painter Guercino to Rome to decorate their villa.

He used his time well. He changed the rules of the conclave: from now on cardinals voted by secret written ballot, which made it harder to bully or bribe them in public. In 1622 he set up the Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith, Propaganda Fide, to run missions from China to the Americas. That March he canonised Ignatius Loyola, Francis Xavier, Teresa of Ávila, Philip Neri and Isidore the Farmer in a single ceremony.
He backed the Catholic side in the Thirty Years War, and the Duke of Bavaria thanked him with the captured Palatine Library of Heidelberg, which went to the Vatican. Gregory died in July 1623.

claims.text: Gregory XV brought in the secret written ballot for papal elections.
claims.note: His bulls of 1621 and 1622 laid down the rules, and conclaves still use written ballots today.

claims.text: Five saints were canonised in one ceremony on 12 March 1622.
claims.note: The bulls survive. Romans joked that it was four Spaniards and a saint, since Philip Neri was the only Italian.

claims.text: The Heidelberg library was war loot handed to the pope.
claims.note: Maximilian of Bavaria gave it after taking Heidelberg in 1622. Most of it is still in the Vatican Library.

reigns.hook: Gregory is dead. The new pope is a poet and a Barberini, and he has long admired Galileo. Galileo thinks his moment has come.

reigns.tagline: The poet pope who put Galileo on trial
reigns.previously: Gregory XV dies, and the cardinals meet in the summer heat of 1623.
paragraphs: Maffeo Barberini was a Florentine diplomat who wrote Latin verse and liked clever company. As a cardinal he even wrote a poem in praise of Galileo. As pope he spent like a prince. Bernini built a giant bronze canopy over St Peter's tomb, and bronze was stripped from the porch of the ancient Pantheon. Most of that metal ended up as cannon for Castel Sant'Angelo.

Then Galileo published his Dialogue in 1632. It argued for a Sun-centred universe and gave one of the pope's favourite arguments to a character called Simplicio. Urban was furious. In 1633 the Inquisition made the old scientist kneel and renounce the idea that the Earth moves. Galileo spent his last years under house arrest near Florence.

Meanwhile the pope's nephews grew rich on Church money. Their feud with the Farnese family dragged the Papal States into the War of Castro, which ended in 1644 in a costly flop. When Urban died that July, many Romans openly celebrated.

claims.text: Galileo muttered "And yet it moves" as he got up from his knees.
claims.note: The line first appears in print in 1757, more than a century after the trial. No witness reports it.

claims.text: "What the barbarians didn't do, the Barberini did."
claims.note: The joke was going round Rome in his lifetime and is linked to Pasquino, the statue where Romans pinned anonymous jibes. Who coined it is unknown.

claims.text: Urban turned on Galileo because he felt mocked as Simplicio.
claims.note: Contemporaries said so, and the pope's argument does end up in Simplicio's mouth. Historians also point to politics: Urban was under attack for being soft on heresy.

reigns.hook: Urban's nephews have made a lot of enemies. The next conclave picks a stern old Roman lawyer who owes them nothing, and who listens rather too closely to his sister-in-law.

reigns.tagline: The scowling pope Velázquez painted too well
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected; made cardinal by Urban VIII
reigns.previously: Urban VIII dies in 1644, and many Romans cheer.
paragraphs: Giovanni Battista Pamphili was a Roman lawyer and papal diplomat, plain-faced, slow and suspicious. France tried to block him, but the veto came too late. Once elected he went after Urban's nephews and their fortune, and they fled to France. Everyone said the real power was his widowed sister-in-law, Olimpia Maidalchini. Ambassadors learned to call on her first.

In 1648 the Peace of Westphalia ended the Thirty Years War and gave Protestant states rights in law. Innocent declared it null and void. Europe ignored him. The days when a pope could undo a peace treaty were over.

His family palace stood on Piazza Navona, so he turned the square into a showpiece. Bernini's Fountain of the Four Rivers went up in the middle, finished in 1651. In 1650 Velázquez painted him, red-faced and wary, one of the great portraits of all time. He died in January 1655.

claims.text: Seeing his portrait, Innocent said "Troppo vero!", "Too true!"
claims.note: A much-repeated story with no contemporary source. He did hang the picture and reward the painter.

claims.text: Olimpia Maidalchini ran the Church through him and was nicknamed "the popess".
claims.note: Her influence was real and widely reported by envoys. The juiciest tales come from hostile gossip writers such as Gregorio Leti.

claims.text: Olimpia refused to pay for his coffin, saying she was a poor widow.
claims.note: Told by hostile writers after his death. His body did lie for days before burial, but the details are coloured.

reigns.hook: Innocent is dead. After an 80-day conclave the cardinals pick his Secretary of State, Fabio Chigi, as Alexander VII. A queen who gave up her throne is already heading for Rome.

reigns.tagline: Bernini's patron, humbled by the Sun King
reigns.previously: Innocent X dies in 1655, and his family squabbles over the bill.
paragraphs: Fabio Chigi was a Sienese scholar-diplomat. As papal envoy at Münster he watched the Peace of Westphalia being made and protested against it. He came in as a reformer, swearing to keep his family away from Rome. A year later he invited them in and gave them jobs. Rome shrugged; it had seen this before.

Christmas 1655 brought a star convert: Queen Christina of Sweden, who had given up her throne, rode into Rome and made it her home. In 1656 plague hit, and Alexander's strict quarantine kept the death toll far lower than in Naples. Then he gave Bernini the job of his life: the two great curving colonnades of St Peter's Square, and the bronze Chair of St Peter inside.

Louis XIV was less impressed. In 1662 the pope's Corsican Guard attacked the French ambassador's palace in Rome. Louis seized Avignon and threatened war, and in 1664 Alexander had to sign a humiliating treaty, send his nephew to Paris to apologise and put up a monument admitting the guilt. He died in May 1667.

claims.text: Alexander kept a coffin in his bedroom to remind him of death.
claims.note: Reported by people at his court and repeated by later biographers; he was known for gloomy piety.

claims.text: Louis XIV forced the pope to put up a monument admitting the Corsican Guard's crime.
claims.note: Required by the Treaty of Pisa, 1664, and pulled down a few years later with Louis's consent.

claims.text: Christina of Sweden entered Rome in December 1655 as a Catholic convert.
claims.note: Her welcome is well recorded; she lived in Rome until her death in 1689 and is buried in St Peter's.

reigns.hook: Alexander is dead and Louis XIV has taught Rome a lesson. The cardinals turn to the late pope's Secretary of State, a gentle Tuscan who once wrote operas.

reigns.tagline: The opera writer who became pope
reigns.cameToPower: Elected with French and Spanish support
reigns.previously: Alexander VII dies in 1667, humbled by Louis XIV.
paragraphs: Giulio Rospigliosi had a past no other pope could claim: he wrote operas. In the 1630s, working for the Barberini, he wrote librettos including Sant'Alessio and Chi soffre, speri, one of the first comic operas. Later he was nuncio in Spain and Alexander VII's Secretary of State. As pope he was gentle, generous and modest, and kept his relatives on a short leash.

He gave Bernini one more job: the angels carrying the instruments of the Passion along the Ponte Sant'Angelo. In 1669 he calmed the long fight with the Jansenists in France with a compromise known as the Peace of Clement IX.
His great worry was Crete. The Turks had been besieging Venetian Candia for over twenty years, and Clement sent money, ships and men. It fell in September 1669. He died that December.

claims.text: Clement IX wrote opera librettos, including the comic opera Chi soffre, speri.
claims.note: Rospigliosi wrote texts for operas staged by the Barberini in the 1630s and 1640s, decades before he became pope.

claims.text: Clement died of grief at the fall of Candia.
claims.note: Said at the time and repeated ever since. He was ill and nearly seventy; the heartbreak is a nice story, not a diagnosis.

claims.text: Two of Bernini's bridge angels were thought too beautiful for the weather, so copies went up instead.
claims.note: Bernini's own two were kept indoors and later went to Sant'Andrea delle Fratte, where they still stand. That the pope wanted them saved is the usual story.

reigns.hook: Clement is dead and the conclave drags on for months. In the end the cardinals pick a Roman of 79 who has been a cardinal for barely five months.

reigns.tagline: The old man who adopted a nephew to run Rome
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected; made cardinal by Clement IX
reigns.previously: Clement IX dies in December 1669, said to be heartbroken over Crete.
paragraphs: Emilio Altieri was a Roman aristocrat and careful Church lawyer who had waited a very long time. Clement IX made him a cardinal in November 1669, days before dying himself. The conclave that followed lasted almost five months, and in April 1670 the cardinals settled on Altieri, aged 79, mostly because he was too old to last.

He had no nephew to run things, so he made one. His family's last heiress married a relative of Cardinal Paluzzo Paluzzi, and the pope adopted the cardinal, who took the name Altieri and took over the government. Romans grumbled that the cardinal-nephew was pope in all but name.

Clement canonised Rose of Lima in 1671, the first saint born in the Americas, and held the Holy Year of 1675. He sent money to Poland against the Turks and quarrelled with Louis XIV over French church revenues. He died in July 1676, aged 86.

claims.text: Clement X adopted Cardinal Paluzzi as his nephew, and Paluzzi ran the papacy.
claims.note: The adoption and the name change are documented; ambassadors complained that everything went through the cardinal.

claims.text: When elected, Altieri protested that he was too old and wept.
claims.note: A common tale in conclave accounts of the time; such modest refusals were also expected theatre.

claims.text: Rose of Lima, canonised in 1671, was the first saint of the Americas.
claims.note: She was the first person born in the Americas to be canonised by the Catholic Church.

reigns.hook: Clement X is dead at 86. The next pope is a thrifty banker's son from Como who hates nepotism, and he is about to pick a fight with the Sun King.

reigns.tagline: The penny-pinching saint who saved Vienna
reigns.cameToPower: Elected after a long summer conclave
reigns.previously: Clement X dies at 86, his adopted nephew still running Rome.
paragraphs: Benedetto Odescalchi came from a rich family of bankers in Como. As pope he was the opposite of the Baroque spenders: he cut the court, paid down the debts of the Papal States, kept his nephew out of power and frowned on carnival and theatres. Romans mocked his thrift. They also trusted him.

He spent his money on one cause, war against the Ottomans. When a huge Turkish army besieged Vienna in 1683, papal cash flowed to Emperor Leopold and to King John III Sobieski of Poland, whose cavalry broke the siege that September. Innocent then helped build the Holy League that drove the Turks out of Hungary.

With Louis XIV it was war of a different kind. The French clergy's Four Articles of 1682 said popes could not overrule kings or councils, and Innocent refused to confirm Louis's bishops. By the time he died in August 1689, dozens of French dioceses were empty.

claims.text: Papal money helped save Vienna in 1683.
claims.note: Innocent sent large subsidies to Leopold and Sobieski and worked hard to build the alliance.

claims.text: Innocent quietly backed William of Orange's invasion of England in 1688.
claims.note: Louis XIV's side said so, since both men opposed France. No evidence shows the pope helped a Protestant take James II's throne.

claims.text: Innocent was beatified in 1956.
claims.note: Pius XII beatified him after a cause slowed for centuries, in part by French objections.

reigns.hook: Innocent is dead and the French want a friendlier pope. They get a Venetian of 79 who means to make up for lost time, and his nephews are packing for Rome.

reigns.tagline: Old, Venetian and in a hurry to reward his family
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected; made cardinal by Innocent X
reigns.previously: Innocent XI, the thrifty pope of Vienna, dies in 1689.
paragraphs: Pietro Ottoboni was a Venetian noble and an expert Church judge who had sat on the Rota, Rome's highest court, for years. Louis XIV wanted peace with Rome and backed him, and soon handed back Avignon, seized in his quarrels with Innocent XI. Ottoboni was 79, and he acted like it. His great-nephew Pietro became a cardinal at 22 and spent the family's new money as a patron of music, hiring Corelli and later the young Handel.

Rome liked him better than his strict predecessor: taxes were cut and food got cheaper. He bought Queen Christina's great library for the Vatican and sent money to Venice for its war with the Turks. But he did not give in to France. On his deathbed he had the condemnation of the Four Gallican Articles made public. He died in February 1691, after 16 months.

claims.text: Asked why he rewarded his family so fast, he said: 'I must hurry, the clock has struck twenty-three.'
claims.note: A famous quip in the old Italian way of counting hours, meaning the day was nearly over. It is told of him but not well sourced.

claims.text: Alexander VIII bought Queen Christina's library for the Vatican.
claims.note: Her manuscripts form the Reginenses collection of the Vatican Library to this day.

claims.text: His nephew Cardinal Pietro Ottoboni became a great patron of Corelli and Handel.
claims.note: Corelli lived in his palace; Handel performed there in 1707–08.

reigns.hook: Alexander is dead after 16 months. The cardinals squabble for five months before settling on the archbishop of Naples, who has strong views about nephews.

reigns.tagline: The pope who banned the papal nephew
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected; a compromise after five months
reigns.reignEnded: Died in Rome in the Holy Year
reigns.previously: Alexander VIII dies after 16 months, his nephews well rewarded.
paragraphs: Antonio Pignatelli was a southern Italian noble, a career diplomat and then archbishop of Naples, simple in his habits and stubborn about reform. He took his name in honour of Innocent XI and went one step further. His bull of 1692, Romanum decet pontificem, banned popes from giving estates, offices or income to relatives, and allowed at most one relative to become a cardinal. The age of the super-rich papal nephew was over.

He spent on the poor instead, turning part of the Lateran into a refuge and building up the great hospice of San Michele. In 1693 he made peace with Louis XIV, whose bishops dropped the Four Articles. In 1699 he condemned a book by the French archbishop Fénelon on pure love of God.
He opened the Holy Year of 1700 but did not live to close it. He died that September, aged 85.

claims.text: Innocent XII's bull of 1692 ended papal nepotism.
claims.note: Romanum decet pontificem was real and largely obeyed. Favouritism at court went on, but the giant family fortunes stopped.

claims.text: 'The poor are my nephews.'
claims.note: A saying attributed to him by admirers; there is no contemporary record of him saying it.

claims.text: He advised the dying Charles II of Spain to leave his crown to Louis XIV's grandson.
claims.note: Charles did consult the pope in 1700. How firm the papal answer was, and how much it counted, historians still argue.

reigns.hook: Innocent dies in the Holy Year, and weeks later so does the King of Spain. The cardinals choose a scholarly Albani, newly a priest, to face a war over Spain's crown.

reigns.tagline: The reluctant pope who split France and lost China
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected; made cardinal by Alexander VIII
reigns.previously: Innocent XII dies in 1700, having banned papal nepotism on paper.
paragraphs: Giovanni Francesco Albani was a polished Roman bureaucrat from Urbino who had been a cardinal for ten years but a priest for only a few weeks. The conclave picked him in November 1700, the same month Spain's childless king died and left his empire to a French prince. Albani wept and held out for days before saying yes. He had good reason to dread the job.

The War of the Spanish Succession rolled into Italy. In 1708 imperial troops seized papal Comacchio and marched into the Papal States, and in January 1709 Clement had to recognise the Habsburg candidate as king of Spain. Louis XIV and Philip V were furious. Neither side trusted him again.

In 1713 his bull Unigenitus condemned 101 statements by the French Jansenist Pasquier Quesnel and split the French Church for decades. In 1715 he banned Chinese converts from honouring Confucius and their ancestors with the old rites, and the Kangxi Emperor turned against the missions. He also gave James Stuart, the exiled Catholic claimant to Britain's throne, a home in Rome.

claims.text: Albani took days to accept his election and had to be talked into it.
claims.note: Contemporary reports describe his tears and refusal; theologians were consulted before he agreed. How sincere the reluctance was is another matter.

claims.text: His ban on the Chinese Rites wrecked the Jesuit mission in China.
claims.note: The ban angered the Kangxi Emperor, who restricted missionaries. Historians argue over how much the decree, rather than court politics, caused the decline.

claims.text: Unigenitus condemned 101 propositions from Quesnel's book.
claims.note: The bull of 8 September 1713 lists them. Many French bishops and the Paris Parlement resisted it for decades.

reigns.hook: Clement dies after 20 hard years. In the conclave the emperor blocks the favourite, and the cardinals turn to a man whose family once gave the Church its mightiest pope.

reigns.tagline: A mighty pope's name on a sick man's shoulders
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected; made cardinal by Clement XI
reigns.previously: Clement XI dies in 1721, worn out by war and the Jansenists.
paragraphs: Michelangelo dei Conti came from the Roman clan that had produced Innocent III, the most powerful pope of the Middle Ages, and he took his ancestor's name. He had spent twelve years as nuncio in Lisbon. He got the job only after the Austrian emperor vetoed the front-runner, Clement XI's Secretary of State, Fabrizio Paolucci.

He was ill and heavy, and his reign was short and cautious. He kept up Clement's line on the Chinese Rites and leaned hard on the Jesuits, who were dragging their feet, threatening to stop them taking new members. He made the French schemer Guillaume Dubois a cardinal and kept paying the exiled James Stuart's pension.
He ruled for less than three years. He died in March 1724, aged 68, and the cardinals settled in for another long conclave.

claims.text: He was of the same family as Innocent III.
claims.note: The Conti of Segni produced Innocent III, Gregory IX and Alexander IV in the 13th century, and he picked his name to honour them.

claims.text: Dubois's red hat was the price of French support in the conclave.
claims.note: Dubois, the French regent's right-hand man, worked hard for it and got it within weeks. A bargain was widely suspected; no signed deal survives.

reigns.hook: Innocent XIII is dead. After ten weeks the cardinals choose a 75-year-old Dominican who sleeps on a hard bed, begs them not to elect him and trusts the wrong man completely.

reigns.tagline: The friar pope and the crooked cardinal
reigns.reignEnded: Died at 81, still living like a friar
reigns.previously: Innocent XIII dies in 1724 after less than three years.
paragraphs: Pietro Francesco Orsini was the heir of one of Rome's grandest families, and he threw it all over at 18 to become a Dominican friar. As pope he still lived like one: plain food, long hours in church and pastoral visits, and he kept his old archdiocese of Benevento. He took the number XIII, treating Pedro de Luna, the Benedict XIII of the Avignon schism, as an antipope.

He had no head for government and left it to Niccolò Coscia, a favourite from Benevento whom he made a cardinal. Coscia and his friends sold offices, took bribes and drained the treasury. The pope never seemed to notice. Meanwhile Rome got the Spanish Steps, finished in time for the Jubilee of 1725.
Benedict died in February 1730, aged 81. The Romans went after Coscia as soon as he was gone, and the next pope put him on trial.

claims.text: He first called himself Benedict XIV, then changed it to XIII.
claims.note: Reported by the standard histories: he chose the number that treated Pedro de Luna's claim as void.

claims.text: Coscia was jailed for his corruption.
claims.note: Under Clement XII he was tried, fined and sentenced in 1733 to ten years in Castel Sant'Angelo, though he kept his red hat.

claims.text: He was pulled alive from the ruins of his palace in the Benevento earthquake of 1688.
claims.note: The story is in his early biographies. He credited Saint Philip Neri, a belief rather than a fact anyone can check.

reigns.hook: The friar pope is dead and the treasury is empty. A long conclave picks a rich Florentine of 78. He will go blind, and he will settle accounts with Coscia.

reigns.tagline: The blind pope who built the Trevi Fountain
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected; made cardinal by Clement XI
reigns.previously: Benedict XIII dies in 1730, leaving Coscia and an empty treasury.
paragraphs: Lorenzo Corsini came from rich Florentine bankers and had once bought his way into a Roman career. He was 78 when elected, and by 1732 he was blind. He ran the Church from his bed, with his nephew Cardinal Neri Corsini doing much of the work. He put Coscia on trial and clawed back what he could.

To refill the treasury he brought back the public lottery his predecessor had banned, and spent the winnings on building. Nicola Salvi won the contest for the Trevi Fountain, Alessandro Galilei gave the Lateran its giant new front, and in 1734 the Capitoline Museums opened to the public. In 1738 his bull In eminenti made him the first pope to condemn the Freemasons.
Abroad he counted for little. The great powers swapped Naples and Parma between them without asking him. He died in February 1740, aged 87, and the cardinals locked themselves in for six months.

claims.text: He went blind two years into his reign and governed from his bed.
claims.note: Every account of his reign records it. His nephew and the Curia carried much of the load.

claims.text: His 1738 bull was the first papal condemnation of Freemasonry.
claims.note: In eminenti apostolatus specula banned Catholics from joining on pain of excommunication. Later popes repeated the ban.

claims.text: The Capitoline Museums were the first public museum in the world.
claims.note: Often said. They opened to the public in 1734, but the Ashmolean in Oxford had admitted visitors since 1683.

reigns.hook: Clement XII dies blind at 87. The next conclave drags on for six months, until a cheerful scholar from Bologna makes a joke the cardinals can't forget.

reigns.tagline: The wittiest pope, and Voltaire's pen pal
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected; made cardinal by Benedict XIII
reigns.previously: Clement XII dies in 1740, blind and bedridden at 87.
paragraphs: Prospero Lambertini, archbishop of Bologna, was a brilliant canon lawyer with a fast tongue. Years earlier, as the Vatican's "devil's advocate", he had written the rulebook for making saints, and it is still the starting point. After six months of deadlock he is said to have told the conclave which candidate to pick for a saint, which for a politician, and that if they wanted an honest man they should take him.

He knew the Catholic kings were stronger than the pope and made deals rather than fights. Concordats with Sardinia, Naples and Spain gave rulers more control over their churches. He confirmed the bans on the Chinese and Indian rites, and backed women scholars in Bologna such as the physicist Laura Bassi.

Protestants and philosophers liked him too. Voltaire dedicated his play Mahomet to him in 1745, and the pope wrote back politely. He died in May 1758, aged 83. Behind him the Catholic courts were sharpening their knives for the Jesuits.

claims.text: He told the conclave: if you want an honest man, elect me.
claims.note: A famous anecdote repeated in many histories. It fits his humour, but there is no reliable record of his words in the conclave.

claims.text: Voltaire dedicated Mahomet to him, and the pope replied.
claims.note: The dedication and the pope's letter of 1745 were printed. Voltaire made the most of it against his critics.

claims.text: His rules on canonisation are still used.
claims.note: His treatise De servorum Dei beatificatione set the standards for evidence and miracles that the process still follows in outline.

reigns.hook: Benedict XIV is gone. The cardinals pick a gentle Venetian, and the Catholic kings are about to demand the one thing he won't give: the head of the Jesuit order.

reigns.tagline: The pope who would not give up the Jesuits
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected; made cardinal by Clement XII
reigns.reignEnded: Died the night before a showdown
reigns.previously: Benedict XIV dies in 1758, liked even by Voltaire.
paragraphs: Carlo Rezzonico came from a rich Venetian family that had bought its way into the nobility. He was pious, kind and stubborn, and his reign became one long fight to save the Jesuits. Portugal's strongman Pombal threw them out in 1759, packing hundreds onto ships for the Papal States. France banned the order in 1764. Spain expelled them in 1767, and Naples and Parma followed.

In 1765 Clement answered with a bull praising the Jesuits. In 1768 he condemned Parma's attacks on Church rights, and the Bourbon kings hit back. France seized Avignon and Naples took Benevento. In January 1769 their ambassadors demanded that he dissolve the order outright.
He called a meeting of cardinals for 3 February. On the night before, he died suddenly of a stroke, aged 75. The Trevi Fountain, begun under Clement XII, had been finished in his reign.

claims.text: He had fig leaves added to the Vatican's nude statues.
claims.note: Widely told, and he did favour modesty, but which statues were covered and on whose order is unclear.

claims.text: He died on the eve of the consistory called to answer the Bourbon demand.
claims.note: He died on the night of 2 February 1769. The meeting was set for 3 February.

claims.text: Pombal shipped the Portuguese Jesuits to the Papal States.
claims.note: From 1759 hundreds were deported and landed at Civitavecchia, to the pope's dismay.

reigns.hook: The Bourbon courts want a pope who will kill off the Jesuits. After three months they get a Franciscan, the only friar in the College. Did he promise them something to win?

reigns.tagline: The friar who shut down the Jesuits
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected; made cardinal by Clement XIII
reigns.previously: Clement XIII dies suddenly in 1769, the Jesuits still standing.
paragraphs: Lorenzo Ganganelli, a doctor's son from Romagna, was a Franciscan friar and the only member of his order among the cardinals. The Spanish and French courts backed him because they thought he would dissolve the Jesuits. He stalled for four years, mending fences with Portugal and dropping the yearly bull that had annoyed every Catholic king.

In July 1773, with Spain pressing hardest, he signed the brief Dominus ac Redemptor and dissolved the Society of Jesus. Its general, Lorenzo Ricci, was locked in Castel Sant'Angelo and died there. In 1774 France and Naples gave back Avignon and Benevento.

He had lighter moments. In 1770 he made the 14-year-old Mozart a knight of the Golden Spur, and he began what became the Pio-Clementine Museum. He died in September 1774, aged 68, and Rome said the Jesuits had poisoned him.

claims.text: He promised before his election to suppress the Jesuits.
claims.note: His enemies said he had given the Spanish a written pledge. No such paper has been found; he may have hinted that it could be done.

claims.text: He was poisoned.
claims.note: Rumours spread at once and his body decayed fast. The autopsy found no proof, and most historians think he died of illness.

claims.text: He knighted the boy Mozart.
claims.note: Mozart received the Order of the Golden Spur in July 1770, after writing down Allegri's Miserere from memory in the Sistine Chapel.

reigns.hook: The Jesuits are gone and the conclave drags on for months. The man who comes out is handsome, vain and about to run straight into the French Revolution.

reigns.tagline: The handsome pope who died a French prisoner
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected; made cardinal by Clement XIV
reigns.previously: Clement XIV dies in 1774, amid whispers of poison.
paragraphs: Giovanni Angelo Braschi was handsome and knew it. He spent freely: a new sacristy for St Peter's, galleries for the Vatican's ancient statues, a palace for his nephew and a costly scheme to drain the Pontine Marshes. In 1782 he travelled all the way to Vienna to talk Emperor Joseph II out of his Church reforms. Joseph was charming and changed nothing.

Then France exploded. In 1791 Pius condemned the Revolution's Civil Constitution of the Clergy, which turned priests into elected state officials. In 1796 a young general called Napoleon Bonaparte marched into Italy. The Treaty of Tolentino in 1797 cost the pope land, millions in cash and a hundred works of art.

In February 1798 the French took Rome and declared a republic. Pius, 80 years old and sick, was hauled away as a prisoner, from town to town and over the Alps to Valence in France. He died there in August 1799.

claims.text: Many said Pius VI would be the last pope.
claims.note: The papacy looked finished in 1799, with Rome occupied and the pope dead in exile. Some French officials and writers said as much.

claims.text: He was vain about his good looks, especially his legs.
claims.note: A favourite joke of Roman satirists. His love of show and building is well documented; the vanity stories are gossip.

claims.text: The art taken at Tolentino went to the Louvre.
claims.note: Many pieces were paraded through Paris in 1798. After Napoleon fell, the sculptor Canova recovered much of it for Rome.

reigns.hook: The pope has died a prisoner and Rome is in French hands. The cardinals scatter, then gather in Venice under Austrian protection to elect a successor.

reigns.tagline: The monk who stood up to Napoleon
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected; from Pius VI's home town
reigns.cameToPower: Elected at a conclave in Venice
reigns.previously: Pius VI dies a French prisoner at Valence in 1799.
paragraphs: Barnaba Chiaramonti was a Benedictine monk, gentle and stubborn, from Cesena like his predecessor. Back in battered Rome, he had to deal with Napoleon. Their Concordat of 1801 brought the Church back to France, on Napoleon's terms. In 1804 Pius crossed the Alps for the coronation in Notre-Dame. At the big moment, Napoleon took the crown and put it on his own head.

The friendship soured. In 1809 Napoleon annexed Rome. Pius excommunicated the invaders, and in the early hours of 6 July French troops broke into the Quirinal Palace and arrested him. He was held at Savona, then at Fontainebleau, and bullied into concessions he later took back.

When Napoleon fell, Pius came home to cheering crowds in May 1814. That August he restored the Jesuits, and the Congress of Vienna gave back most of the Papal States. He even gave Napoleon's mother a home in Rome. He died in August 1823, weeks after a fall that broke his hip.

claims.text: Napoleon crowned himself in front of the pope.
claims.note: Planned in advance and recorded by witnesses. Pius blessed the crown; David's huge painting shows Napoleon crowning Josephine instead.

claims.text: Pius called Napoleon "Commediante! Tragediante!" to his face.
claims.note: The scene comes from the French writer Alfred de Vigny, writing in 1835. No witness reported it.

claims.text: Pius sheltered Napoleon's mother and family in Rome.
claims.note: Letizia Bonaparte lived in Rome from 1814 until her death in 1836.

reigns.hook: Napoleon is gone and the Papal States are back. The hardliners want them run the old way, and their man is Annibale della Genga, a cardinal so sickly he looks half dead.

reigns.tagline: The sick man who ran Rome like a strict headmaster
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected; made cardinal by Pius VII
reigns.previously: Pius VII dies in 1823, his lands restored.
paragraphs: Annibale della Genga was a former diplomat, so ill at his election that he looked like a dying man. He was the choice of the zelanti, the hardliners who hated Pius VII's reforming minister Consalvi, and won after Austria vetoed their first pick. He sacked Consalvi and set out to bring the old order back.

Rome's Jews were shut back in the ghetto at night and barred from owning property. Police spies hunted the Carbonari and other secret societies. Taverns could sell wine only through a grille, for drinking at home. The Holy Year of 1825 brought in pilgrims, but the Papal States grew poorer and angrier.
He died in February 1829, aged 68, and few Romans were sorry. The cardinals looked for someone milder.

claims.text: He banned vaccination against smallpox.
claims.note: Often repeated, but historians have found no clear ban. The story may come from his opponents.

claims.text: He told the conclave they were electing a corpse.
claims.note: A popular story about his poor health at the time. It is told in many forms and none is firmly sourced.

claims.text: Austria vetoed Cardinal Severoli in the 1823 conclave.
claims.note: Cardinal Albani read the veto for Austria. The hardliners then switched to della Genga.

reigns.hook: Leo XII is dead and Rome breathes out. The cardinals pick a gentle, sickly canon lawyer, said to be the man Pius VII had always hoped would follow him.

reigns.tagline: Twenty months of pain, prayer and revolution
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected; made cardinal by Pius VII
reigns.previously: Leo XII dies in 1829, his police state unloved.
paragraphs: Francesco Saverio Castiglioni was a learned canon lawyer, gentle and constantly ill. He suffered from painful sores and a stiff neck that made him hold his head to one side. He loosened some of Leo XII's harsher rules, but left foreign policy to his Austrian-leaning Secretary of State, Giuseppe Albani.

Britain passed Catholic Emancipation in April 1829, letting Catholics sit in Parliament, and Pius welcomed it. In July 1830 revolution in Paris threw out the last Bourbon king of France. Pius decided to recognise the new king, Louis-Philippe, rather than lose the French Church.
Unrest was spreading through Italy when he died in November 1830, after only 20 months.

claims.text: Pius VII used to call him "Pius VIII" as his chosen successor.
claims.note: A story told in older histories. Pius VII thought highly of him, but the nickname is anecdote.

claims.text: He welcomed Britain's Catholic Emancipation Act.
claims.note: The act became law in April 1829, weeks after his election, and he praised it.

reigns.hook: Pius VIII is dead and revolution is spreading through Italy. The cardinals take seven weeks to choose a Camaldolese monk who isn't even a bishop yet.

reigns.tagline: The monk who kept the trains out
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected; made cardinal by Leo XII
reigns.previously: Pius VIII dies in 1830 as revolution spreads through Italy.
paragraphs: Bartolomeo Cappellari, a Camaldolese monk named Mauro, was the last man elected pope before he was a bishop. Within days of his election Bologna and the other northern towns rose up and declared the pope's rule over. Gregory called in Austrian troops to crush them, and when the revolt flared again in 1832 the French moved into Ancona too.

In 1832 his encyclical Mirari vos condemned liberty of conscience and freedom of the press. He kept the Papal States run by priests, with no railways and few reforms. Yet in 1839 he condemned the slave trade, and he founded the Vatican's Etruscan and Egyptian museums.
He died in June 1846, aged 80. Italy was simmering with nationalism, and the cardinals wanted a gentler face.

claims.text: He banned railways from the Papal States.
claims.note: The first papal line opened only in 1856, under his successor.

claims.text: He called railways "chemins d'enfer", roads to hell.
claims.note: A pun on the French chemins de fer. Widely told, but no reliable source has him saying it.

claims.text: His 1839 letter condemned the slave trade.
claims.note: In supremo apostolatus, issued in December 1839, banned Catholics from taking part in the trade in African slaves.

reigns.hook: The cardinals pick a kindly bishop with a name for liberal ideas. Italy goes wild for him. It won't last.

reigns.tagline: From liberal hero to prisoner of the Vatican
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected; made cardinal by Gregory XVI
reigns.previously: Gregory XVI dies in 1846, with railways still banned.
paragraphs: Giovanni Maria Mastai-Ferretti, soon "Pio Nono", began as Italy's liberal hero. He freed political prisoners and eased censorship. Then came 1848. His minister Pellegrino Rossi was stabbed to death on the steps of parliament, and Pius slipped out of Rome in disguise to Gaeta. Mazzini and Garibaldi set up a Roman Republic until French troops crushed it in 1849. Pius came home cured of liberalism.

He dug in. In 1854 he declared the Immaculate Conception a dogma. In 1858 papal police took six-year-old Edgardo Mortara from his Jewish family in Bologna, because a servant said she had secretly baptised him. Pius refused every plea to return him. In 1864 his Syllabus of Errors denied that the pope should make peace with progress and liberalism.

In July 1870 the First Vatican Council declared the pope infallible when defining doctrine. On 20 September Italian troops blasted through the wall at Porta Pia and took Rome. The Papal States were gone after 1,100 years. Pius shut himself in the Vatican and called himself a prisoner. He reigned 31 years, the longest after Peter's traditional span.

claims.text: Edgardo Mortara was taken from his parents and raised by the Church.
claims.note: The case caused an international outcry. Mortara became a priest and defended the pope all his life.

claims.text: Infallibility passed by 533 votes to 2.
claims.note: Many opposing bishops left Rome before the final vote on 18 July 1870 rather than vote against the pope.

claims.text: In 1881 a mob tried to throw his coffin into the Tiber.
claims.note: During the night-time move of his body to San Lorenzo, anticlerical rioters attacked the procession. Police drove them off.

reigns.hook: Pio Nono dies after 31 years. The cardinals want a short, quiet reign and pick a frail-looking man of 67. He will outlive almost all of them.

reigns.tagline: The stopgap pope who lasted 25 years
reigns.previously: Pius IX dies in 1878, the self-styled prisoner of the Vatican.
paragraphs: Vincenzo Gioacchino Pecci was 67, thin and pale, and the cardinals expected a short reign. He lasted 25 years. He stayed a prisoner of the Vatican and never set foot in Italian Rome, but his mind roamed further. In 1881 he opened the Vatican's secret archives to scholars of every faith.

In 1891 his encyclical Rerum Novarum took on the industrial age. It defended private property against socialism, but it also said workers deserved a fair wage and had the right to form unions. It became the founding text of modern Catholic social teaching.

He was the first pope to be filmed, blessing the camera in the Vatican gardens in 1896. He also enjoyed Vin Mariani, a French tonic wine laced with coca, and let his face appear in its adverts. He died in July 1903, aged 93.

claims.text: Leo XIII endorsed a cocaine-laced wine.
claims.note: Vin Mariani's adverts used his picture and said he had awarded its maker a gold medal. Coca wine was legal and fashionable at the time.

claims.text: He was the first pope filmed and recorded.
claims.note: Film of him from the 1890s survives, as does a wax-cylinder recording of his voice made in 1903.

reigns.hook: Leo dies at 93. In the conclave his right-hand man, Cardinal Rampolla, takes the lead. Then a cardinal from Kraków stands up with a message from the Austrian emperor, and the votes swing to Giuseppe Sarto.

reigns.tagline: The postman's son who made war on modernism
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected; made cardinal by Leo XIII
reigns.reignEnded: Died as the Great War began
reigns.previously: Leo XIII dies in July 1903, aged 93.
paragraphs: Rampolla was leading the votes when Cardinal Puzyna of Kraków read out a veto from Emperor Franz Joseph. The cardinals protested, then turned to Giuseppe Sarto, patriarch of Venice and son of a village postman. One of his first acts banned such vetoes on pain of excommunication.

He was warm with ordinary people and fierce with theologians. In 1907 he branded new critical study of the Bible and doctrine "modernism", the sum of all heresies, and from 1910 every priest had to swear an oath against it. He let children take communion from about seven and started a single code of Church law.
France cut the Church loose from the state in 1905, and Pius refused the terms. He died in August 1914, weeks into the First World War. He was declared a saint in 1954.

claims.text: Austria vetoed the favourite, Rampolla, in 1903.
claims.note: The last use of the Catholic powers' old veto. Rampolla's votes actually rose after it was read, but he could not win.

claims.text: A secret network of informers hunted modernists for him.
claims.note: Monsignor Umberto Benigni ran the Sodalitium Pianum, which spied on suspect clergy. How much the pope knew of its methods is argued.

claims.text: He died of grief at the outbreak of war.
claims.note: A pious story told soon after. He was 79 and ill; the war surely distressed him, but no doctor recorded grief as the cause.

reigns.hook: Pius X is dead and Europe is at war. The cardinals pick a small, sharp diplomat from Genoa who has been a cardinal for barely three months.

reigns.tagline: The little diplomat who called the war a slaughter
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected; made cardinal by Pius X
reigns.cameToPower: Elected weeks into the First World War
reigns.previously: Pius X dies in August 1914, weeks into the war.
paragraphs: Giacomo della Chiesa was small, pale and slightly lopsided, a Genoese nobleman trained as a diplomat under Cardinal Rampolla. Pius X sent him off to be archbishop of Bologna and made him a cardinal only in May 1914. In September, with the war a month old, the conclave chose him. Even the smallest white cassock laid out for the new pope was too big.

He spent the war trying to stop it. In August 1917 he sent the warring powers a peace plan that called the war a useless slaughter. Both sides ignored it and each accused him of favouring the other. His office in the Vatican traced missing soldiers, swapped wounded prisoners and passed messages to families.
In 1917 he issued the first Code of Canon Law. After the war he made up with France and opened the Church's missions to local clergy. He died of pneumonia in January 1922, aged 67.

claims.text: Benedict XV called the war a "useless slaughter".
claims.note: The words are in his peace note of 1 August 1917, addressed to the leaders of the warring nations.

claims.text: The Allies secretly agreed to keep the pope out of the peace talks.
claims.note: Article 15 of the secret Treaty of London of 1915, published by the Bolsheviks in 1917, shut out the Holy See at Italy's request.

claims.text: The Turks put up a statue of him in Istanbul.
claims.note: Raised in 1921 in the courtyard of the Cathedral of the Holy Spirit, thanking him for war relief given without regard to nation or religion.

reigns.hook: Benedict is dead. The cardinals turn to a librarian who climbs mountains. In Italy, a former socialist journalist named Mussolini is months from power.

reigns.tagline: The mountaineer pope who made a country
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected; made cardinal by Benedict XV
reigns.cameToPower: Elected on the fifth day of conclave
reigns.previously: Benedict XV dies of pneumonia in January 1922.
paragraphs: Achille Ratti was a scholar-priest who ran the Ambrosian Library in Milan and then the Vatican Library, and spent his holidays climbing Monte Rosa, the Matterhorn and Mont Blanc. After a stint as papal envoy in newly independent Poland, he became archbishop of Milan and, in February 1922, pope. That October, Mussolini came to power.

On 11 February 1929 his Secretary of State and Mussolini signed the Lateran Treaty. Italy recognised a tiny sovereign state, Vatican City, and paid compensation for the lost Papal States. The pope accepted the loss of Rome. The Roman Question was settled. In 1931 Marconi himself helped open Vatican Radio.

In 1933 the Vatican signed a concordat with Hitler's Germany, negotiated by Eugenio Pacelli. The Nazis broke it almost at once. In 1937 his encyclical Mit brennender Sorge, written in German, was smuggled into the country and read from Catholic pulpits on Palm Sunday. Old and ill, he was preparing an encyclical against racism and antisemitism when he died in February 1939.

claims.text: He died before he could publish an encyclical against racism and antisemitism.
claims.note: A draft, later called the "hidden encyclical", was written by Jesuits at his request in 1938. It was never issued.

claims.text: Mit brennender Sorge was smuggled into Germany and read out on Palm Sunday 1937.
claims.note: Copies were secretly printed and carried to parishes. The Gestapo seized what it could afterwards.

claims.text: He told Belgian pilgrims in 1938: "Spiritually, we are Semites."
claims.note: Reported by Belgian Catholic papers at the time; the Vatican's own paper left it out.

reigns.hook: Pius XI is dead and Europe is months from war. The cardinals choose the man who knows Germany best: his Secretary of State, Eugenio Pacelli.

reigns.tagline: The diplomat pope of the Second World War
reigns.previously: Pius XI dies with his encyclical against racism still unpublished.
paragraphs: Eugenio Pacelli was a Roman lawyer's son who spent his life in Vatican diplomacy. He was nuncio in Germany through the 1920s, then Pius XI's Secretary of State, and in 1933 he negotiated the concordat with Hitler's new government. The cardinals chose him on the third ballot, on his birthday, in March 1939. Six months later Germany invaded Poland.

He kept the Vatican formally neutral while Nazi Germany murdered some six million Jews in the Holocaust. In his Christmas message of 1942 he spoke of hundreds of thousands condemned to death or slow extinction, some only because of their nationality or race. He named neither the Jews nor Germany. On 16 October 1943 German troops rounded up Rome's Jews; more than a thousand were sent to Auschwitz. Thousands more hid in convents, monasteries and Vatican buildings.

After the war he was a fierce Cold War opponent of communism. In 1950 he declared the Assumption of Mary a dogma, the only time a pope has formally used papal infallibility since 1870. He died in October 1958. The argument over his wartime record began a few years later and has never stopped.

claims.text: Pius XII did all he could for the Jews of Europe and directed the rescue in Rome.
claims.note: Critics such as John Cornwell (Hitler's Pope, 1999) say his silence failed the victims. Defenders, like the Jesuit Pierre Blet, point to the sheltering in Rome. Since the archives opened on 2 March 2020, David Kertzer (The Pope at War, 2022) and others have added evidence, and the debate goes on.

claims.text: His 1942 Christmas message spoke of people killed because of their nationality or race without naming Jews or Germany.
claims.note: The text of the broadcast survives. Some at the time read it as a clear protest; others found it too vague to matter.

claims.text: St Peter's bones were found under the basilica.
claims.note: Pius XII ordered the excavations and said in 1950 that Peter's tomb had been found; Paul VI said in 1968 the bones were identified. Many archaeologists remain unconvinced.

reigns.hook: The cardinals meet in October 1958. After nineteen years, many want a short, quiet pontificate. They choose the 76-year-old patriarch of Venice, a peasant's son.

reigns.tagline: The stopgap pope who threw open the windows
reigns.previously: Pius XII dies after nineteen years, the war still hanging over him.
paragraphs: Angelo Roncalli grew up in a big family of tenant farmers near Bergamo. He spent decades as a Vatican diplomat in Bulgaria, Turkey and France before becoming patriarch of Venice. At 76 he looked like a safe, short-term choice. He was round, funny and warm, and he took the name John, which an antipope of the Great Schism had used. He calmly declared himself the twenty-third.

Within three months he announced an ecumenical council. The Second Vatican Council opened on 11 October 1962. That night a huge crowd with candles filled St Peter's Square, and he spoke from his window about the moon, then told the parents to go home and give their children a hug from the pope. In April 1963 he issued Pacem in Terris, a letter on peace addressed to everyone of good will.
He was already dying of stomach cancer. He died on 3 June 1963, with the council barely begun. He was canonised in 2014.

claims.text: As a diplomat in Istanbul during the war he helped Jewish refugees escape.
claims.note: His help with transit papers and his contacts with Jewish agencies are well documented, though how many lives it saved is uncertain.

claims.text: He chose the number XXIII on purpose to settle that the Pisan John XXIII was not a real pope.
claims.note: He did say at his coronation that the name had been used by popes of doubtful legitimacy. Whether he meant it as a ruling on the Schism is argued over.

claims.text: He said he got the idea for the council in a sudden flash of inspiration.
claims.note: That is how he told it. Historians note the idea of a council had been floated in the Curia under Pius XI and Pius XII.

reigns.hook: The council has hardly started and its pope is dead. Who will finish it? The favourite is the archbishop of Milan, a careful, anxious man.

reigns.tagline: The first pope to fly, who gave away his crown
reigns.previously: John XXIII dies of cancer with Vatican II barely begun.
paragraphs: Giovanni Battista Montini was a Curia insider who had become archbishop of Milan. He steered Vatican II to its close in 1965. The Mass moved from Latin into local languages, and the Church opened up to other Christians, Jews and the modern world. He gave away the papal tiara for the poor; American Catholics bought it and it sits in Washington.

He was the first pope to fly. In 1964 he went to the Holy Land and embraced Patriarch Athenagoras of Constantinople. In 1965 the two lifted the excommunications of 1054. That year he told the United Nations: no more war, war never again. In 1970 a man with a knife lunged at him at Manila airport.

In 1968 Humanae Vitae upheld the ban on artificial contraception, and many Catholics simply ignored it. In 1978 he begged the Red Brigades to free his old friend Aldo Moro, but they killed him. Paul VI died three months later. He was canonised in 2018.

claims.text: He gave his tiara away and it ended up in Washington.
claims.note: He laid it on the altar of St Peter's in 1964. It was bought by American Catholics and is displayed at the National Shrine of the Immaculate Conception in Washington.

claims.text: He was wounded in the Manila knife attack of 1970.
claims.note: The attack is certain. Officials played down any injury at the time; later accounts by his secretary said he was cut but hid it.

claims.text: He wrote to the Red Brigades "on my knees" to beg for Aldo Moro's life.
claims.note: His public letter of April 1978 survives and was printed in newspapers at the time.

reigns.hook: Paul VI is dead. The cardinals pick someone utterly different: a smiling patriarch of Venice who will last just over a month.

reigns.tagline: The smiling pope who lasted 33 days
reigns.previously: Paul VI dies at Castel Gandolfo after fifteen years.
paragraphs: Albino Luciani came from a poor family in the Dolomites and was patriarch of Venice. He was elected on the first day of the conclave and became the first pope with a double name, John Paul, honouring the two popes before him. He refused to be crowned and had a simple inauguration Mass instead. People loved his grin and his easy way of talking. They called him the smiling pope.

On the morning of 29 September 1978 he was found dead in bed. He had died during the night, after 33 days as pope. The Vatican said a heart attack and there was no autopsy. Its first statements were muddled about who found him and what he was reading, and the confusion fed rumours for decades. In 2022 Francis beatified him.

claims.text: John Paul I was murdered to stop him cleaning up the Vatican Bank.
claims.note: Popularised by David Yallop's book In God's Name (1984). John Cornwell's investigation, A Thief in the Night (1989), and later Vatican research concluded he died naturally, but with no autopsy doubts survive.

claims.text: The Vatican first said his secretary found him, when in fact it was a nun.
claims.note: The Vatican later admitted that Sister Vincenza Taffarel, who brought his morning coffee, found the body.

reigns.hook: Two popes dead in two months. The shaken cardinals meet again, and this time they look beyond Italy for the first time in over 450 years.

reigns.tagline: The Polish pope who outlasted communism
reigns.previously: John Paul I is found dead after 33 days. A second conclave meets.
paragraphs: Karol Wojtyła had been an actor, a quarry worker under Nazi occupation and then archbishop of Kraków. He was the first non-Italian pope since Adrian VI. In June 1979 he went home to communist Poland and millions came to hear him. A year later the Solidarity movement was born. When the regimes of Eastern Europe fell in 1989, many gave him part of the credit.

On 13 May 1981 Mehmet Ali Ağca shot him in St Peter's Square. He nearly died. In 1983 he visited Ağca in prison and forgave him. He made over 100 foreign trips and started World Youth Days. He was strict on doctrine and made a record number of saints.

Late in his reign the abuse crisis began to break, with the 2002 revelations in Boston. His final years were a public decline with Parkinson's disease. At his funeral crowds chanted "Santo subito", sainthood now. He was canonised in 2014.

claims.text: The Soviet bloc was behind the 1981 assassination attempt.
claims.note: Ağca's stories changed constantly. An Italian court acquitted three Bulgarians in 1986, and no firm proof of a Soviet order has emerged.

claims.text: He believed the Virgin of Fátima saved his life.
claims.note: He said so himself: the shooting fell on the anniversary of the first Fátima apparition. A bullet was later set in the crown of the Fátima statue.

claims.text: He was slow to act against abusers, notably Marcial Maciel.
claims.note: Maciel, founder of the Legion of Christ, was only ordered to retire to a life of prayer in 2006, under Benedict XVI. A 2020 Vatican report found John Paul II was misled over Theodore McCarrick; critics say he ignored warnings.

reigns.hook: John Paul II is dead after nearly 27 years. The man who ran his doctrine office, a shy German professor, says the funeral Mass.

reigns.tagline: The professor who did the unthinkable and resigned
reigns.previously: John Paul II dies after nearly 27 years. Crowds cry "Santo subito".
paragraphs: Joseph Ratzinger was a Bavarian policeman's son. As a teenager he was enrolled in the Hitler Youth, compulsory by then, and was drafted into an anti-aircraft unit. He became a leading theologian and, for 24 years, John Paul II's guardian of doctrine. In 2006 he gave a lecture in Regensburg quoting a Byzantine emperor's attack on Islam, and protests broke out across the Muslim world.

The abuse crisis dominated his years: in Ireland, Germany, the United States. He met survivors, wrote to Ireland's Catholics in 2010 and removed hundreds of abusive priests. In 2012 he sent the first papal tweet.

On 11 February 2013 he told a meeting of cardinals, in Latin, that he was resigning. No pope had stepped down since Gregory XII in 1415, and none of his own free will for centuries. That evening lightning struck the dome of St Peter's. He lived on as pope emeritus until his death on 31 December 2022.

claims.text: Lightning hit St Peter's dome on the night he announced his resignation.
claims.note: It was photographed by news agency photographers. Many took it as a sign; it was a storm.

claims.text: As archbishop of Munich he mishandled abuse cases.
claims.note: A 2022 report for the archdiocese said he failed to act in four cases. He apologised to victims but denied any cover-up.

claims.text: Ratzinger was a Nazi sympathiser.
claims.note: Hitler Youth membership was compulsory for boys his age. Biographers find no sign he supported the regime; his family was opposed to it.

reigns.hook: The chair is empty, and its last occupant is still alive. The cardinals look to the other end of the world.

reigns.tagline: The pope from the end of the world
reigns.previously: Benedict XVI resigns, the first pope to do so in nearly 600 years.
paragraphs: Jorge Mario Bergoglio, archbishop of Buenos Aires, was the first Jesuit pope, the first from the Americas and the first from outside Europe since the 8th century. He was the first to take the name Francis. He skipped the papal apartments and lived in the Santa Marta guesthouse. Asked in 2013 about gay priests, he answered: who am I to judge?

His 2015 encyclical Laudato si' made climate change a moral issue. In March 2020, with Italy locked down by COVID, he prayed alone in a rain-soaked, empty St Peter's Square. He made mistakes on abuse, notably defending a Chilean bishop in 2018, then apologised and changed course, making Church officials report abuse.
In early 2025 he spent five weeks in hospital with pneumonia. On Easter Sunday, 20 April, he gave the blessing from the balcony and rode through the crowd. He died the next morning, aged 88.

claims.text: He was runner-up to Ratzinger in the 2005 conclave.
claims.note: Based on an anonymous cardinal's diary leaked to an Italian journalist. Conclave votes are secret.

claims.text: He gave his Easter blessing and died the next morning.
claims.note: The Vatican announced his death on Easter Monday, 21 April 2025, from a stroke and heart failure.

reigns.tagline: The first pope from the United States
reigns.previously: Francis dies on Easter Monday, the day after his last blessing.
paragraphs: Robert Francis Prevost was born in Chicago in 1955. He joined the Augustinian friars, was ordained a priest and spent many years as a missionary in Peru, where he later became bishop of Chiclayo and took Peruvian citizenship. He also served two terms as head of the Augustinian order worldwide. Francis brought him to Rome to run the Dicastery for Bishops, the office that vets new bishops.

The conclave met on 7 and 8 May 2025 and elected him on the fourth ballot. He was the first pope from the United States. He took the name Leo, and two days later told the cardinals why: Leo XIII had answered the industrial revolution, and the Church now had to face another revolution, artificial intelligence.

claims.text: He was elected on the fourth ballot, on the second day of the conclave.
claims.note: White smoke on 8 May 2025; the Vatican announced the result from the loggia of St Peter's that evening.

claims.text: He chose the name partly in honour of Leo XIII, because of artificial intelligence.
claims.note: He said so himself in his address to the College of Cardinals on 10 May 2025.

claims.text: He holds Peruvian as well as American citizenship.
claims.note: He became a Peruvian citizen in 2015, while serving in Chiclayo.
